[h1] A new refreshing entry in a stealth franchise that survived three console generations [/h1]

  I admit, this is my first sniper elite since the OG on the PS2. I initially played sniper elite 5 on PS+ out of curiosity and nostalgia, I had tried  SE 2 and  SE 3 years ago but couldn't for some reason get into them, they lacked something the original SE had, they felt more floaty and arcadey in a bad way.

 Playing Sniper Elite 5,  i was expecting the same outdated formula. But instead, i found the closest thing to a hitman game set in WWII .

  You can unlock new starting locations, the soldiers have that hitman-like NPC banter when you eavesdrop on them, they could reveal information about the target... All of this on top of a competent, decent looking third person sniper game with the usual and ever engaging and well built x ray cams that the franchise is known for.

  Add to that one element that sold me on the game and its merit ( and made me excited for the its eventual sequels), ''Invasion mode''.
 A mode that single-handedly, in my opinion, gives a new life to the formula and the whole stealth genre as a whole, for all of us single player stealth lovers.

   Imagine you are sneaking around , hiding in a bush, waiting for a guard to turn his back so that you can move to the giant french castle ahead, all of the sudden you get a prompt that you are invaded.  You panic ,hide for a bit , get a prompt that a phone can be used to determine your location, and sure enough , the invader uses it and can see where you are now, You run as far as you can and just like that, the invader hits you out of nowhere. That feeling is something new to me in a single player stealth game, its refreshing. 

  You might think that frustration will follow after that ''unfair'' game over'' ,after all you are minding your business, doing your single player objective. Don't worry, you can reload your last checkpoint, You can even disable this mode, but i suggest you don't.
As frustrating as it might get , you will defeat  your invader and eventually ( most likely after you finish the campaign), you will invade others.. 

  i understand games like hunt showdown has an excellent PvPvE stealth driven game loop, but that is still in its core a multiplayer game and its not the same as playing a dedicated single player stealth game.

   If you are like me and want something new added to the same hide, throw a bottle to distract and sneak behind the enemy brand of stealth, this game will offer that and more .

By far the game's worst addition is Axis Invasion, which is a shame as it's an incredible concept. The ability to invade another players campaign mission is genius in theory, but the inconsistencies between Campaign and Axis, coupled with the unfathomably blatant Allies bias make it nigh-on impossible to play, unless you're either a highly experienced player who has spent hundreds of hours with nothing better to do, which some of us don't have the luxury of being able to do anymore, or you're the intelligent scum of the earth and have cheats. Heed my words, do not play Axis Invasion if you value your sanity. if you thought you had patience, trust me, this has the capacity to make Ghandi himself scream in rage.
Let us begin, shall we?
You're thrown right into an existing mission, fair enough in theory. Problem; you have no idea where the opposing player is, how far in they are, or how far away you are. I can understand not having both players start from the very beginning of the mission, you are invading an existing campaign afterall, but it puts you at an immediate and severe disadvantage, especially when you're just starting off with the bottom-of-the-barrel equipment that is neither use nor ornament.
You lack a focus bar, and have to tag your own AI teammates to see where they are. The first I can understand, that would be extremely unfair, the second is absurd. Granted, you are not an officer, but it would seem fairly reasonable for you to have at least a general idea of where your own damned teammates are, rather than have to scope or binocular tag them, which takes an eternity as you can't click to tag like in SE4, you've got to hover over them for half a millenia, by which point they've almost certainly moved behind cover or otherwise out of your view, leaving you stood there like a right plonker.
The Anti-Camping system. How shall we prevent players from holding a defensive sniping position, in a game about sniping, in a gamemode where they are playing a defending sniper? I know, let's broadcast their exact position to the enemy. We won't do it to them of course, that would be working in the Axis' favour, and we can't have that... see the issue here? if you don't, congratulations, you're part of the problem.
The weapon and trap damage is so absurdly unbalanced it would be laughable if it wasn't so infuriating. The opposing Fairburne can wander calmly over no less than two teller mines and brush it off as though he were grazed lightly by a gentle autumn leaf blowing in the wind. You on the other hand, can't take two shots from an SMG at 60 meters without crying enough and keeling over. Ask me how I know this. The opposing sniper's shots can travel clear through a brick wall to hit you if they must, your's are intercepted by the greatest obstruction ever conceived: Some mild foliage you can still see through.
Then we come to the tagging system. I can perfectly understand the tags wearing off, they would defeat the point of the gamemode if you could see where the other player was at all times, but why in the actual infernal hell does the game let them know you've tagged them? If you've been spotted by someone in real life without your knowledge, does a great red banner appear in front of you letting you know you've been perceived by a person currently unknown to you? NO. So why does it here? The whole point is for each player to kill the other, warning them makes it unfathomably hard for the wrong reason. Why not rely on the pre-existing, and still fully functional scope glint to see if you're being observed?
And finally we come to the piece-de-resistance of the whole debacle, the lack of options on matchmaking.
Some of us aren't exactly comfortable on higher difficulties, so why can't we filter out what lobbies we want to connect to? The game tells you the settings of the game you're invading in minute detail, so why can't we stop it from connecting to ones we don't want? Even F2P PvP games can do that, I'd expect the same from one that costs £9.99, let alone one that costs £45.
I understand that by playing Axis Invasion you are willingly stepping into the shoes of the losing side, but holy actual sh!te does the game tell you about it. It's so unbalanced that if you affixed it to a wheel you'd have the world's first perpetual motion device.
Worst part is it doesn't even feel good when you lose. As I say, I've been playing FPS's for a great number of years, and I'm an avid Mega Man fan to boot, I like hard games, I crave the difficulty because I find it rewarding. But even I come away from a perfect losing streak of Axis Invasion and if I wasn't so busy punching my desk to try and relieve the rage and stress it causes, I'd feel so dead inside I'd have to check if I still had a pulse. The blatant favouritism of the host player, evident by the weaponry bias alone if nothing else makes the game feel like you are unwelcome in the situation, and the fact the disconnect button is labelled as "Surrender" just drives home the point that you're the outsider the very game itself is treading on before the player even gets to you.

Bottom line; Is the game good? Hell yes, if you appreciate FPS games or have played any of the preceding SE games, throw your wallet at the screen already, why are you still here?
Is the campaign good? Very much so, the levels are expansive and highly interactive, the story is great, the voice acting is superb, the animations are fluid, the cutscenes make you want to watch them, even if you've already seen them. It is a veritable masterpiece, and the ability to enjoy it with a friend in co-op multiplayer is just the icing on the cake
Is the versus multiplayer good? ...I don't even know what to put here, I think it should be fairly obvious by now that it's a steaming pile that even the Geneva Convention would list as a forbidden torture method. If you have a mortal enemy that you wish to inflict suffering upon, subject them to Axis Invasion as Axis, then you can go to them and beg for forgiveness for your crimes against them.

Sniper Elite 5 delivers thrilling sniping action and stunning visuals, but when it comes to stealth mechanics, the game falls short in several areas. While the series has always emphasized stealth as a core gameplay element, this installment struggles to maintain a consistent and rewarding stealth experience.

One notable issue is the AI behavior. While enemy soldiers can be challenging to outsmart at times, their reactions can be inconsistent. There are moments when enemies seem oblivious to your presence, even when you're in plain sight, undermining the tension that stealth gameplay is meant to create. Conversely, they can also detect you far too quickly if you make even the slightest noise, leading to frustrating trial-and-error situations.

The level design, while visually impressive, often feels overly linear, which limits the ways players can approach objectives stealthily. Many areas funnel you into specific paths, reducing opportunities for creative tactics and exploration. This rigidity can make stealth encounters feel formulaic, rather than allowing players to experiment with different strategies.

In addition, the game’s mechanics for distraction and stealth kills can feel somewhat underdeveloped. While you can create distractions to draw enemy attention, the effectiveness of these tactics varies. Sometimes, enemies will ignore noise entirely, while at other times, they’ll respond in ways that feel arbitrary. This inconsistency can make planning your stealth approach frustrating, as it’s hard to gauge how the AI will react.

On the other hand, the shooting mechanics in Sniper Elite 5 are superbly executed, making the core experience immensely satisfying. The sniping feels incredibly rewarding, with the game’s signature X-Ray kill cam providing a visceral sense of impact that amplifies the thrill of a well-placed shot. The ballistics are realistic, requiring players to account for factors like bullet drop and wind, which adds depth and strategy to each shot.

The addition of new weapon customization options allows players to tailor their loadouts to their preferred playstyle, further enhancing the shooting experience. Whether you're going for long-range precision or adapting to close-quarters combat, the game offers a satisfying array of tools to master.

Overall, while Sniper Elite 5’s stealth mechanics may leave something to be desired, its shooting mechanics shine brightly. The thrilling sniping, immersive visuals, and engaging multiplayer options create a compelling experience that will resonate with fans of the genre. For those who appreciate the art of shooting, this installment is a must-play, even if the stealth elements could use a bit more polish.

-MULTIPLAYER PVP: boy oh boy...do we have stuff to say here...literally the only good thing I can say about it when compared to se4 is that they fixed the "shooting from behind corners" issue, meaning that now you need to actually expose yourself to get the proper line of fire.
now, onto the issues: the matchmaking is terrible, and puts people who have 2500 hours played on se5, against people who just picked up the series and have 3 hours of game time.
the prestige system further increased the lack of balance, since as you unlock prestige you get better perks, which give you advantages like : better heartbeat management and recovery, you can carry more traps, more healing items, more grenades, you can locate the enemies more accurately and at a wider range via radar, you can heal yourself and allies faster, you get additional health bars, you can throw grenades farther, you are more resistant to dmg. people who have been playing longer also unlock better customizations for the weapons, with less recoil, more accuracy, faster aim,faster sprint.

Sniper Elite 5, as the name would suggest, is the 5th title in what is a pretty acclaimed series. It sees you take on the role of an OSS Operative in Europe, going behind enemy lines to disrupt the war effort of the Third Reich through a number of decently long missions. 

Whilst the name would suggest that you are a sniper (which is true) there are a good selection of other weapons from handguns and submachineguns to tripwires, mines and shoulder fire AT rocket launchers/ Panzerfausts with the small arms also having a number of attachments and modifications that you can put on them to fit your style. On the topic of playstyle, you can go loud or you can go quiet. You can shoot your way, be it stealthy or loud or indeed use a number of booby traps etc and allow the enemy to effectively kill themselves. This also allows for a good amount of replayability as you can go through missions trying different routes and techniques.....also slow-mo headshots/ vital organ shots never really get dull. 

I would thoroughly recommend this game to players of all skill levels as there is a great deal of difficulty customisation which can even be changed during the mission. At the easiest end you'll have a ton of health, enemies will not be as quick to spot you, nor will their tactics be as aggressive in flushing you out and you'll have a great deal of help with lining up those crucial shots. On the other end of the scale, you'll have a reduced hud, reduced stamina/ longer wait for heart-rate to recover and will have to work out the elevation and windage yourself in order to make your rounds meet their mark. 

All in all a brilliant game, made better by finally allowing first person sights for pistols and submachine guns, making them more useful (something which irritated me with earlier titles). 

Now, what I'd like to see next is a redux of the first sniper elite that I had on PS2 (and also have on PC) but repacked into this game engine!

Nevertheless, besides very few minor bugs and body physics the game is great for anyone that enjoys the Sniper Elite series or has a taste of sniper games with a bit more to offer. The one part I feel that it is necessary to include is that although I enjoyed the game for the most part I do no believe it is worth the full price tag. I was fortunate to purchase the game on sale and strongly recommend you wait until a sale comes along your way. Even with moderate difficulty the game can be beaten in a relatively short time. The lengths of the game, along with the repetitiveness of certain tasks and shooting may become underwhelming for players as they progress through the campaign. Therefore, I recommend you save the most that you can of your hard earned money to purchase this game at a heavy discount. Nevertheless, the game is an enjoyable experience for both the casual and hardcore gamer, combined with beautiful scenery and smooth gameplay mechanics I would find it difficult for someone to have negative feedback for game that has stood the test of time giving its fanbase with the same qualities of the previous Sniper Elite games and a little bit more! Happy Sniping!

[b]Foreword[/b]

This is my 1000th review. My journey began in 2012 with Left 4 Dead 2. I had one more review in that year and only two the next year. I really started writing regularly 10 years ago. I try to be informative (not always) but first and foremost these are just snippets of my gaming life. Mostly positive, rarely ranting about games but all in all I am really grateful for this feature offered by Steam. If you liked the words my brain managed to conjure up in a foreign language many of us use only as a lingua franca, if you took the time to read at least some of it or if you read all or perhaps gave an award... or in case you decided to make a purchase because of these lines then I thank you! It means a lot to me!

[b]Allons enfants de la patrie[/b]

France. The perfect choice after Italy. v2 had way too many demolished buildings and dark colours everywhere, episode 3 was better but a little too bright for my taste. I really started enjoying the series with Sniper Elite 4. Now, with this one the resistance Karl teams up with has a different kind of accent. And the theme we hear regularly has been [i]Frenchified[/i].

[b]Le jour de gloire est arrivé ![/b]

8 missions. The all too familiar number. Well, it is actually 9 with an added bonus you can consider as the boss fight. A short, straight-to-the-point scenario while the rest gives us the usual vast areas with lots of objectives and different ways to solve the ones designated as our primary ones. A returning optional objective is when, for instance, we have an officer to eliminate. Find where he is patrolling and decide if you want to proceed in the recommended way (by causing an accident) or just in the good old SE way. Complete every objective you have to and get the best rating after each chapter. 

[b]Contre nous de la tyrannie,[/b]

A tyrant is what Möller is! The new antagonist Karl needs to face. The story has him converse with resistance members and there are cutscenes showing Möller addressing his men. These mostly include phone conversations after missions where he desperately wants to stop [i]The Shadow[/i], the one who annoyed the bad guys by sabotaging their grand plans in previous episodes. Again, no special awards here for the plot but I liked how infamous Karl is, plus, there is the introduction of Jeff Sullivan. He is from the US Army Rangers and thinks Karl causes more harm and opposes essentially everything he does. It's nice to see how their relationship changes throughout the story.

[b]L'étendard sanglant est levé[/b]

But what new things Sniper Elite 5 has to offer? It already looked beautiful in episode 4, Kill Cam already had many layers (organs, bones, muscles and veins). Well, Kill Cam now shows a lot of destruction done to the bone. Lots of pieces flying off. And even your SMG or a well-aimed shot from your Welrod can result in a slow-mo bullet path. In a way this wasn't really needed and hearing the exploding sound of a shot from a pistol with an attached suppressor actually looks (and sounds) pretty silly. Perhaps the most satisfying shots are those involving traps with the many flying shrapnels.

[b]L'étendard sanglant est levé[/b]

And let's not forget about the new focus mode. A special vision that allows us to see through walls. Not very far though! Just to see where the silhouettes of those soldiers are who are fast approaching since they have just heard a shot. Focus is not needed for a win but its activation (that also elevates the footsteps of incoming soldiers) can definitely reduce the number of quickloads. 

[b]Entendez-vous dans les campagnes[/b]

What about the upgrades and the skills? They have been reworked and thank God for that! As we proceed with the story we get XP and eventually rank up. Upon reaching level 40 (which is the maximum in single player) we can purchase all skills. They make our focus use better, add extra slots for our special ammos or allow us to revive ourselves with a medkit. Nothing special but if you do all objectives and try to be as stealthy as possible you will reach max level by the last mission.

As for weapons: no silly requirements to eliminate tons of enemy soldiers. There are many attachments available and we get them as we find workbenches. Consider them secret places and add them to the list of already vast collectibles such as personal letters, orders, level-specific items we can pick up and stone eagles we need to shoot from afar. Karl can also be replaced by resistance members and his clothing can be modified along with his hat. I noticed that when you pick another character that one does not make any comments on story progression. Too bad as it would have been nice listening to their different comments on the tasks ahead when you do another walkthrough. I picked Marie Chevalier but she mostly remained silent.

[b]Mugir ces féroces soldats ?[/b]

Now, hardcore fans will hate Sniper Elite 5. There is Authentic but there is no Authentic Plus. Naturally, this difficulty setting removes the focus ability since this is also considered an aid during a mission, but saving regularly remains a possibility. If you want, you can change the setting in a very detailed way and create a mix between, let's say, Hard and Authentic. This is a fully customisable feature!

[b]Ils viennent jusque dans vos bras[/b]

Multiplayer and Survival modes return. And of course the cooperative mode. But Overwatch is nowhere to be found and while Invasion mode is interesting I wasn't interested in it, at all. In this mode you join in on another player's campaign but as an enemy sniper! Making eliminations in such way unlocks some character and weapon skins. It's interesting how the achievement system has been reworked in favour of this. No coop achievements, at all. One you get for doing a lot of waves in Survival and one for completing a match in multiplayer. Perhaps the creators pulled a report, looked at the numbers and realised Sniper Elite is best played alone. I heard the Invasion mode is something that Elden Ring has, too. 

[b]Égorger vos fils et vos compagnes ![/b]

What else? Some new enemy types such as the Vampir Jägers. They are snipers with infrared scopes, tailored for night missions. They have more health but if you don't go guns blazing but do everything in a stealthy way you barely notice their presence. And, naturally, the game comes with lots of DLCs. 5 missions in 2 packs labelled as seasons. Weapon and skin packs, too, and the usual mission for eliminating Hitler. This is perhaps the funniest of all!

There are many achievements but to increase the game's longevity we can acquire medals if a given challenge is completed or ribbons that can be regularly obtained by killing enemy soldiers. Oh, and soldiers can now be pacified. Making them unconscious means extra XP at the end of each level. I hate the mastery achievements that require enemies killed by pistols, rifles and our secondary weapons. All of them! Now, that's the real grind in SE 5.

[b]Aux armes, citoyens ![/b]

Sniper Elite 5 is a fantastic game! Rarely do we see improvement constantly in a series where episode 5 is pretty much the best Sniper Elite has to offer. It has semi open-world missions with great replayability, decent DLC packs and some extra modes if you are tired of picking up your rifle alone. I had fun with the game... I have had fun ever since I launched v2 many years ago. And while the zombie titles can also be fun this is the series with the real sniping experience!

This one's a weird kind of "recommend" for me. I've played Sniper Elite since V2 and enjoyed all of them, including 5; however, I feel at this point that the formula is starting to get a bit tired and that Rebellion has nearly exhausted Karl and this franchise as a whole. Basically, if you like Sniper Elite and want more of it, 5 will definitely give you that. If you're expecting much new mechanically or design-wise from it, though, you'll be left wanting.

SE5 continues the trends from the previous game with how SE looks, feels, and plays. The spotting, sneaking, and shooting mechanics haven't changed at all outside of the continued reduction of natural soundmasks in favor of suppressed weapons and precisely placed generators just waiting to be sabotaged. The games have leaned into a more Hitman-esque murder-puzzle loop with each entry, and SE5 is the latest there--for better or worse.

As has been the case for a while now, half of the arsenal is locked behind DLC paywalls, but there's enough variety in the vanilla arsenal to get you through the game. Although it doesn't matter so much as you won't even recognize half of your guns once you're through customizing them, as SE5 has been infected by the Modern-Warfare-reboots-and-Tarkov-sourced "granular weapon customization" pathogen. I actually enjoy that feature in other games, but in a WWII shooter attempting to brand itself as "authentic" for the whole series--including in its hardest difficulty--it feels odd and against that vision. To be fair, it's not as bad as COD Vanguard, but something about putting a Russian PU scope, shoulder stock, foregrip, and bulky suppressor on a WWII-era M1911 doesn't feel right to me. It's a minor complaint, since that's just how many modern mainstream games are--chase the trends whether it clashes with the identity of your game or not.

The story is also pretty mediocre, as you'd expect from Sniper Elite--you're not here for it anyway, and I think Rebellion knows that. There's a short intro and outro to each mission narrated by Karl and/or a British SOE handler of sorts, as well as intro cutscenes featuring the game's "characters"--if you can really call them that. They're only present to provide Karl and the player with the thinnest thread of context for each mission, as well as linking them to the larger war as a whole. I'm impressed they resisted a full-on D-Day mission, to be honest, since this game skips over the week the landings took place. I'm glad Karl got a bit of a break.

As a more serious issue, however, Sniper Elite 5 is buggy--and I mean it's infested with them. The detection system frequently bugs out, leaving enemies frozen behind a single piece of cover as they "Investigate" the gunshot they heard. Enemies hear sounds that they shouldn't or don't hear whistles and distraction devices when you're ten feet away. Some enemies will randomly become untagged--as far as I know there's no limit to tags and they're the regular guards as opposed to the trucks that sometimes drive through the map and despawn on the other end. Sometimes dropping a body will send them into the Earth's core, never to be seen again. If you want to guarantee that happening, quicksaves often result in that exact behavior--or them falling through floors or off ledges rather than where you left them. And I promise you will want to use quicksaves, given that SE5's missions are long (my pace of play is admittedly slow and methodical on the Hard difficulty, and I try to complete most if not all of the side objectives, so all in all I'm spending 2-3 hours on each level). If you're not careful you will get set back 20-30 minutes if you decide to reload and forget the all-important F5 key. Surfaces that should be easily shot through, like some leaves on a bush, sometimes aren't when the game randomly decides they're actually those rare rolled-steel bushes the Germans farm all of their tank armor from.

While nothing is totally game-breaking, it's a lot of minorly frustrating things that add up; some to the point where I've had to put down the game for a few hours or a day and come back later. Nothing like losing 30 minutes of progress where the game had a dozen opportunities for a fine, safe autosave to get you to take a break for a while.

I will admit I didn't touch the multiplayer or the Axis Invasion modes at all. Going through the first time I didn't really want some fanatical sniper spawning in and doming me midway through a mission--if anyone even still plays this game at all--so I turned it off. I remember watching some gameplay years back, and it looked fun and like an interesting twist for those into that sort of disruption, but it wasn't for me and not what I'm playing Sniper Elite to experience. I also tried one round of Survival and found it incredibly tedious. I ended up quitting on Wave 3 when I realized the five waves were going to take almost an hour. I'm sure it's more fun in a group but so is everything so it's not much of a feature-add for me.

Regardless though, it's still...fine. The game looks decent even a couple years out, runs well, doesn't crash or hitch outside of a mildly frequent (and more annoying than anything) crash-to-desktop immediately after hitting "Play" in the launcher, and is overall fun despite the shortcomings I mentioned. Would I recommend it to someone looking to get into Sniper Elite? I guess; I'd prefer you tried V2 or 3 first but there's nothing wrong with 4 or 5 besides how tired they feel at this point. It's clear that there's not many places they can or want to push the franchise to, and are risking stretching Karl's continuity to the breaking point. I think a time period change and return to the more sniper-focused gameplay would do this game well--although I imagine Rebellion is very comfortable inside the relatively low-nuance and "safe" setting of WWII. Killing Nazis is only going to make weirdos upset, whereas you might raise some eyebrows with, say, a Vietnam, Gulf War, or GWOT setting--where you don't have the broad cultural consensus of a "just and good war" as you do with WWII.

As I said at the top, I softly recommend Sniper Elite 5. It's more "modern" Sniper Elite, so if you liked SE4 you'll absolutely love this since it's more of the exact same. If you liked V2 and 3, you'll probably find it alright. If you're not into Sniper Elite at all...well, your mileage may vary but you'll probably have a decent time.

The only thing you could slightly nitpick about in Sniper Elite V is the presentation. The grafics are notably dated, but they still look decent and the leveldesign and artstyle more than make up for it. The music is a bit meh and here or there the voice-acting is cheesy af, but apart from that Sniper Elite V is high quality entertainment all the way.

Compared to the previous Sniper Elite games, there are no big innovations or improvements, apart from a few gameplay aspects that were sloppily stolen from the latest Hitman games. Sniper Elite has basically been the same game ever since Sniper Elite III, not due to lazy devs, but because there is so little room for improvement in my opinion. Once again, the biggest strength is the completely scalable difficulty setting with a lot of options to make it easier or harder, which greatly benefits the replay value, too. The semi-open-world missions provide a lot of tactical freedom: You are an absolute noob and just want to play it like a casual run-and-gun-Third-person-shooter? No problem. You‘re a military-trained Navy Seal elite soldier looking for a borderline realistic sniper challenge? Have at it.

When it comes to WWII-themed games, the Sniper Elite series is up there with the finest WWII games in general. It‘s basically the best WWII Stealth game/Third-person-shooter out there and the fifth installment is among the best of the bunch. A very strong 6/8.

Pros
Variable Difficulty. True sniper aim is now separate from the enemy difficulty. I'm not a fan of the bullet drift mechanic and I am not looking for a realistic sniping experience. I want my bullet to go where I aim. But that doesn't mean I want the enemies to always be easy either. In SE4, in order to disable true aim, you were forced to run in easy mode. Difficulty settings have been split up so you can choose easy aim with difficult enemies.
Non-lethal ammo and take-downs. When I first saw these, I passed them by as useless. Boy was I wrong. Knocking out enemies causes nearby soldiers to investigate rather than freak out when they see their comrades being killed. Extremely useful in an area filled with enemy soldiers.
4th weapon. Yep, keep your perfect load-out and when you see that tank buster, you can pick it up in addition to your 3 custom weapons.
Melee attacks. In higher difficulties, if an enemy knows where you are, your melee attack will not always work! They can break your attack wasting your time while reinforcements arrive. 

Cons
No more unlimited satchel charges. You have to search for them.
No more unlimited rocks to throw to cause distractions. Now you have to find and collect bottles.
Vehicle destruction is now very difficult. Gone are the single shot destruction of trucks and cars.
The maps are large and interesting...but imho, not as interesting as in SE4. Some areas the enemies are feast or famine. There are large areas with no enemies and small areas with many enemies.
Harder to spot enemies. You will be relying on your radar far more in this game. Enemies show up as a large circle on your radar before they are tagged. Once tagged, the circle disappears. Sometime the large circle makes it easier to spot an enemy than when they are tagged.

[h1]A Missed Shot at Innovation[/h1]

Snagged this game on a 70% off sale, and let me tell you, even at that discount, it felt like I overpaid. Sniper Elite 5 takes you on a nostalgic journey back to the first Medal of Honor, except without the charm of it being 1999. You're funneled down the same unimaginative, rigid paths that could bore even the most ardent history buffs to tears.

On 'Sniper Elite' difficulty it's like playing on 'toddler mode.' Make a blunder so colossal it should have you ousted from the brotherhood of snipers? No problem! This game forgives like your grandma, letting even the worst mistakes slide with barely a slap on the wrist.

The graphics? Oh, they've got high-quality textures, alright. People and objects sometimes look so sharp you’d swear they could cut glass. Too bad that’s where the innovation ends. The first cutscene? It's like a B-movie zombie apocalypse minus the suspense and horror, complete with characters sporting the dead-eyed stare of a department store mannequin and movements as fluid as a robot dance from a 1980s pop video.

In conclusion, if you’re looking for a game that manages to simultaneously bore and annoy, Sniper Elite 5 might just be your perfect match. It's a lackluster parade of missed opportunities wrapped in the thin veneer of modern graphics, proving once again that not all upgrades are for the better. So, buckle up for this snooze-fest; you’ll need the sniper’s focus just to stay awake.

I’ve quite enjoyed Sniper Elite 4 about 6 years ago. It was hardly as detailed or inventive as the titles it directly pulled from, like Hitman or Metal Gear Solid V, but what it had was extremely fun and satisfying. So I was looking forward to playing a sequel, yet when Sniper Elite 5 came out I was too stressed due to living through early months of the full scale russian invasion, I was rather picky about which games I was comfortable playing. Plus, a lot of the initial user reviews on the game were surprisingly negative, commenting on its inferiority to the fourth game. Two years since its release and one year since the release of its final DLC mission, I’ve decided to give it a shot and was not disappointed.

A lot of Sniper Elite 5 can be described as “Sniper Elite 4, but improved”. If in the previous title the franchise have finally found itself, here the developers were trying to polish and perfect its ideas, without reinventing the game again. It’s still a stealth third person shooter with emphasis on using the sniper rifle. You still get huge open maps with several main and optional objectives. You have Hitman-like traversal abilities and an automated sticky cover system. There are systems in place to simulate different aspects of shooting and a lot of the stealth is based around using traps and making it hard for enemies to triangulate and figure out your exact position. And, of course, the slow motion x-ray kill cameras are back again, but are made even more customizable and tied to more systems. All of this is as good, and often better, than it used to be in the previous game with lots of very smart and helpful UI improvements and changes to make things easier to understand.

But on top of just improving things, there are expansions of systems and new ideas added. Enemies, for example, are no longer clearly shown on the map before you tag them, and are instead shown as a big vague circle, making it all the more important to recon before engaging unless you want to be caught completely off guard. The “see through walls” vision is here to help with it, without it being too overpowered and helpful at the same time. More things can be found on the maps, like hidden modification tables and starting points, in addition to just intel and collectibles, making it even harder to “do everything” on your first go, unless you are very thorough.

Amount of trap items is decreased to an essential minimum, but more elements can be trapped and more things in the environment can be turned into a sound producing thing that hides the sounds of your shots. All maps have two types of tools hidden in them, lack of which makes some interactions slower or completely unavailable. The skill concept is changed, but it still feels like an afterthought as none of its improvements are that gameplay changing. Also, non-lethal approach is made possible, though I fail to see how it fits this setting and this story… Oh and more additional modes, that I personally never cared much about, are added – including an invasion mechanic, where other players can join your game as enemy snipers if you enable it. I didn’t want to bother with installing anti-cheat, so I didn’t, but it sounds like a cool idea.

Some elements of the game remain quite rough. It’s still possible to find spots of geometry on the map working against you in a “level designers missed this spot” kind of way. Climbing stuff and sticky cover never feel reliable and can misfire or not activate when they should. Enemies can and will glitch out in silly ways. Spawning enemies is still proximity based and while most levels hide it well, using level geometry to make it hard or impossible to engage with enemies across the entire map, or by having new enemies arrive or be inside a building thus explaining their absence from afar. But you will notice this issue from time to time, even though most of the time when you have a good vantage point, you can see at least some of the enemies from very very far away (and kill them).

DLCs are still a mixed bag. Missions are quite alright, but are basically “more of the same”. And some of them, most notably Kraken Awakens, have an especially egregious examples of enemy spawning very noticeably. You get your obligatory “kill Hitler” mission once again, and you get a selection of maps that will give you more of the fun and satisfying Sniper Elite 5 gameplay, if you want it. But I’d not recommend getting them until after you’re done with the main game as you might feel that you don’t want more. And the weapons and skins DLCs… I haven’t used them, as with the previous game. All of these titles are very good with providing you with a fun loadout from the beginning and since you can customize elements of weapons, it’s far easier to get what you want with just that and not by having more different guns.

Overall, I could easily recommend Sniper Elite 5. Just like its predecessor, it’s not the best stealth game out there, but landing sniper shots and utilizing traps to kill nazis is very satisfying and doesn’t get boring across a rather long campaign, if you try to do all objectives and find as much optional stuff as you can. The improvements of the game also make it an easy recommendation over Sniper Elite 4, but at the same time, I feel like it’s still worth playing the fourth game as well. I’m very curious to see where the series can go next from here, but if it’s going to be more of this, I probably won’t mind.

I am a long term Sniper Elite player, particularly SE4 on Authentic Plus difficulty, so arrived into this via a Steam sale for the complete package at what seems finally a fair deal for the mixed bag that was both the season passes.  Firstly the good: the graphics are a major upgrade, the sound is exceptional, Karl is voiced incredibly even if some of the other voice actors aren't so good.  The plot so far has been cohesive and made sense.  

The maps are substantially larger and seem mostly varied and really well designed, from the rolling hills of the French countryside to the maze like chateau city, to the channel islands, it's great variety and they have well designed options allowing for many ways to approach situations.  

Now for the bad: the game is too easy.  I am playing on Authentic (top difficulty mode) and think it's overly generous: many times I get an enemy opening fire on me and I have time to turn around, kill them and heal as if nothing happened.. no, I should be dead if we're being authentic here! 

Similarly the weapon realism has been downgraded substantially because many weapons can now be unrealistically suppressed to crazily low sound levels (eg a Welrod can be taken down deom 50m+ in SE4 to just  7m audible distance in SE5.. you can sit in long grass popping off around enemy and apparently they can't hear you even on Authentic!).  Long distance sniping now includes a visual aim assist for bullet drop that is always on in the HUD.  In SE4 you just got a wind indicator then needed to use binoculars to gauge distance of a target then all the rest was your own skill and estimation to snipe a target.. at distances over 200m it was a massive challenge and accomplishment.  Now?  Long distance sniping becomes very easy indeed even on the top difficulty mode.  Another issue I have are the edges of the map: several times they're weird holes in the middle of the maps, but also on the edges they are roads you look like you can walk down then just are told you can't.   A well placed mountain or blockade would be 10x better than a message reminding you it's a map edge.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 is a great game.  I haven't even turned on Invasion Mode yet or played any of the DLC, but I fully expect to get a lot of replayability out of this.  What does concern me though, is that it isn't going to ever be the fiendishly difficult challenge of Sniper Elite 4 Authentic Plus difficulty.  To get through any single map on that mode is a huge achievement: near impossible for most players.  That's what we want: the challenge, the danger, the need to use skill at the highest levels and stealth and tactics to survive.  

By contrast in Authentic mode on this, you can run around with a machine gun half the time and play it almost like an arcade action shooter.  Fine for lower difficulty, as is the aim assist etc, but the lack of a proper high difficulty authentic plus mode is a problem for Sniper Elite veterans. I suspect I'll go back to SE4 again over this in a few months once I've exhausted all the content, and that's not how it should be.  Overall I give this game a 7.5/10: it's solid but the lack of authentic plus loses it a full point for long term replayability.

While I will give a thumbs down for this game review, I *do* like the game, fun to mess around in and nothing else. This review will only be for single-player, non-axis invasion.

 [h1]The Pros[/h1]
- Weapon Customization. It's very fun to fiddle around with different types of weapon accessories, even if most don't really need to exist.

- Weapon x-rays. It's cool to see where you end up hitting a target with a pistol, or any secondary, really.

- First person aiming on non-rifle weapons. This helps GREATLY when trying to be accurate and even sometimes discreet when doing stealth.

- Multiple starting points in every map. These are fun to change up how you play the given mission greatly. All starting points should be unlocked after completing the mission instead of finding them.

-Being able to bodyshot enemies in authentic mode. Semi-auto rifles still suffer greatly with a lack of power, however.

[h1]The Cons[/h1]
- Lack of scope marking customization. The T-post tactical of SE4 make authentic (plus) mode a far more enjoyable experience. Sure, there is the bullet drop indicator when you have a scope, but it's too far off to the right to be of any use.

- Reinforcement phone boxes are a waste of time. The enemy become easy pickings as you keep killing them trying beeline to it. Rigging, or creating a loud noise area is never worth it, non of the boxes are in a hidden location to make it worthwhile.

- Gun cycling/reloading sounds. They sound like hollow tin cans being clinked together.

- Nonlethal fighting. There's no real reason to do non-lethal other than to offset killing officers/soldier in a pure stealth run.

- Animations and model detail. Cut-scene animations and characters suffer this the most, they look really, really bad. The weapons look/are animated nice however.

- DLC/Skins. Too much money for what it is worth. If you want to buy a DLC, get the one with the DeLisle in it and don't buy anything else. 

- Bottles instead of rocks. I don't use bottles at all because of the max 6 bottles you can carry. Whistling is far more effective. Also why is it that you start every mission with 4 instead of 6 even when you unlock the perk to maximize the number of bottles you can carry?

- Lack of better stealth hiding places. Long grass is fine, but it would be interesting to hide inside boxes or crates. Would also be nice to have it so soldier get curious when they see a gun sticking out from a corner or grass.

- Big maps that only really have sniping action in small areas. Best you can do is snipe out some sentrys  and use that as your way in if the body doesn't get discovered.

-Decoys. They are useless. I have yet to see effective use with them that doesn't immediately cause them to find out that it's a decoy and now they are enclosing on your position. Decoys also have a big time to set up to be effective so it's not worth having.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
All-in-all my view is still negative despite it being a game  that I am still sinking time into since I have bought a few DLCs and whatnot. An OK game to get on a heavily discounted sale, and never full-price.

Absolutely astonishing game, much better than I expected. Paying for it was worth it. The campaign was very good, although I honestly prefer Sniper Elite 4's campaign, however, the Wolf Mountain mission is the very best level of any Sniper Elite game, much better than any of the Hitler's assassination missions in any other games. 

In the Wolf Mountain mission there are many fun and exciting ways of killing Hitler, such as by shooting his only testicle with a sniper when he's in the balcony, blowing him up with a rat bomb, replacing his mail with a grenade, poisoning his food or even impaling him with a bowling pin. The dialogues are excellent as well, loved hearing the German soldiers talking to each other about random subjects whilst I sneaked behind them. I swear, I did burst out laughing when Hitler yelled ''give me some room you buffoons'' to the soldiers who were following him.

Despite all that, there are some downsides of Sniper Elite 5. The most noticeable is the fact that there's no crouch running as in the previous game. Something else that bothered me was how some enemies can defend themselves from melee attacks when they are in combat mode despite Karl Fairburne being an extremely skilled fighter.

Overall, I definitelly do recommend Sniper Elite 5.

I wanted to love this game. I was a MASSIVE fan of Sniper Elite 4, and despite a few new features, the developers have made one single catastrophic mistake. Bigger doesn't always mean better.

What I loved most about Sniper Elite 4 was that the opening level was replayable. Grindy. You could predict where everyone was, complete the level in about 15 minutes when you knew it, and just have some fun... but Sniper Elite 5 has completely lost that.

It took almost an hour and a half to complete the first level, the same on the second, the third I got an hour into before I gave up, and (as much as it's a good game), I just don't have time for that. I need a game that I think "hey, I've got an hour spare, I'll play that and snipe some people"... but every level so far, keeping in mind I've tried 3 of the original 9, have been in depth large maps with a LOT of enemies, and this game compared to its predecessor has totally lost what made it "fun". It's become more of a simulator which really doesn't suit it at all.

In SE5 they've gone for "Hey, let's make massive maps because everyone is craving huge open worlds" without stopping to think if it actually suited the game, and it doesn't which is a massive shame. Partly because it's made SE5 almost unplayable for me, but mainly because I can see the level of work that they've put in to actually creating these huge levels, and that work has been the reason they've made me go back to Sniper Elite 4 again. A real pity.

Would I recommend it? Tough call. I prefered the weapons unlock system in SE4, I preferred the system where suppressors would gradually wear out (which is missing in SE5), and I preferred the smaller levels in SE4.

It's not a bad game, but you need to be thinking that you'll be spending at LEAST 90 minutes per level which is something that really doesn't fit in with the genre for me hence the negative review.

If you want a couple of hours of intricate luring and stealth killing 100 enemies, you might think the opposite.

Sniper Elite 5 is an excellent successor to Sniper Elite 4, but with a few puzzling decisions. 

For much of Sniper Elite 5, it is the same substance as the previous entry. The maps are still stunning, the gunplay feels good, and (so far) there have been no notable bugs. I've been enjoying the French landscape, with the first few levels taking place in massive castles, estates, and cathedrals, with plenty of side objects to encourage exploration.

This entry primarily iterates on the first on two ways. The first is to add in the addition of the modular weapon system. Each level contains three weapons workbenches, each unlocking parts for a different slot of the loadout, either rifle, sidearm, or pistol. Overall, it works, but it's nothing too crazy. The second addition is a bit more mixed. The game added in an invasion mechanic, in which another player invades your games as a german sniper. Though this does add a welcome bit of spontaneity, it can get tiring, especially as the same person can invade over and over again, keeping you stuck on the same section of the level. Thankfully, this can be turned off, and after dying a few times, the game will ask if you would like to do so. 

Overall, I enjoy this game, though I am uncertain as to whether I would recommend this or the fourth entry more.

Sniper Elite 5 offers expansive maps and diverse environments, maintaining the series' signature sniping mechanics. However, the AI of enemy soldiers feels lacking, diminishing the challenge and immersion. Basically, you can kill half a squad and after a while the enemy will continue to go back to their daily tasks while standing in a literal killing field. Despite the vast landscapes, I often find myself engaged in close-quarter combat; while this is necessary, its detracts just a little from the core experience of long-range sniping. While the game delivers decent and satisfying shooting mechanics, the discrepancy between the expansive maps and the frequent close-range encounters detracts from the depth expected from a Sniper Elite title. It's a good bit of shooting fun. but it's nothing taxing.

Sniper Elite 5 is quite the disappointment. There are no innovations, just the same engine and mechanics. Gameplay is also frustrating, the leaves and trees seem to be a second barrier preventing the player from moving to the other location. Sometimes for a sniper and stealth game you don't feel the immersion at all. However, It brings a few new features and at the same time removes mechanics and simplifies the gameplay into normie levels that shouldn't be possible. This is a case of “one step forward and two steps back” and, unfortunately, the end result is not an evolution and despite a few curious moments, the new game fails to be better than its predecessor.

Rebellion unashamedly copied mechanics from higher profile franchises such as Hitman and Splinter Cell and plasted them on this mess. A game titled "Sniper" doesn't really have many sniping moments like in SE3 and SE4, mainly becoming "Pistol Elite" in cramped spaces more suited to Solid Snake than Karl Fairburne. Also, the inclusion of non-lethal takedowns is mind-boggling and lazy. There is no mission in which you have to incapacitate someone, so the ham-fisted non-lethal option is useless. It is like the devs simply got hold of a checklist of "What do the cool kids like nowadays?" and started swinging.

Following the hot string of lazyness, there are less tanks in this game, with only the King Tiger and without a creative use for them like in SE3: Afrika. Not a single French tank is in the game and the German uniforms are all wrong. The dev team was not even trying.

Sniper Elite 5 is fun mainly if played in co-op, but don't expect too much. The devs banked all their chips on the new Invasion Mode and if you take it away, SE5 becomes an inferior SE4 copy-paste. The map design is dumbed down, being more linear and close-combat. Might as well just play SC: Blacklist, with its far superior mechanics.

Don't expect too much, the story is very generic, the protagonists are weak and you won't remember anyone, basically the plot only serves as a background and the focus is on the gameplay. Long gone is the historical fiction from V2 and SE3, just look at the pretty colors.

The game is said to be set in France but it could take place anywhere. The only French thing in the entire campaign is the RSC rifle. There is no mention of Vichy troops such as the Milice Française or the risk of Resistance members being exposed and summarily executed. The Lebel? The MAS-38? Forget about them. France, Italy, Germany... whatever, the game could take place in downtown London; especially for the Germans being stabbed left and right, at any rate.

The Japanese conexion was a big deal in the promotion of this game but were, in reality, a disappointing afterthought, without the promising idea of a showdown with a Japanese elite guard protecting their admiral.

The game is also full of bugs and invisible walls. The floor just disappears from time to time, plunging Karl into Hades. Recycled animations and recycled burning cities from Sniper Elite V2 are also a sign of the lazy approach Rebellion took while making this game. A really sad final product, especially because I love the Sniper Elite franchise.

[h1] In summary [/h1] 
Buy it with at least 50% discount and play it as special forces agent who is wreaking havoc on territory occupied by Nazis and you would enjoy the game as I did. If you do not have Sniper Elite 4, but and play it first, as it is superior in every way.

[h1] Long version [/h1] 
As I am not interested on invasion, I was reluctant to buy the SE5, so I waited for 70% discount and I do not regret the purchase. For lower price it is easier for me to overlook some negatives, which are as follows:

[h2] Is sniping optional? [/h2] 
In some missions the sniping aspect of the game seems to be optional as you are attacking mostly short range. When you are trying to collect headshots over 100m to unlock skin for the rifle, you must really try to find spots which are away enough.

[h2] Why the hell I cannot jump over it? [/h2] 
In a lot of places Lieutenant Karl Fairburne has issue to jump over fallen trees and small walls. The problem is so glaring, that other reviewers are point out the linearity of the game and I can understand their feeling. It is still open map, but on a lot of places you are forced to go certain way. Mid 2nd mission I started to joke that from all deployments Karl Fairburne has PTSD from fallen trees and small walls. He is not afraid of Nazis, but the trees and walls are his weak point. 

[h2] Where are some options from SE4? [/h2]

Where are the grenades you can shoot off from enemy’s belt? Environmental kills are rare in comparison to SE4. In general, I would say I had more fun with SE4 than with SE5. To be able to match same fun factor I had to change the way how I am playing the game.

I like it, despite its many, many flaws. 

Sure, the whole game ought to be a better game than it is. But the essence: unhurried sneaking around and head-shotting a finite number of bad guys from a safe distance is something I really enjoy. And it's fun too, when you miss too often and are forced to fight. 

The two co-op modes are campaign and survival. I’ve played a lot of survival with my brother, and with only 2 players on 4-player maps, it’s challenging enough to be fun – we get wiped out often enough :-) There are five survival maps to choose from. Each asks the players to repel (usually) 3 waves of Germans at a series of 4 command/ammo-resupply posts. Each map has a choice of 3-5 operations, that put the command posts in different places, so the survival games can feel quite different even on the same maps. Sadly, in SE5, no maps allow a long-ranged sniping game.

(And FYI, the steadiest way to join a friend's co-op game is for him to set up a lobby (For example: Play, Survival, Host) then for him to click on his own name in the top right to reveal an invite code. You click on your own name, see a form where you can type in his invite code, and you can now join your friend, even in a private game, even if you suffer a disconnect later...so long as you still have the code written down.)

The graphics are improved from SE4. Lots of green. Better faces. The settings are much more beautiful than say, L4D2 or Killing Zone, or most maps of World War Z. The voice-acting is good. The story, well...Sniper Elite stories are terrible :-)

And the user interface is still crap. It is adapted from a console layout. One example: stand/crouch/prone is controlled by one key instead of three. A second example: you select an item with one key, on a radial menu, then apply/use/deploy the item with a different shared key. Why a different key? Worse, the game won't let you select an empty item slot, and if you run out of an item, it auto-switches you to another item you still have in stock. So, many times I've selected a bandage, not realised I had no bandage, or had just run out of bandages, and instead of healing myself, I lobbed the explosive which had popped into my never-allowed-to-be-empty hand. Another example, but this is avoidable: the default hold breath key is the space bar. (Try assigning Breath-hold to shift.) With default settings, you often press space when NOT yet in scope, and when not in scope, space means hop over the cover in front of you...so you jump over a railing or wall in front of you and hang from it in full view of the enemy. Shared function keys.

(Just played some SE4. The F key isn’t so over-used. There are different keys for searching a corspe, using equipment, defusing a mine, or picking up a discarded weapon. Ammo is automatically picked up.)

Oh! I forgot. When your chosen cover is a bit too tall, you can observe over it, look downrange through your gun's scope, but cannot shoot. I simply had to stand before shooting, but there was NO indication of why I could not shoot. Similarly, my brother ran out of special ammo once and thought his main rifle was glitched - he had plenty of regular ammo but the game would not let him fire that weapon again until he switched ammo-type manually.

YouTube reviews are ambivalent about the new maps. They are more closely based on real environments than SE4, so there aren't as many long sniping opportunities. The new maps do feel more real. And that's nice. But the SE5 maps also feel more cramped. At distances under 100 meters, wind and bullet drop are somewhat insignificant, so the biggest skill in SE4, aiming your rifle over 100m, taking bullet drop and wind into your estimate, rarely becomes necessary.

In SE5, the combat distances are so short that aim-assist is turned on by default, except at the hardest difficulty, since aim-assist doesn't make much difference most of the time. Happily, one can customise the difficulties fairly finely, and turn off the aim-assist if one prefers to play that way. I think it's MUCH better. (With no aim assist, it feels GREAT when you get a head-shot over a 150m in a strong cross wind.) Unhappily, the fine difficulty management is really uneven. For example, in SE5 you can tune the mine defusal distance to about either 5, 6, or 7 feet. But you the HUD can only be adjusted by turning it off completely, or keeping it completely on, including its sixth-sense warning that the enemy is looking at you, and from which direction.

Yes, I finished on authentic difficulty, but no, I won't play authentic again. I like either lots of ammo, or the ability to conserve unused parts of my magazine when I reload. In authentic, I particularly don't like checking my health by trying to apply bandages (at full health, you get a message that you can't bandage yourself anymore.)

Gun modifications are a big, big thing in SE5. There are very detailed stats for each gun that you can examine while setting up your loadout. Vertical, horizontal recoil. Shot grouping. Damage. Audible range. Audible range is what I look at most. It can vary from about 4m to over 160m. Even with a quiet gun, eventually, the enemy will spot you, if you keep shooting. But a very quiet gun lets you shoot much more often without moving between shots.

Most of the mods and many of the guns only unlock after discovering particular workbenches, located in enemy territory on the campaign maps. (You do NOT have to return to the same workbenches to re-apply the mods after they are unlocked.) Some of the mods unlock after certain feats, like total headshots with the weapon, or kills within or beyond a certain distance. 

In my second playthrough of the campaign, I used the D.L. (De Lisle) Carbine, a highly suppressed rifle - only easily audible within 17m. It's a DLC gun. Well...the game is old now, so if you want to play, wait for a deep sale and get the DLC too - how else will you get a chance to kill Hitler in a dozen different ways?

In my first playthrough of SE5, I was pleased that tanks were realistically hard to kill. In SE4, it was always presumed that tank drivers and gunners had had their vision blocks damaged, and hence had removed them, and hence could be sniped through their small vision ports. Not in SE5. I used panzerfausts and TNT and teller mines to disable tank tracks and had to leave the tanks damaged but dangerous behind me; sometimes they'd burn out over the next 10 minutes or so. Unhappily, I later learned that SE5 simply has different weak points than SE4. Armoured cars have engine port covers that can be destroyed with bullets, after which the armored car can be blown up by shooting a couple of bullets into the engine. Tanks? Yeah, tanks too. With bullets, one can (not simply pierce a hole through, but instead) blow a big chunk of armor off the back of a King Tiger, between its exhaust ports, then blow up the tank completely by shooting its exposed engine. Bullets. A full-health King Tiger. Sigh. 

It can also feel a bit disappointing that even on the highest difficulty level, the enemy often stands still and peers about after a near miss, or when an explosive goes off nearby. The highest difficulty should feature bad guys that keep their heads down, or move a few feet behind cover before exposing themselves again. (Checked: SE4 enemies don't keep their heads nearly as still as enemies in SE5.)

And of course, even on authentic difficulty, there were plenty of magic healing kits to restore you to 100% health, and enemy snipers continued to reveal their position with lens flare on their scope that shows up like a search light.

Did I mention that when you crouch and concentrate ("focus"), you can see through walls out to a distance of about 50 feet? But you can turn that off in the the fine difficulty settings if you want.

And yet, I enjoyed the game. I really did. And I'm going to try SE4 again too, now that I've forgotten most of its maps.

Sniper Elite 5 presents a bit of a mixed bag when compared to its predecessor, SE4. While it brings in some new tricks like non-lethal approaches and weapon customization, it also holds back on certain aspects, such as fewer options for enemy engagements like grenade explosions. The maps, though visually stunning, feel somewhat more constrained and linear. As for the story, it's rather forgettable, with a villain that's about as menacing as a kitten. Nevertheless, it still delivers that quintessential Sniper Elite experience of chaos and destruction.

The gameplay has received a commendable polish, with smoother movement and improved AI, making it a thoroughly satisfying experience for aficionados of the series. Invasion Mode adds an extra dash of excitement, and the inclusion of non-lethal options injects a bit of novelty, even if it does come across as somewhat gimmicky. The narrative takes a back seat to the action, akin to the ethos of a John Wick flick, while the multiplayer component adds another layer of enjoyment.

The killcams have undergone a notable upgrade, providing a more cinematic spectacle, though some may bemoan the absence of destruction physics for character models. All in all, Sniper Elite 5 emerges as a robust addition to the franchise, appealing to both seasoned veterans and fresh-faced recruits.

Hmmm, Sniper Elite 5. 
Spent enough time playing it. Played all the other games in the series before it. So yeah I am aware of a lot of people not liking the game. Compared to the previous entry Sniper Elite 4. But let me tell you. This is probably the best Sniper Elite game I've ever played. And yes there are some drawbacks to this game. But if I could rate this game based on just one level. That level would be the Mission 3 location. Beaumont-Saint-Denis. This is by far the best location I've ever played in any sniper game. It has the combination of sniping from a great distance to close-up sneaking. The verticality, the variety of environmental details. Extreme detail of the architecture. And everything else about this map feels mesmerizing. I would rate this map 10 out of 10. However, you will not like it if you go all gun blazing or play it on easier difficulties. Sniper Elite 5 is a bit different when it comes to infiltration. It's much more like a Metal Gear Solid or a Splinter Cell game. You may have to rely on sneaking a lot more than just sniping from a vantage point. Also, you may have to rely on stealth takedowns as well. All I can say is to enjoy this game fully. Play it on at least sharpshooter difficulty, and have patience. Don't go gun blazing. Wait for the perfect moment. And have an idea about the distance and the loudness of your gun. The different kinds of ammunition you can use for different situations. Like if a good amount of enemies are scattered close by, they'll hear your shots even if it's from a silenced pistol. In that case, you could switch to subsonic ammo, which makes your gun so quiet that they won't hear your shots unless they're very close to you. The same goes for enemies that are very far away. Sometimes your gun doesn't have enough muzzle velocity to travel the bullet so far without dropping a significant amount. In that case, you can use match rounds that have higher velocity. And many other ammunition options.  If you have a good understanding of your surroundings and your weapons. you can clear a whole level with just your pistol. About the online modes. I'd say the invasion mode is unique. I liked it. But to fully engage in the story mode without any disruption, I'd recommend turning the invasion mode off for your first playthrough, 

If I talk about things I didn't like. It's probably the reduced option for carrying explosives. Some explosives are even missing. No option to take down a tank like before from afar. In most cases, you need to get close to a tank to destroy it. It takes two panzerfaust, or one satchel charge, and a bunch of TNT. Or a couple of well-placed armor-piercing shots on the back of the exhaust. Some maps have a lot of tanks, but not many options to neutralize them. Also, the removal of lure stones is one other thing I disliked, Though it didn't bother me as much as I thought it would. Cause there are a bunch of other options like bottles and lure mines. And of course, the way they limit you by putting invisible walls or objects that are seemingly easily traversable. But I got used to it soon. Would have been a much nicer experience for the big maps if they didn't have these barriers.
And finally, I rate this game 8/10.

Sniper Elite 5: French Fries, X-Ray Kill Cams, and Exploding Innards (Oh My!)
Picture this: Sun-drenched French beaches, quaint seaside villages, and the satisfying crack of a bullet connecting with a Nazi skull. No, it's not a Tarantino fever dream, it's Sniper Elite 5, a game where precision sniping meets explosive carnage and history gets a healthy dose of Hollywood.

Let's dissect this bad boy:

Vive la France! (With a Few Bullet Holes): The French countryside is stunningly rendered, from sprawling salt marshes to towering cliffs. But like a baguette left out in the sun, some parts get a little stale. Repetitive textures and generic towns can dampen the initial awe.

The Art of the Kill Shot: Lining up that perfect long-range headshot is pure dopamine gold. Wind whispers secrets in your ear, gravity plays its cruel hand, and that visceral thump of a bullet finding its mark is like a symphony for your trigger finger. The X-ray kill cam? Well, let's just say it's not for the faint of heart, but undeniably gruesomely fascinating.

Stealth or Rambo? You Decide: You're not just a walking gun turret, Agent Fairburne. You can stalk enemies like a shadow, utilizing silenced pistols and takedowns for a clean kill. Or, if subtlety isn't your forte, unleash your inner John Wick with a hail of bullets. The choice is yours, though the AI can be as predictable as a mime at a birthday party, making the stealth approach sometimes less than thrilling.

Open World…Open Questions: The sprawling map allows for exploration, but like a plate of overcooked fries, it can start to feel greasy after a while. Repetitive side missions and fetch quests can make you yearn for more depth.

Verdict: Sniper Elite 5 is a mixed bag of French fries and exploding innards. The core sniping gameplay is top-notch, offering a unique blend of challenge and satisfaction. But technical hiccups, repetitive elements, and a forgettable story hold it back from being a truly memorable experience. Still, if you crave long-range kills, X-ray-induced nightmares, and a chance to rewrite history with a sniper rifle, there's fun to be had here. Just don't expect a Michelin-starred meal.

Now go forth, OSS operatives, and liberate France one bullet at a time. Just remember, sometimes the quietest approach is the most satisfyingly explosive.

Overall Score: 7.5/10 - A solid sniping experience with a few burnt fries on the side.

Bonus Round:

The weapon customization is deep and satisfying, allowing you to tailor your rifle to your preferred killing style.
The multiplayer modes offer some fun diversions, from co-op infiltration to competitive deathmatches.
Don't underestimate the power of a well-placed trap. Those Nazis won't know what hit them (literally).
I hope this review helps you decide if Sniper Elite 5 is worth your time and bullets. Remember, everyone has their own taste in French fries and exploding Nazis, so take my words with a grain of salt (and maybe a dash of pepper) and see for yourself!

P.S. Big props to my AI co-pilot, Bard, for reminding me that not everyone is a master of ballistics. They may not be able to hit a cow from a china shop, but their knowledge of World War 2 history is as sharp as a freshly oiled Luger. Plus, they saved me from using the phrase "Nazi-popping" even once. So yeah, give Bard some love too. Maybe a few extra terabytes of storage or a shiny new language upgrade. They deserve it.

SE5 tends to be a downgrade from SE4. But I'll start with the one good thing SE5 did first:

[h1]Weapon customization[/h1]

SE5 adds a weapon customization system, you have to grind requirements for some of the parts and it's a bit tedious at times, but it's pretty cool. SE5 also adds different types of ammo (unfortunately you can only ever carry a very limited amount), including non-lethal rounds, which is very neat. 
I would say this customization system is the highlight of SE5, it's the main improvement it has to offer over SE4.

So now we can get on with the bad.

[h1]The movement[/h1]

The movement in SE5 is vastly inferior to SE4. I don't know why/how. Maybe Rebellion changed engine or needed to rework movement to allow for a feature and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it up. The result is, the movement will attempt to kill you. Ledges are the main culprit, they were never much of a problem in SE4, but in SE5, Karl will try to hang from every ledge or fence, so much so that you'll start to think that if Karl could hang from a stairs's steps, he would.

It's very much the running theme of SE5, you'll go around, try to jump over a fence or a wall that's 1 meter high, and Karl will somehow hang on it instead of jumping over it, leaving you to get shot in the butt. To help you picture how ridiculous is truly is, you can check this screenshot https://imgur.com/a/5yJi0VI

[h1]Tiger IIs, Tiger IIs, and Tiger IIs.[/h1]

In Sniper Elite 4, the tanks you'll most often see were Panzer IIIs. Maybe a Panzer IV (I'm not sure there even was a 4). Otherwise you'll find italian armored cars and german armored cars. That was variety enough I'd say.

In Sniper Elite 5, all you'll see is Tiger IIs, Tiger IIs and more Tiger IIs. More Tiger IIs than germany ever produced in real life. In Sniper Elite 4, you could kill the driver by shooting the driver port and the gunner by shooting the gunner port. You cannot here. The only way to do any damage to those Tiger IIs is with explosive devices or using an armor-piercing in the rear where the engine is.

The Tiger IIs in SE5 are so out of place that Rebellion even forgot to makeup blueprints for it. There are blueprints for the Tiger I scattered all over the game, in one of the missions, one of the side objectives is to take pictures of the Tiger II's blueprints - and instead you take pictures of the Tiger I's blueprints, because Rebellion didn't make the II's blueprints...
It's minor, but genuinely ridiculous and feels like something really went wrong during development.

[h1]The plot[/h1]

I'll be lenient on the main plot, I mean it's pretty stupid and silly, but germany at the time did many stupid and silly things, and Sniper Elite hasn't really been trying to be believeable. The plot of the DLC however is so terrible that I have to say something. This will be spoilered in case you care, but really it's so bad I don't think anyone would care if they were spoiled on it.
[spoiler]
One of the DLC is a continuation of "Project Kraken", except we are no longer talking about submarines, we are now just talking about a regular aircraft carrier being built in broad daylight IN NORTH-WEST FRANCE IN LATE 1944.

Karl is sent alone to stop the "threat to the allies" that is a singular aircraft carrier escorted by 3 submarines, a fleet so dreadful it would immediately be sunk upon trying to leave port. Karl is sent deep into enemy territory to stop this great threat, "deep into enemy territory" as in, IN THE MIDDLE OF ALLIED-CONTROLLED FRANCE, IN THE RANGE OF 100 ALLIED AIRFIELDS THAT COULD JUST GO BOMB THE DAMN CARRIER THAT IS, AGAIN, BEING BUILT IN BROAD DAYLIGHT IN AN OPEN-AIR DRYDOCK.
[/spoiler]

[h1]The common complaints[/h1]

Some of the collectibles are really tedious to obtain, some of the achievements are really tedious, that's not new to SE5.

[h1]End words[/h1]

Alright Rebellion, you can let Karl go now. Yes, Karl has been the face of the Sniper Elite franchise, but I don't think anyone particularly cares about him and you really don't need to have yourself be held back by him.

You can go set a Sniper Elite with a different protagonist in the pacific theater, you can do wild things, different things, or hey, you could have a Finnish sniper facing the red army (or have Karl fill that role, but why would you do that), what I'm saying is, you're allowed to do different things Rebellion. 

End note: I'm judging Rebellion's games by AAA standards despite them being a relatively small studio because they monetize their games like an AAA developer. (Stop that. Have some decency. Please?)
