Early on you'll need the "bullet time" to estimate bullet drop for the long shots, or to slow things down... and as you get used to the rifles you'll start estimating the shots yourself (and making them).

This entry has silencers you can equip to most of the weapons, which detracts a little bit imo from the old system of finding a vantage point and having to time your shots to nearby artillery or a malfunctioning generator or whatnot, to mask the sound of the shots. Now you just make sure you're far enough from enemies, and you can shoot whenever. Definitely don't feel as encouraged to explore to find the "sniper's nest" spots.

Overall though, a great entry from Rebellion!

My Sniper Elite V5 Experience. A story for the ages.

I am going to be refunding this game as I was willing to give it a chance, but as most of the reviews here have stated, the traversal in this game takes me back to the Playstation 2 days. Im honestly quite shocked on how much of a step back they have taken compared to Sniper elite 4 in terms of blocking certain paths. This made it "difficult" for both myself and my co op partner. The first mission right off the bat has me in tears of laughter however. Upon us exiting a SUBMARINE with our allied friends onboard, one of them shouts something on the lines of "Dont get us killed by getting alerted". It couldnt have been 15 minutes later, that a German artillery gun fires a single projectile onto the SUBMARINE and killing the entire crew. My friend just goes "you guys were in a submarine, why the **** didnt you go underwater.

After that PTSD causing event, the main objective now requests us to enter a base to blow up some huge electrical dish  (I dont even care at this point for proper terminology of that thing) but instead, we decided to do optional missions. Out of the 8 "destroy aa guns" that I believe there was, we only blew up 3 because the game did not give us enough satchel charges (and we did explore to try to find some). So after making the easy decision to not let this game waste anymore of our time, we decided to push forward. We kept to the left side of the map, this time, heading straight for the main objective. Before reaching the main objective, we navigated ourselves through a labyrinth of evil bushes that blocked easily openable areas not considered by the devs. We attempted to climb the treacherous "10 degree incline of doomed dirt" that Karl is somehow unable to climb (I suppose we forgot to equip the climbing gear before starting the mission).I myself got stuck on the "infinite reloading" animation on my rifle. And finally, we were forced to open our maps numerous times to see our current location and strategize  a game plan to overcome the evil dirt and bushes.

So we did this, and after navigating for 10 minutes, we finally made it to the main objective. Or so we had thought. As we stood there, on the main road, both my friend and I looked at eachother in a state of disbelief. Presented before us was this massive steel door that casted its gaze menacingly. It was so massive that we knew something fishy lurked in the air............and fishy it was.

 It had 2 of the same symbols painted onto it. "No entry".

My heart sank. The journey that led us here was all for nothing. I thought about my non existent wife, kids, brothers, and most importantly, my love for my country. I decided to walk further down the road to see if there was a hidden path, but it was to no avail. We were now back to square one. We busted out the map and devised a plan to take the main road. I told my partner "This life as a sniper isnt for me anymore, screw the stealth approach". He nodded as we pushed forward. Every enemy that entered our line of sight, we layed waste to.  The evil bushes and dirt tried to come for us again, but I was determined to complete the mission. In the midst of me trying to complete it, I decided that after I escape this horribly designed map, I was going to shoot myself in the foot so that I could go back home. 

So now, here we are. Ending right on back to where we first were before doing the side missions. I said to my partner "I wont make the same mistake twice; well take the right side". He agreed. After partially letting out our frustration along the way, we finally arrived. We immediately opened fire,  killing everyone in sight like we decided not long ago. We realistically disabled the dish with a crowbar, then we destroyed the circuit breaker (with our bare hands). As we nagivated  to the end of the location, we saw it. The menacing steel door. I was on the other side now, how could this be a "no entry"?!?! I shouted. Then I heard it say to us quietly. "No entry".  Just as I was about to take my own life, my partner spotted a hidden bunker beside it. We investigated, and came to the conclusion that this indeed would take us to the other side where we first met the steel door. We entered the rabbit hole, and after about 40sec of jogging through the concrete jungle, we reached the other side. Once we exited the bunker, we indeed were on the side we thought was a dead end. I stopped and put my hand on his shoulder. I looked at him in the eye and said "how the hell were we supposed to know we had to go even further down the road to the right to see this?". "It makes no sense" I further added. 

It didnt matter in the end, nothing did. After busting out the map the 3rd time, we finally made it to the rendezvous point, only to be greeted by some angry french woman that had no reason to be angry. After speaking to her, I shot myself in the foot and I am now talking to HQ. They say my refund is being processed.

SE5 could have been just SE4 (which was superb) with new maps, but Rebellion have continued to evolve the series, and Karl's latest adventure is highly enjoyable so far.  

Other reviewers have held up bottles replacing rocks as a problem; I think it's an excellent change.  A thrown rock never did strike me as something a German would react to; it's a neutral sound, and would blend in with the ambient sounds of nature.  Breaking glass is the complete opposite; it's guaranteed to attract attention, and the fact that your supply of bottles is limited forces you to choose your moment carefully rather than just hide somewhere and throw endless stones until one of them has the desired effect.

Weapon customisation at the workbenches is great.  Tough choices have to be made, as most of them penalise you in one area to improve another, but you're now able to choose how you want your guns modded to suit your play style.  If you're run-and-gun, choosing lighter weight at the expense of accuracy or range, or the patient assassin camping out for the perfect shot, going for the ultimate long range kill at the expense of a heavier gun and less mobility.

All in all, I'm very happy, and fully expect to love SE5 as much as I did SE4.  Thoroughly recommended  if you liked any of the previous games in the series.

Ultimately, I will have to leave a positive review for SE5 because while it has a LOT of glaring issues at launch, I'm sure most will be fixed over time through things like patches or content packs. There's definitely a lot more polish to be brought to the game. Now with that out of the way:

Bugs:
There seems to be a good chunk full of bugs in my playthrough so far. Karl getting stuck on slight geometry on paths that are clearly meant to be walked through. Being caught on an infinite slide animation because of one stray rock. Enemy bodies completely disappearing when I take them down in tall grass. Animation locks when hugged up on cover. Enemies just not registering the fact that you're right in front of them sometimes. It's a good handful but that being said, I do expect these to be addressed later on and as of right now, none of them feel super game-breaking.

Gameplay:
SE5's big new appeal is having this new hitman-inspired approach to the missions, basically taking SE4's maps and then making them a bit bigger and a lot more open-ended for player agency. It actually works out a lot and makes it feel a lot more fun planning approaches or having a completely different approach to go with the next playthrough. It really does encourage replays of missions and that'll help SE5 in the long run. The new weapon customization is also extremely rewarding and fun to tweak BUT it's completely stunted by two things, a complete lack of weapons to experiment with (there's 15 weapons total, 5 per category) and no shooting range to test out your new build like you could in SE4. Hell, I realized there weren't even any shotguns in the game and that sucked because I LOVED the M30 drilling. Also, they got rid of S-mines and Trip mines and only brought back the Teller mine, we got the Schu mine but that's just a non-lethal mine. Rocks were replaced with bottles (now a limited amount) and added the decoy which is eh. I hope a lot of this is addressed over time but I'm skeptical, though the gameplay is still fun.

Setting:
I think this is SE5's saving grace, the authenticity of WWII is so prevalent here and I absolutely love it. I liked Italy in SE4 but it felt weird for a WWII setting. You are experiencing everything from a German war factory, to the Atlantic Beachhead of Normandy, the Occupied Austrian Alps, to the French Countryside akin to Operation Market Garden, all militarized by the German occupation of the area and it was just so completely atmospheric. The German's have proper loadouts for their time and I found that extremely impressive because it's the entire standard issue equipment for your basic Wehrmacht soldier on the western fronts. Your Jaegars and Vampr Soldiers actually look authentic this time around vs SE4's style of just a basic get uniform. I personally found that to be an extreme nod to historic authenticity. 

Conclusion:
The game is pretty good as is but there's definitely a lot more polish and a lot more content that needs to be added to further reinforces the game's gameplay systems.

It pains me to write this review, because I loved the previous game dearly, and while I certainly don't hate this iteration, I'm just... disappointed. Short version: this game is one step forward, 15 small steps back.

Longer version - Oh boy, let me list you my grievances:
- Our protagonist appears to have been dropped on his head between games, and while he still remembers how to pick up guns from fallen enemies, he is entirely incapable of conceiving of how to reload them, and will instead simply discard them once the initial ammo runs out. Or any time you switch weapon, for that matter.
- Speaking of weapons, the initial selection (including unlockables) is a travesty, with basically every well-known rifle from the period suspiciously missing from the list (which is made up of a lackluster 6 rifles of mostly obscure models... almost like someone was planning to sell back the fan favourites as DLC down the line. Almost.)
- Then there's the elephant in the room - invasion mode. To be fair here, I am in no way protesting its existence, and I wish anyone excited by it a jolly good time - but to have singleplayer PvE unlockables gated to not only participation, but performance in a PvP mode, that's gonna be a hard yikes from me. Insult to injury that turning it off results in a penalty to all xp earned.
- Along with reloading enemy weapons, our protag has also forgotten how to pick up rocks from the ground for easy throwing, and must now rely entirely on whatever glass bottles he can find along the way.
- (As a trade-off, he appears to have learned to harness his latent psychic abilities in order to sense enemies through walls. YMMW on this one)
- Your mileage may also vary on the gun customization feature. While it's not COD-levels of bad, it's certainly taking some historical liberties - and every single attachment available somehow make some aspect of the gun worse, a design decision I personally loathe.
- Traversing is great, until it ain't. When it works, traversal feels... very decent. But there's a lot of times where there are no visual cues and even less logic to what you can and can't climb, and at least the first map is plagued by knee-high impassable obstacles, invisible walls, and long stretches of ditches, vegetation or fencing that any normal human should be able to traverse with ease, but our protag inexplicably cannot.
- Finally, there's a lot of things that, while not outright bad, also just aren't as good as they were before. Tagged enemies don't show up as they used to, making visibility sometimes an issue. Empty lung looks and feels just a little worse than before (in part because it now has a wind-up time of sorts, making repeat shots less fluid). The kill-cams, while now available from just about any weapon (which is great) just look... jankier, somehow - which is kindof impressive, to be honest.

All in all - it's hard not to come across as someone with a vendetta writing this, but I feel it is an accurate representation of the game in it's current state. It's not that the game is not fun, and I definitely plan on putting more hours in it - but I've already paid for it, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't disappointed. I feel overall let down with some of the choices made by the design team. I'm sure a lot of this will change and improve with patches and DLC, but in its current state, I really cannot think of a reason to recommend anyone buy this over Sniper Elite 4.

There are two big problems with this game, and it isn’t the invasions nor the freaking traversal mechanics; it’s the obtuse way that the game has to present its mechanics and systems, one, and the other, is the absolute horrid progression and unlocking systems in this title.

The way you unlock attachments and weapons in this game is by progressing through the game and finding workbenches in the levels corresponding for each of the three types of weapons you can carry (rifle, assault rifle, pistol). The guns are varied and the attachments are detailed and change your weapons significantly, not only in how they worked but also on how they look. The issue?

The best attachments and weapons can only be obtained after the halfway mark of the game, literally the most silent silencers and rifles, the more damaging machineguns, and the best attachments for your pistols, can only be obtained after the third mission or so. This missions also last around two hours long or so by the way… What does this mean?

It means that the players will get a really bad first impressions from this game, and most people won’t make it into the 6 hours or so it takes for the game to supply actually good equipment that you can use to experiment with the game systems and mechanics and… It’s a shame.

It’s a shame because I persisted after the third mission despite wanting to quit the game, partly out of curiosity, partly out of desire of wanting the game to become better, and it eventually did; I loved Sniper Elite 4, now I think this has taken the throne as the best one in the series, even surpassing its predecessor.

Just know it takes a while till you can actually sneak around and stuff. The game also makes a poor job at emphasizing how important the new bullet types you can use are, subsonic ammo is essential in stealth approaches because it literally makes it so your gun is virtually silent, you can shoot an enemy from 20m away and they won’t hear you, armour piercing ammo by comparison makes it so you can take out vehicles in just a few shots, assuming you’re targeting their vulnerable parts, which you can see after you mark them either with your binoculars or weapons… This last thing is never explained… Might be common sense to some but, the last couple of games never had this mechanic, all you had to do if you wanted to destroy a vehicle was to shoot at its vulnerable sections once with simple, regular, ammo.

So, yeah… This is going to be yet again another underrated game from Rebellion and in a way, it’s entirely their fault. I don’t agree with the complaints about the invasion mode because you can turn it off, the same as you can choose to not install easy-anti cheat (thank God for whoever in the dev team suggested this). I also don’t agree with the traversal being worse here because it’s not a matter of the mechanics being worse is a matter about the game not explaining them enough, not in tutorial sections, not in its design, you can still drop from high ledges and Karl (protagonist) will hold on to ledges below him breaking his fall in the process, you can also jump from one ledge to the next, climb through vines, etc. The issue is with how these systems and mechanics are delivered, not in the mechanics and systems themselves.

It’s a shame, because if you persist with it, it truly becomes a fantastic game, but I’m nearing the end of the game, sixth mission or so, and only 17% players have reached it to begin with…

Match: More velocity and damage, but also louder when fired, good against targets from afar as well.

This game is alright for single-player. Nothing special. Decent sized maps, albeit, nothing that screams "Awesome". NPCs have been dumbed-down in comparison to SE 4 (and even SE 3) NPCs. Ballistics have been simplified somewhat as well.

Biggest downside is the inability to freely replace your weapons by picking up dropped weapons from NPCs. You can pick theirs up, but it is a limited use item, then it's right back to your gear. Hence, don't expect to be able to tote an MG42 or Panzerfaust as a secondary while you play. Flare-guns are no longer treated as equipment. They, too, are an item meant to be used, not carried to where they are useful. You will find yourself constantly toting useful flares, panzerfausts, and MGs a few feet, dropping them, picking them up again, and repeating just to get them to where you want to use them.

A lot of the old SE 4 game mechanics never were incorporated into this game, or were half-assedly added in so they failed to function properly. Best examples of this would be the lack of ability to jog while crouched (perhaps the most used feature of SE 4), and the lack of an ability to toggle-aim via a hotkey (either you set toggle aim on, and your regular aim key has to be pressed to aim, and then again to go back, or you get used to holding the aim button all the time, and ignore the toggle-aim setting).

While the weapons sandbox is pretty big once you include all the upgrades each weapon can have (especially with DLC packs), only a handful of the customizations are worth use in both MP and SP modes, or even at all.

Customization of your weapons is nonsense, too. Suppressors might cut sound, but unlike their IRL counterparts, they DO NOT reduce recoil, making your weapon more controllable. In fact, they do the opposite. Additionally, a component that on one rifle makes it equip/aim faster will on another rifle have the opposite effect. Needless to say, anyone who spends enough time playing with the sandbox of weapons and their component upgrades will find the whole of it generally counter-intuitive.

Add to this the fact that some weapons/upgrades have a massive advantage in MP, in the most ridiculous of ways, and your MP experience is guaranteed to agitate most players. Unfortunately a 6.5/10 for me at the moment. Core elements remain the same as in previous iterations, but new mechanics are implemented very poorly and detract from the overall experience. Most notably, the developers added vertical movement (a la Assassin's Creed), but--unlike in AC--while you can climb *some* surfaces such as vines, you can't even walk up the bank of a road or hop over a small pile of rocks. This leads to extremely awkward gameplay where you are never sure whether you can climb over something or not (usually not), and have to try first to find out.

The aforementioned problem also means that the large open map, another new feature, is actually not large at all. For example, there are some roads that you simply cannot walk off of because you are somehow unable to ascend a 15 degree incline, despite being able to climb the side of a house. Compounding this problem are barriers that have absolutely no reason to be barriers, such as slightly-dense foliage and low walls. Why can I climb over medium walls but not low walls?

The worst is when you find out you can actually climb something, such as as a side of a house--only to realize that it leads to a dead end (i.e. you cannot top out) and your only option is to climb back down. Remove the ambiguity, please.

The redeeming quality is that, once you get past the fence that could only be cut in one place but not another, and actually get sniping, it's the same old goodness as before.

Anyway, so far it's been a mixed bag. I'm liking the customisation and the more personalised game experience with custom difficulty and all, but the game itself is pretty lacklustre. As of the completion of mission 2 a few things stand out to me the most.

-The AI

The AI is either aimbotting and hits every shot it takes the moment you step out of cover (snipers especially) or cannot see you when you're crouching literally at it's knees. There is barely any in between and it almost ruined the experience for me at times.

-The map design

The maps feel almost claustrophobic, especially mission 1, where you can't move through or hide in incredibly thin bushes and are railroaded to running often 40+ meters around hedgerows and stupid walls that you for some reason cannot vault, coupled with weird terrain that you can relatively easily get stuck on. I'm hoping since I've only completed mission 1 and 2 that this is just an issue in those examples.

-The visuals

The game kinda looks like ♥♥♥♥. The textures and lighting are all *fine* but the anti-aliasing implementation really genuinely hurts my eyes at times. That bundled with the fact that it runs at just over 100fps (ultra, 1440p) on my 3070ti and lacks *any* DLSS implementation at all is grating, although considering the job they did with AA it might be a good thing after all that they didn't implement DLSS. FSR 1.0 is there, though. For some reason.

-The bugs

I know it's day 1 but.. come on. The x-ray camera doesn't really work right a lot of the time, enemies just ignore shots at some angles (an infantryman i encountered was manning an mg42 and shrugged off 12 headshots in the first mission) and killing some enemies breaks others pathing. It's kinda sad that this is the state of almost every newly released game these days, but i trust these issues will be ironed out over the next couple patches.

-On the other hand, the good

I still like the game so far and despite the issues i have with it, i'm having fun. that being said, i cannot particularly recommend the game in its current state due to the aforementioned issues, especially at the price point they are presenting. The classic SE gameplay loop is still as good as ever (it wouldn't have survived like 7 games if it wasn't) and the new customisation options are pretty cool, but the game has pretty big issues, most of which I'm hoping get patched in the near future, but some I'm more worried about being permanent dampers on the overall experience.

Finished the campaign, updating the review. Yes, indeed, this is a good one. Sniper Elite as a series finally finished its growing pains and developed into a remarkably nice stealth action game. One that I might just put on the level with other pillars of the genre.

First of all, this game is finally a proper sandbox. The levels are vast and complex, to the points of being a bit confusing on your first run. There are multiple entrance and exit positions, and enemies are semi-randomized, which makes replaying them still feel fresh. And you will want to replay them, because there are collectibles, additional objectives and lots of other stuff you will probably miss on your first run. Especially since a lot of objectives can be completed in different ways — for example, you can climb up to the radar and set charges, which you will later detonate with a precise shot, or you can fight your way into the bunker underneath and overload the generator. 

The enemies are smarter than they used to be, they now flank you and organize proper search parties. You can still setup maneater bushes and serial killer corners, but be prepared that while you are having your fun, you are probably getting pincered by the other squad. Mobility is key in Sniper Elite 5, especially since there are very few truly silent ways to kill an enemy — even the best silencer in the game is only rated for 8+ meters.

All of this creates a very addictive type of gameplay where planning really pays off and you need to think through both your approach, execution and escape from each encounter. Especially if you are going for the challenges — some of which are really ridiculous in the best possible way. 

But it isn't all about sneaking — sniping is still the name of the game (literally). It can be as complex or simple as you want it to be, but I highly recommend you to set its difficulty at least to Hard. Having gravity and wind pull at your shots makes sniper duels a lot more satisfying. And there are some shots in this game that are truly rewarding to nail.

As for the rest — Sniper Elite 5 is pretty par for the course. It probably won't blow you away with its graphics, story, music or characters. All this is perfectly servicable but overall par for the course. But it has amazing gameplay and that is by far the most important part.

Download SnakeBite. Get yourself that mod that let's you wear a skull prosthetic mask, and the Cyborg skin for the MSF sneak suit. Roleplay as a cyborg assassin. Be a villain and build Outer Heaven. Maybe Kojima really believes the game is as it should be, but this game should've been about being a super villain. 

You should not use the tranq pistol. The game should've made stunning and sleeping enemies more difficult, given the tranq pistol more limitations. You should have every reason to murder your enemies, the demon that you are. Use only limited stun/sleep grenades to kidnap soldiers to build your private army. Everybody else dies silently or in a blaze of gunfire (your choice, "Venom" Snake). 

You even look like Eggman when you pilot D-Walker. That's what this game should've been like; an open world littered with "Eggman Moments". You are literally playing as a NES era super villain.

The gameplay is really tight and the story, which is OK but not exactly stellar, doesn't get in the way *too* much like it does in 4. If you are into it for the story, it is structured almost as if it is some kind of ARG. You piece things together with casette tapes, and the cutscenes don't reveal, like, anything. The twist, which is frankly the gamer equivalent to the Empire Strikes Back twist these days in terms of how hidden it is, is pretty cool but it should've had more of an effect on your in game avatar. Rather than a dumb, surface level character creator, you should've had a "Snake editor" where you edit Snake's appearance in ways that make sense for a 9 year older Snake. Eyepatch optional, scars are editable, hair color can be changed to reflect age. Stuff like that.

The online elements show some really interesting potential. You build the new Motherbase and compete against other Motherbases, foreshadowing the coming war economy of the later games. I never played MGO, but it looks like generic deathmatch stuff. Not my thing. The "Journey/Death Stranding" like multiplayer should have been MGO's whole thing, and with concentrated attention being given to it, I honestly think that the system could've been something really special. Frankly, as it stands, it is pretty cool and a little addicting. But it is little more that "number go up".

As it stands, this game is fantastic, but the story it tries to tell is caught up in trying to portray Snake as a legendary mercenary while also somehow turning him into a villain. Give us more villain gameplay. Let me be the supervillain "Big Boss" is in the MSX games. 

Check it out and kill a bunch of dudes. Have discretion when it comes to the men you enlist for your Outer Heaven. Create your own scenario where you imply that Venom Snake is the first Cyborg Ninja. And don't become addicted to silencers or tranq guns.

I can’t emphasize enough how spectacular and simultaneously disappointing the experience of [i][b]Metal Gear V[/b][/i] is. 

It’s been 10 years that I’ve been trying to finish this thing. I’ve had at least one copy on every platform the game was released on, played at least 20–30 hours on each of them, and after so much time and so many abandoned attempts, I finally managed to gather enough patience to push through this brick.

And… well, I can’t say I was very surprised by the result.

I knew exactly what I was getting into, and why I had quit so many times before, just as I knew why I kept trying to finish it.

Technically, from top to bottom, the game is an extraordinary production. A state-of-the-art achievement for its time—what was possible to deliver with a huge budget and a near-psychotic obsession with polish. A landmark of quality in open-world gameplay and the still-unmatched peak of the stealth-action genre.

Not to mention the cutting-edge presentation, with a level of attention to detail and clarity that gives the entire game a convincing texture, making it feel like an interactive film.

It’s a game that still runs circles around most modern productions, even after all these years.

The animations and controls are almost flawless. Mechanically, the game is so diverse and dynamic that just five minutes of casually roaming the maps will naturally generate hundreds of interactions between the player, the systems, and the enemies.

The game features the most reactive and manipulable enemies in the genre—completely consistent to play against, capable of reacting in dozens of different ways depending on the player’s actions, and perfectly integrated into multiple dynamic difficulty systems that span the entire map.

A lethal and non-lethal multitude of weapons, gadgets, advanced movements, and versatile stealth rules, all in perfect sync with level design, provide complete freedom for the player to improvise. The game gives you that liberating feeling that no matter the situation, there is always a universe of possibilities right in the palm of your hand—fully viable—and you never need to rely on the slow, tedious tactics typically associated with the genre.

There’s a certain mastery in the level design in offering so many distinct areas, realistically crafted yet overflowing with possibilities and inviting to conquer, while somehow always providing a clear sense of layout and threats. At no point did I feel like I was going in blind on any mission, deprived of anticipation—being caught off guard always felt like my fault. 

The skill ceiling is in another galaxy, and the game’s ability to react accordingly—and even retroactively scale the difficulty of previously completed missions—ensures things never feel static or repetitive. They made sure that at least most of the main missions are highly replayable, whether through the vast range of ways to complete them or simply through the living dynamism that emerges during gameplay.

The game retains that classic slapstick sense of humor from the series. The juxtaposition between the seriousness and realism of the setting and the inherent comedy of the gameplay is pure gold. It maintains a lightness that makes the experience very enjoyable, especially because the game goes a long way in encouraging a kind of almost “friendly” playstyle.

Throughout the entire experience, you also have a highly addictive time-based progression system that is fueled by your actions in the field, where you unlock a constant flow of new tools that drastically extend the game's lifespan.

But even with such a strong core design and countless hours of replayable content, it’s hard to ignore how unfinished the game feels—and to not miss something that should give your actions a compelling context, but instead leaves everything feeling a bit… hollow?

Perhaps, in yet another of the many dumb allusions to the term “Phantom Pain,” the lack of a real story is what killed my enthusiasm every single time.

I can’t describe how high my expectations were before release. The trailers promised an unforgettable, intense, cathartic journey worthy of a legendary blockbuster. Ground Zeroes had already given a taste of the technical quality we could expect and a glimpse of a more mature and efficient Kojima, shedding much of the sluggish, intrusive, indulgent exposition that defines his narrative “style,” while daring to push the franchise into more politically charged and complex territory (with questionable results).

If Phantom Pain was going to be even better, it had everything to become the epic masterpiece that would conclude the saga once and for all. It had everything to be special.

And well, the game came out amid stories of controversy, backstage tensions, and cut content. Then I played it. I was initially mesmerized by the gameplay’s potential. But after many hours, the story seemed like it hadn’t even begun… That exciting adventure never started—the essence that should drive everything just wasn’t there. Instead, I got background monologues and a plot thinner than tissue paper. My goodwill lasted about 20 hours, which is more than enough to finish any game in the franchise. Then I quit—and repeated the process several times over the years, always growing tired of gameplay not being enough to carry everything.

And I didn't even know how much worse the whole thing was. Before, I had only glimpsed the emptiness—now I experienced the slog of Chapter 2, which is so poorly made that it makes Chapter 1 seem cohesive and substantial by comparison. The endgame is purposeless, incoherent, and frustrating, filled with the worst missions in the game, repeated content, mandatory side quests, and the most predictable and irrelevant twist imaginable.

The thinness of the context behind almost everything that motivates you, and how unengaging every piece of the glacial-moving plot is, drains all enjoyment from the experience. It’s a complete emotional vacuum—no character development, no tension, no meaningful antagonism—filled with literal HOURS of audio tapes discussing topics you don’t care about, because the game does a terrible job of making you care about anything. 

Even well-known characters have completely lost their personality.

When "Sins of the Father" starts playing as the credits roll at the end of the first act, the game seems to be trying to evoke a sense of dramatic conclusion that simply isn't there. It just feels awkward.

Under the truckload of redundant exposition typical of Kojima’s games you at least used to have a genuine story, with memorable characters and scenes, and a healthy dose of drug-infused Japanese absurdist humor that managed to shine despite the author’s constant attempts to kill your engagement.

This is just… nothing. A complete void. 

The Metal Gear game that pushes the mechanical boundaries the most, but fails to deliver on the aspect for which the franchise has always been best known. It's a bizarre and depressing contrast.

You know what my favorite part of the entire "story" was? Miller talking about hamburgers.

It was the only crumb of humanity in the whole thing.

I'll probably continue for the next few weeks, replaying missions I enjoyed, experimenting, and taking on self-imposed challenges. I have no doubt it will be a lot of fun, now free from the burden of a narrative that never really existed. But I'll never want to start from scratch again.

[h1]War Crimes, Cassette Tapes, and the Greatest Stealth Sandbox Ever Built for a Man Having the Worst Midlife Crisis on Earth[/h1]

[h2]1984: Snake Wakes Up and Immediately Makes It Everyone Else’s Problem[/h2]
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN kicks off with a hospital escape so deranged it feels like someone filmed a fever dream with military funding. Then it drops you into 1984 as Venom Snake, loose in Afghanistan and Central Africa, chasing revenge, rescuing Miller, rebuilding an army, and generally behaving like therapy has failed on an international scale. It’s officially sold as “tactical espionage operations,” which is accurate, but not quite accurate enough. This is tactical espionage operations if tactical espionage operations also included horse poop, child soldiers, cassette tapes, and a helicopter that arrives like it’s billing overtime.

[h2]Fox Engine Still Looks Like Black Magic in Combat Boots[/h2]
This game still looks filthy in the best possible way. Not just “good for its age.” I mean properly, obnoxiously good. Sunlight bouncing off sand, floodlights cutting through dark outposts, rain slapping across metal, faces half-lit in the chopper, all of it still has that expensive, clinical shine that makes a lot of newer games look like they were assembled out of damp cereal. It’s not trying to be pretty in a fairytale sense. It wants to look like dust, steel, blood, and bad intentions. Mission accomplished, you magnificent bastard. Did I mention it's disgustingly well-optimized as well?

[h2]The Soundtrack Has Taste, the Helicopter Has an Ego, and Both Are Right[/h2]
The audio in this thing is absurdly sharp. Every suppressed shot has that nasty little cough to it, every alarm feels like your luck just got audited, and the helicopter may as well be a supporting character by the end. Then there’s the music. The licensed tracks, the synthy unease, the mission intros that make you feel ten times cooler than your actual performance deserves, it all works. MGSV understands a crucial truth: if you’re going to sneak into a Soviet base at 3 a.m., you should at least have bangers. Otherwise it’s just unpaid trespassing.

[h2]Every Outpost Is a Puzzle Box and You’re Allowed to Be a Complete Freak About It[/h2]
This is where The Phantom Pain goes from “excellent video game” to “frankly a bit rude to the competition.” The stealth is incredible. Every mission gives you room to improvise, sabotage, scout, ghost through, tranquilize half the map, or turn the whole operation into a flaming HR incident. The open mission structure, all the tools, the buddy system, the supply drops, the weird little emergent disasters, everything clicks effortlessly. It's one of the few games where messing up is often more entertaining than succeeding cleanly. And the controls? Sharp as hell. The game trusts you to experiment, then quietly smirks while you invent some deeply unhinged tactic involving decoys, sleeping gas, and a cardboard box.

[h2]A Great Story Until It Starts Leaving Pages Stuck to the Printer[/h2]
The story is fascinating right up until it starts feeling like it lost a fight with a chainsaw in the edit room. Early on, it’s strong stuff: revenge, identity, manipulation, trauma, all wrapped in that wonderfully self-important Metal Gear tone where everyone talks like they’re delivering classified poetry. I like that about it. I really do. But the back half stumbles. Hard. Important threads feel underfed, emotional beats get stranded, and the whole thing eventually gives off the unmistakable vibe of a masterpiece with a missing wall. Also, Quiet is a ridiculous character design. Not subtle, not clever, not “symbolic,” just Kojima looking you dead in the eye and saying, “No, seriously, she breathes through her skin,” as if we all just fell off the idiot truck yesterday.

[h2]An All-Time Great Game with a Hole Blown Straight Through the Middle of It[/h2]
That’s the maddening part. The Phantom Pain is simultaneously one of the best stealth games ever made and one of the most frustratingly incomplete-feeling blockbusters I’ve ever played. Its moment-to-moment design is so damn good that you can forgive almost anything for a while. Then the repetition creeps in, the narrative starts wobbling, and you realize this incredible machine is running with a few organs missing. Even so, the highs are ridiculous. Mother Base building is weirdly addictive, the freedom is intoxicating, and the game keeps producing those perfect little “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, did I just pull that off?” moments that most open-world games would kill for. So yes, it’s flawed. Very flawed. It also absolutely wipes the floor with most games that are technically more “complete” but have the charisma of office carpeting.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

[b]Sound:[/b] [u]9/10[/u]
Rotor blades, tape hiss, and mission music doing criminally good work.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] [u]10/10[/u]
An elite stealth sandbox that lets you play like a genius, an idiot, or both at once.

[b]Story:[/b] [u]7/10[/u]
Brilliant in stretches, then suddenly held together with duct tape and denial.

[b][u]Overall: 8.9/10[/u][/b]

METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is the kind of game that annoys me by being phenomenal. If it were merely bad, fine, easy, throw it in the bin. But no, it has to be astonishing for forty hours, occasionally transcend the genre, and then leave a giant crater where a fully satisfying ending should be. Bastard. I still love it. Not because it’s tidy, and definitely not because it wraps up neatly, but because when you’re actually in the field, sneaking through a base while a sandstorm rolls in and your helicopter is blasting 80s nonsense on the horizon, it feels untouchable. Broken in places, yes. But untouchable. And honestly, that’s a very Metal Gear way to be.

“It is no nation that we inhabit, but a language. Make no mistake; our native tongue is our true fatherland.” - Emil Cioran

These words presented at the beginning of MGSV finally gave voice to something that had bothered me for a long time, and changed the way I saw games forever. After seeing Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, subbed in English in the theater for the first time, I couldn't understand why people didn't prefer the original audio track over the dub when both options were available. The dubs were often cheaply acted, mistranslated, and culturally whitewashed, leaving me with a sour feeling as I could sense something wrong, but not place it.

The events of MGSV are disturbing to say the least. But, the thing is, it had something to say at a time when seemingly no one else could or would. I looked around at the other titles I'd been playing and realized that ultimately they were empty, vapid action movies with nothing more to say than "Good people good, bad people bad". Damn near my entire gaming history up to this point I reviled the MGS series through my own unfortunately learned closed-mindedness, until I saw the quick look shown by Brad Shoemaker on giant bomb dot com, and I gave it a go. 

MGSV changed me in a real, fundamental way. Not only was it just a top notch tactical survival action experience with just about every kind of wonderful mercenary management my autistic ass could hope to ask for, it had real things it wanted to say. Not only that, it had things to say that I wasn't clever enough to understand until many years later, and I'm [i]still[/i] trying to understand all of the symbolism. But what I caught immediately onto was the game's message of the colonization of language, a concept that I had been bothered by for many years, but could never place it, it just wasn't talked about. 

And I looked around and asked, "Well, if not Kojima, then who the ♥♥♥♥ is gonna talk about this? Because we really gotta be talking about this!"

MGSV is not for the faint of heart, narratively. It presents you with many sickening situations, and shows you in no uncertain terms, that you shouldn't confuse the term "protagonist" with "hero". These concepts are important to understand, and the game confronts you with the weight of these actions. However, if you can steel yourself, you might find yourself in for a one-of-a-kind stealth action experience only surpassed by its spiritual successor, Death Stranding 2.

(Reviewer also plays a Playstation copy)

As a longtime fan of stealth games, I believe Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is the best and most ambitious title the genre has ever seen.

The difficulty hits a perfect sweet spot. It’s never too frustrating thanks to the "Reflex Mode" when spotted, yet it remains challenging due to the clever enemy AI. These enemies feel like they were truly built for stealth gameplay; once you have some experience, you can predict how they will react to certain situations. This removes frustration and rewards actual planning. To my knowledge, Phantom Pain is the only game that has successfully pulled off a true Open-World Stealth experience. From riding your horse to infiltrating countless guarded outposts, the mechanics are incredibly well-thought-out.

The main missions are a highlight, even if they vary in uniqueness. The world feels alive because things are always moving—like a convoy transporting a VIP that won’t wait for you. If you’re too slow, they leave. This dynamic nature creates immense immersion. My only gripe is the optional mission checklist. On your first playthrough, these objectives are hidden, and some are so random or difficult that they feel impossible to complete without an online guide.

The side missions act more like activities and can feel repetitive. A minor annoyance is that they often reappear in the world, meaning you sometimes have to leave and re-enter an area just to let the next set of missions appear. However, the amount of content is staggering. Between expanding Mother Base, unlocking tons of gadgets, managing personnel, and even the base-raiding multiplayer (FOB), you can easily spend over 100 hours here. There’s even a separate PvP mode I haven't even touched yet!

Story-wise, it’s typical Hideo Kojima: philosophical, complex, weird, but a bit more grounded here so as not to overshadow the gameplay. However, the plot is super hard to fully understand, even with research. It follows Ground Zeroes, which itself requires knowledge of Peace Walker from the PSP. Even then, some plot points remain unanswered, making it unnecessarily complicated for newcomers. If you’ve never played a Kojima game, the beginning might overwhelm you.

Still, even years after its release, Metal Gear Solid V remains bombastic. It is a true AAA masterpiece that I will remember forever. Absolute recommendation!

I came off 100%ing Delta AND Ground Zeroes so this review will be comparing this game to the general market AND it's competitors of the same franchise

Delta is a masterpiece, it took the weakest parts of 3 and fixed them, then left what was already perfect ENTIRELY untouched, the story, the voice cast, the music was all left alone and the controls were molded into a hybrid of this game and something new. I think Delta is the best stealth action experience of our generation. Ground Zeroes story and level of polish far exceeds The Phantom Pain, it has the same engine, mainly the same gameplay, 100% the game gunplay, cast, and style, but the vibes, amount of voice acting per mission and detail put into creativity for missions and dynamic changes for how you handle the situation are definitely beyond The Phantom Pain.

So where does The Phantom Pain excel? Time sinking, I 100% delta in a fraction of the time, a quarter perhaps, a full run of Delta on the hardest difficulty if you play well is 3 hours-ish. This game has slogging moments where you want to be done but it also has incredible moments that make you wish it went on for 200 more hours. Each mission is poorly balanced around the idea of bringing anything you HAVE researched up to that point, with some tasks actually being LITERALLY impossible unless you stopped at mission 3-4 and did sidequests first, thankfully the only mission that REQUIRED research was basically after the main game's story, but for those perfectionists (of which Metal Gear Solid as a franchise has many) it stings to be told you can't complete this mission 100% until 20 hours have passed and you have a research team to develop the 45 minute timer to completion

Research in general is the main feeling of progression, your mother base doesn't have enough customization to make it feel home, but it growing in size is a nice thing all the same, but the research is where it shines, you control how you progress the tech tree, what you focus on and dedicate manpower, resources and time

As you play, this becomes a downside, research times turn from instant into 14 minute timers into 45 minute timers into hour long timers and eventually where I am, they are online timers (meaning IRL time exclusively and can ONLY BE SPED UP WITH MICROTRANSACTIONS) that go on for days and for 2 items now A FULL WEEK, so when I called this game a time sink, keep that in mind, alongside the fact that there are 150+ sidequests that are basically copy and pasted around the map with some not even being any different at all (tank squad and armored vehicle squad might as well be the same) and every single one requires a loading screen, a flight to the location, dropping off, completion, then getting back either by helicopter (or if you are lucky and can fulton yourself, that speeds things up) into another loading screen to do it all 150 more times

"But.. I literally just wanna play the main story, thats all"
Then its fine, Delta is better for that but if you want to enjoy the gameplay mixed with free-roam elements, this game is the only one of its kind for this

Compared to all games on the market, its one of those rare diamonds in the rough that give more value then they cost, in league with something like Factorio or Slay The Spire where you can get thousands of hours from such a cheap game, but my only warning is that its flaws are evident, the game IS unfinished (as much as some disagree) and the story will leave you unsatisfied alongside the endgame EXCLUSIVELY turning into PvP as you invade the same model of base 1000 time for meager returns

8/10, Go play Delta if you can afford it, if you are coming from Delta, this might be the second best MGS game to ever be released, so enjoy it well since god knows when the next Remake or Mainline game will ever come out

Probably the best Espionage-based tactical game ever made, one of Kojima's memorable, and the last before his departure from Konami, which never seems to recover from it and keeps trying to capitalize on his work even long after he went away.

- Let's start with the music: it blends the OST's from all the old MGS games, and also you will hear known pieces such as Take On Me and The Final Countdown. - The setting of the 80's Afghanistan and Central Africa, occupied by the Soviets and CFA forcer respectively. The maps are a huge sandbox for the player to experience, with bases and outposts which you can raid for resources, or "steal" enemy soldiers to come working for your own private army: the Diamond Dogs.

- The companions: the trusty horse, the fluffy good boi, D-Dog(which you find abandoned as a pup, and extract him and raise him as one of your best), and the sniper, Quiet(initially, an assassin sent to kill you, which managed to realise the mistakes she made and tried to make amends by collaborating with you).
- You can extract almost every single thing you see on the map(which makes MGS-V an actual EXTRACTION shooter) from plants, wild animals to vehicles, even TANKS.. with their crew still inside. 
- The game runs on almost anything, and is incredibly well optimized for a game that has a pretty big open world

Cons:
- Well.. I tried finding but couldn't.. maybe one: one of the final story missions: a tank having aimbot, managing to hit you from almost any angle possible, which makes that mission incredibly difficult in comparison to others.
- Nothing else really

This is one good action game, but that also rewards stealth if the action scene is not forced, so I Highly recommend getting this game, because we may never see a MGS game as good as this one

Tactical Masterpiece

The game stands as a masterclass in stealth design and narrative craftsmanship. The mechanics can feel somewhat weird at first, as the gameplay is strikingly unique compared to most conventional action games, but once you become acclimated to its rhythm, the system reveals itself to be somewhat satisfying. Movement, stealth, and timing feel deliberate, rewarding players who take the time to really understand and master the intricate flow of the game.

The weapons are crafted for the experience. Due to the fact you can only carry a limited number of guns and items, certain missions require you to carefully and thoughtfully choose the precise loadout before stepping into the field. This limitation surprisingly enriches the game with an additional layer of what stealth should be in a video game. When situations spiral into chaos, the ability to call in weapons and supplies becomes incredibly clutch, often rescuing what would otherwise be a mission failure.

Some players may feel that portions of the gameplay become repetitive, but the game is truly about refinement, improvement, and discovering increasingly intelligent ways to approach every mission. Truly one of the greatest stealth games of all time.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain has some of the best stealth gameplay ever made. The freedom you get in missions is insane, the mechanics are polished, and every encounter can be approached in a ton of different ways.

The problem is the game feels unfinished. The story isn’t nearly as strong as earlier Metal Gear games, and the later missions start repeating content instead of adding new stuff.

So you end up with a game that’s an incredible stealth sandbox but a disappointing Metal Gear story.

The field operations in Metal Gear Solid V offer an incredible level of agency that keeps the gameplay fresh even 50 hours in. One moment I am a total ghost, carefully tailing an interpreter through Operational Guard Posts and larger Camps to secure a perfect stealth run, and the next I am leaning out of a helicopter door to shred comms dishes in a two minute speedrun. The game balances these high tension sneaking missions with moments of absolute chaos, rewarding whatever approach I decide to bring to the AOR.

While the action is the main draw, the management side back at Mother Base provides a sense of long term progression. There is a real satisfaction in optimizing my roster and hunting for specific specialists to push my R&D levels higher. Unlocking advanced gear like the Battle Dress or specialized buddy tech for [spoiler] Quiet [/spoiler] makes the logistical grind feel worthwhile. The constant drive to improve mission scores and secure elite recruits creates a loop that is consistently rewarding and technically deep.

If you are fan of previous Metal Gear Solid titles, or you are just getting into the series, this game is great to jump into. The story is a little dry, and I do miss David Hayter as Big Boss, but the action and stealth in this game are unrivaled. 8/10

Right off the bat, this game is a perfect 10/10 for me, and I'll tell you why. 
This game gets a bad rap from hardcore fans for being 'unfinished'. I don't see it that way. 
The gameplay is fantastic, probably some of the most fun I still have over 10 years later. It's very easy to get into with a lot of emergent gameplay as a result. Compared to the older games, this is a very easy bar for entry into the series as MGSV has THE best gameplay imo. Very few games scratch that indescribable itch that MGSV hits. Ghost Recon Wildlands comes pretty close, actually, but given it's a Ubisoft game with that Ubisoft 'polish', it lacks the refinement and passion to be a truly great game. Helldivers 2, actually, also plays very similarly in terms of combat, movement, etc though the gameplay loop and core mechanics are radically different. No other game touches my tism when it comes to infiltrating an enemy base using any tactic and gear at my disposal, and then getting out alive. I could meticulously knock out all of the soldiers and kidnap them for my private army; I could start a running gunfight just for giggles; I could blow up a vehicle or radar tower to cause a distraction and nab the target before bugging out, or call in a helicopter to shoot up the place. I can use decoys to ♥♥♥♥ with a single soldier for several hours before I bowl him over in a running leap and then extract him while he's unconscious in the seat of a jeep. I can throw empty mags at a guys head repeatedly just to annoy him. I can use a water gun to fry electrical equipment for easier infil/exfil or to cut off enemy comms, I can beat up my own soldiers endlessly and they'll love me for it, I can even attack another players FOB and steal his ♥♥♥♥. The options are near endless, and always fun. 
Graphics are definitely dated by today's standards but man was it cool in 2015. 
The story is amazing. It's very hard to follow, I'll be honest, but I'll straight up say I think it's the best story of the MGS series in my very biased opinion. Themes of identity, trauma, revenge, betrayal, intrigue, acceptance; MGSV: TPP is absolutely a spy thriller with multiple layers of storytelling going on at once that obscure what is actually occurring in the foreground and the background. Revenge is used as a carrot, pointed at a nebulous and ghostly antagonist that's absent for most of the game. It makes you think; are they actually the bad guy here, or is there more to it? In typical Kojima fashion, there's absolutely more than meets the eye, it's just not made obvious unless you look at the evidence the story, the characters, the dialogue, the context, and the clues that you start to piece it together and realize; you've been played like a damn fiddle, and Kojima wasn't the fiddler, he's the conductor. 
This game is a perfect 10/10 for me, I will always love this game and the memories I have tied to it. As much as I would give for a sequel or another game in this same vein, sometimes less is more, and MGSV has captured my attention and fascination for a decade.

A Masterpiece of Mechanics, a "Phantom" of a Story
Rating: 7.5/10 — A Series Veteran’s Perspective
(Played on PS5 / Also tested on PC)

As someone who has completed Metal Gear Solid 4 more than twenty times, The Phantom Pain feels like the ultimate paradox of the series. It is technically the most refined and mechanically sophisticated Metal Gear ever made — yet emotionally, it often feels deliberately distant, like something intentionally incomplete.

The "Paper" World vs. the Cinematic Opera
Coming from the tightly directed, handcrafted environments of earlier entries, the open world initially feels strangely artificial. Afghanistan and Africa function brilliantly as systemic playgrounds, but their repeated outposts and familiar structures can weaken the sense of place that once defined the series. However, this design increasingly feels intentional. The repetition mirrors the player’s role as a soldier trapped in endless operations — efficient, tactical, and emotionally detached. It creates freedom, but sacrifices the cinematic identity that made Shadow Moses or the battlefields of MGS4 feel unforgettable.

The "Wow!" Factor vs. Operational Routine
In MGS4, I looked forward to every Act, savoring every conversation, and at the end, I’d just say: "Wow, that was a blast!" In MGS V, that feeling fades. It often turns into a routine checklist: eliminate, rescue, destroy. Even with perfect mechanics, I find myself asking: "Is this story beat even relevant?" The emotional weight of MGS 1–4 is diluted into endless missions.

The Pros — The Technical Zenith
• God-Tier Optimization: The Fox Engine remains astonishing. On both PS5 and PC, the game runs flawlessly at 60 FPS with near-perfect stability — it is still a benchmark for optimization.
• Mechanical Perfection: As a stealth sandbox, this is the genre’s peak. Movement and CQC reach a level of responsiveness few games have matched.
• Quiet as a Lifeline: Quiet brings exactly the kind of bizarre and fascinating "Kojima feel" that the rest of the game sometimes lacks. She emotionally saves the experience and reminds us of the series' roots.
• Adaptive Enemy AI: Enemies dynamically responding to player habits (helmets, decoys, night vision) remains one of the smartest systemic designs in gaming.

The Cons — The "Phantom" Pain
• Story in the Shadows: Moving major lore into cassette tapes fundamentally changes the storytelling rhythm. It feels less like participating in a grand saga and more like reconstructing one from fragments.
• Friction and Waiting: Constantly calling the helicopter, waiting for extraction, and repeating opening credits for every mission becomes tedious over time and breaks the stealth atmosphere.
• The Sound of Silence: While the 80s soundtrack fits, the absence of sweeping orchestral compositions leaves certain emotional moments feeling restrained rather than monumental.
• A Deliberately Hollow Finale: The lack of a traditional narrative resolution leaves a lingering incompleteness — a literal "phantom pain" that something meaningful is missing.

A Final Thought for the Veterans
For fans of the original tetralogy (MGS 1–4), this game can ultimately serve as a refreshing departure. It’s a chance to experience a "different Metal Gear" — one that trades linear epic storytelling for base-building, resource management, and a vast array of tactical missions. It’s a unique escape that lets us see the franchise through a systemic lens before we inevitably return to the narrative style we love most.

Verdict
MGS V is a 10/10 stealth system and a 6/10 Metal Gear story. It prioritizes player agency over authorial spectacle. I’m finishing this journey out of respect for the series — but emotionally, I already feel myself returning to the cinematic masterpiece of MGS4.

My real journey continues with the Master Collection Vol. 2. I’m going home soon.

MGSV has always been one of my favourite games, and I am heavily biased towards this game. Unlike many others I really enjoyed the story in this game and the accompanying gameplay that this game provides only adds to the spectacle. People who critique the story or dog on it for being the "weakest story entry in the series" may or may not be correct, but it doesn't in any capacity detract from this game whatsoever.

The gameplay of MGSV is borderline perfect, there is absolutely nothing like it, the only things like it are derived from it. The controls are responsive & snappy, Boss moves as you would expect him to and in quick fashion with little restriction to how fast or slow you can play the game. The game being an open-world makes it by far the least linear entry in the series and it provides the player with freedom unlike any other game to explore alternate paths, do side-quests, bonus objectives etc. It's open ended to the point where the game could become trivial with even half-decent gameplay, but that's where it excels the most. This game has the advantage of player expression and it does it in spades, whatever you did to clear an outpost someone did in dozens of other ways, straightforward or elaborate, and that's why it's so good. The choices the game provides to the player, while not the most plentiful nowadays, were designed in such a way where the limitation seems non-existent. This game's controls were so good to the point that one of the most popular multiplayer games ripped off the controls & movement of this game (Helldivers 2). The absolutely ginormous variety of weaponry & equipment at your disposal, along with attachments for said weapons, even if they look ridiculous, add so much to the feeling of the game once you're deployed. You can make the absolute perfect rifle, shotgun, any loadout you need for any specific niche you need to fill.

The level design in this game for an early-open world game is as you'd expect, a bit empty. There's no two ways about it, this game is akin to Far Cry (Drive) 2, a lot of the map is just a big open desert with some convoys going back and forth, however outposts and mission areas are designed very well, to the point where I kind of wish that the game had more facilities, industrial areas like MGS2, or urban areas like MGS4. The game is by far at it's peak in these areas, where there's loads of buildings, cover, guards everywhere and less terrain to abuse without any hit to the gameplay. I think the only thing that would've completed the package in totality is more scripted events ala Ground Zeroes with the truck being board-able to ride into a facility and similar things like that to abuse and play around with. Overall, the boring parts of the map travelling can be solved with the cardboard box transport thing, which can teleport you between points of interest whilst keeping immersion.

The aesthetic of this game is just awesome, whilst the PMC that Boss runs is a bit unrealistic, the aesthetic of it certainly isn't. It really captivates you in that 80s environment, whilst still keeping true to the sci-fi aspects of MGS that it's known for, with more advanced technology being seen as prototypes, etc. I absolutely love and eat up the aesthetic of this game, and with some mods it can make the kind of goofy uniforms of the Diamond Dogs seem genuinely legit, and I feel like this game could've excelled in showing off a more caggy, yet still conforming to the sci-fi feel of MGS without any detraction from it. Personal preference aside, the building of the PMC and it's growth is far more organic and convincing than it was in Peace Walker, and is a significant improvement from it in every single way, from the narrative to the characters and their build-ups, everything. Even your soldiers have some secrets they talk about whilst on the platforms, there isn't a single other game that displays such a unique competency in making a military leader setting genuinely feel real.

The story of this game is a point of controversy and it requires a detailed look to fully grasp it, although it's not roll-slop levels of garbage, where the story doesn't exist, and is told through """""environmental storytelling""""". The story can easily be grasped in a single play-through without any sort of guidance or pointers in regards to the direction of the story, and since it starts relatively early in the timeline, some prior knowledge may not even be necessary to start playing the game to be invested. The game still leaves secrets and unanswered questions, whether that's on purpose, or because the story was rushed because of tension between the lead developer and Konami, I couldn't answer it better than anyone else could. Ultimately it is my favourite, even if it is a point of contention. Everything surrounding the story displays it in such a fashion where, despite it's flaws, like not using real-world names for weaponry and locations as MGS was known for, which detracts a good amount from the immersion, still somehow speaks to me the most. All personal of course, it's just the most memorable story to me by far, perhaps because of the controversies, conspiracy theories, or because of it being an enjoyable and amazing narrative idea.

The game, in general, excels in everything it does, and I have no complaints. The content of the game is plentiful, there is much to explore, unlock and experiment with, with tons of main story missions and an enormous amount of side content, MGSV on it's own is a game packed full of content. However, there are still some critiques of this game I must add:

Quiet. probably the worst MGS character ever conceived. Only exists for goonbait (along with the posters). Everything related to her in the story could've been sidestepped completely and told in a different way, or simply plays out and the game tries to tie relevance to her. When the story hits you with a 4D chess move, you answer back, and the game is already placing down a new chessboard to play on. Quiet is annoying to play with, annoying in the story, unnecessary and generally just garbage.

Fictionalised naming schemes, guns, vehicles, etc. Everything in the game represents a fictionalised equivalent of an already existing thing. For example the famous Stinger anti-air missile launcher is represented as the "Honey Bee" and bears a very odd resemblance to it. There aren't any Sikorsky H-60's, instead in their steed is the "UTH-66 Blackfoot", to name a few examples. Some of the guns also just look horrendous and ugly, like the """AK's""" that this game has.

Trash DLC + microtransactions, is this really still necessary?! For a full price game too, you might as well be offering an extra "rip off my customer" button below your game's purchasing options. The game has a very well designed online base-raiding / defending system in which you can buy extra platforms to get more resources. What do these extra platforms cost? "MB coins", which are basically the gem equivalent of any other mobile game. They offer you 2000 for ten euros, seriously, who is buying this? The outfit DLCs I can understand, maybe. But they are unnecessary, add them as rewards, not as stupid paid-for garbage.

The final con? Probably the last good MGS game that will exist.

Ah, man, this game slaps! One of the best open world stealth games I've played ever and one of the games I've connected with emotionally in a way I can't quite explain. People can ♥♥♥♥ on it and claim it was unneeded all they want, I'll always defend it (and yes, I have played the other games, this is one of, if not my all time favourite video game series). There are so many things about this game that I wanna talk about but I don't wanna spoil it for anybody (even though YouTube and Reddit are already doing a pretty good job of that), I'd recommend you play it for yourself instead.

The game is a brilliant subversion of everything from traditional game storytelling to what you think you know, and forces you to re-evaluate everything from what you are told to what you see and experience in the game. It is a master work in linguistic engineering, with language and interpretation being undoubtedly the major theme in the game. 

In the words of Neitzsche (in a quote flashed on screen right at the start of the game) "there are no such thing as facts, only interpretations." MGS V uses its very gameplay - the very act of you playing - to subvert its own narrative as well as the player's expectations of what an MGS game should be. 

It's a brilliant essay in hypertext. For example, race and white supremacy are arguably key themes in the game yet never talked about directly in the narrative, merely hinted at indirectly by what you see and experience in the Angola-Zaire border region. 
Further, early audio tapes from Miller hint at Diamond Dogs' involvement in real-world conflicts in Africa like the higly controversial Rhodesian Bush War in the 1970s, where mercernary groups, particularly American soldiers disillusioned with their own country's reaction to the Vietnam war, flocked to. All of this before Snake even wakes up after the events of Ground Zeroes.
If you think this is a stretch, consider that the basis for the Diamond Dogs logo is a Rhodesian Ridgeback dog. And I haven't even touched on Afghanistan and the Mujahideen - another proxy war in which the USA played and funded both sides at certain points. 
The game brings new light to, and asks new questions of, these conflict zones and the overall setting in which the game takes place.

I concede that sometimes the gameplay can become boring and repetitive - particularly in the late game - monotonous even. But that's a key aspect of the world post the global 'war on terror' that the game attempts to convey, and we will see fully realised years later in MGS 4 - a world where mercerneries fight in 'proxy wars without end' that blend into each other, without nations or creeds: A world where the very nature of war and conflict has been reduced to nothing more than a boring 'chore' that must be carried out in order to ensure the status quo is maintained. 

Over a decade later, I still find myself coming back to this game to try to glean more meaning, interpret more context, and find more hidden themes and references. It truly is a masterpiece.

Minor Spoilers included: 

Prior to anything, it's worth mentioning that my first, and likely last, playthrough of this game was done immediately after playing all prior main installments in the series. 

Had this game been called anything but Metal Gear Solid, I would have loved it. Unfortunately for it, having that IP attached to it makes it one of the most frustrating experiences I've ever had in my life.

Overall, it's a good game, but its flaws ruin it completely for me. The story is lackluster to say the least. Most missions don't result in any progress story wise, or when the plot actually moves forward, it's via a radio call. On the few occasions you do get cinematics, its fine, but nothing in comparison to the rest of the series. Even worst is the fact that the game finishes it's main plot, but then continues with useless filler which doesn't do anything for the player, nor the game.

Venom snake is not likeable at all, mostly because he has no presence. It feels like he's a complete passenger of the story. He barely talks, or does anything, and has no personality to speak of, which contrasts massively with all previous MCs of the saga. Side characters are also quite boring, if not completely unlikeable. Huey sucks, and that's the point, but Kaz and Ocelot aren't doing much for me either. Specially in comparison to their other appearances. It's also an MGS game with no boss fights, which doesn't help at all. 

On the gameplay side, the game is quite decent. It shines when you're left to tackle an infiltration mission, but waiting times to develop equipment take too much out of the fun. It also lacks any big infiltration missions, and by the time you get a sniper with tranquilizing bullets, the game plays itself. The game only becomes fun after you mod it, and make it so that you can do all missions with no equipment.

But the biggest problem I have with this game is how completely unnecessary it feels. It only serves to add context to the early Metal Gear games, and nothing else, and It doesn't even do that properly. MGS 4, flawed as it might have been, provided closure to all plotlines. It gave a conclusion to one of the greatest videogame franchises of all time. That makes MGS V feel like that much more of a cash grab.

Had Kojima been able to finish this game, my feeling might've been different, but I can't wholeheartedly say that I like, nor enjoyed this game.

Still, if you've played all prior entries, I recommend you play this, specially if you are willing to mod it (It's quite easy to do so).

Edit: It's worth playing to see the end of the franchise with Kojima. I wouldn't reccomend it otherwise, as I found it quite disappointing. Not a bad game, just not what I wanted. 

Regarding the bosses: None of them require any thinking, nor are they interesting set pieces. The "attempts" are either too easy, such as the fight with quiet, which can be beat by dropping supplies on her head without leaving cover, or deeply boring, like the one with Sahelanthropus, which is just running around airdropping tanks until it's finished.

The game wants to punish you consistently for running around like a headless chicken relying on headshotting people with silenced pistols, it lets you do that, but the things you miss out on by killing every soldier you see far outweigh the convenience of making Snake be a ruthless killing machine. Kojima has stated that one of the main driving points of player freedom is that MGS will guide you towards playing non-lethal, but won't restrict you to only doing so. Violence is nearly always an option. It's refreshing, it adds character and healthy difficulty. I could praise this game endlessly for gameplay design alone, but under that, it's still a Metal Gear Solid game.

[h1]The Overarching Story[/h1]

 Metal Gear has always been borderline absurdist, enjoyably so, but teetering that line can easily drag the player out of immersion. This story is believable, with some caveats. Particular elements, namely the Eli arc start to cross the line unenjoyably. Easily forgivable, just noteworthy. The comments you will hear about the disjointed and rushed nature of the storyline have truth to them, but it's not nearly as heavy as you'd expect. A lot of it is purely derived from the push and pull of open world gameplay. There's a lot of sudden stops between missions, the motherbase, and the open world. If you were to only look at the story, ignoring the jolts, a very compelling and engaging story is there, I'll get into that shortly. This is probably the most grounded and least silly entry in the series, maybe not in story, but at least in presentation.

[h1]Snake 'n Friends[/h1]

[b]Punished "Venom" Snake.[/b] 
          Where to start.

 This version of snake is older, experienced, maybe cynical. He's tired, the commitment to his role is there only because he's stuck there, there is no real way out of his position. This approach to his personality directly results into this being one of the most human portrayals of Snake. The restrained compassion and humanity creates so much tension, half the time you'll be thinking "Oh my god please say something"
It's surprising how much attachment can be had to this version of Snake who almost acts like a proxy for the player. A main critisism of this game was that Snake didn't talk a lot, and that he wasn't voiced by Hayter. It's true, he doesn't talk a lot. The dialogue is restrained in a way that makes the moments where he does speak have so much weight, nearly always quotable, and offers a glimpse into the way he's perceiving the world. Those moments where he talks are without a doubt some of the best in the game. Sutherland does an amazing job portraying this hardened version of Big Boss. Ocelot's character is genuinely likable, he's smart and logical. Sometimes serving as a way to ground the events occuring. Miller is in my opinion, deeply unlikable. Not in an intrusive way, he's just very intense and hard headed. It serves the story well. Quiet's story arc was surprisingly interesting and nuanced, her appearance really does harm the weight of it though. Oh Kojima... All things considered, i really enjoyed her story, and really the stories of the entire supporting cast. HEAVY SPOILERS: [spoiler]It's a real shame that the Snake you play as isn't really Snake. The reminder of it is almost painful, thinking that this story, this character progression, does not carry over to the Snake you play as in Snake Eater and Peacewalker. It's easy to let that fact suck you out of the story.[/spoiler] The post quarantine arc is almost taxing to play through, ending with one of the most heartfelt speeches you'll hear in gaming. Bonus points for the demon symbolism, but I wont spoil that.

 It's saddening that this was the farewell installment of the series, with Kojima "leaving" to create his own studio. Does it wrap the series up well? It's arguable, it's a messy ending. I would've loved to be able to play as Venom Snake again. I think anyone could play the series as is and be happy with it. Saying goodbye to Snake really does hurt though. Nearly 40 years ago, almost double my age, we got to meet him. One of the true gaming icons. 

MGSV is without a doubt one of the best gaming experiences you can have, for fans of the series, or as newcomers.
