Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an excellent tactical stealth/shooter game. I think its one of the best out there due to its unique gameplay mechanics and setting. The cinematic sequences of the story follow Hideo Kojima's over-dramatic style of storytelling which further differentiates the game from others in the same genre. There are a lot of things to do in the open world, and the player is always encouraged to pursue different tactics when tackling objectives. In a gameplay aspect, MGSVTPP is amazing and offers hours of replayability. 

However, my biggest problem with this game is in its story. Unlike my previous experiences with MGS titles, I find it really hard to be engrossed in the story of MGSTPP. I find myself feeling indifferent towards characters in the game, not being able to take sides or favor certain characters because I find the game's overall narrative to be very detached with the player. This problem only worsens in Chapter 2 of the game, where missions from Chapter 1 are reused with no contribution to the story whatsoever and are made to be challenge missions instead. I found this really disappointing, and at some points in my playthrough I even thought of just dropping the game. Although, I understand why it turned out like this due to Kojima not being able to push through with his version of the game after parting with Konami.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is probably the best unfinished game I played. Although it sucks that it was never truly finished, I'll take what I can get. If you're fan of stealth shooters with high replayability, then purchasing this game would be a good idea. I must warn you that this game will disappoint you at times, especially with its story, but that does not hurt the fact that this game is still a great MGS experience.

I am just finding this absolutely impossible to get into, and I see roughly half my friends on steam are too. About 50% of people seem to drop this game before the first 10 hours, the rest playing 60 or more. To me, this game just feels like a massive identity crisis, asif Kojima wanted to hit all these different genres at the exact same time and ending up subpar at all of them. For example:

Foraging herbs and dealing with wildlife in the open world- the Far Cry series does it much better and it feels more organic (foraging for herbs.... for some niche medical item.. in a combat zone.. when you have a whole army at your disposal... really?!)

Army management and building a fighting force- Shadow of Mordor/Shadow of war does it infinitely better with much more interesting characterisation and more actual input from those on your side.

Stealthy/loud infiltration of enemy camps- the Sniper Elite series does it better with much more thought out maps and more interesting level design than just "desert town". The AI is also much more interesting and deep than is seen here.

For pure stealth the game feels too imprecise and not fleshed out enough- Styx being an example of a "pure" stealth game which stands head and shoulders above this. 

Sandbox-style item research and deployment to ♥♥♥♥ around with- Just Cause 3 does it better. A game actually built around the mechanic rather than having it jammed in.

Base building and management- the Xcom series does it better and makes it feel more intuitive than a load of different options, menus, buttons and other nonsense you have to dredge through.

I really wanted to enjoy this game but it just feels like a mess of interesting ideas jammed together into a mediocre product. Maybe if Konami gave Kojima more time and funding the game would feel better. Who knows.

This is a difficult game for me to assess. I am a HUUUGE MGS fan. Grew up with the games and love them dearly. I really wanted to love this game as well. However there are a few things that really make it hard for me to recommend it. The core game play is REALLY GOOD. It's SUPER FUN to sneak around, try different methods, have companions, etc, etc. However the level design is incredibly boring. Don't get me wrong, what's there is decent and even good but there's no variety what so ever. The missions quickly become the same thing over and over again. And there are A LOT OF THEM. The story has great potential and awesome stuff there but it's all over the place and poorly written with a very strange pace. Especially after Act 1. 
So, let's talk about Act 2... 

The game is clearly unfinished and this is when you really notice it! Was it really necessary to add repeated missions? Were the side ops not enough? Cut-scenes start showing up randomly after any unrelated side op mission and most of the new missions are the ones you already completed but in hard mode. Sometimes the enemies are extra hard, sometimes you can't be seen at all or it'll game over, but they are the same exact missions! There are a couple new ones but most of them are just repeats. Hell, the last 4 missions aren't even new! Yes, the real last mission is the 4th to last! Why even bother? The core story is actually really good!!! With pretty good twists, all metal gear style! That's what's so frustrating about all this. The game had everything to be easily the best in the series!

And now let's talk about Quiet....

Minor spoiler ahead (I wouldn't care as it's not important at all for the story but oh well, you've been warned).

Quiet is one of the things that tipped me over the most. There is NO EXCUSE to have the only female character be basically naked all the time purely for the pleasure of 10 year olds. Because seriously, there is no other reason for this decision. And I refuse to believe a grown man finds this funny/entertaining (I know a lot do)... It's embarrassing really. Are the devs and for that matter, Kojima, 10 year olds? That's seriously disappointing. Like seriously, it's the most immature crap I've seen. The given "reason" for it makes no sense and has no bearing on the story. It's absolutely ridiculous in this day and age. And the saddest part is that the character itself could have been an incredibly interesting and awesome strong female personality that is much needed in the video game industry.

I finished the game. In fact, I have 100+ hours in it. There were still many things I liked but my feelings are incredibly mixed and I feel, as a fan, I can not recommend this game. It saddens me to say that, but at the end of the day it was a big disappointment on many levels. If you're not a fan of the series definitely don't touch it. If you are, well... It is what it is but I understand you want to play it. Go for it I suppose.

Ground Zeros was meant to be the way to introduce this game and it was an utter trainwreck. Bad controls, terrible console port and awful mission design. The only interesting part of of course was the lore it provided. When I started to play the main game I was baffled how differently it plays.

As for the main game, it really started of better, it was promising, it feels like it were so close to be one of the best games ever, but sadly it failed to deliver fully and what was good got tainted by design as the game gets worse as you progress. And I'm not talking about the typical console port weaknesses even tho this game isn't free from them, nor the fact that story is full of holes because appearently you don't get the full story without knowing all Metal Gear games. I'm talking about the promised 'ultimate freedom', where the game punishes you (including buffing and giving "cheats" to the AI enemy) and withhold rewards, if you don't play the way the devs intends you to play. I'm talking about the often nonesense events as the game takes control over you way too often in important story moments, to force the player into stupid decisions and situation during missions which could've been avoided by applying common sense, all that to fit the narrative of the game and the narrative of all the other Metal Gear game as well. These are really what mostly turns this game from enjoyable into a sour experience as you progress, but there are other gameplay things as well.

Some missions are great but some are just as rage inducingly terrible as Ground Zeros, which can really poison some meant to be important or even emotional story moments (I'm looking at you 'A Quiet End'). The techtree is really extensive, but as I said, the freedom is really just an illusion in this game, so you'll most likely not gonna utilize 90% of that stuff. The basebuilding seems cool at first, until you realized it's pretty much based on the F2P empire building browser games of that era, which are very time consuming and nobody enjoys playing them really mostly because it comes with tedious grind for resources and waiting for timers to tick down. Not to mention that after a certain base  expansion it comes with unavoidable PvP participation which is just incredibly dumb.

The game bleeds from thousand wounds and often gave of the vibes as they just ran out of ideas at the end, almost became a masterpiece, but so many element was just put together wrong, and regardless of it's good qualities, it has left a bad aftertaste. I fathom most of the very positive review comes from the people's love for the series, but objectively it's far from deserving such a high praise. It could've been much better. It's a shame, really.

This is an unfinished masterpiece. Kojima's vision for this game was grand, maybe even unrealistic, yet they managed to actually implement a huge amount of their ideas into the game. The attention to detail is astounding and I am pretty sure you could do things you haven't done before even if you played this for 300+ hours.

Quick rundown of the game concept:

You have an open world, from which you can access main and side quests. There is not too much to be explored in the map itself, but the game play is so well done that you will not get bored. You also have a base with different departments that you can improve by extracting soldiers from the map and making them part of your team. These soldiers all have different abilities and you will need to find the right soldiers for the right department. E.g. if you want a better R&D team, then you will have to extract soldiers that have a good ability in R&D. The better your team is, the more things you unlock. And there are a LOT of things to unlock in this game.

I could go on for a long while about what exactly you can do in this game, but that would fill an actual entire book. The most important part is that this game was conceived with a very clear vision in mind and it was crafted incredibly well by an obviously very talented and passionate team. 

Sadly, Konami cut the funding for the game before it could be finished because they got tired of Kojima wanting to make revisions and additions to the game. As you probably know, they also fired him after this project, so this is the last work of Kojima under Konami.  The fact that the game is not finished is really showing in the last 30 % of the game.

Anyway, this game is incredibly well done and a whole lot of fun. You should buy it. Now.

I am 27.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

This is one of the best, semi open world games, I've ever played. Honestly, as unfinished, not [b] rushed [/b] this game is. They definitely prioritized gameplay over story, and I am somewhat grateful. To cut it short, you can do so many things, until you get bored.

2. You capture knocked out/Stuned soldiers, depending on their skills, can unlock your cool weapons and stuff, and the more soldiers with higher skills, the higher the level of your Mother Base and its departments. (You also earn Karma points if you knock soldiers out instead of killing)
3. When you want to complete all missions task, you can also find yourself completing said the mission in a multitude of ways. Most of the missions are not linear, necessarily. But they can be completed in a multitude of ways.

I will say this. Why did Konami scrap the Fox Engine? Instead of selling it? I mean they aren't even using it, they just abandoned it. Scrapped it all together.  It is a really good engine, which houses photo-realistic environments and maps. The Afghanistan one. Is just fantastic. It feels and is beautifully crafted. It's extremely immersive. I swear it never gets old for me. Think about it, your a badass soldier, a phantom, and the fact the Russians refer to you as the "Dushman" gives this world a sense of lore, a sense of realism. because on the battlefield, stories emerge. Stories, turn to myths, and myths turn into legends. But regardless, imagine how terrifying it would be if a mythical figure snatches your allies/comrades one by one, and you cannot do anything about it. Think about that,  

But yeah, the story is just a tacted-on thing. I wish Konami gave Kojima more creative freedom instead of breathing down his neck. But do I recommend this game? Absolutely.

Depending on the kind of games you like, MGSV may have near infinite replayability. Unlike previous MGS games playing it like a pure action game and killing everything that moves is a viable strategy, but also like previous MGS games it's far from the most interesting or rewarding way to play. If you enjoy stealth games you'll want to ignore the letter grading system in the main missions and instead focus on the hidden NO TRACES bonus you get for completing a mission with perfect stealth, no kills, and no trace you were ever even there. You can't throw an empty mag as a distraction, knock an enemy unconscious and dunk him in a dumpster, or even put out a trash fire with the water pistol for a little extra cover of darkness. Playing for the NO TRACES bonus really makes the enemy AI, level design, and silky smooth controls shine.

However, if you fall into the trap of letting D-Dog or Quiet mark all the enemies for you and systematically tranq and recover everything systematically the fun emergent gameplay turns into an unfun systematic slog, so either go for no traces or go Rambo because the middleground option is rather bland. Disabling reflex mode is also an absolute must, if you're taking an approach that involves shooting at things it basically drops the difficulty to zero. The great thing about MGSV is that if you disagree with what I consider the fun way to play it and think that reflex mode headshots make you feel like the ultimate badass, you can really play in the style of the 80's action hero of your choosing and have a great time doing it.

If you're a long time MGS fan the story adds some fun and interesting context the previous games, but the overall plot kind of blows and doesn't matter overall to the series chronology. There are some interesting themes brought up, but they're so barely there that they merely present the veneer of meaning. But that doesn't really distract from some of the most fun stealth action ever created. Also Quiet is stupid. I have absolutely no issue with sexy ladies in video games, but the justification for her running around Afghanistan in her underwear is so stupid that I would have preferred no justification at all. Not to mention that they bring up a character from a previous game that had a similar condition but wore a full body ghillie suit. I get it, Kojima likes sexy laides with damage, and his excuses for the T and A in his games is about as good as Quentin Tarantino's reasons for close ups of Uma Thurman's feet. But if you're the kind of person who thinks pointless sexiness adds to a game's overall value then bonus for you because you won't have to alt-tab out for a mid game wank.

[h1] You're either going to love it or hate it [/h1]

70 hours spent in-game. At the moment of writing this review I'm half way through the story. 
Metal gear V is a weird game. It surely captivates old fans of the series, while bringing some innovative elements that you might either love or absolutely dislike with all your heart. This is not to say the game is bad, far from it: even calling it "Joe's Stealthy Adventures: the chick with no voice and huge boobs V" and not Metal gear, this is a quality product, masterfully crafted that will give you hours of fun. 
There are however some aspects of it that made me dubious at best.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

- [u] Graphics [/u] : at 2k Ultra settings with a 144hz monitor the game looks STUNNING. No other way around it. 
- [u] Audio [/u] : some of the best 80s hits paired with some really good orchestral pieces. 
- [u] The FREEDOM [/u] : MGSV takes the path of the "Open World", which is both a good and bad thing. The good part is surely the freedom you are given, every single situation can be approached in several different ways to achieve results. 
Let's say you have to infiltrate an enemy outpost. Do you want to go busting out big guns and shoot every single guard around? Do you want to stealthily infiltrate? Wanna use decoys and trick the enemies? Wanna hop on a single pilot mecha and wipe out everything? Wanna FALCON PUUUUNCH your way with your prosthetic arm fired like a rocket? All of these are viable options, and I could go on for an hour. 
- [u] The Online component [/u] : I haven't tried yet the actual multiplayer (deathmatch etc to understand each other) but I did try the FOB infiltration mission. To put it simple, these are side mission available after proceeding enough through the story. 
No worries, NO SPOILER for now! 
This is how they play out: you infiltrate the Mother base of another player to steal resources/soldiers. While this sounds easy, as the AI is decent but far from perfect, the difficulty rapidly increases with each infiltration: enemies start to wear heavy armor, drones start to pop around, mines, and all sort of devices to stop you. Soon enough it becomes much, much more difficult than the base game. And keep in mind the other player is alerted of your infiltration and CAN DEFEND IT actively or take revenge in a second moment nullifying all your efforts. 

[h1] The bad, or rather, the boring. [/h1]

- [u] Repetitiveness [/u] : I mentioned before having an open world game is both a good and a bad thing. The bad thing is that basically every side mission (side ops, they are called in game) and also some main story mission tend to repeat themselves. A. Lot. 
There is a decent variety of side ops, but these start to repeat themselves quite quickly. I don't even remember how many times I went to point A to kidnap a guard to add to Mother base, sometimes even to the exact same enemy base. 
There is literally a side-op that consists of [spoiler] recruiting a certain gunsmith, who turns out to be just an apprentice of the REAL gunsmith. This unlock the next side-op, that asks you to.. kidnap another lad... who again turns out to be an apprentice. This unlocks the next side-op, that asks you to... kidnap another lad. No, I did not accidentally write it twice. This repeats a few times til you reach the last step of kidnapping yet another guy who finally turns out to be the real deal [/spoiler] . This could have been such an interesting quest instead you are basically doing the same thing over and over, and it's not the only side op that plays like this. 

Thing is, every game that has to prolong its life has to somehow achieve one objective: make the player do the same task, while tricking him into not noticing that he is doing the same task over and over again. There are plenty of examples of this, but MGSV in my humble opinion, does not a great job at it. 

- [u] Repetitiveness, part 2 [/u] : dedicating this to Mission stories, this is going to be somewhat of a spoiler but I promise to keep any detail regarding the events completely out. [spoiler]After about 30 something story missions, the game ends its first chapter (it sort of plays out as in a movie, with each story mission having intro text presenting characters as actors, a nice touch indeed). Then, after the aforementioned 30 something missions you unlock a bunch of new story missions and A LOT more of the same, initial 30 missions who give you NO extra lore, and are literally THE SAME MISSION played on harder difficulty. [/spoiler] This literally feels, for me, like they ran out of ideas/budget and they said "you know what, let's just repeat the same ♥♥♥♥ again". I am a big Kojima fan, but this is just.. disappointing. 
- [u] Goodbye Codec conversations [/u] : this is kind of a let down for me, I am used to basically every Metal gear having Codec conversations, but they are just not present in this game. Hell, even Metal gear rising had memorable codec conversations, in this game they are just not present. I suspect they knew about it and tried to "fix it" by adding cassette tapes you can listen to, for extra info about story/lore. But they are in no way comparable and it boils down to you just listening one character brief you about one topic. I know this is HIGHLY subjective so I advise to take this part of the review with a pinch of salt, it might not be an issue at all for you but for me, it kind of is. No more epic Tank Made of Poo codec call, no more "Uhhh Snake, why the hell are you in a box...?", no more 5 mins call about ethical AI development, or movie recommendation from the 60s. 

Even after this I definitely, definitely recommend this game. There is an uniqueness that makes it so different from any other Metal Gear game that you don't really want to miss out.

I was very hyped about MGS V since the very first announcement trailer. However, I've finally completed MGS 4 before MGS V was released, and found its story and mechanics somewhat meh. So wheh reviews mentioned weak story and lack of cutscenes, I was not enthusiastic, and was hesitant to buy. However, I kept in on my wishlist still. 5 years later, in the depths of the 3rd lockdown, and amid the winter sale, I decided to give it a go - and never regretted that. My impressions from various aspects of the game are below:

[h1] 1) Gameplay [/h1]

This should be the main reason for anyone to buy this game. In my opinion, any advances in PC/console hardware can only be justified by new gameplay, unachievable before because of technological limits. MGSV's flexibilty and multiple interlocking systems are a good example of that. In most missions, you are given main objectives, and some directions as the mission progresses, but how you achieve those are up to you. Both in main story missions and side quests, this, and wide variety of tools available to you gives an ample space to improvisation and trying and testing the laws of the game world.  Although you are nudged towards stealth pacifist approach by design, nothing forbids you from recreating Rambo III scenes here (well, apart from the lack of bow:(  
There is also a simplified base-management level, which some people complain about, but I find it ok. The fact that most tasks (eg sending troops on missions, expanding the base, researching new weapons) progress only in-game, and in real time, was baffling. But I got used to it, and servers the concept of parallel rewards, as every 5 minutes a task is completed and you get something nice. 
There is some farming/grinding, inevitably, but mostly is not required for story progression - I did most of it to explore the world/get resources to unlock weapons I wanted faster. However, in the latter part of the game, missions lack variety, and if  you want to go for 100%, you'll have to revisit same locations multiple times, doing basically the same actions.

[h1] 2) Story[/h1] 
The second pillar of MGS series in general. To me, it seemed ok (worse than MGS 1/3, better than 2/4), even the final twist, and there definitely were cool custscenes along the way. It also touches on themes rarely approached in mainstream, triple-A games (eg survival of smaller languages). However, to those unfamiliar with MGS lore it may seem overtly complicated, and wacky at times.
My 3 main concerns around it are: i) slow pace - at least 1/3 of main story missions could have been moved to side missions, as they add little to main story. This is even more evident in chapter 2, as after the main baddy has been dealt with, there is little to drive the plot forward; 2) some mismatch between what the story teased in trailers, and what was actually delivered. Trailers heavily implied that this will be the story of Snake's descent into madness, following his quest for revenge (all Moby ♥♥♥♥ references pointed that way too). But although he does some terrible things along the way, he does them out of necessity, and overall is shown as a noble soldier, caring for his men, and having a moral compass. So the phrase "Kaz, I'm already a demon" rings hollow to me even at the end of the story. Same about 2 main antagonists - their intense hatred towards Snake is given little credible explanation; 3) one of the main subplots remains unresolved in chapter 2. It is unclear whether it was left for a DLC, or sequel, of the team just were forced to cut it (as the press reports suggest). Also, chapter 2 feels more like a 10-hour epilogue to the main story, finishing subplots for most  characters introduced in chapter 1, rather than a continuation of the story. The mission leading to the true ending just appears in the mission list, without little explanation as to how events lead to it.

[h1] 3) Graphics [/h1] 

I would say the graphics are standard for PS4  / XB1 era games, in terms of technical quality. But level design, and attention to details are amazing. Night showers in Africa, and night alerts in Afghanistan, with flares descending slowly, look very pleasant.

[h1] 4) Sound & Music [/h1] 
High quality voice acting, satisfying sound effects, good original and licensed soundtracks. Note that a significant portion of the story is delivered in audio, via tapes you receive after missions. These are much like voice diaries in Bioshock and other games, but some are quite long (10+mins), and resemble actual radio plays (you'll hear more than just people speaking)

[h1] 5) Technical performance [/h1] 

Overall ok - I played at max graphics on 2016 gaming laptop (i7, 960M, 8gb), and FPS mostly stayed in 30-40 range. It dropped to 10s-20s in one mission, and in some custcenes, but that was not a big deal . There were no glitches/bugs that I can remember, apart from 1 time where it failed to transition between the missions - I just restarted the game and it was ok then.

[h1]  Conclusion [/h1]

-) How you're taught some things but not others. First of all I realize there's "Tips" describing just about everything in the game. But that little timeline you use to scroll through what's probably several hundred of them is ridiculous. They really couldn't have made a better menu for that?

-) Teaching about enemy encounters, as well. Glaring example: tanks.
In mission 8 they expect you to destroy a moving convoy of 3 vehicles, including 2 tanks... 
while at this point you've probably never fired a rocket launcher before (maybe the Honeybee despite how they told you not to)
and have no idea how durable tanks are, to boot. So yeah, great experience trying to set up an ambush without any prior knowledge. Watching all dumbfounded as your first 2 rockets/explosives can't even destroy 1 of them so they're just gonna pass and probably spot you.
Stuff like this could so easily be resolved by forcing a fight with a single tank that's not trying to outrun you, first.

-) Mission ratings on your first playthrough. Where you get to review:
. How many times you were spotted because of things you feel like you had no chance to predict

Having played every other title in the Metal Gear Solid franchise, it's safe to say that you're not missing a whole lot from this one from the story perspective. It feels like a lazy sequel-prequel in a fashion similar to the "first" three episodes of Star Wars - except it doesn't feel that it goes anywhere. It feels self-contained in the sense that if you had played prior titles, there's nothing that feels groundbreaking or revealing to later sequels. 

My main frustrations stem from a lack of early stealth options or upgrades from the early game. You are given a lot of lethal weapons to work with while decent non-lethal options are hidden behind grindy resource gathering mechanics. Grab a person. Interrogate. Reveal items. Gather people. It just felt that I constantly had to extract people in the same way everytime in large environments that felt recycled. The vastness of desert plains littered with small shanty cities feel underwhelming more than atmospheric. At best, it feels like a game that should have came out 2 years after MGS4 instead of 7 as more of a guided experience as opposed to an open-world environment that begins to feel too similar after a few missions.

If you're coming in hot right after MGS4, I say go for it. New to the series? Despite being among the few places to start chronologically, you'll appreciate the simplicity of the game's controls after its story rich older predecessors. If you're just reading reviews to validate your own positive opinion of the game, then I'm sorry. It's less of the same due to a lackluster story and fantastic stealth weapons being locked away to boring grindy missions.

OVERALL REVIEW: 8/10

Gameplay 10/10
-Pretty much top tier, with very few weak links. You just need to want to go out and try new things, since it's very easy to go through this game with just a tranq pistol/sniper and do every mission the same way. The replayability of the game is about as high as it gets, with a load of weapons, ranks, and side objectives in every mission.

Visuals 7/10
-Very solid, still holds up very well 5 and a half years later, plus now the game is pretty easy to run on high/ultra. Unfortunately the setting for half the game, Afghanistan, doesn't have much to offer, it's just brown and sand. The second area, Africa is better with a good mix of red and green though.

Audio 8/10
-Sounds are all meaty and intense, exactly how they should be. Plus you can easily add your own music in game, but even so there is an ok selection already in the game.

Difficulty 7/10
-Getting through the game isn't too hard, a mixture of the buddies being a little OP and a very generous reflex mode. But to pull off a perfect mission is quite the challenge and very fun one. 

Story 7/10
-Even though this is a metal gear game, it feels like it lost a bit of its special touch. The codec is gone, replaced with a basic radio, I suppose to try and make the game more of a "game with a movie" rather than a "game in the movie". Still it was part of the charm of the games and I think MGS3* did the balance best. The cutscenes are beautiful with almost everyone of them being a single long take, and they absolutely capture your attention. However only about 25-30% of the story are in those cutscenes, with the majority of the story taking place in cassette tapes given to you throughout the game. In theory this means you can listen to them anytime, either at Mother Base, in the ACC, or while deployed in a mission or side ops. But in practicality, it's hard to understand them while playing, and it's hard to play while listening to them, so while I don't mind them, I think it could've been handled better. Overall the story is interesting, but it could've been handled better.

*I've played MGS 1, 2, and 3, but I have not played 4 or Peace Walker

The Rest
-It's a game everyone can play, the story is, as I've said above, very much optional, and the gameplay is enough for everyone to pick up the game once.
-I have a RX580 and a R5 2600, and this game runs on high never dropping below 60 (which the game is capped at), so it's not that much of a demanding game.
-At 20 dollars, you can easily get 50+ hours of solid gameplay, which I would say is definitely worth the price. When it's on sale for 5 dollars, it's definitely a steal, though you may want to get the definitive edition so you can get Ground Zeroes as well.
-I've had pretty much no bugs throughout my playthrough, it's a non-issue

Rating: 9/10 
Genre: Open World Stealth

THE GOOD: 
+ The fox engine is incredibly optimized. Even my 8 year old computer can play this at 1080p 60fps with medium to high settings with little trouble. Everything runs smoothly, and the game provides a lot of graphical options. The game itself look gorgeous, the environments, the landscapes, and scenery feels alive and the load times are fast. 

+ Given the variety of options and weapons, the game has very responsive and tight controls. You always feel in control of any situation. 

+ The amount of content is staggering. With over 45 main missions each one giving you a rank based on your performance, optional tasks, over 150 side missions, and online raiding other peoples bases there is no shortage of activities. Many side missions are repetitive, extract enemy soldier, kill armored units etc. but they all feel satisfying to complete. 

+ Weather plays an important role in stealth. Night time makes it more difficult for enemies to see you, sandstorms make visibility impossible for everyone but also provides a good opportunity for stealthy excursions, rain makes it harder for enemies to hear you etc. 

+ The game tries to have some semblance of realism; In order to go on missions, you have to outfit your gear, the better the gear the more expensive it will cost per deployment, you have to call a chopper to extract you from the field, you have to visit your home base regularly to boost staff morale etc. Little details like this helps to separate this game from most other open world games.  

+ You get a companion whenever you go on a mission. You start off with a horse but also get other companions as you play. Each companion provides different support and you can choose who you want depending on the mission. The more you use a companion the greater trust you earn and unlock more skills for them to use. For example, earning the trust of your horse allows you to make it poop on command slowing down vehicles. You just don’t find that level of quality in other games 😊 

+ There is a staggering number of weapons and items for you to try out. There is no shortage of ways to tackle any situation, and experimenting with different load outs is fun.  In addition, each weapon and item have an insane number of upgrades. 

+ Keeping enemies alive and extracting them to your home base is how you increase your overall stats and allows you to unlock new equipment and gear in addition to providing better support and intel on the field. I thought it was a genius mechanic, other games reward experience from killing enemies where as this game, the game incentivizes keeping enemies alive. Although you can manually assign captured enemies to different positions, I found it much easier to let the game automatically assign positions based on rank level.  

+ Half way through the game you are given the ability to invade other peoples home bases, to get resources and money. Although not required, it does make things easier and does provide a nice change from playing the game every once in awhile.  

The Average:
+/- The story is typical Hideo Kojima fare. Over the top characters, super human abilities, and crazy plots, villains go on long monologues about their motives. The execution and production values are insane, the voice acting sells the story and does a great job of holding the entire game together. There is a fine balance between realism and absurdity and this definitely veers into the more absurd aspects. You can listen to cassette tapes to listen to more of the backstory and motives of each character.  

+/- The enemy AI can be a bit hit or miss. Sometimes they will spot you a mile away and other times they will stare right at you when you are 10 feet away.  


The Bad:
- The amount of money and resources to upgrade your base and equipment is arbitrarily very high. In addition, there is a timer to how fast resources can get processed, a timer for how long to upgrade certain equipment. These are arbitrary restrictions for no other reason so that it takes longer to play, and to incentivize playing online where you can grind out getting money and resources. Its not necessarily a bad mechanic, its just not properly balanced. 

- Certain in-game mechanics are not explained very well. If I didn’t check online, I would have never known there is a fast travel option, or that I have to manually customize my helicopter after upgrading certain components to reap the benefits as well as some other aspects. I would recommend reading a beginner’s guide after playing for a few hours. 

Conclusion:
I love how this game has so many different gameplay systems/mechanics and how they all fit so perfectly together. The game has such a positive gameplay feedback loop that you constantly want to keep going back into the field to extract better soldiers, or replay the main mission to get a better score etc. Its always interesting to go online and see how other people completed missions and all the different ways it can be done.

It's strange, but a good kind of strange. The kind of strange that makes you wonder what could possibly happen next. It's a game that plays like a movie...that plays like a game, if that makes sense. But, that's just how Kojima does it; he did want to be a movie director, after all.

There is so many, perhaps too many things I want to talk about how messy Phantom Pain is, but I will just focus on the main disdain points I had with it.

Skull Face, such super cool voice he has, such intimidating he looks, such dangerous the way he schemes things, even has the background considering him to be the Shadow versus the Light of Big Boss Snake, all of these should make him an epic antagonist, perhaps might surpass Ocelot too, right? RIGHT? [spoiler]only then to be shot a like dog on the street[/spoiler]. I admitted every encounter with him is freaking chilling and hype, only to be let down with plot armor “I am the boss, can easily finish you, but I’ll just let the other cool guys do it instead so that you can escape and we will have the next conversation similar to this… or till I got PK by another. Too late Snake!”

Okay the main antagonist is wasted, who else can I chat to? Miller? Nope, only mission briefing. Ocelot? Nope, only boring and repetitive codec talk. Quiet? Feel free to watch her booty while showering but that is all, [spoiler]and her department is total unnecessary and pointless[/spoiler]. Huey? That is the last person you would ever want to face. Aside from the cool cutscenes randomly appear you won’t get to talk to anyone or anymore. 

To summarize, MGSV:PP has the weakest plot in the entire series.

Okay what about the classic codec talk? We should get insight on the locations, events, side quirky stuffs to aid the missions, right? “A Soviet soldier... A lot of them came from Central Asia before, but lately they've been using more and more Russians.”. Then [spoiler] A Soviet soldier... A lot of them came from Central Asia before, but lately they've been using more and more Russians[/spoiler]. Sure there are lot of tapes, but it’s just hearing, not active talking about something, with genuine reactions. And I doubt Kojima hired Kiefer just to say a few lines and a few grunts.

Now to the missions and stealth gameplay, the stealth play is superb, smooth, flexible, allows for variety of playstyle, the mission area designs are open enough for multiple entries and covers, yet the mission variety is lacking – ranging from capture/rescue prisoners, neutralize/eliminate/destroy certain targets, retrieve intel and equipment. There are side-tasks for you to revisit, though just extend on the previous or escape via certain ways, nevertheless, you must do them all anyway if wanted to see the true ending, plus it is the only good way to increase funds. But if you are not satisfied enough with those tasks, here is another 150+ side-ops doing the same thing over and over again – capture/rescue heavy armored/”highly-skilled” soldiers/prisoners, eliminate tanks and troops, and the f*** helicopter requiring you to go loud always without alternative silent method, two new minor tasks which are disarming mines and capture wandering soldiers. Devs tried to be clever by turning some side-ops into main ones, but the surprise wouldn’t last long. In the end, as the game is extremely incomplete, they forced you to REPLAY the past missions, but with higher difficulties, and slap the title chapter 2. From there on the cutscenes, the plot went out of order making it a mess to comprehend what just happened, and how.

Talking boss fights, remember how unique the fight was each time you face the Fear, the Fury, Ocelot, Volgin and more in MGS3? Or the sleek Vamp, Fatman, pure swordfight with Solidus and even a freaking fighting Jet in MGS2? Let see what we got in MGSV:PP – yes there is jet fight which is a cutscene only, one sniper fight with Quiet, two encounters with the Skulls (one is totally optional), another one with but armored this time, then another sniper fight with 4 skull girls, and lastly metal gear Sahelanthropus. Thus 5 boss fights in total, and 3 of them are just facing Skulls. And what is the general experience of fighting these Skulls you ask? Shoot and run nonstop! Shoot as you want to deplete their HPs as fast as possible, run as they can just teleport jump around your location with precise, leaving much less room to even think of a proper strategy. Indeed, you can stealthily snipe the Skull snipers, but it is about sitting in one place, using thermal and binocular to pinpoint their locations, then shoot one of them, wait till they recover and relocate their positions, repeat. Because it is way riskier trying to sneak around from cover to cover, as they just automatically pinpoint you regardless of slow crawling, camouflage costume matching the environment you are in, and at foggy night! 

The whole base building is pointless and empty. Getting all 7 departments upgraded to the fullest (and costing real-life time) only to realize they are just giant structures of nothing, as there are no facilities you can enter/interact with, you can’t find core characters like Ocelot, Miller to chat, or even DD to pet him more properly while he was young. Yes there are a few things to collect, but just suitcases containing emblem and some diamonds. There is target practice minigame, but it gets boring too quick. And traversing between bases is long, tedious both by air and by land, it is better to use box teleportation. 

Nevertheless, if you want to get better gears and gadgets, you must upgrade and scout higher rank staffs, and this severely affects your variety of playstyle said above, mainly you must stick with non-lethal all the time, fulton-ing a lot and a lot of soldiers whether you like it or not. Therefore, almost every mission turns into neutralize everything in the first half just so you can up your base decently. Ironically, the amount of non-lethal tools and gears is too limited, yet the amount of AK, M4A1, heavy machine guns is too many, yet you won’t be using them anyway because of high deployment cost. There do be one mission helps you to grind S rank soldiers, but you will need certain tools to make it efficient and quick everytime -> grind to get them first. Still, the game loves to point middle finger towards your capturing efforts, by having scenario that gets many of your high rank staffs killed… TWICE! BECAUSE F*CK YOU CAPTURE THEM AGAIN!.

By this point, you already got so tired of the game, the playtime is already too bloated, just want to 100% and quit forever, don’t even have any mood left in trying out different things, unless you are so obsessed with it. And no, I don’t want to do anything related to MGO.

I was initially turned off of this game (*GASP*) because the stealth felt unintuitive compared to the games I was used to (namely dishonored) and the fact that I seemed to mess up an ungodly amount early game without an especially tough difficulty or modifiers. I immediately assumed this must be some kind of insider thing for die-hard stealth fans and Kojima worshipers and that a simple FPS (Doom not COD) normie like me would never be privy to it's mighty secrets. 

Later down the line when I learned to be more OK with failure in videogames (and life in general lmao but that doesn't belong in this review) I came back to give it a try since I was feeling a little burnt out on the games I normally play and remembered how I hadn't even come close to finishing this one. I won't say I had a godly shift in perspective, but I can now confidently say that everyone can enjoy this game, and perhaps should if they have the means. 

It wasn't smooth sailing getting started for me, given that most of my experiences are with shooters (and among all of them that could be counted as stealth, pretty much only dishonored could be considered a proper stealth game). Laying aside that ever present attachment to perfect success was how I learned to start enjoying the game, experimenting, and keeping the tape rolling even if something did go wrong. The resultant experience was much more engaging, and IMO is the way the game should be played.

Note that I still have not finished the game, and I still think that gameplay alone it's already paid it's dues.

Story wise, you kind of have to learn to shut up and enjoy the ride. Nothing makes any kind of real sense, even with significant MGS lore backing you up, and Kojima has this crippling habit of both overexplaining and underexplaining which leaves the player even more perplexed. For example, the game will horribly underexplain why we should even care about half the things that happen or go on in it, but will horribly overexplain ridiculously basic stuff (like that one tape of Huey basically spelling out the ABC's of cloning like one would to a middle schooler). It might just be 'lost-in-translation' or alternatively just due to a Japanese style of narration/storytelling which just doesn't appeal to me.

Atmosphere is another story though. Through gameplay, cutscenes, travel, everything is this brilliant sense of atmosphere which builds the tension and meaning of the 'scene' we play/interact in. And the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes range from normal to surprisingly smooth and seamless.  Honestly I think it carries the lackluster story VERY hard, and makes literal frothing-at-the-mouth gibberish seem emotive and impactful. I suppose you could lump it into story because it's technically very related, but the Metro series has taught me that there is a tremendous difference between the atmosphere (which is more closely tied to the art and gameplay) and the story (a justification for the gameplay, and why it works the way it does, as well as being a sort of string to tie the experiences of the game into a recognizable whole).

So, as of now I have two ratings for this game. A rating for comparison with the masterpieces and greats of the gaming world, and a more general score comparing it with more general games.

General Score: 9.5/10
Reasoning: Delivers a very unique and worthwhile experience compared to most normal titles within and adjacent to it's genre.

Masterpiece Score: 7/10
Reasoning: Definitely has some good stuff, but on top of not being properly complete, it's story is an absolute mess. Basically five Michelin stars when taken in specific slices, but taken as a whole it's like an unceremonious buffet of mismatched delicacies; expensive, high quality, often tasty, but lacking all the things a coordinated meal gains from being that way.

I am 50.

That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

The stealth is jank, you're basically invisible if you're prone/crawling, but if you're crouching, you'll be spotted from considerable distance even in the dark.  Similarly, there's a mechanic regarding covered/uncovered vehicles, you'll be spotted at around 70m if you're driving an open-top truck, but if it has a roof, you can get closer.  This doesn't translate well to tanks, where you can post up at the gates of a guard post and gun down everyone there, but they'll have no idea where you are because you're not moving, unless one of them gets within 10m of you.
All friendly vehicles are basically paper mache despite the analogues used by enemies taking many, many explosives to take out.  This includes the support helicopter you can call in, which either kills foot-soldiers with modest efficiency, or gets shredded by anything more than small arms fire, or gets one-shot by a tank at its highest health upgrade because it hovers in place.
Despite trying to emphasize stealth, the story will drop head-on showdowns on you, which are a pain to get through if you brought a sneaky loadout, or worse, didn't R&D any significant firepower, in which case, you can expect to wait 18 minutes to an hour to be able to bring a weapon that makes the fight less hellish.

On mouse and keyboard, you'll face additional problems, like being unable to do light throws with grenades and similar items, you're meant to tap the attack button (LMB) for a straighter throw, and hold to throw with a higher arc, but the window for a "tap" must be less than a tenth of a second, and you'll always end up with the high arc.
You also can't crouch walk at a speed that will let you catch up to an unaware soldier without them hearing you on account of the binary nature of a keyboard.  You *can* hold a button to walk slower, but it's so excessively slow that it's impossible to reach someone who isn't standing still.  Others have said that you can tap the slow-walk button to stay under the noticeable noise level, but I was never able to get the timing/frequency of presses right to make that work.  These sneak-walking issues are removed by the sneaking suit outfit, since it makes your non-sprinting movement silent, but you have to get through a bit of the game for it, then pay to use it every time you deploy.

With few exceptions the side missions mostly consist of 7 or so tasks repeated 16-20 times each in different locations.

One redeeming, but unintended detail relevant in 2021 is that the indirect pvp of invading/defending player bases has gratuitous payout with next to no challenge or risk on account of online being a ghost town.  This allows you to skip a ton of grind and required waiting for money and resources.  I spent the last 60-70 hours of gameplay not giving a single thought to rare material cost to develop or go into the field with certain items, because I had Bezos money and more resources than I could exhaust if I *tried*.
My strategy for these was to use the heavy battle dress (more health) and either use an LMG and mow down the guards or to activate the night/thermal vision goggles, pop smoke grenades directly on guards and rush into the cloud to beat them down and repeat.  The 3-4 hours I spent invading bases (over-)funded the majority of the other 91 hours I won't get back from this.

Although the story is incomplete, Metal Gear Solid V manages to deliver one of the finest and most love towards the franchise. MGS V: TPP manages to deliver promised gameplay importing the same Mechanincs that are found in the "Tech Demo" MGS V: Ground Zeros. Unlike previous Entries, MGS V: TPP manages to offer players a more open gameplay design. Offering player countless of different ways to tackle on the Open World of MGS V. The amount of tools is simply huge, and a great balance of Non Lethal - Lethal Weapons. The base development mechanics, are complex at first however becomes ADDICTING to manage. The controls feel like its the best its ever been and the game manages to work flawlessly with PC's Mouse and Keyboard, however it is suggested to use a Controller since the game's manual and hints mainly revolve on using a Controller. Sound design is amazing, and guns sound ever so punchy and beefy. The gameplay finally allows for a Gunfight aproach where going loud is not a huge punishment unlike the older titles. The story however is missing the "Metal Gear" trademark  of using very flashy boss fights, and using a complex story line. I have previously completed Metal Gear Solid (1998) and Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater (2004), What we got is decent enough however comparing to previous games, the story is the most lacking along with Ground Zeroes. It also lacks the beloved CODEC calls. Since mostly all MGS games featured CODEC which is sad that it does not exist anymore. Snake feels like he is a bit quiet since in most cutscenes he barely talks, only giving out some dialogues comparing to his counterpart in MGS 3. A big highlight for me is the love for the PC optimization. The game works flawlessly with low end config PCs. I use an I5 8250u, 8gb ram, UHD 620 (Or simply a laptop), and at medium - low settings the game delivers outstanding performance if capped at 30 fps. For an intergrated GPU gamer this means alot, since having a consistant 30fps is a very hard task, and manages to stay consistant in Combat scenarios and Gunfights. 

The only downside is that driving is a little bit floaty, but that is my looking for the smallest of details. Story is unfinished due to production time given by Konami. The lack of Dialogue for Snake makes him a bit underwhelming, however it might symbolize a more Mature Snake. However this still is a bit of a sad pill to swallow for long time fans. 

Overall this game is an outstanding piece of work and a well deserved end for the Metal Gear timeline (Survive ur not part of this jack off). Kojima has done his absolute best in hard times with Konami, and if the budget and development time would be more friendly to Kojima, the game would have been a PERFECT stealth game. However even at this state the game manages to get a solid 9.5 in the end (Since the story can be more developed).

MGSV is a very strong game when it wants to be. I'm still in awe of the sheer amount of options, both lethal and non-lethal, that are available in this silly stealth game. Every time I return I find a new way to play. This is largely thanks to the many companions that Snake takes with him, each providing their own playstyle and set of upgrades to unlock. And even after the campaign is finished and the bonus missions are complete, there's an entire world of asynchronous online bases to infiltrate and explore. I haven't even mentioned how well the game plays in a vacuum— did you know that the controls for this game are intuitive [i]and[/i] as smooth as butter?

This comes at a bit of a cost, though. The game's narrative is engaging and cinematic, but it ends up being full of holes, particularly towards the end. Even at the best of times, the story goes out of its way to make sure that every female character is a sex object and every child is a throwaway plot device. In other words, this story has a lot to say, but it rarely manages to say it elegantly— and it's made entirely worse by the fact that the game is missing a huge chunk of both story and gameplay after corporate meddling.

12 hours in and I'm not wasting another second on MGSV. Every design decision seems to be intended to re-invent the wheel in the most over-complicated, nonsensical way possible. If the developer wasn't Japanese and the game didn't have Quiet in it, it would've been criticized as the frustrating mess that it is.

- A vast array of menus that should have been consolidated into 3 or 4 will cause you to waste valuable refund time as you scratch your head wondering what all of this stuff does and why the developers chose to implement half the game in a menu.

- Tons of unskippable in-game events. Devs thought it was a great idea to force you to watch a 60 second "playable cutscene" of Snake entering and existing a helicopter, among other inane things. But you're encouraged to skip actual cutscenes in order to get a better rank on missions! *facepalm*

- The game delivers instructions via audio only. If you play with sound off or turn your attention elsewhere, you can easily lose track of what the game expects you to do and have to restart. I found a way around this problem by pressing Alt+F4.

- There's a "staff management system", aka Pokemon mini-game, that doesn't matter, has a terrible UI, and caused me to waste precious refund time.

- The open world is not actually open. You are forced to traverse it without fast travel, and the vast majority of it is empty desert.

- There's no point in using stealth, unless you enjoy repeating areas dozens of times for the sole reason of learning enemy locations. Hiding to wait out alarms isn't an option unless you enjoy staring at the screen doing nothing. You either 100% an area, or wind up setting off alarms and resorting to gunning everything down. Which would be fine, except that soldiers respawn at most camps, which means you can't actually play the game running & gunning...

- Alarms prevent you from completing objectives, but only sometimes. The game doesn't feel a need to point this out.

- Your animations control the player, not your input. If you want to strafe right, the character will jankily turn Tomb Raider 1 style. If you are in the prone position, you need to maneuver as if you're using tank controls. This is a video game. I expect my input to take higher priority than my character's dumb "immersive" animations.

- There's a resource grind and a research tree the size of the moon. If you intend to suffer this game, do yourself the favor of downloading mods that remove costs and timers on research.

- Apparently, this game has an online component. I couldn't find a way to shut off online features reliably, so I resorted to blocking the game in my firewall.

No amount of "finishing touches" or attention to detail when porting to PC could fix this mess.

There is a lot of different weapons and items to develop, lethal and non-lethal whichever matches your play style best. You also get tactical buddies you can take with you to help you out on missions like D-Horse, D-Dog, D-Walker and Quiet, each with their own abilities and customisation.

Another thing worth mentioning. While undertaking missions or just free roaming, you can find cassette tapes of 1980's songs and listen to them on your walkman or develop a loudspeaker for your chopper to annoy your enemies with. Try it out if you haven't already, the game just hits different with Gloria or Rebel Yell playing in the background. Even better, put your own music in the game! It's hilarious calling in a chopper to attack an outpost with Caramelldansen being blasted from the distance.

About the multiplayer... Technically there is multiplayer. I'm not talking about Metal Gear Online, that's a separate game. I'm talking about the FOB missions in The Phantom Pain. In this mode you invade other player's bases and try to capture staff and resources from them or you defend your base from invaders. In my opinion it kind of sucks, it's not really as fun as it may sound. The only way you can play with your friend is when they support you and you get invaded at the same time you are both playing the game so that they can help defend it. That scenario is very unlikely to happen. Eventhough I don't really enjoy the mode that much, there is some unique story content to it that I like that I've never seen in any other game before. I won't spoil it too much but you must know this story content is basically impossible to trigger alone and is extremely rare to happen in game. [spoiler]Players will eventually get the option to develop a nuclear weapon. You will have to invade every nuclear equipped player on your region's server and dispose of their nuclear weapons. Once the amount of nukes reaches 0 a special cutscene will play for everyone as far as I understand how this works.[/spoiler]

With that said I wish that we got a proper co-op mode too. I'm sure many others feel the same. I know Snake is a master solo infiltrator, but he still has his buddies to help him like mentioned in the beginning of this review! Imagine you could invite a real person to your game using your buddy slot. Then they pick one of your available combat unit staff or maybe even Quiet, since you can already play as her in FOB. Heck there's even enough seats in the chopper, and what kills me is the multiplayer component is already there! I can literally see and interact with my friend in a FOB training session!! We just need a co-op mode!!! I know this is all easier said than done, but I can't help to look at it and think wasted potential.

Now let's talk about the story, don't worry I won't spoil anything. You've probably heard it before and yes it's true, there is a pretty big part of the story missing. The first chapter is really good and feels complete. I was sucked in and eager to reveal more of the story as I played. After finishing the first chapter I had this kind of melancholic feeling because I've gotten so much into the game and people said the story is not all there. Knowing that, I didn't know what to expect next and I tried keeping my expectation's low.

The second chapter doesn't nearly feel as high quality as the first one and it's probably because of the Kojima breakup with Konami that happened at the time of this game's release. The second chapter has very few new missions and this is also when missions form the previous chapter starts showing up with higher difficulty. With only six new missions and the rest repeats, it really feels rushed in the end.

The game was literally not finished. There was supposed to be a Mission 51 that never made it into the game and if you bought the collectors edition you got an extra disc with it that contains cutscenes explaining the missing story parts. This clearly shows that there were more plans for it. I can understand why it got people upset who didn't buy the collectors edition at the time of release, I think everyone at least deserved to see what we could've gotten as a last mission. Fortunately these clips can easily be found on the internet so don't worry and go look it up after finishing the game.

I'd like to add my view on the story cassette tapes you obtain while progressing. I heard people say that this was how Kojima decided to shorten the cutscenes for MGSV. I think the tapes are a great way to get more details of the story if you wish to know more. You can put them on and listen to them as you are doing missions or side-ops. To me they were a lot better than finding long written notes that require you to pause to read them like a lot of other games do. Maybe longer cutscenes would've been nice, but I do get it that some people find very long cutscenes frustrating and MGS is apparently known for it's lengthy cutscenes.

I have to say that I did enjoy the story. Some older hardcore fans may say otherwise but I think it was great. Especially that twist in the end. It stuck with me for couple of days. (You'll know what I'm talking about if you played it). Like I mentioned, some disliked it, but since this game is set in a time before the event's of some of the previous MGS games, it makes sense and I wouldn't have wanted a different ending. I just wish the last ending made it into the game.

Overall this gets a well deserved 9/10 for the flawed masterpiece it is. It's painful to imagine the game we could have gotten if the rest was included. Maybe one day Hideo Kojima gets the rights back to his creation and finishes the story he wanted to tell. We can only hope, but for now we are here just to suffer.

This is a good game, it's just not a good Metal Gear game. The open world mechanics are cool, the environments and vista's are really neat and the time and weather dynamic all make it feel more realistic. The 'menu' option of the iDroid where time doesn't stop and the fact that you have to swap weapons or call for support in real time also help to make it feel less 'videogamey' in a good way. The first half of the game is just very good in general.
The problems of the game arise with the story. Metal Gear games have always toed the line between ridiculous, super serious and ridiculously serious but this is the first game I've played in the series where the story falls flat. The start of the game is incredibly brutal and edgy, almost comically so. The villains Skullface, the parasite unit and the Burning man are nonsensical. The zombie plotline is stupid and an incredibly tired cliche and Eli, Code Talker and the African children are flat characters at best and excruciatingly annoying escorts and hindrances at worst, both in terms of story relevance and gameplay. The further you get into the game the game also gets more difficult, which isn't a bad thing at all. The problem is how the game gets more difficult, particularly with extreme mode and perfect stealth mode. In these missions enemies deal ridiculous amounts of damage or you are stripped from the Reflex ability. Either you can die in one hit to almost anything or lose a core game mechanic that has carried your sorry ass throughout the first half of the game. The game makes a habit of taking things away from you, and while this is thematically accurate to the story it's also infuriating. Why build up Mother Base when some story mechanic happens where half your men die offscreen if you don't manually quarantine 200+ people? Why build your bond with DDog or D Horse if the story keeps forcing you to take Quiet in important missions? Why try to play full stealth when story missions every now and then force you to have strong rocket launchers you may not have yet developed?
Mother Base itself is also a bit problematic. The idea of a homebase that keeps growing is really cool, but the area itself is incredibly boring. You only go there for cutscenes, to take a shower or do dumb training missions.

Overall, MGS 5 is a good game, but not a great game and not a good Metal Gear game. If you enjoy open world games with stealth mechanics you'll enjoy it a lot, but in the sea of open world games out there it doesn't stand out too much apart from it's title.

First, a disclaimer: this game's only noteworthy female character is named "Quiet," and her whole thing is that she's always comically close to nudity and she never speaks. She's as loyal to you as a stray dog you can pick up, but you earn her loyalty by kicking her ass in a fight and then ordering her around. (You earn the dog's loyalty by hanging out with him and petting him.) Unless you're willing to point-blank shoot an unconscious, mostly nude woman, she's going to be living in a cage in your sea-castle for the bulk of the game. There's so much to say about the way this game seems to see women... That's the dark side of having a franchise that feels like it's made by an incredibly talented team who are under the full control of a 14-year-old boy.

The juvenile and insulting way that the game tries to make sense of what, exactly, women are isn't far off from the rest of the series. Quiet is just another way that this franchise pays homage to its roots. If MGS had two pop culture parents, they would be 80s action films and James Bond. The dialogue is campy, mullets are somehow cool, everyone has eye patches, the bad guy is named "Skull Face," and death can (of course) be overcome by being a furious badass muscle dude.

You should also know that this game is obviously unfinished, story-wise. I guess there was a lot of drama involving Hideo Kojima at Konami during production, and that resulted in about a third of the planned story just... never getting made. And it looks like it never will be. It's a pretty dissatisfying end to the MGS series (but still not as bad as Mass Effect 3). It seems like a lot of people knew about this going in, but I didn't know about it until I finished a mission and the game was just suddenly... done. Since MGS5 is the last game in the series and it takes place in the middle of the franchise, I thought it would try to tie things together. It really (and I cannot stress this enough) did not. If you're the sort of person who is seriously bothered by that kind of thing, maybe keep that in mind.

That said, I am the type of person who is seriously bothered by that sort of thing, and I still really enjoyed this game. It's STUPID fun. I'd be a huge hypocrite not to recommend it. Even if the story left a lot to be desired, the stuff that did make it into the game was pretty damn enjoyable. If nothing else, it was amazing to finally see Ocelot in his natural element (which is almost-secretly in love, if you were wondering). I can't think of any other game where you can make friends by using a rocket fist to knock a bunch of dudes unconscious and then use a balloon to rip them violently into the sky. Ten minutes later, they're somehow ready to die for you. Where else can you live out that kind of experience? I give this game a 4/10. Highly recommend.

There's a lot to be said about this one, so I'll divide this review in topics, trying to be as brief as possible. 

MY PERSONAL HISTORY

This is the first "Metal Gear" game I play to completion. I played a bit of "MGS 2" when it came out, but had to stop when my father sold our PS2. Recently, because I wanted to know more about the lore while I was finishing this one, I watched playthroughs of the first 3 games. Now I intend to play other titles, besides replaying "Ground Zeroes". 

DURATION

It's huge: took me 170 hours to finish chapter 1, then a few dozen hours more to finish chapter 2 and I still have plenty of side ops to play, besides FOB missions. Since you can replay missions and side ops, there's actually no time limit for this one, so it's a guaranteed "bang for your buck". 

STORY

Even without the cut content from the endgame (damn you, Konami), this is maybe the best and certainly the most complex story I've experienced in a videogame. It baffles me that several other reviewers wrote that the story on this one is not very good _ either some of the other games are better (the first 3 are not, although "MGS" is pretty good) or these people didn't listen to the tapes. I also find it strange to see on YouTube videos that explain what happened, because everything is painstakingly explained in the cassettes, with no mysteries left behind. In a nutshell: [u]listen to the tapes[/u]; I did it over and over while I was traversing the maps (as a rule of thumb I never fast travel when playing a good open world game) and they're amazingly written and acted. You'll be missing out big time if you don't.

For fans of the previous games, it's great to see [spoiler]younger versions[/spoiler] of [spoiler]Liquid Snake[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Psycho Mantis[/spoiler]. Also, [spoiler]Otacon's father[/spoiler] is such a fascinating character! To me it seemed that this title really connected well with the others and the overall story arch of the series is nothing short of epic, with deep roots in History and Science. It's almost like a "great American novel" in videogame form.

GAMEPLAY

A great stealth game, specially in the beginning, when you don't have the best gear or the most advanced buddies: Quiet (for combat) and D-Dog (for infiltration). This is an example of a game that only gets easier as it progresses (except for some of the dreaded "boss fight missions", like [spoiler]the Skulls[/spoiler], [spoiler]Volgin[/spoiler], [spoiler]Sahelanthropus[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Quiet's rescue[/spoiler]). 

I had the most fun when I was simply clearing outposts by myself in Afghanistan, crawling on the ground and patiently waiting to choke and Fulton everyone without being seen. Ghosting in this game is amazing. 

Long range combat is surprisingly good, although I didn't use sniping much because it alerted enemies. Most of the time I only used nonlethal methods and on the first time (after dozens of hours) that I actually shot someone with a live round, the poor electronic soviet soldier went writhing on the ground, bleeding and begging me to not kill him. It really hit me in the feels. (It's amazing how pacifist the game is _ not a surprise coming from a country that used to be warmongering but suffered such a crushing defeat _; the enemies are always portrayed as complex human beings, as you can overhear them talking about their lives, like some soldier who lost a brother or another who can't wait to go home and see his daughter.)

The weakest part is the driving, but besides not being mandatory, it's not really advisable, since it will draw enemy attention. Just strolling through the map while listening to the tapes is the best way of transportation (you can also use the cardboard boxes to be sent to several points of the map, but I never did that _ or carried several other optional stuff, like dummies, mines, walker gears, shields, cigarettes, night vision goggles etc.; all you really need is the nonlethal pistol for when you are spotted and, on few occasions, some explosives).

There's so much more to be said (from having to extract interpreters to gain access to subtitles to the development of Mother Base, its army and all of the collectibles), but let's try to keep it short.

ONLINE

The proper Online section of the game, with PvP battle maps, is the least interesting portion. More alluring is the possibility of invading other players bases through FOB missions, stealing personel and resources _ you can make enemies and allies this way. 

PERFORMANCE

Very well optimized, with very fast loading times. Not the largest or the most beautiful open world game, but good enough.  

CONCLUSION

Really an excellent game, although not perfect. If you like stealth, look nowhere else. If you want an epic story, you got it. 

Also, Hideo Kojima's ego is obviously huge (but he can pull it off).
