I've suffered through a lot of games which felt like distractions rather than entertainment. I felt obligated to complete them, as if it were my job or some sort of meaningful accomplishment. MGS5 reminded me what it felt like to be genuinely excited to play a game. I was surprised that I enjoyed the gameplay so much, when Metal Gear games are usually more story driven.

Pros:
* Gameplay stands apart from most other games - stealth and even combat feels different in a good way
* Deep plot (though probably not the best in the series)
* Fox engine is great - I wish more games used it
* The game looks beautiful, and small features like water glistening on skin really make visuals stand out
* A ridiculous amount of features and tricks (the "horn" on your head grows if you kill a lot, enemies sleep at night, you can shoot out lights, you can add pictures to cardboard boxes to lure enemies etc.)
* Controls can be somewhat odd but strangely easy to get used to
* Works great with a controller
* The base building aspect really adds some variety and longevity to gameplay
* You can pause cutscenes
* A decent selection of "buddies", each having their own strengths
* Smart AI difficulty which adapts to the way you play
* The many upgrades to your base, weapons etc. will keep you busy
* Quiet is cool
* Lots of side missions and an online component which create a decent endgame
* Night and day, along with a weather system affects gameplay

Cons:
* Chapter 1 was great but Chapter 2 was a mess. It would have been better to include all critical story elements in Chapter 1 and wrap up the entire story
* Helicopter rides take way too long - you're often forced to sit through long chopper rides, or wait for supply drops etc.
* Too many minor features which probably took a lot of development time away from creating missions/ story (you could lean sideways on your horse to avoid enemy detection, you could climb cracks, you need to wash off blood to feel mentally and physically refreshed, morale system for soldiers in your base, the horse can poop and enemies will slip on it)
* Maxing out upgrades takes very long - you'll be way past the the end of the story before you start getting the best items in the game, and by then you won't really need them
* It takes too long to gather resources and earn in-game currency
* Weapons, supplies and even the helicopter all cost in-game currency. It doesn't usually make much sense to max out the items you carry. It also defeats the purpose of upgrading items, since they then cost more to equip
* Bad fast travel system
* Side ops are trickled in, stretching out the amount of time you'll take to complete them

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is not only the most "game-y" of the Metal Gear series, but it is actually so good that it outshines all the others in both good and bad.  For those new to the series, you'll DEFINITELY want to pick this one up first.  (I haven't played Ground Zeroes yet.)

First off, those lengthy cutscenes that get drawn out more and more for each main MG game actually serve a purpose as they make you feel like you're a fly on the wall and actually feel like you're there in all the gritty universe this game sets itself in. You're not just sitting back and watching 2 characters in action or talk or hearing long speeches.  In fact, the cutscenes are actually short, simple, and to the point with hardly any dialogue. And yes, you can skip them if you like (which will probably be necessary anyway if you want to replay certain missions).  All the expository dialogue is communicated via cassette tapes which are ENTIRELY optional if you so choose to listen to them.

Second, I haven't had this much fun infiltrating a base in years since the first MGS1 game.  You can do anything to your heart's content and ANYTHING can happen ANYTIME.  Want to go it alone?  You can?  Want to change the weather?  You can.  Want to go in guns blazing? You can!  It's all there and fun to enjoy.

But for every improvement this game has from its predecessors, there's always the bad, but I won't go in too much detail as it's basically been said before: cut and repetitive missions, voice actors not returning for their roles (except f**king Otacon, I always hated him in MGS!), wonky controls, etc. etc.  The only REAL issue I have is that you don't start any missions with a FULL CLIP of ammo.  Every gun you have has 1 bullet less of a full clip.  How the hell do you mess that one simple programming error!?

But other than that, this game is worth getting on sale for the Definitive Experience.  I managed to get it for only $9.98!  How can you beat that!?

This game is good, but there are some major inconveniences that keep it from being great. I'm probably in the minority here, but I actually think Ground Zeroes is the better game in the MGS V chronology. That's not to say this game is bad - it's not - this installment just tends to be much more frustrating than its predecessor. In terms of storytelling, this game is top-notch (of course it is, it's MGS after all), but there are a handful of things that bug me to no end:

First off, the easiest way to score an S rank on missions is to run in guns blazing and not worry about being spotted or shot at by enemies. Speed is the name of the game here, which is disappointing for a series that defines stealth gameplay. 

Second, the maps are too big for no good reason. If you were rewarded for exploration or if the enemy bases served a purpose other than farming resources, then the enormous size of the maps would be justified. As it stands however, the amount of time you spend travelling from point a to point b is tiresome. Overall, the worlds feel empty and the repopulating outposts are more of a nuisance than anything.

Lastly, some missions are frustrating to the point of wanting to rip your hair out...not because they demand a high level of skill and preparation, but because they seem to be up to luck more than anything. Every time you see the words Skulls, Mist, or Parasite in your mission intro, prepare to have a bad time. Combine that nuisance with the baffling decision to lock the true ending behind more difficult reskins of past missions, and you will start to resent the amount of time you've put into the game.

If you ignore the baffling insistence of going in guns blazing all the time, and you can be bothered to look up tips and tricks for completing the most obnoxious missions, then you'll be rewarded with a solid stealth shooter. Just don't expect it to stack up to the rest of the MGS catalog.

Five years ago, I decided this was my favourite stealth game ever. Today, it's still my favourite stealth game ever. After playing through Death Stranding again, I felt the urge to return to the game that introduced me to the epic mind of Hideo Kojima, for old time's sake. I want to talk about Metal Gear Solid V.

Games like MGSV are a rarity. It amazes me how even after all these years, very few video games have managed to truly recapture the scale, freedom, and AI intelligence of this espionage shooter. And what's really worth appreciating is how there is virtually no penalty for playing the game however you'd like. Even if you don't like stealth, that's fine. This game accomadates every playstyle through an astonishing degree of variety in level design, equipment, and mechanics. You can choose to go in quietly - assassinating every enemy in sight. Or, you could take them out nonlethally and recruit them to your cause (aka "fulton extraction" - best thing ever in video games). Maybe you're my brother and hate stealth, so you'd opt to ride on a bipedal machine of death, laying everything in your path to waste. This degree of open-endedness is undeniably the game's greatest strength, and contributes so much to its replayability.  

It's also worth mentioning how incredibly well the graphics have held up. I don't know if it's just me, but there was something so mesmerizing about the visual direction of games released in 2015 that makes them look so much better than some of today's triple A titles. Bloodborne and Witcher 3 are two great examples of this in addition to MGSV. In MGSV, It feels like you're playing a movie the entire time due to the game's photorealism and masterfully directed in-engine cutscenes. Each of these cutscenes transitions into gameplay and back in one fluid shot, which maintains a perpetually engaging experience for the player. The intro sequence has to be one of the most kickass openings I've ever seen in a video game, and most if not all of the other cinematic moments in this game are going to stick with you for a while. All of this was made possible with the fox engine, which was was truly ahead of its time. It's sad to see that it never ended up making any other quality games like this one. May it rest in peace. 

The only gripe I have with this otherwise perfect game is its story. It's not that the story is bad in MGSV. The problem with it is that it's incomplete. If I understand correctly, there was some turbulence between Konami and Kojima during their production of MGSV before he cut ties with the company. This prevented him from telling the complete story that he wanted to with the game, which is a damn shame when you consider what he is capable of making when he possesses full creative control over a project. Just look at any of his other games in the Metal Gear series, or even Death Stranding which came out more recently. Every single one of these games delivers a solid beginning, middle, and end, which leaves you craving more but having experienced enough. Here, in MGSV, you are left craving more without having experienced enough. The game builds up towards so many exciting plot points that would be a joy to experience with its beautiful engine, but ends short of letting you experience any of them, which is a bummer. It's clear that these teases were Kojima's way of letting us know that he wanted to do so much more with the story, but alas could not because of Konami's influence. However, he was still able to provide a compelling and memorable narrative, despite his limitations. You play as the iconic Big Boss, now damaged and reduced to the moniker "Punished Venom Snake." It's up to you to amass a team of familiar faces and loyal troops to get back at those who took everything from you - "All for revenge," as the slogan of the game goes. Despite the rather freestanding nature of this narrative, Kojima still managed to wrap up the MGS franchise in a meaningful way, expressing his heartfelt gratitude to his fans. This was the perfect send-off to the series, in my opinion, and I walked away feeling immensely satisfied with everything I had experienced.

All in all, MGSV is a hell of a game. Its variety, freedom, and replayability is staggering and makes for some of the most fun gameplay you will ever experience in an action-oriented video game. And the story, despite being incomplete, is still thoroughly enjoyable. Yes, it does suck that we didn't get the whole narrative package here, and it does hurt to imagine how much better this already amazing game could have been had Konami sympathized with Kojima's passion for video games as an art form. But at least when an auteur's abilities are hindered, you still end up with a solid fraction of their vision. And this fraction is well worth your money.

- They call for support.
- They will build a search party to look for you in the area you've last been seen.
- They'll fire with artillery at your last known position.
- They will call for support from the base or a neighbouring base.
- They can give up if they see they have no chance.
- They start fights with wild animals and animals can kill soldiers.

There are lots of things that made me laugh, for example the Wolf kills enemies with a Knife, that's almost as retarded as it is funny. Some of the tapes are really funny as well and there are lots of funny easter eggs.

Most people don't get the base and why it's there. I will explain it: If there was no base you would basically just kill everyone, but with the base you really want to get anything you can get, so every mission also becomes a heist for ressources and also a kidnapping mission to increase your base members. It's also relaxing to come back to the base and look at what you created, drive around do some target practise.
Same thing kinda goes for the zoo, the animal hunting was a nice addition and I really liked hunting for specific species sometimes.

I'm not sure what I can say about the story, it was a convoluted mess. I liked most cutscenes and there were some decent storybeats. The characters were pretty good for the most part. I don't really get why people would criticise Quiet for her outfit, my biggest issue is that she doesn't look fit enough for her physical abilites. I didn't really care for her at first, but my god is she cool. I also loved my horsey and doggo, both very usefull.

There is also an insane amout of stuff to unlock and I'm a sucker for that kind of stuff. And you can costumise so much stuff and up to the guns themselves and build whatever you need.

Turns out this is one of my top 10 favourite games, I was really surprised to find that out.

- Why can't I just bring the stuff back that I didn't use during the mission instead of paying for everything all the time?

2015 + 2016 was one of the best years of video games bar none. I've played games since games began and while I loved the 90's and noughties era, the people who state "games aren't what they use to be" don't know what they're talking about. They're just looking through rose tinted goggles. Whatever their reasons, they're always weak answers. Sure, graphics don't make a game, this is true but games today are more than just graphics. Depth? Modern games often have more depth. Size? Never been bigger. "Games today hand hold!" Sure SOME do, but there are PLENTY of harder games out there. "It was about the gameplay" Yeah, as they are today. Games today have progressed graphically, in size, mechanically, depth, writing, voice acting and story telling. If you want a platformer where your only ability is jump, you can still get them today. 

Unfortunately, 2015 & 2016 were so good, it feels like everything after has struggled to compete. Around this time, my cat was poorly and if anyone knows cats, they'll know they despise you playing on a PC, sitting on your keyboard and whatever else. Despite being a PC gamer (or computer gamer even since there was many before PC) I don't subscribe to the pathetic "PC master race!" card, I'm a gamer, I'm not going to limit myself, so while my cat was poorly, I bought myself a Ps4 (which, I loved so much I bought an xbox 6 months after...which gathered dust) so I could play in bed with my kitty. The Witcher 3, Arkham knight and of course, MGSV all came out and playing these on a huge TV relaxed in bed was incredible, and some of the best times I had in a SINGLE player experience for gaming. I put hundreds of hours in each of these titles and loved them so much that I bought them all again on my hefty gaming PC once my cat died. 

The problem is, these games were so good that I've felt nothing has really competed with them since. There's been some good games yes, but since this generation that has allowed developers to push the boundries in gaming, most of the large studios prefer to water down the games and give you less content, for more money, while throwing microtransactions at you. These games proved that modern games were better and now, it's like they don't want to continue creating such masterpieces, and it's sad, because gaming has always been a major hobby for me and I want this feeling back again. 

As for MGSV! Well, as I've stated, obviously I love it. It isn't perfect, none of the games I listed off were in fact. Like The Witcher 3, you won't know if this game is good or not if you've only played 4-5 hours. It's quite boring at the start even. I guess you shouldn't need to play a game for so long to work out if you like it or not, but it's because there's so much content in the game, you won't know what it's about until further in, despite the fact it throws everything at you including the kitchen sink. After every mission you're unlocking new gear, and there's so, so much of it, and for once, most is actually worth it, completely allowing you to customise the way you play. 

So you should ignore anyone who's played 3-4 hours and leaves a negative review because they haven't seen what the game is about. If they say they've played more on a different platform (like me) then ask yourself, if they thought it was a bad game, why did they buy it a second time around? Now, on the other end of the spectrum, there's people leaving negative reviews after 900 hours. What? What type of idiot plays something they dislike for 900 hours. 

Ultimately, the game isn't perfect, it clearly changes in the second half (which, you could still spend hundreds of hours before getting to if you desired) and it is completed per se, but you can tell there was issues and had content cut, which was a shame because it could have made this one of the best games ever made. It STILL is a contender though IMO.

The graphics are dated compared to today's top titles, but it still does look good, very good and runs perfectly. Sound is great, music is awesome. Story is brilliant...but kinda whacky, gun play and mechanics are superb, mechanically it is sound and it has a lot...and I mean a lot, of depth. For its price you really get your monies worth, and that's what counts right?

Also, I played MGS4 on Ps3 once, but I didn't care much for the older generation consoles (that era were pure console-esk games that had little of anything IMO, but I get that many have some beloved titles from that era) but I honestly don't remember much about it at all, so practically, I went into this game knowing nothing about Kojima or MGS franchise. So you don't need to know anything either. 

I'm also not a third person lover, nor am I a stealth game lover...but boy, do I love this.

Reviewing this game is difficult for many reasons but I will attempt to sum everything up in sections.

Gameplay: The way it feels and plays is bar none the best in the series. Lots of tools at your disposal. Infinite ways to take on a mission, super solid here.... for the first 10 hours. 
you see when it came to the other games in the series, notably the original PS2 trilogy, it had a foundation which the level design, the boss fights, and the enemies complimented amazingly. The games woud build upon themselves within their each respective entries. Everything had a purpose. Here, its not like that at all. While the level design is good, you would be better off playing a different open world game. Empty stretches of land bring it down hard. And within these small sandboxes you get with each mission, it quickly dawns on you how useless everything is. Take a tranq and shoot everyone. Its quick and easy. But here is where this game differs. It relies heavily on the player making their own fun. And unfortunately the game does not compliment this philosophy with the endless amounts of grinding needed to unlock the interesting gear and abilities. The first 5 or so hours is what this game should have been throughout. Instead it becomes a mindless chore by the end.

Online: Piss Poor. FOBs are busted with everyone using a set of strategies, terrible net code, and boring gameplay. MGO3 is a laughing stock compared to its predecessor MGO2, with its lack of content, lack of interesting and well thought out maps, terrible net code, horribly balanced classes, and countless other issues I could go in depth on. Which I will.. somewhat. 
FOBs are plagued with spammers and cheaters on PC especially. Combined with balancing being non existent, and net code being absolutely horrific, its no wonder this game never made it. MGO3 is an even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Balancing is non existent here as well. One class rules above all! Maps are horribly designed, open, does not compliment gameplay. What I will give them credit for is that these maps has some substance to them. Multi layered playgrounds is about all I can say about positives. This game needed to be supported. It should have. It could have been something more. But the rushed nature of it shows.

Story: Surprisingly, there is a lot to say here despite what others might think. The themes, subject matter, philosophies, ideas and experiments in place here are second to none. But, you can have all of these and still come out with a piss poor story. Its all about the execution, and this game would rather say these things are here rather than build on them. The themes of loss, identity, revenge, progression, and many more present here are not utilized efficiently. This game opens in what can be stated as the most memorable openings to a video game. This opening is far different than the rest of the game, being a horror filled escape through a hospital being destroyed and people being slaughtered before your eyes. The game is at its absolute highest here. After this sequence, you are left pondering the identity of the man by the name of "ishmael" or so this game wanted you to be. Its clear as day he shares the same VA as Big Boss does so unless you are not paying attention, you might believe he was a figment of your imagination or just the real Big Boss. From the first mission to Mission 31 is just repetitive missions with hardly any story progression. What we have here is a jumbled up story told through weeks and does not pick up unless you are invested in everything thats going on. Like the bodies in the oil mill, or the skulls that show up every now and then. If you want the full experience of the story prepare to listen to what amounts to a few hours worth of tapes explaining everything in boring exposition. But it is at least something and gives you insight in what the game wont show you or just gives you a glimpse of. To sum it up, you are on a revenge quest to find the person that blew your base to hell almost a decade ago, and by doing so lead to you being in a coma during this large gap. You leave the hospital broken, skinny, and a warped mind confused on why you feel the way you do about the situation presented. As you make your way through the desert, you encounter jobs and different people linked to this man named Skull Face. And in doing so leads you to Africa where he is supposedly. After a lot of time passes, saving a child soldier or two, building up your base and taking on contracts, you eventually catch up to Skull Face which can only be amounted to the second best part of the game. OKB Zero. This place is the only time where the gameplay is complemented by the well crafted level design and enemies which test your skills quite nicely. All of this just to lead up to Skull Face telling you his whole plan over a car ride... anyway. His Metal Gear which was designed by Huey, which we will get to him at his most relevance, goes wild due to a young Psycho Mantis controlling it. You fight off the Metal Gear and put an end to Skull Face, rendering this games main plot resolved. The second chapter is a jumbled dish which was undercooked and thrown together just to make the deadline for the customers. To best sum it up, it is a mash of all of the side plots concluding, being left unresolved, new plot threads coming in, some just to be resolved the moment they are introduced. The one thread to get a complete resolution outside of this games second main thread is the Parasites thread. It culminates in a platform being quarantined and you having to go in and slaughtering the people you once knew as fellow soldiers who would live and die by you. This sends Venom through a downward spiral. It turns out Huey caused all of this, and I mean literally caused this games main story to be set in stone. Killing his wife along the way, and intentionally starting a pandemic because... he's just that kind of guy. Despite this revelation, Venom is sent down a spiral concluding in this games ending, where it shouldnt have ended.... This games ending is just a cutscene explaining why you arent Big Boss, and why you are. Essentially talking to the player. It ends in a cliffhanger.

Overall: I cannot give it a rating. I will say I recommend it if its on sale for one go around. With every positive MGSV has, it is plagued by flaws.

Pase 5 años dudando de si comprarlo o no, luego de estar en oferta a solo 5 dólares decidí probarlo. Mi análisis se resume a esto: ¿Han visto a gente pasando el Dark Souls con una guitarra de Guitar Hero? Pues bien, el mal llamado capitulo dos básicamente te obliga a jugar con hándicaps similares a este. Para poder ver el resto de la historia o el resto de cinemas, tendrás que pasar ciertas misiones que poseen una dificultad bastante obscena, no señor, conozco mis límites de paciencia y este juego los sobrepasa con creces. La campaña del juego está incompleta y no recomiendo jugarlo ni comprarlo, se nota que no pudieron diseñar las últimas misiones y reciclaron misiones previas, pero con detalles hermosos como el no poder usar tu equipo, el equipo en el cual gastaste horas y de alguna manera definían tu estilo de juego; otras misiones se terminan si te descubren, cuando la filosofía era adáptate e improvisa; en resumidas cuentas misiones desafío que entierran los últimos detalles de una historia que tampoco está muy buena. 

Es triste, metal gear solid está grabado en las memorias de muchos jugadores y toda la novela que Hideo Kojima versus Konami nos dejó una última entrega con sabor amargo. Tenemos el mejor gameplay de la saga envuelto en polémica y con una historia sin terminar y los pocos detalles se ven enterrados por un último tramo que traiciona al jugador y lo que ha venido construyendo.

Cuando compre el juego sabía que esto iba a pasar, sabía que la decepción llegaría tarde o temprano, las reseñas de medios más independientes mostraban su desdén al tramo final, pero una vez llegas y lo vives en carne propia te frustra tanto que un gameplay tan sólido, con una historia que trata de compartir ideas interesantes, no sea bien acompañado por el diseño de misiones, el cual parece más una lista de desafíos, que en otros juegos serian opcionales. Metal Gear Solid 5 es un juego que seguirá dando de qué hablar entre sus fans, por un lado, tenemos un buen juego, mecánicas excelentes y un sistema de progresión que nos motiva para seguir avanzando y por el otro lado tenemos una historia errática que se diluye a medida progresamos en el juego y no termina de cerrar bien ni concretar sus ideas.

Me hubiese gustado un mejor final para la saga, porque si, el Metal Gear que nos fascino es parte de la historia y no volverá, hubiera preferido que esta entrega no existiera, que fuera otra franquicia, una nueva IP, pero las cosas son como son y mañana seguramente habrá otro juego en oferta y yo estaré contando las monedas de mi alcancía esperando poder comprarlo sin desajustar mis gastos mensuales.

Metal Gear Solid V is probably the best stealth game I've ever played. Unlike its predecessors, which were more linear and plot-heavy, this game continues the story of Big Boss as a direct sequel to Peace Walker both in terms of story and gameplay. The gameplay of Peace Walker has been refined to absolute perfection in MGS V and the missions take place in two massive open-world maps. The game gives you countless tools to complete missions in any way you choose, with the most rewarding and fun approach being a fully stealthy one. Getting to a high ground, marking out enemy units with your binoculars, and carefully planning and executing missions with the numerous tactical options available is extremely satisfying. You can even bring certain buddies with you, such as a doggo that can sniff out enemies and even stun or kill them. And yes, you can pet him too. The base management system from Peace Walker returns, and you can even visit your base, which you couldn't do in PW. The story is decent, although it does have some dips in quality towards the end thanks to Konami not letting Kojima finish the storyline. This is probably the last game in the legendary Metal Gear franchise, and while Konami could continue to milk it, it wouldn't be a true Metal Gear game without Hideo Kojima's touch. If there's one thing I dislike about this game, it's the replacement of David Hayter with Kiefer Sutherland as Snake's voice actor. Other than that, the game is packed with content and is an absolute joy to play. It's a must-play for any fan of the stealth genre. a must play.

Despite this, the game's fun lies in its impressively enjoyable gameplay, which gives a reason and justification for every little mechanic. Even seeming incomplete, it's a wonderful experience.

So this will be one of the longer reviews i wrote. Here it comes!
Although i never played any of the Metal Gear games before this one, this one really hooked me even though people say it is the second worst in the franchise. Here are some of my thoughts:

[h1] The good [/h1]
You are the best soldier that ever lived, The Big Boss [spoiler] not really him, but his body double who shares his memories somehow, and you know everything he ever did [/spoiler]. 
The buddy system is pretty good in my opinion, and going on missions with each of them D-dog, D-horse and Quiet is a pretty good idea of "bonding with them".
The story is good, but you can see that it is really rushed and it is not finished. I mean there are a lot of plot holes. But never the less the story is one of a kind. We kinda see Venom Snake descend into darkness more and more.
The fulton extraction is also really good touch. You can extract anything from the battlefield, be it a sheep, a donkey, a bird, a material container, a tank, a soldier, you name it.
The weapon arsenal and weapon customization is really huge. Also you get to customize almost everything, from your base color, to your helicopter equipment, to modifying your weapon.
The game also has a lot of ways of playing, you can sneak your way without killing anyone or you can go full Rambo and wreck havoc. 
I would also like to say that the feeling of having your own base and your own private army is pretty good.
Also the optimization of this game is needless to say, out of this world.

[h1] The bad [/h1]
I honestly have no clue, but i feel that the game is not finished. I really wanted to see Venom Snake take down Cypher (I dont know if he takes them down at all). The death of Skull Face was not enough for me.
It feels repetetive after 30-40 hours (kill heavy infantry, rescue prisoner, gain intel...)
MB coins, really lame way for more FOB's. 
The grind, grind, grind.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Although the game has flaws i think that it is really good and engaging game. It has a lot of replayability. All in all i would give it 8/10. Would recommend buying it on sale though, and Definitive Edition (You get both Ground Zeroes and Phantom Pain plus every DLC).

I wanted to like it. I really did. I love stealth games, the graphics look gorgeous, the cast has some top-tier voice actors, I've heard great things about the MGS series, and Kojima is a legendary developer whose name is often used as an example of an innovative force in the modern AAA industry. So I had pretty high expectations from this.

But... I didn't like it. The stealth was very janky, with Snake sometimes not going in to cover when he should, enemies spotting you when there really is no reason they would, and then just walking slowly over to you like morons so you can kill them quietly even if you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and got spotted.
The inability to tie knocked out enemies up, means that they're gonna wake up eventually and there's nothing you can do about it (we have insane gadgets like a detachable rocket-arm and some kind of super-balloon that abducts people, but we can't get some rope?), so if you want to do a no-kills no-alarms run, you have to be really fast - which is pretty hard to do on a first playthrough when you don't know the map layout and what you need to do. This means having to replay missions to actually do them well, which is a little too much to ask from a game that started feeling repetitive after less than 10 hours of gameplay, where I only beat a tiny fraction of the game.

The story is... nonsensical. B-movie spy stuff with very weird names, a quirky sense of humor, and some pretty cool supernatural stuff thrown in. There are some pretty good cinematic set-pieces that are really quite fun and exciting, at least in the first few hours of the game. It's generally pretty cool, even if it does make little to no sense and feels like it was written by a 10-year-old with a very wild imagination, but it wasn't enough to grip me. Mostly because the characters are pretty boring (that may be because I don't know them from the previous installments). Every single one of them is just a gruff badass tough guy. That's all there is. I know there is a girl named Quiet that shows up eventually (didn't get to that part) but I assume she's just some gruff badass tough girl. There was nothing that made me connect with any of them, and if I don't feel anything for the characters then a "cool setting" alone is not enough to keep me interested.
I was actually pretty into the supernatural stuff, but there was this very weird dissonance between how you're supposedly playing a super-stealthy espionage game, until a supernatural thing happens and then it goes full-on over-the-top action-adventure-shooter. The two aspects didn't seem to flow naturally from and into each other, but rather the genre just switched at random. At times I didn't know if I'm supposed to try and sneak or just shoot and run for it, until I was killed and realized sneaking is not possible in this section.

But janky gameplay and boring characters are not usually enough to put me off. There was still enough good stuff in there, and I was definitely planning to push forward and finish it in spite of all the problems.
So what killed it for me?
The base building. What an absolutely pointless, useless, terrible mechanic to have in a game like this. You have to recruit people, assign them to teams based on their skills, build platforms for the teams to use and slowly expand your base. You literally have to manage hundreds of people and lots of different resource types. This is done through large, overly-complicated, information-filled menus. Every time I had to do something regarding base building, I lost some of my will to keep playing. And every time a new tutorial popped up, adding YET ANOTHER LAYER to the convoluted mess that is base building, I wanted to just quit and go play something else.
Until, eventually, I did.
I wish the base building was an optional thing, with a button for "do this automatically" that just lets me be a badass spy and not a logistics officer, but it's not. You have to do it, or you're not gonna get upgrades, and you need those upgrades if you want to do well.

Oh well. I guess Kojima's games really aren't for everyone

Maybe I went into this with the wrong expectations, especially not having played any of the previous installments. I expected a fun stealth game with a reasonably serious story; what I got was as abstruse as it gets, mixing attempts at conveying a half-interesting story with supernatural garbage.

I could overlook this if the gameplay was great; alas, this is a mediocre console port in that regard, which doesn't even manage to show keyboard bindings half the time (probably making me miss out on a bunch of helpful maneuvers and movement techniques). Even the in-game controls overview shows a controller, making absolutely no sense.

There are some interesting gameplay elements, but overall, the controls are too poor for most of them to be enjoyable. There's a half-baked cover system, making Snake duck behind cover when running into it, but this often doesn't work and is very finicky. Many actions also require either pressing a button or holding it, which makes performing the action you want to do when multiple are available needlessly annoying (probably a leftover from the console version). In stressful situations, I often wanted to quickly perform an action, only for it not to work because I wasn't standing perfectly still and perpendicular to the object.

There's also a whole base-building component tacked on that doesn't add anything worthwhile to the game; yet, without spending time managing staff and resources, you won't have access to most gadgets and weaponry, making it essentially mandatory. This is worsened by the game's very busy and convoluted menu system.

On the plus side, the graphics are decent and the game is well-optimized, running very smoothly. The score is also pretty good, not to mention the great selection of licensed songs.

To conclude, you'll probably only enjoy this if you've played the previous games and know what's going on and are either playing with a controller or very frustration-resistant.

[i]This game is a masterpiece, yet it didn't even reach its full potential.[/i]

[h1]The Negatives[/h1]
• The story feels cut short.
• Act 2 is padded out with mission replays.
• The numerous Side-Ops can grow repetitive.
• Sometimes Snake slips on rocky terrain.
• Draw distance could be better, especially when using the binoculars.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]
• The Phantom Pain is an amazingly open-ended experience with incredibly polished gameplay, everything feels smooth and fluid. 
• The missions mostly allow you to approach them from any angle offering terrific tactical stealth opportunities while also providing the tools for a less covert approach. 
• There are plenty of interesting items to develop and deploy with, some are useful and some are just for fun. Developing more equipment is also useful to upgrade your favourite guns with other components which is pretty neat.
• The game offers a selection of buddies to accompany you. Unlike many games they are more than just AI Companions that only get in the way, once your bond is fairly high buddies can provide essential help to Snake during missions.
• The map is varied with compounds, ruined structures, deserts & jungles. While it isn't ground breaking I definitely enjoyed exploring it's areas across missions.
• I enjoyed the story & I enjoyed uncovering the "Truth". I found most of the key characters interesting & unique and felt the primary story was fairly self-contained without requiring prior knowledge of the series to enjoy & understand on a basic level. 
• Mother Base is a perfect meta-game, encouraging collecting resources to expand it and extracting soldiers to build up your army. The management aspect of Mother Base is fairly light and not too involved but it offers a constant incentive when out on the field to capture soldiers instead of just carelessly eliminating them.  
• The game has a lot of charm and Kojima’s unique style really shines. I enjoyed watching most of the cutscenes as well as discovering details in other areas of the game such as the Fast Travel system, uses for the Tape Player & Cardboard Box on the field & visiting D-Dog on Mother Base. 

[h1]Bonus[/h1]
If you finish the game and find yourself interested in the story you can find on YouTube “Metal Gear Solid V: Episode 51”. This 19 minute video is from the Special Collector’s Edition of the game and details the concept behind the ultimately cut 3rd Act of the game.

The more I play this game the more I see the flaws in it. This game has truly awful mission design. It's a game that emphasizes stealth but almost all of the missions take place in large, open environments that don't offer enough routes to approach and neutralize enemies. Most of the time you're going to find yourself abusing magazines or decoys to position enemies how you want, or proning and trying to flank around them right in the open. Enemies can spot you from absurd distances and even when you're concealed by cover or foliage. This adds up to a game that can feel very unfulfilling. When you successfully complete a mission without detection it feels more like luck than skill. The cardboard box, a mainstay in the series, is almost always a worse option than going prone. That isn't to say there aren't some really cool stealth mechanics in this game. I love having the ability to roll, love the decoys, grenades, C4, and awesome variety of weapons. This game could be the ultimate stealth game if the gameplay didn't feel so inconsistent.

I still think the game is worth playing for the story and presentation alone, but man, this game really infuriates me. I've also played Ground Zeroes and that "game" (more of a demo) actually plays way better than The Phantom Pain. The map in that game is actually well-designed and gives you plenty of ways to approach and neutralize guards and complete objectives in a stealthy manner. 90% of The Phantom Pain on the other hand feels like they just made an open world without giving much thought to stealth and then set you loose in it. Sure, you can pull off some really cool stealth moments, but as mentioned earlier, pulling them off feels like it involves more luck than skill.

One other annoying thing, if you're playing with mouse and keyboard controls (which you should, they're far better than a controller) you're basically forced to use the sneaking suit because your default movement speed just walking forward pressing W is loud enough to alert guards. You can't effectively use anything but the sneaking suit which is a pretty huge design flaw IMO. If you use a controller you have analog control over your movement speed but unfortunately the controller controls suck.

From the serfs of the Middle Ages sprang the chartered burghers of the earliest towns. From these burgesses the first elements of the bourgeoisie were developed. The discovery of America, the rounding of the Cape, opened up fresh ground for the rising bourgeoisie. The East-Indian and Chinese markets, the colonisation of America, trade with the colonies, the increase in the means of exchange and in commodities generally, gave to commerce, to navigation, to industry, an impulse never before known, and thereby, to the revolutionary element in the tottering feudal society, a rapid development. The feudal system of industry, in which industrial production was monopolised by closed guilds, now no longer sufficed for the growing wants of the new markets. The manufacturing system took its place. The guild-masters were pushed on one side by the manufacturing middle class; division of labour between the different corporate guilds vanished in the face of division of labour in each single workshop. Meantime the markets kept ever growing, the demand ever rising. Even manufacturer no longer sufficed. Thereupon, steam and machinery revolutionised industrial production. The place of manufacture was taken by the giant, Modern Industry; the place of the industrial middle class by industrial millionaires, the leaders of the whole industrial armies, the modern bourgeois. Modern industry has established the world market, for which the discovery of America paved the way. This market has given an immense development to commerce, to navigation, to communication by land. This development has, in its turn, reacted on the extension of industry; and in proportion as industry, commerce, navigation, railways extended, in the same proportion the bourgeoisie developed, increased its capital, and pushed into the background every class handed down from the Middle Ages.

[h1]A gem crushed by grinding[/h1]

As I start to write down the review for this game, I get a bittersweet feeling. Sweet because it is very difficult to express how precise and refined this game is. Bitter because it is very easy to say that this game has one of the poorest grinding systems I have ever seen.

Let us start with the undisputed good points about this game. For example, the gameplay. It is just so good and so satisfying. I love stealth games, especially when the stealth component is fair and realistic, and this game manages to deliver a very rich formulae to approach the different missions making you feel like the ultimate snake. A lot of gadgets, options and a lot of combinations can make every single mission of this game different from the others: go to one mission with your tranquilizer sniper rifle, do another with your rocket arm, what about a personal challenge to only subdue the enemies in hand to hand combat…? There is a huge array of options for you to take down every mission, and it will only feel repetitive if you always rely on the same equipment over and over again (being honest, like every other game, right?). Apart from the gameplay, everything concerning technical aspects of the game, like graphics or BSO and sound is very good too (specially some of the original tracks included as part of the BSO). About the story, I am not a MGS fan, but I will say that it was at least good (you may not understand a lot of things going on, but MGS is a not a cult franchise or something like that, it is as easy as going to Google to search information about moments or things you don’t understand, if you are too eager to wait to the game to unfold itself). 

And, up to this point, I believe you will say, is this game perfect? Sadly, it is not. Because everything I stated above gets ruined by the worst grinding I have ever seen… To not enter into too much detail, the game has a lot of missions. Good, right? Well, not that good when you have to do hundreds of the same missions all over again. The maps of this game are beautiful, and big, but not big enough to carry on the good feeling over all that repetitive missions, where you will have to take the same posts over and over again…it is very sad, but if they created this game with a goal of around 50 hours of gameplay for the completionists players, with meaningful missions that are not copy pastes one of another, this game could have been way better. But no, they decided that it was better to say: [i]Hey, let us plague this game with four types of missions, the only difference being the number of enemies in each one…they will love it...![/i] …ok, I did not.

To conclude, if you like stealth games and you find this game cheap, go for it. If not, this may not be the game for you because even for someone like me (who likes grinding when it makes sense) this game was so tedious from the second half to the ending (ending, let’s say, that I had to watch on YouTube because there was a point when I was not willing to put a ton of hours of just doing the same stuff all over again).

Let me preface this review by stating that I have never played a Metal Gear Solid game or even a Kojima game before.

MGSV is an incredible disappointment - not because this game is terrible, but because it is on the verge of greatness. The core gameplay loop of MGSV is excellent: You drop in from the helicopter for a mission, scout out an enemy base and then take the base either through stealth or by going loud or a combination of the two. The gunplay is excellent, and the stealth mechanics are great. It comes together really well and provides a very good experience. One big disappointment is that there are only two zones (Afghanistan and Angola) for you to play in. MGSV would have benefited greatly from adding another 1-2 zones in other environments and in particular if it included any indoor segment (the entire game takes place outside).

As a result of the excellent gameplay, I find it incredibly frustrating that [b] MGSV forces you to spend so much time not actually playing the game. [/b] From forcing in an unnecessary base development and gear research mechanic, to excessively long cutscenes that don't say anything of any importance, MGSV seems like it really wants to waste your time. This is very apparent upon getting started on the campaign. It took me over two hours to get through this first mission and during this time I estimate I was playing the game for about 5 minutes. I'd also like to mention that that MGSV puts you into a character creator during this sequence - but you don't get to use your painstakingly created character at all. This character design is only for online play and MGSV in no way makes this clear (or the fact that you can change this design later at any time).

At times due to being forced into doing base management and gear development MGSV can feel like a menu simulator. I spend so much time trawling through menus to find what I needed. This is exacerbated by loading screens between menus. This bleeds over into the gameplay - if you want to call a supply drop for more ammo, you need to go into a menu. If you want to order your sniper companion around, you need to go into a menu. If you want to call the helicopter to end the mission, you need to go into a menu.

Another complaint on my long list is that MGSV never seems to shut up and let you play it. It constantly bombards you with an absurd amount of dialog, almost all of which really didn’t even need to be said. Every single time I run into a sniper I get a radio call to tell me what a sniper is. Every time I run into an enemy helicopter, I get a warning about an enemy gunship and what they are. It was of no surprise to me that when the pandemic happens, that MGSV feels the need to explain to you exactly what a pandemic is, what quarantine is, and what we can do about it. 

As far as the story goes, MGSV is a completely incoherent mess. Nothing really makes sense, unless if you spend hours trawling fandoms/wiki to explain things and even then, the plot still doesn't make sense. I’m not going to go into detail here, but to me the plot was unsatisfying and clearly incomplete.

After mission 31 missions just start repeating without any explanation of why. The reason behind this is that MGSV is not a finished game, and the developers copy pasted the first part of the game for you to play again. This game could be a great game if not marred by various bad elements.

The good:
-Good stealth game, several ways to complete a mission.
-Many ways to take down enemies aside from killing them: you can stun, tranquilize, chokehold, or drop supply box on them.
-Open world map. You can travel by horse, by car, by riding a bipedal robot, by hiding behind enemy truck, by hiding inside cardboard box and let the enemy deliver you to another point.
-There are 50 main missions and more than 100 side missions.
-Lots of weapons to choose from.

The bad:
-Once the enemy get alerted to your position, they suddenly become super soldier that can notice tiny movement from far away. The enemy will now focus on your location and ignore all other explosion and distraction caused by you.
-Some missions have super tough enemy appear at the end without warning. So you might not equip a proper weapon on your first playthrough.
-The game run on autosave, but it's only triggered when you pass through certain area. There are times when I looted the whole base, killed almost all the enemies by stealth, but get killed by the sniper hidden faraway. During all this time, the game never autosave, hours of gameplay wasted.
-The story is bad. Don't take it too seriously while you play.

The ugly:
-By default, you open doors by slamming it hard, potentially alerting all nearby enemies. This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a stealth game. Even the buddy dog can open the door quietly.
-Lots of waiting in the game. Start a mission, loading screen, then wait for animation of chopper slowly fly to location. When mission is done, call for chopper, wait for it to arrive. Board the chopper, wait for it to depart. Chopper departed, wait for animation of chopper slowly fly away from the area. It wasn't so bad the first few times, but after several missions, it gets annoying since the animation can't be skipped.
-If you are a skillful player, the enemy gets 'stronger' eventually. It sounds good on paper, but it is annoying in practice. First enemies will wear helmet to better protect them from headshot. Then they wear body armor. Eventually they will wear face cover and full body armor, so you can't even head shot their face. If the game think you are still good enough, the enemy will wear night vision googles to spot you in the dark. Then they will place landmines around the location where you could potentially sneak in. They will also put some snipers in the area. The enemies get more difficult not only in side mission, but in main mission as well. You would think later in the game you want to redo earlier missions with better gear to achieve higher rank. Good luck with that, because the enemies get stronger as well.
-Some weapons require extraordinary amount of money and resources to upgrade. I wanted to try out the strongest sniper rifle in the game, but after I look at the upgrade requirements, I give up. I have put in almost 200 hours in the game, and I am nowhere close in getting that upgrade.

Conclusion: The story is bad, there are some bad elements, and you will need a lot of grinding to get the best weapon, but I still think this is a good stealth game. The original price is too expensive IMO. I got this game around 75% discount, so it's worth it.

MGSV is super tightly designed from the mechanics to the control scheme. though you can play this with mouse and keyboard, i highly suggest using a control to experience how deliberate and genius the control scheme is. keyboards have the advantage of many buttons to which actions can be assigned, but controllers have few. in MGSV, however, many actions are assigned to the few buttons, and, not long after u get into it, these quick split-second actions of pressing certain buttons while holding others becomes second nature; it's that intuitive. as for gameplay, you enjoy a great breadth of missions that put you in various environments where you will pursue various objectives under various limitations. if you add the many weapons, tools, and play-styles into that equation, you have a foundation from which every player will have a unique and fun experience. admittedly, the story get's kinda complicated, but the way that MGSV is designed allows for its deep and complex lore for those who want it, while also keeping the individual missions episodic and intelligible on their own. of course, like any game, MGSV isn't perfect, but i'd be willing to make the argument it's right at the cusp; it's a must-own.

tldr:
+super tight control scheme
+hyper-focused design
+foundation for many unique and fun experiences from player to player
+story and missions allow for enjoyment of the overarching, deep lore and/or simple episodic and digestible missions
+80s music can be collected and listened to as you play

Pros:
Graphics are good. The transitions in sunlight when exiting a building are a nice touch. 
Sound is good. The fact that you can play the games soundtrack while you play is a nice touch.
Lots of variety in the way you can take down enemies
Open world design lets you approach things your way
Lots of controls, a bit of a learning curve, but I think the UI handles everything well
Interesting storyline with a lot of audio content for you to listen to
Good variety of weapons, and interesting design of your command post with its different staff doing different tasks

Cons:
The game becomes repetitive quickly. Though the game is open world, that world is largely empty. Despite the decent graphic engine, there is only so much you can do with the drab desert color scheme. 
Though the map may seem large initially, there are really only a handful of bases and villages. The missions and side missions will send you to the same places over and over again. And the locations themselves are pretty lacking in design. Why would russians be guarding the equivalent of a bombed out building in the middle of nowhere?
The variety of research that you can perform for new weapons and items is interesting, but largely irrelevant. Though you can approach the game as a rampaging marauder killing everything in your way, you will be penalized for not playing stealthily. That means you will likely be staying with non-lethal takedowns, making only a few weapons viable.
The harry-potterish backstory of mystical enemies vaporating here and there is a bit hard to swallow for a war game. It's also unnecessary. As is displaying the cast of level designers EVERY TIME you finish a mission. It's just an odd, narcissistic choice that I have never experienced in any other game before. 
Some of the design choices are also really, really cheesy. Your intelligence gathering comes in the form of literal cassette tapes that you pick up along the way. Yet, you have an 'iDroid" PDA that you work off of. Its a strange mismatch of technologies that makes no sense, and it comes off as just being plain tacky.

If you don't mind repetitive games to take up some time, you won't be dissapointed in this game. If on the other hand you like more variety on the level of a Fallout 3/4 open world, this is probably not the game for you.

Metal Gear has always been a staple in video game industry: mindblowing plot twists, great characters, incredible gameplay and breathtaking soundtrack. Alas, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain lacks a lot of what made the previous games perfect.

First of all, let's get gameplay out of the way. It's great. Probably the best stealth gameplay I've ever experienced. I have no complaints on the gameplay, literally none.

Little note about the OST. I especially loved some of the cult tracks included, like Take On Me or Gloria. Sins of the Father is a good track as well but i think that [spoiler] the way they played it in the game was really stupid and with no sense at all [/spoiler].

The plot is hilariously bad. It had a very strong start but after Chapter 2 it's just so boring and useless to the lore (except for one specific mission). Just for your interest, Chapter 2 not only is just really, but REALLY short compared to the first one, but it completely bores you even with such an amazing gameplay. The characters are so useless. Really. They have little to no impact to the plot. Even [spoiler] Ocelot [/spoiler], who is my favorite character in the series, is just an useless NPC throughout the game. This game aimed so much on the drama that it even forgot what the word means. Going back and rewatching the trailers, it looks like a very different game. After finishing the whole plot, it just feels like this was what Kojima was intending but it was executed so poorly by Konami that it hurts. 

It took 46 hours to finish the game (true ending), and now everything just feels like empty, an empty world with empty characters but full of ♥♥♥♥ to do. My last and least important complaint is the difficulty. This game is just easy. Maybe it's because I've already played and finished all the previous games so I'm pretty acquainted to the genre and that's it. But man, what a [strike] thrill [/strike] way to end such a memorable series.

[h1] Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is one of the best games of all time in terms of gameplay and in terms of story. However, it is by far the worst MGS in terms of story. [/h1]

STORY (6/10)
The plot really did feel incomplete as many people have already said. While the plot was "cool", if this was any other game I'd be talking about how deep it is, this is MGS. We hold Hideo Kojima to higher standards. Characters such as Huey and Quiet had very interesting character development, but a lot of things weren't truly explored. I loved the heavy nature of the game and the themes that this game plays around with, but it was just missing something. For one, it was missing a LOT of story, and the missions were inevitably repetitive. The boss fights were also just not quite up to par with some of the old Metal Gear Solid games. EVEN PORTABLE OPS did a better job!

GAMEPLAY (9/10)
The mechanics, fluidity, game optimisation is absolutely excellent. Never has an RPG game felt so immersive and the tactical espionage action allowed for such creativity. However, while the game should have used the amazing Fox engine with all its capabilities, it SHOULD NOT have been open-world. That significantly contributed to detracting from the story. 

GRAPHICS (9/10)
This is by far the best looking Metal Gear Solid game and will go down as having one of the best balances of graphics, realism and frames-per-second. That said, I'm not a sucker4visuals.

VERDICT (8/10)
Probably deserved GOTY back in 2015. But for an MGS game: Best gameplay, worst story. Nonetheless, a very important game and a must-play for any Metal Gear fan.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#475 out of 633)... it's time for Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.

I'd have to have my head pretty firmly lodged up my own ass to think I have anything new or worthwhile or revelatory to say about a Metal Gear Solid game, huh? It's a Hideo Kojima game: everything that could possibly be said has already been said, shouted into the void by a thousand different voices a thousand times over. It's impossible to overstate, I think, just how compelling a subject Metal Gear is for media criticism—professional and amateur alike.

For my purposes here, I'd like to really narrow in on just one single aspect of the game: the one thing that struck me more than any other while playing. For all of its excess, for all its ambition, I think The Phantom Pain is a game that is both far too strange, yet paradoxically, not strange enough. It's a Kojima game without enough Kojima in it—but just enough that you can tell it's missing something.

And look, I know what you're thinking: I played Metal Gear Solid 4, too—and I'm just as surprised as you are. Who'd have thought that less Kojima in a Metal Gear game would be a bad thing? The world has gone all topsy-turvy and nothing makes sense any more.

If you're unfamiliar with the Metal Gear series, I imagine you're quite confused by this point (why haven't you stopped reading?)—too quickly explain, series director Hideo Kojima is a very unique and ideosyncratic person who creates very unique and ideoscyncratic games. And if you're sensitive to misogynistic portrayals of women... you may want to mentally prepare yourself before diving into any one of them. Kojima games are quirky and bizarre—but also very often intriguing, compelling, and revelatory. They also feature some of the most finely-polished and mechanically-enthralling systems and mechanics in the stealth genre. Every Kojima game is iconic, and most of them are classics. And while the Metal Gear series may shamble on without him, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain marks the end of Kojima's involvement with one of gaming's strangest and most memorable series.

Assuming you've read anything about MGSV before, including the above, you likely understand that it's an open-world stealth game like no other, filled with engaging mechanics, challenging AI, and a world that adapts to your tactics forcing you to constantly think on your feet. I honestly spent far more of my time with the game than I'd care to admit clearing the same enemy bases of hostiles again and again just because the core mechanics were so rewarding and the AI kept things so unpredictable that each run felt properly distinct from the others. I suspect I am not alone in this. MGSV offers up an enormous world filled with play opportunities... all of which is strung together by a narrative that embodies most of Kojima's usual excess.

But there's just not that much story there relative to the gameplay, and what is there just doesn't feel as fresh or interesting as prior entries in the series. As engaging—enthralling, really—as MGSV can be, it doesn't quite reach the same level of brilliance as Metal Gear Solid 2 or Metal Gear Solid 3: both of which married equally excellent gameplay to extraoridnarily bizarre, finely-crafted, frequently too-meta narratives. No matter what you're doing in MGS2 or MGS3, you're constantly at the edge of your seat, wondering what crazy, insane nonsense you'll see next.

And don't get me wrong—The Phantom Pain is still a Kojima game, there's still crazy insane nonsense to look forward to... it's just the exception, not the rule. Most of your time will be spent scouting out enemy bases and expending your mental energies on decidedly mundane challenges—when a giant killer robot or evil ghost demons pop up in the story missions, they feel like invaders from an entirely different, somewhat more interesting game.

Note: also played on Sony Playstation 4.

I know some of you have played this game, and you probably know what I'm talking about when I say it's a masterpiece. But for those of you who haven't, let me tell you, this game is a trip. It's got more twists and turns than a rollercoaster, more espionage than a James Bond movie, and more "WTF" moments than you can shake a stick at.

And speaking of "WTF" moments, have you ever wondered what it's like to be inside the mind of Hideo Kojima? Well, let me tell you, it's like being on a really strong dose of... well, let's just say Kojima's marijuana must be pretty potent. But don't worry, folks, it's all in good fun.

Now, some of you might be wondering, "Hey, Hyrden, how do you know so much about Metal Gear Solid 5?" Well, let me tell you, I've spent more time playing this game than I care to admit. In fact, I think I've got our friend in the front row beat - they've played it for a thousand hours on their PS4! That's dedication, folks.

And you know what's even more impressive? They went and bought it again for their PC! That's like buying a second copy of the Bible, folks. But I get it, I really do. This game has it all. Stealth action, incredible music, and some of the craziest plot twists you'll ever see in a video game.

So, to sum it all up, Metal Gear Solid 5 is a game that will leave you speechless, make you question reality, and keep you coming back for more, no matter what platform it's on. So, if you haven't played it yet, what are you waiting for? Trust me, it's worth the thousand hours.

The game isn't perfect. It had a massively troubled development and has a lot of shortcoming as a consequence. The game is in fact missing an entire final third of the story, and the second third of the game is a nothing more than the first third of the game with different mission variations and difficulties sprinkled with some new missions mostly for story. 
The game also had a contentious monetization scheme of offering insurance for you FOB(Forward Operating Base) for real money, but this was all optional. The game also offered development shortcuts for real life money. The currency is called MB coins and you can now earn a decent amount of them with daily logins.
The FOB section to the games multiplayer is almost completely ruined by hackers. So you can try and compete in this mode, only to feel like you have been spat in the face after a hacker with max stats on the FOB with only 50 hours play time stomps you.
The new version of Metal Gear Online is unfortunately very lacking in content. The games troubled development meant that the online released a few weeks after the base game, and it too suffers from hackers, but was almost completely abandoned at launch due to the failure to attract a large player base. Today it it usually only possible to find one semi full lobby, and it is filled with high rank players who are dedicated to the game. The games online progression system means that you unlock better gear at higher levels, so the higher tier players who are more skilled at the game also have better gear than you do starting off. But you can still get some kills with the base gear.

Overall, the game is fun but lacks a lot of polish and content. It is the weakest MGS game by far, and I can only recommend you buy the game when on steep steep sales.

This is without a doubt the best open world stealth game that I have ever played. I completed my game missions when I was around 40 hrs into the game and I am still going. Repetitive doesn't mean boring however, the sheer scale of mission may be enlarged or the difficulty of the mission may be increased depending on your level. The AI in this game is unpredictable most of the time and it's not dumb like other stealth games. The game expects you to change your way of approach depending on the playing style you are following the most. For example, If you tend to infiltrate the enemy bases at night, the soldiers will be equipped with Night Vision Goggles in the subsequent missions, etc.

As a major fan of the Metal Gear series having first played the original back on PS1, picking this up was a simple "no brainer” for me. The concept of Metal Gear moving into an open world format was difficult for me to grasp at first due to my familiarity for the series not being in this format. However, once I was used to it, all I can say is bravo as it really enhances the experience and gives you the feeling of being in full control of how missions play out. One disappointment was the lack of cut scenes and storytelling compered the previous Metal Gears. For me, I feel this is what really makes you connect with a Metal Gear game so much. Please don’t misunderstand me, I appreciate in previous games the cut scenes were very long and some people may be even put of due to this, however for me it was part of the experience of the game and one of the reasons why I was so hooked onto the story and each in game mission. MG5 doesn’t give me this same connection, I feel that this is due to the fact that missions are selected and rarely acted, you land onto the battlefield, complete the objective and leave the battlefield in what feels to be a repetitive process at times. 
If you’re new the MG franchise and you’re thinking about picking this up, I would certainly recommend getting up to speed with the story as the game pretty much throws you in without really explaining who you are and the characters you’re interacting with.  
To simplify, MG5 has great game play and once you’re used to format and understand the games mechanics, it simply gets better and better. The freedom to do what you want and how you want to is what separates this from any other Metal Gear game. Although the story as times is exciting, I don’t feel that this will go down as a classic in terms of storytelling.

At that point, I had seen very little that even resembled an MGS game.  By the time I got to the first mission, I was already so let down by the tutorial stage that I had very little hope for the rest of it.  Traveling by horse?  An open world concept for an espionage and infiltration game?  I gave up after three hours of game play.  I would NOT recommend this game for anyone.  If I had wanted a movie with scripted game play, I would've played The Last of Us.

I just wished Konami gave more trust, faith, and funding to Kojima to complete this game. It could've been the best stealth game of all time (and Kojima's swan song to the Metal Gear franchise).

But was it really being on the PSP that made me dislike the game? In the end I think no, I just don't really like any of the content made for Big Boss after 3.

TPP in particular has this feeling of soullessness in comparison to the rest of Kojima's game that I can't quite shake. The rest of the franchise is a ghost that kind of hangs over the game. Touted as a 'Missing Link' of sorts when it comes to overall MGS lore, it's more like a filler arc that you don't really understand the necessity of its existence. To its credit, MGSV's gameplay is everything in Peace Walker taken to its ultimate end. It's well refined and easy and smooth to play. Kojima perfected Metal Gear's gameplay. It's just such a shame that the framework around that perfectly tuned gameplay is window dressing, Nothing of what I loved atmospherically from the rest of the franchise is present in this game. I know there's no wild twist to keep me playing on the edge of my seat like the twists and turns of MGS1, no real biting commentary like in MGS2. It is a video game and it is a video game that plays well. But I think Metal Gear is more than that, and this game never really gives me any of those things I wanted.

If there's a choice between this and anything else, replaying MGS1-3 is what I'd say, and you'd still beat it well before a run of TPP would naturally end with all the filler content it has. Or maybe play Death Stranding instead - a game Kojima made following this creation that makes me feel like is where all his soul and heart went to instead of this game.

It is difficult to put into words how much I recommend this game. How much I love it and how much it has shaped how I feel about games.
This game is masterful. It is very well designed and the systems work together with such beauty and such attention to detail that if you can think of a solution, it has an incredible likelihood to work. Not only does this make things fun, and never feels like the developers didn't think enough or weren't open minded enough, but you can play this game so many different ways. I did my first play-through without killing anyone, and it just worked. I was simply able to, there was never a time where I was required to kill an enemy soldier. Let that sink in. This is a war game.
That said, this is a war game about how horrible war can be. What other game would have you rescue a bear from a minefield as a side mission? [spoiler]What other war game has you fight a parasitic pandemic?[/spoiler] Not only that, not only are you able to play non-lethally and rescue animals from a war zone, but there are also superhuman zombie soldier things [spoiler]and mechs[/spoiler]. It's fantastic. The story is of course incredibly well done, and I highly recommend you listen to all the audio things. This game showed me the emotions that this video game can inspire, and I am not exaggerating. This is the only video game that has made me cry. Not only this, but the final twist is certainly the most well-executed in any game, movie, TV show, or other piece of media that I have ever encountered[strike], AND HE DANGLES IT IN FRONT OF YOUR FACE BECAUSE HE KNOWS YOU WON'T NOTICE!!![/strike].
The gameplay and level design is fantastic. In Mission 11 [spoiler]you face off against a sniper[/spoiler], and soon every single aspect of the terrain, every lump of raised ground, every tree, every bush, every turn of the river even, becomes so important. You literally see the world differently, and while I was playing I was blown away by the level design on display. It is intense and fun and exhilarating and it's one of my favorite pieces of gameplay of any game.
Finally: the optimization. This game is a legitimate miracle. I used to have a really, really, really bad graphics card. I didn't actually know how bad it was when I had it, I just thought that's how things were, but now that I've upgraded I realized that what I had was legitimate garbage. Off the top of my head I believe it was an AMD R7 240. Anyway, the point is that I COULD PLAY THIS GAME!! I could run this game WELL! Nearly any other 3-D game I had to play at 720p with lowest possible settings, and I would pull about 20-25 frames. Old games, too, stuff that had no right to cause performance issues. I could play MGSV at low settings at 1080, or even medium graphics settings with shadows and light effects and all that at 720 or 1080 if I was fine with 15 fps. I can't communicate how insane this is looking back on it. If you are worried about performance, and you can run ANY GAME that came out after 2010 on settings you deem acceptable, heck probably 2005, you should be fine.

So there you go. That's my review for what is literally my favorite game. At its price, you owe it to yourself to play it. At almost any price, you owe it to yourself to play it. It is a masterpiece. My final bit of advice is that, in the hospital escape at the start, you do not have to use the gun Ishmael gives you. He will take care of it eventually, just wait. If you want to do non-lethal, you can do so from the moment you hit start.

If, like me, you've played all the previous MGS games and were expecting a sequel, then you'll be sorely disappointed. The boss fights are almost non-existent, Snake is now basically mute, and you'll have to go out of your way to have the exposition stuffed down your throat. All the cheekiness has gone too, leaving only angry grim soldier men with the smallest vestige of the old MGS charm. The whole thing is riddled with questionable design choices, such as mandatory mission replays on higher difficulties (the harder versions being waaay more fun and should have been standard the first time around), and barely-utilised mechanics, which may or may not be due to the game's release being rushed. What's for sure is Kojima tried to be even more ambitious than 4, and it didn't quite come together. One mercy is that the change of VAs for all the main characters, along with Kojimbo's insistence that it's MGSV not MGS5, made it very easy to scrub from my headcanon of the series.
The gameplay on the other hand is phenomenal, but got repetitive and frequently mind-numbingly boring. This made the difficulty extremely jarring in places. If all the hard missions weren't interspersed with hours of outpost raids, faffing about in mother base, and trivial non-plot relevant side and main ops, it could have been a fantastic game. Hell, there is about 10-20 hours of truly amazing content in MGSV, just spread thinly over 60+ hours of ehhhhhhh. 
For me the most fascinating part of this game is the potential of what it could have been. There is so much unexplained symbolism, mechanics that are foreshadowed but never used (hem hem battle gear hem hem), and Kojima weirdness, as well as some seriously great sections that shine through the cracks. Unfortunately, its just a phantom pain, as we'll never get the game we lost.
