I'm bored, I couldn't sleep last night, and the Rona is going so I'm just pissy,

I can't fault the writing for being itself, I mean, it's Kojima. But the constant credits and unskippable bits are are obnoxious and distracting. The controls are terrible, and playing with a mouse and keys involves some awkward mashing. Actions like picking up a body and a item are bound to the same key, so often I'll pick up a rifle while quickly trying to move a body, or start attaching a balloon to a car while I'm trying to get into it. Not to mention the damn menus. All of the tutorials are for a controller even though I don't even own one, and the audio doesn't work so I can't change the music, voices, or VFX volume. None of the keys are explained for a keyboard so who know what button does what. A few minutes ago I commanded my horse to take a ♥♥♥♥ while trying to interrogate an enemy.

Snake handles like he's drunk, and input seems to lag all over the place. I can't seem to stop, and I'm not sure if it's a bug or not. Snake, the horse, and the walker all won't stop moving most of the time and require me to mash the movement keys until they do. Which is hell when precise movement is the key to being spotted or not. There were so many points where I was spotted or shot because I stepped out of cover while just trying to turn around or back up. And on that topic, why the hell does the camera switch to a dramatic angle and play a musical cue every time I'm trying to get on. It screws with my direction and when I'm trying to escape it makes me lose precious seconds. The animations are wooden and screw with the character's movement.

I can't believe this is a stealth game. There's no cover button, just awkward "auto cover" that's janky as hell. The movement is a liability and you can't effectively look around you and run without getting stuck on a random rock or step. The FOV is fixed and way too low so situational awareness is a dizzying display of spinning the camera around while Snake's ass takes up the whole bottom part of the screen. There's no quicksave or quickload, and many missions involve trying to infiltrate a compound in a canyon with barely any cover. Maybe I should use the box more. I like the observation mechanic of watching your enemies but there's no point in spending time casing the place when you might be spotted and have all your work undone with no save. I don't have time to replay a mission over and over to explore. Plus, Snake can take an absolute pounding so I'm not really motivated to sneak around using the janky stealth system. I'll quietly subdue the first few guys but eventually it's murder mode. 

The "open world" is a joke, it's just a bunch of levels stitched together with desert roads. It gets repetitive fast. I feel like I live in some of those compounds. The helicopter is just an extended unskippable cutscene and I'd rather just walk, or gallop, or robot wheelie to the next level across the dust.

To round off, ♥♥♥♥ the base building system and its bizarre layout. Why are all my platforms 1km apart with nothing in between but ocean? I have to take a 3 minute drive across the open ocean in a jeep to just get to the medical or R&D platform. There doesn't even seem to be anything to do but wander around tortuous staircases and have occasional cutscenes. Oh, and beat up your men because they're all masochists who thank you for punching them or shooting them with rubber bullets. I hate micromanaging the crew and having to play Pokemen and capture enemies I want to take home with me. It's funny but it gets old fast.

Why am I still here?
Just to suffer...
The time not playing the game i lost.
The real life lost.

Edit Update on Review:

I`ve played this game more... A LOT more. And I think I should add more of what I think to this game.

It`s a LOT more indepth than I initially expected, I`ll detail the main bits.

1. The missions are quite varied from the usual stealth to tank busting.

2. The soldier security AI is very good. If take off X-Ray and marking on the soldiers, you`ll notice how good they are. At the beginning they`re relatively relaxed, and you think you can take out a soldier or two which is easy on tiny outposts of 3 men. But any bigger and it`s not that easy. Even if you have a big ambush advantage and take down a few sentries, someone (I guess the section leader), will make a comms check. When he gets no reply, they go on alert. Sometimes they`ll just call for support which will make things even worse. Also when on Alert they usually stop walking about alone where it`s easy to pick them off, they start searching in pairs. Some soldiers are quicker on the ball than others.Even when you take out an area it`s only for a while since you often get these security trucks that come by to check everything`s ok! Very good security measures, though they are still a bit short-sighted.

3.When you blow a situation and they all go into combat mode, life can get really tough, especially in daylight. They`ll mark where you are and gather to attack it, even flanking. You need to get away from that spot fast. I usually have a back up plan like a bomb planted elsewhere to get their attention if I have to run.

4. Pretty much all missions let you do a job how you want. The missions almost never end unless you get killed. For instance, I had to find a prisoner through an enemy  interpreter, but I didn`t think and used a Tranq on the interpreter knocking him out instead of following him. So I sent him to base and they interrorgated him giving me info on where the prisoner may be found. You can even kill the interpreter, but then you have to find the prisoner yourself.

5. As the game goes on you`ll get all kinds of help from a dog (if you want him) to others. You`ll also have access to military support such as artillery. Very useful, but they all cost money.

6.You get a base (an oilrig) that at first seems empty, but then you employ staff, extra stuff and can really expand the base with medic station, R&D, military, etc. There`s way more to it than meets the eye. You can even customise it to your colour pref and even Logo. It`s almost like a 3D version of the Xcom 2 base and I wish Xcom 2 had a base that you could run around like this! 

7.You manage staff, you even manage missions staff can go on.

8.You can customise your Helo and even add music which really adds to flight in and out of missions or around the base.

9.It isn`t feminist/sjw nonsense which I really, really like, ie Quiet and most fighters are men.

10.It has some strange thing like animal conservation on your base and saving animals (but it does help get in money).

11. Weird story, but it`s ok.

12. Very realistic in some aspects (most the military and stealth stuff).

13. Some people said all you do are Afghanistan missions. Untrue. I`ve been doing African ones too, facing a lot of Africans and South Africaners so far and I`m only 12% into the game!

14. No Fast Travelling that I can see, except by realistic means, vehicle, horse, chopper, even on the base. I like as i`ve never FT in any game even when it tried to make me! Very old school.

Neutral:
1. The fantasy stuff, but now I realise why it`s called `Metal Gear Solid`. The fire man, the girl in the gasmask that`s actually a bloke. I don`t mind it, but it can be  `weird`.

2. the naming of things has that weird Japanese Final Fantasy feel, ie the simplistic names for things such as "mother Base" (nobody Western actually calls their base `mother base`) and other names that are just too on the nose at times. It likely sounds better in Japanese.

4. Campaign story is ok so far, but I`m more interested in the `open world` stuff.

5. It`s not really open world. it`s quite open but many mission lock you between impassable hills so you can`t go approach from a different angle.

6. Each mission can be LONG, as in an hour or more, depending how you approach them and I approach realistically.

7. No FT. Some people will probably hate that as they`ve been spoilt by FT.

8. If you keep failing a mission (by dying), the game gives you the option to go easy by wearing a chicken hat- I refuse! But it`s funny and then becomes annoying when it keeps asking me!


Negatives:
1. I still find doing everything in 3rd person annoying. A dedicated optional 1st person mode would make this 10\10. I`m sure I`d be 50% more efficent in 1st person.

2. A few missions are hugely annoying such as the one where I had to find a lost Wanderer. It took me absolutely ages trying to get him. Fortunately they`re the side missions.

3. Sometimes you aren`t given a choice when it looks like you should have one in the story.

I`m only 12% of the Campaign in! It`s one of those games you have to play for at least 5 hours before you see what it has to offer.

Forced PVP, a cynical money-grabbing scheme and no option to save manually ruin what would otherwise be a flawed but amazing game.

The issue here is that 90% of the resources and equipment you gather in your supposedly single-player game are kept 'online' in the cloud where other players can steal them.  Even while you are offline.

Want to protect your investment in time and effort?  You can buy 'insurance' from Konami but only for real money.

Honestly it's a scam worthy of a mobile game, I'm almost impressed.

And of course, even if your stuff doesn't get stolen, you can't access it yourself if you lose your internet connection.  Fantastic game mechanic.  To make matters worse it only really starts to affect you after you are about a quarter of the way through the story and have hours invested, so good luck getting a refund.

Other than that, well, it's a Hideo Kojima game.  Don't worry, you won't forget, he makes sure to have his name up on the screen at least twice an hour while you are playing - writing and level design credits roll after every single mission.  Oh and also before, during the briefing, so you can't skip them.

The first level of the game consists of half an hour of cutscenes, which can thankfully be skipped, and half an hour of crawling along the ground, which can't.  Every time you start a new game.  Make a save point after the intro so you don't have to play it again every time?  Sorry, no manual saves.

That autosave is the other massive drawback of this game.  It's inexcusable in a supposedly open-world game to not allow you to save when you want.  It's unreliable as well: it's not tied to completing missions, or moving to different zones, or even to the passage of time, it just seems to save when it feels like it.  Sometimes three times in as many minutes, sometimes not for an hour.  Which, inevitably, means at some point you are going to lose hours of progress. 

The interminable cutscenes, the constant rolling credits, and the lack of what I guess they considered an 'immersion breaking' save option can sometimes make it feel like you are watching a movie rather than playing a game, but if so then it's a movie aimed squarely at tweenage boys.  Obviously the character of Quiet is well known about these days; I won't go into the dubious lore that tries to explain why she is walking around in ripped fishnet tights and a bikini, I will just point out that every cutscene involving her seems to start with the camera zoomed in on her chest.

As for the actual gameplay?  It's a lot of fun with lots of different options for completing missions, but the mouse and keyboard controls suck.

It's a Hideo Kojima game.

So I'd never played a Metal Gear Solid game before. It's weird. Not necessarily bad. The gameplay itself is good. Guns, sneaking, the buddies you get to help you, the sheer amount of options on the tale for how you wanna play is awesome. Every variety of lethal or tranquilizer weapons, using balloons to abduct people and animals, bipedal mechs. It has a lot of good stuff, and many beats in the story are pretty good or at the least they ham it up so much you'll chuckle at how serious they take things. 
Positive notes I will say. Sneaking is great, everything about the sneaking feels right. Hiding in darkness, taking cover etc. They give you lots of ways to hide like hiding in toilets, dumpsters or cardboard boxes. There's lots of little bits of polish and mechanics that are neat. You get a recording of a guy having violent diarheaa and if you play it while a guard might suspect you're hiding in a toilet, he gets grossed out and leaves. And you can move around as the cardboard boxes not only to sneak,  but to fast travel. The cardboard box stuff is just great. 
One of the best things in the game is your buddies. You start with a horse. D-Horse is cool. Great horse, comes when you call, can later on poop on command. You can hang of his side and hide while riding. The you get D-Dog. D-dog is amazing because he shows you where all the enemies nearby are. Which is super useful because up until that point, you keep getting caught by dudes who you didn't notice. He also later gets the ability to distract stun or kill enemies. Super good dog. The you get Quiet, who is a sniper. As a buddy, she's probably the best because you have actual backup in the game. In addition she can also scout places. She's not always as efficient as D-Dog, but she can cover your butt when you need it so she's great. Probably wouldn't have made it through the game in the time I did without her. Final buddy is a Walker vehicle. Barely used it but it's neat. Goes real fast, and super all terrain. 

That said it does have a number of negative aspects worth discussing. First off, unless you played other Metal Gear games, you won't know a bit of what people are talking about is, except for context clues. That's normal for a game that's part of a longrunning series but this is some next level stuff where they really don't explain a lot of who people are prior to this game.
Secondly, it starts with this hospital level where everything is really weird and confusing and you have severely limited mobility at first. Now all the weird stuff does get cleared up, but you have to play the whole game to learn why all the crazy stuff in the first level makes sense. A lot of people have also said that the game doesn't have an ending. No it does. They just make you replay the first hospital level. Which is annoying because even though you now understand all the crazy stuff, you're also just replaying the same low mobility tutorial level and all they changed was that there's like 1 little cutscene change. And then there's a bunch of cutscene at the end that end it. 
So yeah, the end doesn't have a boss battle or a clear ending point due to something you did. Which sucks because there are a couple of loose strings that don't get tied up, that they clearly wanted to make into a final boss and didn't. 
It's also really clear everything that happens the way it is, happens just so they can set up the games that already came out, but take place in the future. 

All in all, good game. They just go a weird direction sometimes.

There are hardly any cutscenes at all (plus one really long and awkward car ride with Skullface), and the story is a meandering mess. At the end, when the stupidest twist of all time is dropped onto the player, you must completely redo the tutorial mission WITH ALL OF THE TUTORIAL STUFF STILL IN THE GAME--remember that you've played at least 100 hours to get to this point--just to see the one thing at the end that's different. 

The entire third act of the game was cut and there's basically no ending, and most of the missions are copy-pasted with minimal differences. The game has 50 missions technically, but you run out of new ones at 25 and then have to do slightly changed versions over again in order to reach the "true" ending. And once you do reach the "true ending," once you do replay that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorial--which, by the way, everyone raves about; it's boring, linear, and not anything like MGS should be, and it tipped me off that this game would blow right from the get-go--you magically receive a dozen extra audiologs that explain all of the rest of the story to you. That's it. The final chapter of the Metal Gear saga, and its conclusion is a podcast. Not even a cutscene where Big Boss explains everything. Just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ podcast. 

We were supposed to receive the origin story of Big Boss. If you haven't already been spoiled, that's not what this game is. It was supposed to tell a tale of a descent into darkness, bridging the gap between the idealist of Peace Walker and the warmonger of Metal Gear. Snake even has a horn! Look how dark this'll be!

But MGSV isn't dark. In fact, it goes out of its way to be not-dark. There are child soldiers, but you're not allowed to murder them--in fact, you get a game over if you try to. By the midpoint of the narrative, Venom Snake has basically started his own daycare, and Kaz makes sure to always remind us that the kiddies are being treated well. Huh? What? Aren't we supposed to be evil? Isn't Venom the bad guy? What is this? Is Kojima really this incapable of writing a thematically cohesive narrative, or could he just not stand to be mean to babies in his game? 

If you can't tell, my disappointment in this regard is immeasurable. For years I was desperately awaiting MGSV's release. MGS3 is my favorite game of all time. I love Peace Walker. I like MGS2 and 4 a lot. And even after falling for the scam that was Ground Zeroes, I was still unbelievably excited for V. 

Then I played the game. 

#2. The Gameplay

On the surface, MGSV has an excellent primary gameplay loop. The sneaking has never felt better. It has one big problem, though: 

IT SUCKS. 

The issue is that the primary gameplay loop doesn't feed very well into the base management systems. You can beat this entire game without ever thinking about it, and so you're hardly ever incentivized to actually engage with the mechanics. You will anyway, because everyone likes cool stuff, but the unlocks basically do nothing. Not in the literal sense; literally, they're very valuable, for the most part, but MGSV is too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy. You can beat the whole game by shooting everyone to death with rubber bullets. And you HAVE to take rifles every mission! No OSP, unless the game decides it's an OSP mission. 

Every stealth game, and especially every MGS game, struggles with this problem, but you have so many tools in MGSV that it's the worst it's ever been. A sneaking mission? Why not just take a tank instead?

Yeah, you can drive a tank in this stealth game. 

The entire game has been balanced around the slow-mo Splinter Cell alert mode, where you have a free three second window to get a tranq headshot when spotted. This will make even the most inept players feel like a god. It trivializes stealth. But if you turn Splinter Cell mode off, the game suddenly becomes impossible--sneaking just isn't practical over long distances without it, not in a game set mostly outside. More on that later. 

Ironically, Ground Zeroes is the MGSV we really needed. A focus on open-ended stealth action in conjunction with clear objectives and linear narrative. A game that is narratively cohesive, just like MGS 1-4. Peace Walker works because it's, basically, a mobile game. But when I sit down to play a game at my PC, I don't want a mobile game's structure. It's too disjointed. It doesn't work. Every mission in this game ends before it feels like it's gotten started. It's not engaging. 

This, in conjunction with the complete focus on overworld stealth, ruins the game. Sneaking around Afghanistan, which is all brown and tan and ugly, is not nearly as interesting as sneaking around Shadow Moses. Understand that there is basically NO inside stealth in this game. There's a very small number of vaguely urban levels, but most of it is in the desert or the jungle. This is repetitive and uninteresting, and the focus on exteriors means the level design is completely without merit. There's just nothing there.

I'd like to remind you at this point that all of the best parts of MGS3, the game that takes place in a jungle, were actually when you were inside of a Soviet compound. 

And there are just so many other issues. Flying in with the helicopter every mission, seeing Kojima's name over and over and over again, dealing with clunky menus, handling countless bugs (many of which have probably been fixed by now; i haven't played this game in 4 years)--basically, ♥♥♥♥ this game, don't play it.

#3. ♥♥♥♥ this game, don't play it.

In summary, if you want a TL;DR: "Vocal chord parasites, son." That should explain my review. Oh, wait, it doesn't? ♥♥♥♥ YOUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUU

The gameplay is fantastic - you basically move around in a sandbox type of environment where you can tackle mission objectives the way you want. This is the greatest strength of the game, to choose your own playstyle, to develop your own tactics in order to get the optimal result.

At least as long as the game won't interfere with its ridiculous cut scenes. It's simply annoying to be suddenly put into the passenger seat to watch your character which you had sneaking around so stealthily plunge into the middle of something. Like an entire enemy combat team which appears out of nothing. Or a giant robot which is out to kill you. Or a burning apparition which wishes to turn you into charcoal. 

It's frustrating to watch how your protagonist remains rooted to the spot, waiting for whatever is out to kill him closes in, while you wonder if he got a death wish nobody cared to inform you about.

Because that's the second major setback of the game: The story. It's somewhere between nonexistent, confusing and outright bad. Nothing really adds up, neither the motivation of the characters nor the general plot. It's just a giant mess of "because we need something in there".  The general lack of story presentation is best described by the main way it is conveyed: Via audio logs that simply appear in your inventory after you've finished a mission. If you care listening to them, you might find some clarification, but after a while you will give up listening to them, because it feels like a chore to work your way through a piling stack of audio tapes.

On the bright side, you've got a few very interesting companions to take along while roaming the countryside. They add some interesting layer of tactical gameplay, giving you even more variations about how to capture the next enemy outpost or base. The use of various vehicles, from a simple 4-wheeled drive up to a full blown MBT adds some spice, but is actually a departure where the game shines most.

Bottom line, MGS5 would have been even better, if they had cut back on the rather atrocious story and added more complex main missions focused on the superb commando style game play.

Extra points for the excellent 80s soundtrack and the attention to detail which went into the game. Some things are outright hilarious and make you wish to experiment more to find all the hidden easter eggs. (Stay 3 days hidden in a dumpster and then return to base.)

Where to start with this one? Perhaps, with the fact that I've never played a single MGS game before this one, not even MGS: Ground Zeroes. I picked it up on Steam as a stealth fan and I was blown away completely.

Saying that I was overwhelmed by the sheer number of possibilities at the start is a huge understatement. It might a while to figure out what's what and what are the best ways to use each gadget. I have to give the game props on how original some of the stealth mechanics are. I don't think I've seen any other game, where you can run around in a carton box or kidnap soldiers from the battlefield. Amazing stuff!

The story is even more confusing for a newbie. The game almost expects the players to thoroughly know the characters and the events that happened before the game. I still have more questions than answers after spending 100+ hours in the game. I guess I'll have to blame it on the lack of experience with the previous MGS games. All I can say is that the cast, the voice-acting, and the cinematics are top in the industry. 

MGS V: The Phantom Pain is also an amazing looking and optimized game. I have encountered zero issues during my lengthy playthrough. Some of its environments are photorealistic, especially in Afghanistan. The African levels are just as immersive and believable, if not more. 

The one complaint I have about MGS V, which does not concern the overabundance of gameplay mechanics, is the game's monotony. The side-missions are extremely repetitive and get increasingly more tedious to do, once you get to a certain point in the game. It's either: 'Go rescue that hostage' or 'Go blow up this convoy'. It gets boring the more you play them. I haven't tried out the multiplayer aspect of the game, but from what I've heard, it's pretty much dead. 

Overall, incredible game, which offers an immersive sandbox experience with literally thousands of toys to play around and experiment with. Use them wisely and don't forget to summon your in-game buddies if you get lonely. They have some cards up in their sleeves (or bras...)!

Disclaimer: MGSV is the only Metal Gear game I've played, so I can't compare it to its predecessors.

[h1]Content[/h1]
The game consists of 50 main missions and 157 side ops. The missions are basically the levels/episodes of the game in the form of contracts to kill/capture/destroy something within a specific mission area of the map. Half of them have actual plot relevance, while the other half are self-contained assignments. All the missions in the first half of the game are unique, even if they take place in the same mission area, but some of the missions in the second half are just higher difficulty versions of previous missions. All missions rank you based on completion time, avoiding kills and being spotted, rescuing prisoners etc.. You can repeat any of the missions after completing them if you want to go for a better rank or want to loot resources/personnel. Each mission also has some bonus tasks to make things more interesting or give you more stuff to do; some of them give extra points for your mission rank. Based on your playstyle, you can get missions done in just a few minutes, or take your time with them, as all of them can be completed in stealth.

Side Ops, on the other hand, are basically a free roam activity. They're very repetitive: 10+ capture a specific soldier, 10+ rescue a prisoner, 10+ wipe out an armoured battalion etc.. Basically, the same task over and over again, but in a different area of the map. Oh, and only a certain number of them are loaded into the map at a time; you have to leave the map and return to get a new set of them. So, these are just there to give you something to do in free roam and they are pretty repetitive.

If you're connected to the online server, you can also invade the bases of other players to steal their stuff. Or invade AI-controlled bases to avoid retaliation. But all this means is that you deploy to their base on one end and have to reach the other end without getting killed and without being able to resupply (you can steal personnel and resources along the way too). Could have been interesting if it had more variety, but it is what it is.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game is divided into two chapters. The first chapter spans up to mission 31; it's complete, has some surprises in store, but has quite a bit of room for improvement. Chapter two, on the other hand, was where the game ran into budget/deadline issues: most missions here are just the exact same missions from chapter 1 but with extra gimmicks for a challenge; a few missions are new and contribute some details to the plot, but there aren't a lot of them. Additionally, one plot point never got resolved in the end, since the end to it was cut from the final game. Instead, the game ends [Spoiler]by forcing you to replay the prologue level but with a few changed cutscenes in the very beginning and the very end, where the game reveals a plottwist; otherwise, the level is exactly the same as the prologue. Couldn't even be bothered to let you play from a different perspective or something[/Spoiler]. So, it's pretty open-ended and feels like it came out of nowhere.

[h1]The World[/h1]
There are two maps in the game: an area in Afghanistan and an area in Africa. The Afghanistan area has occasional sandstorms and is pretty annoying to navigate since the abudance of rocks forces you to take very specific routes to reach certain areas. The Africa region is much easier to navigate and has a bigger variety of terrain.

However, both maps are pretty desolate: there are no civilians or rebels or any other third parties in the game - only you and enemy forces. There are several enemy bases (outposts) per map that are pretty well set up, but the areas in-between feel pretty empty. Aside from various guardposts that block your way (though they can be avoided by taking detours) and a truck driving between outposts, there's nothing else to find there. There aren't even that many animals you can encounter, even though there's a laundry list of animals you need to catch for an achievement.

There is a fast travel system where you can ship yourself to other outposts by hiding in a box on a cargo pickup area, but that spawns you right in the middle of an enemy-controlled outpost with (usually) no checkpoint nearby.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay, on the other hand, is the best part of the game. Plenty of freedom offered: develop the weapons you want, you can choose what to bring to a mission (and the more stuff and upgrades you bring, the more the deployment is going to cost), call in a supply drop mid level, call in a chopper for support or pickup, or just call in an airstrike. The stealth mechanics are neither too complicated nor too dumbed down: enemies see worse in the dark, get suspicious at first if you come too close to their field of vision, and only go on alert if you're very close or are running when they see you, but there's no lighting meter or camo compatibility value to worry about. Enemies also react to your playstyle by taking appropriate measures to protect themselves - if you use headshots a lot, they start wearing helmets; if they catch you sneaking at night - they start using nightvision goggles more often etc..

My only issues are:
1) Interrogations are pretty dumbed down: you just point a weapon at them at 3 m range without them seeing you (or after knocking them down non-lethally and then kicking them to wake up) and then just tell them to talk. There's no difference whom you interrogate either, as the first enemy or two you interrogate will have all the information you need. The interrogations aren't even voiced.
2) If you grab enemies, they can escape your grip before you even have the chance to press anything
3) If one enemy spots you, the entire base goes on alert without having to call in to report an intruder
4) Hard to select items from your inventory that are placed in diagonal slots on keyboard. Plenty of times I threw a frag grenade when I actually intended to throw a sleep/stun grenade solely because the game didn't register that I had pressed two keys at the same time and so it selected the wrong item.
5) Base building is pretty boring - just buy expansions to be able to employ more people at the same time.
6) You can only have 700 staff members per base. That's also how many people you need to fill all positions on a fully upgraded base, leaving you with no wiggle room and the next time you fulton some guy for a mission, you'll lose an existing staff member.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
A game with pretty decent gameplay, but lacking in plot.

The good:
+Freedom to choose your loadout and how you play each mission
+Can call in support during missions (both additional items/ammo and fire support) at the location of your choosing
+Decent stealth mechanics
+Incentives for neutralising enemies non-lethaly
+Plenty of secrets
+Replayability
+Nice graphics
+Day/night cycle that affects gameplay
+Enemies adapt to your gameplay
+How long enemies stay knocked out depends on how you knock them out

The bad:
-Incomplete and not-so-interesting story
-Hard to select needed items from your inventory
-Limited variety of vehicles, outfits
-Poor vehicle maneuverability
-Desolate world
-No third parties in the game
-One of the maps is hard to navigate
-Credits played for each mission spoil surprises
-Dumbed-down interrogations
-People escaping grabs before you can even press anything
-Boring basebuilding
-Restrictive limits on staff count
-Some grindfest achievements
-Can't pilot helicopters or travel from one area to another quickly with one
-Fast travel exists, but you basically end up in the middle of a base filled with enemies with no checkpoint nearby
-Poor connection to servers for online content
-Cutscenes counted towards mission completion time

Other:
Other players can rob your base, but these days you aren't likely to have to deal with that unless you attack other players or have a nuke.

Sadly, I think MGSV is a highly overrated game. It has a lot of things going for it -- good stealth combat, good graphics for its day, some nice Kojima weirdness -- but the game is also frustrating and a slog at times. Side missions are repetitive and get boring very quickly. Even the main story missions can get annoying from time to time. They mostly consist of assassinating X guy, or rescuing X guy, and they lack variety. When the game shines -- in the intro level -- in your sniper duel with Quiet -- in your battle against giant Mechs -- it can be a lot of fun -- but there's too much nonsense in between the good stuff. The game should have cut about half the missions. While it's an open world game, it's a boring, lifeless open world. There aren't really any NPCs to interact with. No shops, or interesting areas. Afghanistan is just a giant rocky, ugly desert. And while the weapon and gadget variety is astounding you have to slog through side missions to earn enough money to develop the better stuff. And don't get me started on the base management -- you constantly have to scroll through personnel lists to eliminate "troublemakers" who send your soldiers to the infirmary, and you upgrade your base to make new facilities that look... exactly like the other facilities. Your base is boring, generic, and not terribly customizable. If there was a way to put my thumb in the middle, I'd do it, because it's not a BAD game. It's just a frustrating, frequently boring game that has some really spectacular content stuffed in between a lot of filler.

Where to begin. Death Stranding publicity prompted me to finally get started on Ground Zeroes and TPP which loomed large in my back catalogue for some time. Got 20 solid hours out of GZ before finally embarking on TPP. After the slow start and first couple of missions all the systems clicked. When it clicked I was totally hooked. More than 200 straight hours hooked. I’m still hooked. MGS5’s supreme gameplay loop never gets old. Prepping for a mission and dropping into either Afghanistan or Africa with my preferred 80s track playing in the background never gets old. Levelling up Mother Base never gets old. I’ve never played a game that’s kept me fully engaged for this stretch of time. I’m finally getting onto other things not because I’m over MGS5 but because other games need to be played. I’m still dropping back into MGS5 develop items, manage my FOBs, level up my staff, knock off side missions, S-rank and complete all story mission objectives. The mission-based structure and ease of per-mission replayability allows for it. Currently at 80% completion. Gameplay is always touted as the most important thing and MGS5 gameplay is glorious.

Kiefer is excellent as Snake and I prefer him. I like David Hayter’s earlier MGS performances but for me he started overcooking it in MGS3 and it got worse from there. MGS5 story and performances stood up for me though MGS3 remains the standout of the series in this regard. We can see and have had confirmed how unfinished the published MGS5 story is. I’ve gone through most of the cassette tapes where a tonne of plot, revelation and voice acting reside. I liked this method of plot delivery. I’d whack some tapes on while doing side missions or free-roam staff recruiting. The story ending took me by surprise and I’m happy I managed to somehow not cotton onto any spoilers. It’s disappointing the game was cut off but what we got is still incredible.

If I must criticise I’d say adding higher difficulty repeated chapter 1 missions in chapter 2 was bit of a let-down after an amazing in-game chapter 2 preview trailer got me pumped for more. Still greatly enjoyed the previewed character moments during chapter 2 but would’ve dearly loved more new missions instead of the ‘extreme’ repeat mission filler. This is where the game’s rushed ending is evident. I ended up S-ranking these on my first go as completing them under the imposed restrictions generally ensures S-rank anyway.

It’s an easy 10/10 from me and if I’m being objective, taking into account my far and wide enjoyment over hundreds of consecutive hours, I’d have to say it’s my GOAT.

A Masterpiece Forged in Stealth and Storytelling
In Memory of Elena
★★★★★

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain" is nothing short of a modern masterpiece, even nearly a decade after its release. As a continuation of Hideo Kojima's legendary series, it brings a cinematic story, tight mechanics, and an emotional depth that is rarely seen in games today.


A Story of Revenge, Loyalty, and Tragedy
The Phantom Pain, which takes place during the height of the Cold War, puts you in the role of Big Boss, also known as Venom Snake, who, nine years after going into a coma, awakens to seek revenge and reestablish his private military empire. A deep tapestry of betrayal, sorrow, and power weaves across the narrative, as characters like as Snake and Kaz Miller battle their inner demons. You're captivated from beginning to end by the poignant emotional weight of Quiet's silent presence and mysterious past, which adds a depth of tragedy and mystery. Because of the story's dealings with the brutal reality of war and the personal costs of retaliation, it transcends beyond mere gaming to become an immersive experience.

Stealth-Revolutionizing Gameplay
However, the gameplay elements of this game are where it really excels. You can use a variety of strategies to approach tasks because of the open-world layout. Whether you're utilizing heavy artillery to take out foes or sneaking around in the shadows, the gameplay feels fluid, responsive, and really enjoyable. Top-notch stealth mechanics let you outsmart the opposition by utilizing surroundings, camouflage, and even your allies. The game is enhanced with the distinct dynamics of D-Dog, your devoted dog companion, and Quiet, the silent sniper with lethal accuracy. While D-Dog assists you in finding adversaries and traps, Quiet may silently dispatch enemies from a distance, giving gamers a range of tactics to try out.

A Group of Unforgettable Characters
The characters in The Phantom Pain are its core. The legendary Snake is a person whose quiet frequently talks louder than words. Their task is made more emotionally complex by his tense and implicitly loyal relationship with Kaz. Snake's more melancholy, gloomy demeanor contrasts with Kaz's unwavering determination to reconstruct Mother Base and exact retribution. Then there's Quiet, whose quiet conceals one of the game's most poignant narrative threads. These people serve as more than just plot devices; they serve as important pillars that emphasize the game's themes of sacrifice, devotion, and the dubious morality of war.

Various Strategies, Endless Opportunities
Quiet and D-Dog are two examples of the buddies in this game that are more than just entertaining extras; they are essential to the action. The surgical precision of Quiet's shooting transforms how you deal with opponent confrontations, and D-Dog's scouting and threat-marking abilities are crucial. With these allies, you can change your strategy based on the circumstances. Regardless of your preference for stealth or a full-on attack, the game provides an extensive range of tools and strategies to suit your needs. With complete control at all times, the gameplay system has a broad yet personal feel to it.

In conclusion
It's not just a game, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an experience full of memorable moments, tactical mastery, and emotional highs. This game will immerse you in its world and keep you thinking long after the credits have rolled, regardless of your familiarity with the series or the saga. The characters, plot, and gameplay come together to create an immense yet intimate experience. Trust me, if you haven't played this masterpiece yet or are thinking about giving it another go, now is the ideal moment. You won’t regret it.

A Personal Tribute to Elena
Elena and I originally connected via her Steam review of The Phantom Pain. Her comments were what drew me back into the Snake universe and persuaded me to play the PC version of the game again. We were separated by distance—I was in the United States, she was in Russia—but we grew close through our shared passion for video games. Time zones didn’t matter; we’d both make more time by staying up a bit later than usual just to keep chatting about the game. We talked about The Phantom Pain strategies for hours on end, particularly how to use D-Dog and Quiet in different missions and how those decisions affected the gameplay. We talked about more than just that, including old-school Splinter Cell titles and Splinter Cell: Blacklist, as well as Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Despite our remoteness from one another and the difficulties we face in the real world, gaming has become our common language.

In 2021, though, we had a falling out. Elena had passed away by January 2022, but I often miss our late-night conversations. I miss our discussions about our favorite games, our conversations about Metal Gear Solid, and our thoughts about the world during COVID-19. Though we lost touch, I still miss those moments, and I’ll always hold dear the memories of the time we shared, even across the divide of time zones and countries.

I actually 100%-ed the game several years before, but seeing it's on sale on Steam made me did it again :D

Pros:
+ Optimization! the best PC-port optimization I've ever played. The game runs really really well on my graphic laptop even in high settings.
+ The gameplay system. The gameplay is the best in the MGS series. It was quite a departure even from the previous games like MGS4 and MGS:PW it was based on. For example there's now dedicated button for binoculars... making the item an essential piece in sneaking. In previous games, binoculars/scope is merely an item which players almost never used. The gameplay is also very detailed in almost everything that we often find some unexpected stuffs, like how you actually can destroy electrical poles to fall on enemies... and it can electrocute if there's a puddle nearby. Basically enabling even more options in our missions. Truly outstanding technical feat.
+ Animation. Every moves and transitions are smooth and pretty realistic.
+ Cutscenes. Kojima loves movies, and since MGS4 he succeeds to make the cutscenes really feel like a movie.

Cons:
- Story. One of the times where Kojima's antics don't work out. Many elements deviate from the usual MGS but doesn't impress. No more memorable bosses, the concept of parasite and language felt really out of place, and there's barely any connection to the necessity of nuclear and giant walking tank, both of which are the core theme of MGS stories. The storytelling wasn't clear and felt really jumbled. Lack of cutscenes and the cassette tape format only makes things worse. Sure, we can still understand the story through the tapes, but the audio-only format makes it difficult to enjoy. The first chapter of the story is still okay-ish, the second one is weird, and the third one is infamously missing from the game~ making the game feels like a true embodiment of phantom pain
- The villain. After his reveal, he's just not as terrifying as he was intended to, despite how well MGS:GZ built the anticipation of him.
- Soundtrack. Almost nothing is memorable. I prefer the previous composers such as Kazuma Jinnouchi and Akihiro Honda
- Kojima actually pulled another "MGS2" in this game... if you know what I mean.

All in all, despite the heavy negatives, the gameplay itself eclipses them. It is that good, even to the point of addicting. Hell, who ever thought that it'll be that fun to play with balloons and abducting people? Most of the time we go out on a mission exactly just to do that! XD

The Phantom Pain: Abundant gameplay, mediocre storytelling, boring open world

MGSV: The Phantom Pain is the only MGSV I ever played. Before I played Ground Zero, the demo of Phantom Pain, and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance, an ACT title. Not having much knowledge of the previous story, I won't go deep into what was going on before and focus on the Phantom Pain itself.

Ground Zero is not a good narrator of the previous story, and The Phantom Pain does not require you to have a full understanding from previous. Viewed it as a fresh start, a man waked up in the hospital and recruited his crews, becoming a powerful mercenary and warlord taking his vengeance. Plus, with some persons he meets, his adventure is a little bumpy, yet not affecting the main story a lot.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The Phantom Pain is a really fun game to play with abundant gameplay. As a third-person stealth game, you can choose to go stealth without a kill, do stealth kill, go into hardcore fight and massacre or even call airstrike to your enemy. You have lots of ways to play, along with huge weapon and gear choices, and very differentiated buddy you can bring. Depending on what weapons, gears and buddy you choose, what style you like, and what objective of your mission, you have lots of options on your missions, being the reason why I say this game has abundant gameplay. Other than that, it has a looter/farm game mechanism and a big upgrade system, both of which are very easy to master. If it is what you like, you can really lose yourself into it.

However, it has drawbacks. Side op missions are very much similar. They are not easy to get tired of, with abundant gameplay, but indeed they are repetitive. Worse still, this game has two chapters. But after Chapter 1, the dev clearly ran out of budget, causing a very imperfect and incomplete Chapter 2. Basically, missions of Chapter 2 just repeat missions in Chapter 1, with an upgraded hardcore difficulty. They are hard and most of them are far from being enjoyable, given the fact that this game is not really designed to go into hot battles (fight mechanism is not perfectly designed so it is not handy) which you are forced to get into quite often.

[h1]Storytelling[/h1]

Hideo Kojima is a talented director. He is indeed great at creating immersive scenes, making stunning visual effects, and showing intense emotions. Particularly, the Prologue is a work of genius in showing the intention in a meticulous and immersive way that I have never seen in any other games. He shows players lots of cool stuff as well. I guess it is every boy's dream in childhood to have his own secret base and here you have one.

That being said, Hideo Kojima is more of a Michael Bay type of director, who is good at visual but not good at the story. With all due respect, he is not a good storyteller and scores low in the script. The script has some interesting ideas, but it is a mess and the story is incomplete. A significant part of it shows unnecessary and unimportant details, which are useless for the story. There are some logical loopholes in the script as well. For example, [spoiler]why Snake doesn't kill Quiet when they first met, just because she is a girl?[/spoiler] It doesn't make sense as you don't see a very solid reason for it. Another example, [spoiler]why Paz is not dead? I remember she was killed by the bomb from her stomach in Ground Zero.[/spoiler]Anyway, the script is not perfect. As for storytelling, it is bad. For all the characters, there are no characters that are really impressive. You don't see emotions from the characters themselves, but from the scenes and plots created. Such as, [spoiler]in the quarantine area where Snake is forced to kill his comrades,[/spoiler] it is designed to show emotions not from the character but from the environment. It is executed very bad and the emotion seems fake. The only good and genius emotion expressing I have seen in the game is [spoiler]in the part where Quiet[/spoiler] Other than that, the part where [spoiler]Skull Face brags about his plan in a truck[/spoiler] is really bad. Why there is music in the middle? Make it as a CG is so much better.

[h1]Open World[/h1]

It is a boring open world. It is said that the best open-world game so far is the Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, which I did not play. I don't really know how to judge an open world, but as far as I can tell, this game is not a good one. The world is featureless and not impressive. There is no interesting place on the map and you have no desire to explore this static world where everything stops when you are not around. 

There are lots of outposts that block your way and restore when you leave, causing lots of unwanted and annoying crossfire. Full disclosure, I've never played a Metal Gear game prior to this one. So I have no idea as to how it compares or even relates, beyond a nigh-impenetrable block of lore that's equal parts compelling and retarded.
But the gameplay though, THE gameplay. It lies somewhere between poe-faced stark realism and absolute ridiculousness. To wit: I'm so used to dealing with AI that, despite having a light machine gun, will still fire at me in controlled bursts like a sensible person. So imagine my surprise when I was busted by this Russian Rambo fella and that commie bastard unloaded on my ass like a lead dispensary. I hear it's a regular thing for MGS AI to act in surprising ways, counter to other games, and it's on full display here.
And then on the other foot, you can not only hide in a cardboard box, but you can put a picture of some anime girl on it and these dumbasses will come up and ogle the box like a 14-year-old. You can tell your horse (you get a horse) to poop, and it does. And if a jeep drives over it, the jeep will lose control and spill off the road. It's fantastic. Also you can attach what is ostensibly a fulton extraction device to an unconcious soldier, a gun emplacement, a wild animal, a vehicle, a shipping crate, what have you; and watch it pause for a moment and rocket into the air. And if it's a person, with an accompanying and totally understandable shriek of terror. It's not yet ceased being funny.
There's a pretty complex base-building mechanic, which is what all this fultoning serves. It ties directly with what resources you can have and deploy in the field, and so it synergizes well with the primary gameplay loop of sneaking, killing or knocking out, stealing ♥♥♥♥, rinse and repeat.
The endgame is pretty elaborate too, though with the usual dumb Konami ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fare behind LONG waiting times that you can skip with microtransactions, on top of in-game resources that seem to exponentially increase in the endgame. You can also raid other players' bases and steal materiel and personnel, and I would've loved to see it in its heyday, because if the defending player is online, they absolutely can jump into said match to defend it. At that point it's super one-sided and terrifying, as you play a game of cat-and-also-cat with a human player, doing ♥♥♥♥ that decidedly isn't AI-like. On the one hand, you're about boned if it happens, but on the other hand, on the rare occasions that they showed up (and it IS rare nowadays), it was an absolutely terrifying and engaging affair.
Now, the story, from an outsider's perspective, is a complete mess. It doesn't help that it's all Kojima-y, who seems like he's VERY close to understanding what humans are. Like David Cage, if you splashed in a little bit of hallucinogen. It took hours of reading the MGS wiki to understand what in the hell they're on about, but y'know.
Anyway, to sum it all up: dumb story, superb and occasionally meme-worthy gameplay, meh endgame, practically nonexistent meta, get it.

Let me start by saying that this game is both addicting, and agonizing.
Not only do I absolutely love Kojima's storytelling, but I marveled over the limitless feeling of the game. You can customize so much about your weapons and gear, much like previous installments, but you also build up a base for you and your on-hand army of mercenaries, forge bonds and functions with four different allies that you take into combat, and have access to an open world filled with opposing forces, animals to rescue, resources to collect, ruins and bases to explore, weather systems, and some interesting new threats.
As I originally stated, this game is agonizing though, but not for the usual reasons you'd find a game agonizing. This is, as far as I know, the last Metal Gear game Kojima will have ever worked on. 
This isn't so much a problem in function, so much as it is in vision. Most people can't repeat stories in the same way the original storyteller did, much less continue from where the last story left off with the same momentum and passion. That's not to say Konami can't do it without Kojima, but I know they haven't inspired any confidence after Metal Gear Survive.

Don't get into this game expecting to finish it.

On a mechanical level the game is wonderful with countless ways to approach each mission.  The sheer variety of ways you can either take-out or sneak past an enemy are staggering to the point where I feel that in my 40 hours of playing the game I barely scratched the surface.

There are three things that heavily detracted from my enjoyment:
The real-time wait times.  If you want to improve your home base you'll be given a timer you'll need to wait to expire in real-time.  Personally, I think that is a mechanic best left in money-grubbing mobile games.

The second is the god awful, nonsensical story.  I won't attempt to try and explain it because I can't; suffice to say you will spend the first hour of the game crawling on your belly (you don't have a choice, your characters legs are atrophied) and running away from a physic mental patient and a man who can summon flaming unicorns.  Later on full-scale building-sized mechs show up.  

Finally, the repetitive nature of missions.  While you have in your arsenal a near limitless bounty of gadgets and weapons, by the time you reach the second map you'll have been asked to extract the prisoner from the enemy camp so many times that I personally chose to stop playing at Africa.

Pros:

*Improved CQC

*Weapon selection

*Tactics

*Computer combat AI

*Improved characters

*Use of alternate characters other than Venom Snake for game play

Cons:

*Repetitive menial tasks to gain GMP

*GMP (gross military product) is bound to online/offline. If you use GMP to research an item, offline GMP resources are used first, leaving you in the red if you do not remain online. Basically, forcing a player to remain online if they do not want soldiers to desert mother base, lose soldier platform levels, and the ability to research items.

*Cut Scenes do not use selected character; cut scene default is Venom Snake

*Head shrapnel is unrealistic. Real soldiers would be forced into retirement.

*Antagonists lack substance

*PVP is dead. Only seen 3 in there and they were game veterans using gimmicks to win a match.

*NPC auto-missions are capped by PVP. Forward bases of operation are required to achieve more beneficial NPC auto-missions.

I've played this game for a fair amount of time. I enjoy the open world aspect very much. Researching weapons or gear. The buddy system is fun (DD is my favorite buddy). NPC Buddies fulfill a specific role in the game. A horse for travel, a dog for stealth combat, a chopper for air strikes. I enjoy the deployment of vehicles, weapons, gear, and buddies in the field. Air strikes are fun too. As to the possibility of others enjoying this game, I can not say. I've been a fan of Metal Gear since the Nintendo console. Close quarters combat, weapon selection and tactical abilities have all improved over the years. As for the story characters, not so much. I found myself ignoring much of the story line to enjoy the game mechanics. 

The only major drawback I find in this latest and (supposed) final rendition of Metal Gear is the Online and PVP system. Some of the online auto-missions are bound to FOBs (forward operating base). You may think it is not a problem until you try to maintain a FOB. It is difficult to maintain a FOB when other players are destroying what you have built online. Now compound that with the fact everything you obtain online remains online and your offline GMP is used FIRST, with no way to transfer the online items to your offline resource pool. Unless you remain online indefinitely, your GMP will fall in the red. You'll lose research soldiers, access to GMP, and resources gathered while online all for research. As of now I have over a million GMP and resources sitting in my online pool because of the lack of combined resources while offline.

I recommend this game if you like stealth, CQC, and are not dependent upon PVP for enjoyment. I suggest you read the game forums for a more in depth explanation. Ultimately, only you can decide if this game is good for you.

Metal Gear is one of my favourite series. I've played MGS 2, 3  and Peacewalker. This is my favourite out of them all. MGSV takes all the base building and item development from Peacewalker and polishes it. It takes the stealth features honed from each game and refines it. It adds an open world environment for good measure. The story is up to the usual MGS standard: conspiracy wrapped in conspiracy. There are twists you may see coming, or others you do not. 

Gameplay:
Finally do we get the ability to prone crawl and crouch move. Decide what degree of stealth you need. Or throw caution to the wind and sprint. 
There are a variety of vehicles to make movement easier: ranging from jeeps to tanks. 
The open world means gameplay is not limited to missions. The very same map you play missions on can be explored. 
Companions. There are various companions with their own bonuses and equipment. Also a dog companion you can pet. Need I say more?
Base building: Unlike Peacewalker you can walk around the base. When you add a platform you can walk around it. You can also assault your employees (Non-lethal weapons only)
Kidnap soldiers you find on the field and make them work for you. I jest: you can extract people you meet in game to your base. They will then add their talents to Mother Base.
Eliminate your way: Want to slaughter everything in your path? Here's a wide variety of lethal weapons ranging from machine guns to rocket launchers. Want to fight non-lethally? Here's many rubber bullet and tranquiliser weapons. Or just CQC them. CQC is MGS talk for Close Quarters Combat, or slamming your opponent against the nearest object as violently as possible.
Intelligent enemies: MGS AI is generally good. Enemies investigate noises, and report things to command. They will flank you during combat, and bolster their equipment to combat your tactics. (For example, they may deploy helmets to protect soldiers from head shots if you're good at hitting their heads.) They also report to command: if a soldier finds a dead body he will inform the rest of the base and put them into alert. 
Many tools to help you: from the classic cardboard box to a binoculars that marks enemies you have lots of tools to help you. 

If you care about story order, this game takes place just after Peacewalker. It contains spoilers for MGS 3 and Peacewalker. Both are very good games and I'd recommend playing them. But don't let that stop you: MGSV knocks the gameplay of those two out of the park.

Overall I feel this game is a fitting send-off for Kojima. I cannot possibly capture all the nuances in this review. I got it for around ten euro in a sale: it is easily worth several times that.

Played for several hundred hours and more than half a dozen play-throughs on PS4, one of the first games I bought when making the transition to PC.

Both Ground Zeroes and Phantom Pain are two of the most divisive games in the franchise, and rightly so. The treatment of Kojima by Konami and his eventual departure from the company show heavily in Phantom Pain's narrative and design. You can pretty much tell exactly when things got bad. 

The controls for PC are quite a culture shock for someone who's only ever played on consoles, and I had to resist the urge to plug in my controller. I rebind the (Walk/Run) key assignment to the Spacebar and the (Dive) button to the "T" key, as trying to move with WASD and hold the CTRL key is nigh impossible unless you have a digit growing out of your wrist... 

Other than the minor nitpick of swapping the keys to more my liking, the PC versions of this game are the way they're meant to me experienced. My laptop maxed all the graphical settings out, and beholding the visual masterpiece that is the FOX engine's horsepower brought a tear to my eye. Truly a very well rendered and realized game world.

I'd recommend grabbing this on sale, because Konami deserves as little money for their awful treatment of Kojima as possible, but other than that I whole-heartedly recommend this game if you like action/stealth shooter adventure games. It's definitely different than any other MGS game in the franchise, in both good ways and bad. But it's worth a playthrough, both for series fans and newcomers alike.

Possibly my favorite game of all time. 
I could spend hours, days even, talking about Metal Gear Solid and this game in particular. How it feels to run around as a random mercenary in his appropriately camouflaged undies, terrorizing the poor PMC conscripts of central Africa with your highly customized, shotgun-shells-firing assault sniperrifle which you exclusively use to point at people's back so they go "Oh shi.., don't shoot", only for them to watch helplessly as you proceed to attach a self-inflating balloon to some random cargo container before riding it back to your mobile home, a neon-pink Apache attack-helicopter that you outfitted to blast ghetto music to weaken the enemy's morale.
The game is wild. And it doesn't lie about "offering you tactical freedom to carry out open-world missions."
If you need a TL;DR about it, this sentence is all you need: it's the single best description to what MGS:V is at it's core. 

It is - ultimately - one of the most flexible and solidly executed pieces of work ever in terms of raw gameplay. Every single weapon, item and tool has it's merits. Everything has one to several hidden mechanics and applications waiting for you to explore them. The gameplay is, in my opinion, the pinnacle of action/stealth thus far. Period. 
Going on a nuclear rampage with your self-replacing, exploding rocket arm is as legitimate as crawling past unaware guards in a sandstorm at nighttime while wearing camouflaged fatigues. The choice is yours.
The gameplay is rewarding, intricate and smooth to no end. MGS:V-TPP falls flat in many ways, but gameplay is none. If TPP has anything, it's gameplay. And in times where developers like to put out unfinished half-assed attempts at games, TPP at least got this done. I respect that.

The progression is ... hm. I like it. Many other's don't, which is fair. You have to find and unlock blueprints for new weapon designs while increasing both your physical resources in terms of money and materials as well as your army's numbers to develop them - and you need enough resources to deploy them in the field. It's an interesting mechanic that adds depth to the game - which is why I personally enjoy it.
 
Also, the PC port is amazing. My potato garbage dumpster fire craptop could handle it with ease while still having it look good visually. 

Where there is praise, there are also negatives ... which are mostly everything else, to various degrees between neutral and bad. 

The story, oh dear... Story is one of the most important aspects in every MG game, and this one really doesn't hold up in that regard. 
I believe it's common fact by now that the story isn't finished, and you really do feel it. The story lacks from serious communication problems. Sometimes, you just don't know what's going on even though the game practically shoves it into your face. Some elements on the other hand are so stupidly subtle that you don't even recognize them unless your perception check happened to hit an imaginary number. 
It's too much talking and too little telling, effectively. Unlike in older Metal Gears, where exposition was tied to critical information, everything here develops in a sort-of linear fashion with story missions happening in the order you choose them. All of which deliver a lot of talk, but don't tell you a lot.
 
The game's tone is jaded and gritty, which works for the story it tries to tell, but ultimately felt exhausting to follow for prolonged time. Take a shot whenever Miller mentions revenge or Cipher. You'd be the one in a nine-year-coma even before the game has really started.  
TPP only really hits the nail once in terms of atmosphere. Once. Which is the sad negative record of the franchise. 
Ironically, MGS:V - Ground Zeros is a far better Metal Gear in this regard, as it tells a story while featuring the grim, oppressive atmosphere, sense of urgency and permanent feeling of anxious paranoia which every Metal Gear tries to achieve to various degrees. TPP, however, has an interesting but mediocre story to tell and outright fails at the story-telling aspect.
The dev team and the community (myself included)  came, after their collective hand-wringing, to the silent cope that the feel of having it unfinished is what "The Phantom Pain" ultimately truly means. It's up to the player to decide that.

The biggest issue I personally have, going along the lines of "phantom pain", is that I see wasted potential. The game, and I'm not exaggerating with this, has the potential to be one of the best if not THE best game of all times. Sadly, you are restricted to two different sandboxes == maps that allow you a lot to try but not much to do. The online experience does provide another aspect and experience to the game, but it's fairly hard to get anywhere without having another friend on standby. You can invade their Forward Operation Base, or they can invade one of yours. Nothing else. No coop, nothing - which is an incredible waste; MG:Survive did it in the same engine. Why not implement it into the original game, too? 

One particular thing that you need to consider with this game is it's repetitiveness. The basic cycle, while enjoyable and extremely flexible, at one points boils down to scout - infiltrate - reach objective - exfiltrate. It requires you to set your own goals, which gatekeeped a lot of people I feel. Paired with the progression mechanic I mentioned above, the game is prone to feel like a grindy chore at times where you'd only try to accumulate resources to unlock the next thing. And here it is at this point - the point where people feel like "so I just go in, tranq everybody, go out and that's it?" - where many players dropped the game.
In order to enjoy it, you need to set your own goals. Be prepared to do so, because once the fresh feeling of the first 5-10 hours wears off, you will need it. 

So yeah. That's MGS:V. There's still so much more to talk about, but I've edited this review already once and I don't want to go on eternally. Browse other comments and form your own opinion, but I do recommend giving it a go either way.

At the end of the day, the game is what it is. An amazing, stupid, powerful and strange little sandbox that could've been much more, but also could've been much much worse. 
It's best to enjoy what we have instead to mourn what could've been, in my opinion. 

So, all in all: 
MGS:V - TPP is not a good Metal Gear, but a good game. 
I found it best to enjoy it once in a while instead of playing the fück out of it. Keeps it fresh and allows you to relax while sneaking around unaware Soviet goons while wearing a stupid cardboard box over your head.

This is one of those games which I would really give neutral review if that was an option. Some missions in this game are really well thought out, and some are just really boring and repetitive. This game has mostly really confusing story. In fact this whole franchise has one of the most confusing and complex storyline out there to understand. 
At the second chapter this game hits a new low. it reintroduces SAME OLD missions and just makes them harder, barely adding any new content you to play and understand better the lore behind this game. I actually think that chapter 2 is mostly old missions which many of them you are required to beat to get the ''real ending'' after chapter 1. Even after this real ''ending'' this game has still a LOT to explain about certain events and characters, but the game just ends. I have heard that konami had cut content from the original game and didn't give kojima enough time/resources to finish this game properly. So there's that. 

Now about the gameplay... I think that this game has solid and fun gameplay with really nice weapons and vehicles, but I must say that vehicle physics are awful in this game. Vehicles and weapons look really nice and they become super helpful especially at the end of this game. Stealth works quite well and you have good control over your character and items you handle.

AL is bad tho, because sometimes AI can't see/notice you even at a close distance without cover, But sometimes AI can see you at a great distance. This is really annoying because you are not entirely sure how the AI ​​will react to your movements and at what distance.
visually the game is spectacular. The game also has good sounds and voice acting, and the animations are well done. The cutscenes are well made in this game in my opinion, although sometimes certain cutscenes can be quite ''cheesy'' and ''scripted ''

I also think  that there's way too much fanservice and grind. I've already explained this  grind aspect earlier in this review but here's some other things wrong about that grind. For example if you want good weapons and enough resources to upgrade your base and arsenal, you have to do quite a lot of side quests and other extras. I don't mind if the grind is '' fun'' but I mean it's mostly really boring grind that you ''just have to do''.
Now about fanservice... I mainly mean Quiet, because I think the reason why Kojima put her in this game was to create some sort of '' waifu '' -like character that the player could cling to because of his ''appearance''. Quiet constantly plays a certain kind of shy but at the same time tough (in my opinion) half-naked woman in the game, which you can take on tasks and missions. Quiet does add certain aspects to the story, but I think there were a lot of plot-holes in that character, especially at the end. For me the fanservice was too over the top in this game and ''cringey''. 

In my mind this game is fine if you can get past these things in game. HOWEVER, this game IS NOT 10/10 game, because some people say that this game can be and is 10/10 game. For me that's just too big rating for game like this. It has OK-ish story, which is really confusing and hard to follow, repetitive story missions and side missions, really awful grind and fanservice. Even AI can be iffy in this game sometimes and for a stealth game you must have a good AI to let player feel like they are in fact playing proper stealth game with good and smart AI. This game has some of those aspects, but not all. 
Sometimes I felt that these negative aspects are just too overwhelming to me to give this game thumps up, and sometimes I felt like this game has it's downsides, but it was still interesting enough for me to beat this game. However, I will give this game thumps down because I feel like this game has too many major negatives to give this game a thumbs up. If Steam had neutral review option, I would give this game a neutral at the moment I am writing this review.

Somehow manages to be an amazing game while also managing to be a soul crushing letdown for any MGS fan. Though it has its moments when you can tell there had at one point been a grand vision in place, this is an unfinished product through and through, and will likely be the last sliver of genuine promise for this series going forward for obvious reasons to anyone who knows the controversy behind the scenes. I love this game, while also lamenting what it could have been. But I've also made my peace with what it is, and that thing is still something that I've lovingly given a great deal of my time to.

The repetition in the side missions can get monotonous if you're chasing a specific type for some reason, but the variety of them when you just go roaming across one of the maps bouncing from one op to the next is entertaining.  After finishing the last of the main story missions (which I'm still not sure was a middle finger from Kojima to Konami or simply a lack of time/funds) I kept playing the game for another dozen or two hours enjoying free roaming before I finally uninstalled it.

I enjoyed the game up until this point. I felt like starting a new game so I did then when I finally understood what was going on I realized that all my online data did not reset and at the beginning of my game I saw that I have over 100million gmp and thousands of resources available. So I dug through forums and such and nobody seems to know that you can't actually start from scratch once you have beaten the game. In this regard the game has no replayability and I do not recommend it until or if ever they decide to fix this heap of steaming dog sh**!
