You know how every school has these cool kids, with whom practically everybody wants to be their friends? When you finally get the chance to befriend these cool kids, you don’t find them as great as you’ve heard. They’re nice and of course, cool. Yet, despite popular opinion, you can only see yourself as their acquaintance. For me, [I]Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain [/I] is that group of cool kids.

The [I]Metal Gear Solid [/I] series is undeniably cool. If it were not, it would not have stood a chance given the ridiculous names of its games and characters, the convoluted yet intriguing storylines, and the outlandish mix of military action, stealth, science fiction and fantasy. A game, let alone a game series, with these qualities should not have worked. Yet, under the meticulous direction of Hideo Kojima, it improbably did.

Up until [I]Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes [/I], I’ve never played a [I]MGS[/I] game as I am primarily a PC gamer. [I]GZ[/I] allowed me to finally appreciate Kojima’s craftsmanship and artistry firsthand on the PC, and [URL= https://steamcommunity.com/id/CharlieLima79/recommended/311340/]I really enjoyed it[/URL]. Needless to say, [I]GZ[/I] got me excited about what [I]TPP[/I] would deliver.

[U][B]What I Liked[/B][/U]:
[I]TPP[/I] has stunning, photorealistic graphics. The stealth action in the main missions are intense, with each set piece designed to encourage you to devise your own plans for infiltration and exfiltration. The cutscenes are cinematic and of high production value. [I]TPP[/I] is without a doubt an ambitious and loaded game that invites you to spend time with it, bit by bit.

[U][B]And Yet…[/B][/U]:
It pains me to profess that [I]TPP[/I] is not the game for me. If it just features what I just mentioned, it would be easy for me to praise it to no end. Instead, what I experienced was a bloated stealth action game that also includes open world exploration, base-building, resource gathering and management, and online multiplayer. Because I’m not a fan of the latter three, I found a good part of [I]TPP[/I] tedious because base-building, and resource gathering and management are obligatory.

[U][B]But First…[/B][/U]:
Let me state unequivocally that the stealth action in [I]TPP[/I] is spectacular. It has been fine-tuned for optimal challenge and excitement. I love this part of [I]TPP[/I], and I wish there was more of it in the first 20 hours of gameplay, during which I completed the prologue, the first 8 main missions, and at least 10 side ops. Yet, I feel like I’ve spent more time than I had liked on tasks that are superfluous to the stealth action gameplay that I expected.

I want to describe a few aspects of [I]TPP[/I] that irked me most, ones that I wished I knew about before purchasing it. If you believe I’m wrong, or at least you can accept these shortcomings anyway, just know that I’m still recommending [I]TPP[/I] because the stealth action bits are truly fun.

[U][B]Open World[/B][/U]:
As an open world game, [I]TPP[/I] is disappointing. With the setting being a rocky, hilly desert in Afghanistan, there are hardly unique locations to explore like in most other open world games. The wide, mostly barren landscape is dotted with small outposts and makeshift bases occupied by enemies, joined by pretty much a single road and the occasional slightly hidden canyon path. With your enemies ready to shoot on sight, open world exploration is hardly a carefree experience.

You can travel from A to B by helicopter as means of fast travel, but it’ll cost you money and is actually not that fast. There are a lot of cinematics that accompany this fast travel, likely because the game uses them to hide its loading times. After watching these cinematics several times, the whole process got tiresome. 

[U][B]Pacing[/B][/U]:
Many open world games have uneven pacing, mainly because the players are likely distracted by all the side missions and hidden discoveries that the games offer. Given that, open world games should have main missions that are varied and that will move the story along at a brisk pace. Unfortunately, [I]TPP[/I] does not.

The prologue/tutorial of [I]TPP[/I] is exciting, with hardly any moment for you to breathe or let the chaos sink in. It’s a grand way to open up a game, but that was the last time I experience that type of excitement 20 hours into the game. Once the proper game begins, the pace is much slower. I was constantly waiting for the next big action set piece, but it never came.

This game is also very repetitive, and its side ops feel like work because in many ways they are. Side ops are obligatory because you need to collect resources in forms of personnel, blueprints, and materials to build your private army, develop new weapons, and expand your Mother Base. In the first 20 hours, I revisited the same locations 2 to 3 times. Although the time of day, weather conditions, and enemy patrol patterns might have differed, I was still in the same locations and not visiting anywhere new.

After my first 15 hours of playing [I]TPP[/I], I found myself still in the Afghanistan desert. It’s only then that I realized I’d be stuck in Afghanistan pretty much forever. (Perhaps it’s a sly commentary by Kojima?) I was still sneaking into outposts occupied by Russian armed forces to clandestinely recover X (usually weapons or weapon blueprints) or extract Y (usually a prisoner or a skilled person who can benefit my private army).

You would think, for a game that has 31 main missions, over 150 side ops, as well as post-game missions, there would be more to see 20 hours in. Yet, given all the time and effort I’ve invested, I’m reportedly at 7 to 8% completion. For game that has this much content, a little more variation to its gameplay and setting to keep things interesting would have been appreciated. At the very least, [I]TPP[/I] could have moved the story along.

[U][B]Too Much Other Stuff[/B][/U]:
The repetitiveness is made worse by all the other stuff that you can/have to do in the game. In between missions and side ops, I found myself:
[LIST]
[*]searching for fuel, minerals, rough diamonds, etc.
[*]building new platforms to expand my Mother Base
[*]reassigning staff in my army to optimize efficiency
[*]researching and develop new weapons
[*]listening to many mission cassette tapes so the game can fill me in on [I]MGS[/I] lore and world history
[*]picking herbs
[*]rescuing wild animals
[*]stealing music cassette tapes
[*]collecting posters
[/LIST]
That’s right, all of the above is part of [I]MGS[/I]’ tactical espionage action. Fun.

The game also encourages you to return to Mother Base regularly to boost your soldiers’ morale. You do that by going up to each of them so they can salute you. The soldiers are scattered throughout the many platforms that you can build, which you can “quickly” travel to by driving or by hailing a helicopter. Tactical espionage action indeed.

[U][B]Final Thoughts[/B][/U]:
In the end, [I]TPP[/I] is not the game I expected. The fantastic core stealth game is surrounded by too much clutter for me to enjoy it properly. I now find myself appreciating [I]GZ[/I] more because it’s a leaner, no-nonsense stealth action game. I also find the level design of Camp Omega in [I]GZ[/I] to be more stellar than what I’ve seen so far in [I]TPP[/I].

Now that you’ve taken time to read why I like and dislike some parts of [I]TPP[/I] (thank you), I hope you can make an informed decision about whether or not to buy or try this game. Chances are, if you’re an [I]MGS[/I] fan, you’re likely to give it a go anyway. However, if you’re unfamiliar with the game series or are new to it like me, I hope you’ll enjoy it more than I did.

METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is an open world third person stealth (optional) game. It is a combination of a movie and a video game, it got hours of cutscenes and the lore is more complex than any other video game or movie i know. I am not a big fan of lore in games and sometimes i just skip it and go straight after the gameplay, but it is not the same for this game. It made me read lots of long wiki pages on some characters, organizations and places (Do not do the same before completing the game for your own good. Spoilers are not fun).
The gameplay is great, as i mentioned earlier the stealth is optional and it can be played and enjoyed by loud and ruthless players too. It is a really long game so it is worth your money 3 or 4 times more than the average AAA title without counting replayability. There are a lot of options in weapons, vehicles and backup and you can choose one of the 4 available buddies to help you in your mission. Each buddy has different abilities that you unlock by increasing the bond level (which is also pretty easy, just don't let them get hurt and order them to do stuff a lot). The enemies also get small upgrades along the story, you have to change your techniques if they don't work anymore and i find this a great way of stopping the gameplay from being repetitive. I personally finished all the main missions and a few side ones in 100 hours and still have some other side missions and new difficulty ones to do. There are FOB raidings too, pretty much the only online part that is still alive. MGS online seems dead, couldn't find anyone to try it out with. FOB missions are about invading player bases for stealing resources and crew, its cost is that if you fail or get spotted the one invaded knows who you are and can invade back.
The graphics are pretty damn good and the optimization is great, i ran it on almost max settings with stable 60 fps (capped) on GTX 1050 4GB (laptop), i5-8250U and 8GB RAM DDR4. My laptop didn't even make a lot of noise and it didn't get very hot, so if you got a similar system i bet you can run it on max easily. The soundtrack is nice and there are featured licensed songs released in the early '80s, which is good for the game's atmosphere, since that is when the story takes place. There are a lot of menus in this game, they look good and have satisfying sound effects.
 
There are parts i didn't like too. The helicopter takes too much time artificially. After doing a mission you are all bloody and want to go to Mother Base and take a shower. You have to call the helicopter, wait for it, get in, wait for it to traver long enough so you would close its door, wait for the game to load and press a button, use your idroid and go to mother base, wait for the loading screen again to press a button, waiting for it to get down and FINALLY getting out of the helicopter. It takes too much time and you can't do something else meanwhile, because you still need to press a few buttons. If you want to get to other platforms of the Mother Base you have to drive there in a vehicle. The road is too long and again, you can't do other stuff while doing it, maybe listening to cassettes at best. There is no reason for them to be this long, i think the road to other platforms should be at least half as long.
The upgrades take too much time. I understand it would be ridiculous to upgrade weapons instantly, but it goes from instantly for low tier to 18m, 36m, 1 hour and a few minutes, a few hours and to my surprise, one weapon that i didn't really need, but that i upgraded only because i had money made me wait 4 days. If i really wanted that gold tier heavy machine gun i would be pissed off badly.
The DLCs are ridiculous, at how much content there is in this game they are almost nothing and shouldn't cost money, yet they do. I never used the suits, i have them only because the bundle that included Ground Zeroes had them too and was only a few dollars more. Honestly there is no reason to buy them, you're wasting money.
The main story wasn't finished, Snake gets robbed of his secret weapon by an annoying brat and you don't get to see him again. If that scene wasn't in the game i would consider it complete, it's like starting a new chapter and leaving it after the introduction.
You see credits everywhere. Even if you don't want you will remember Hideo Kojima's name. At the start of every mission you will see his name credited, then some other credits for the people that made the missions. I think they did a great job making this game but i'd rather have all the credits at the end of the game only. I guess it's just his ego.

The man who sold the world. Kojima has once again crafted a masterpiece of both a story as well as introducing the idea of a bigger threat then your traditional nukes and looks at language. Now some may see this game as unfinished as the situation between Kojima productions and Konami went for a deep s*** around the time this game was getting released. However if you are willing to look past all that you will find a well fleshed out story that connects in interesting ways to the previous games.

At the games core this is a third person shooter with your usual mixture of cover, shooting and stealth mechanics. This game provides players plenty of ways to both play it fast and loud or quiet and sneaky. What's great is the amount of freedom this brings to the gameplay in that you can adapt to the situation on the fly without the need to worry unless you are going for the S ranks in which case the sneaky way is your best friend but still. The option to go loud is there if you feel you must go that route. Just be ready as cover isn't always plentiful out there in the wild open world map. So make sure you are ready if you choose to do that. One of the unique things is that this game allows you to take along a buddy so to speak in missions. Now these have to be unlocked over the course of the game and you cannot take a friend along. These buddies take the form of a horse, a dog, a sniper and a robot. All of which can be custumized to an extent. You can also take people and animals home back to your base via ballon. Which lets say can be quite funny at times.

At the end of the day this game can be quite fun and for what you pay you can easily get around 50hrs+ in terms of gameplay and missions to take part in. While some may feel this game in incomplete it does have plenty of a moments that  may stay with you after the credits have rolled. Highly recommended.

There is a lot to be said about the game. It's a game that doesn't really need to exist, and maybe shouldn't exist. The MGS story was pretty much wrapped up with MGS4, and just like that game, this one's got some controversial contents (I'm looking at you, story). Story aside, the gameplay of MGSV is really REALLY fun. This is a big game with lots of optional side missions and a some decent sized open world environments. There's a buddy system where you can bring an AI partner with you. The partners range from a horse (good for traversal), a sniper (good for backup), and a Dog (my favorite). The partner system is a lot of fun and very useful for the many missions you'll be going on. The game play is solid, but how about that story? So, the story is kinda fun but kinda dumb at some points, but also kinda cool sometimes. That pretty much sums up a lot of MG stories. I should mention for those of you who are unfamiliar with this game's development, the game is somewhat unfinished. And what I mean by that is that the game and the story just kinda end abruptly. Unfortunately, there was some development troubles, but the game is still bery fun and playable in its current state. You can easily spend many hours playing and enjoying this game. It's pretty different from past Metal Gear games, but it's (in some ways) a nice upgrade and also a nice alternative to the MGS norm. If you've never played a Metal Gear game, I highly recommend them! You could start with MGS1 or MGS3. MGS2's story is very reliant on MGS1, so definitely wait to play that one until after MGS1 (MGS4 is the same way). That being said, MGSV is also a fine way to enter the world of Metal Gear, just remember that this game, despite still being a stealth game, is pretty different from the rest. Definitely check it out when it goes on sale sometime!

In spite of a flawed, incomplete, and inconclusive ending, MGSV is the logical evolution of the franchise's formula that gives you more freedom and options than any game prior. Each mission zone feels less like they're a spot in an open world map, and more like a microcosm of the MGS gameplay loop. It's hard to even perceive MGSV as an open world game because there's only two maps, and the way enemy NPCs and structures are set up in hot zones makes it feel like I'm playing a prior MGS in condensed bites.

However, because this is a Kojima joint, it's got his token style of over-the-top sci-fi military fantasy that's been an obvious staple since MGS2 (when things got the most obtuse they've ever been). The first Part's villain is undercooked in spite of his charisma, and I feel that his VA is miscast. The second Part has no villain, and it was meant to but Konami is a troubled entity to say the least. The new Metal Gear Sahelanthropus has stylistic cues that reach both forward and backwards (because this game is the final prequel), but some of the tech that's in it feels like a pseudo-retcon because it never shows up again. The big twist at the end feels like a convoluted attempt to make the canon of two MSX2 games made in the 1980s more sensible, even though most people don't care.

If you can get over the hamfisted, excessive script, MGSV has the best gameplay in the series.

MGSV is an absolute masterpiece of a game, and totally deserves all the praise it gets. It's fun, it's really weird, and it will keep you busy for many hours without getting stale. There are a few areas to complain about, mainly a few BS missions and an unfinished second act, but all that pales in comparison to the good on display here. This was my first Metal Gear game, but I found it actually quite approachable as a newcomer to the series. This is a must-play for pretty much anyone.

Visually the game is top-notch. It goes for ultra-realism, with great facial animations, lighting and textures. The fact that this real-looking world also includes things like giant robots and ghostly soldiers just adds a kind of quirk you don't get from other games. The audio is also very good, and it can help you out a lot when you're trying to make your way around undetected. The visuals and audio combine to make the kind of atmosphere where you're transported to Big Boss' shoes and can just enjoy inhabiting this world. It's hard to describe, but when you're out in the countryside (probably doing silly things like sleep-darting wild donkeys) and are scoping out the base you want to infiltrate, you really feel like you're there and part of it.

Now, the gameplay and feel are really where this game shines. It's so polished it's ridiculous, with all kinds of little systems and details in play that can impact the way you play. Maybe you usually do your missions at night, and like head-shotting guards with your sleep darts. Next time, they might have night vision goggles and helmets. Sneaking around feels great, and it's fairly forgiving if you make a little mistake. If you're seen, you have a few seconds of slow-time to respond appropriately, usually with a sleep dart to the face. That said, it's not always a walk in the park; timing and boldness pay off big time. There are a few parts where your approach needs to differ completely based on the mission, and sometimes it takes some trial and error before you figure it out. Some of the story missions were quite challenging, too. Aside from the stealth, there is a pretty involved meta-game of building up your base, supplies and private army. You collect objects and people with a "Fulton" device, which attaches a powerful balloon to the object and shoots it into the sky (hilarious when you do it to people). There is a whole multiplayer segment of the game which I mostly stayed away from, but some people can spend hundreds of hours just on that. The possibilities in this game are vast and various.

The story, while often totally absurd, is generally very interesting. It immediately hits you with mystery after mystery in the opening segment, and just when you think you're maxed out on WTF, it dumps your into this huge sandbox and says "go play!" Eventually the plot opens up a bit and you learn your place in all this chaos, but it's teased out in a way that keeps you pushing to know what's next. The story does of course falter in Chapter 2, in that most of the "story" missions become re-treads of previous missions with challenging modifiers, but these are actually optional. There are still a few new missions, and I enjoyed them. A lot of the story is told through audio tapes, so you can actually get parts of the dialog while you're still out doing things, which is nice. Some people say the story is bad, and I can't really judge based on other Metal Gear games, but I definitely enjoyed the characters, the ridiculous and cinematic cutscenes, the weirdness, and the general direction of the plot.

My biggest gripes were just a couple of sticking points. There is one part that involves going through your whole army list and separating some of them out, one by one. Since I had like 800 guys by this point, it took me a solid 30+ minutes of just scrolling down and occasionally hitting a button. It... was... terrible. Also, if you leave a mission area by mistake, there is no confirmation given and you can pass the point of no return very fast. I was running away on horseback from a giant robot at the end of one mission, and accidentally crossed over the invisible line. It abandoned the mission instantly and I lost a good 90 minutes of time I put into sneaking around. That really made me mad. They didn't ruin the experience, but things like that occasionally just made me question some of the design decisions.

Overall, MGSV holds a spot among the best open world games, stealth games, and video games in general that are out there. If you're on the fence, just take the plunge. I am very glad I took the time, and you will be too.

This game is simultaneously the best Metal Gear Game and a somewhat bad Metal Gear Game. 

From a gameplay perspective, this is one of the finest stealth action games ever crafted. The systems that make up the base game such as sneaking, combat, cqc, pretty much everything that makes a Metal Gear game good are present in tight form. Add onto that an enormous tree of new toys that can add variety to your game, and you have some satisfying as hell stealth gameplay. There's also a base system that incentivizes silently capturing strong guards instead of just going in guns blazing. Really fun, 10/10.

From a story perspective, this game is one of the worst Metal Gear games. It is clear that this game is unfinished with missing final missions that could help complete the story, but are unfortunately absent. While the moment to moment storytelling is still cinematic and interesting, the overarching plot doesn't really go anywhere. Without spoiling specifics, this game really ends for no reason. The final mission shows up randomly and doesn't have anything to do with plot events occurring in game.

Now it is totally possible that Hideo, being the mad genius that he is, purposefully left out the final chapter of this game after having teased it in earlier trailers. Much like how the ending of Metal Gear Solid 2 left you wanting for more at the time, but in retrospect has been analyzed and shown for the incredible ending that it is. It would make sense, as the themes of this game involve feeling the pain of something lost that once was there (I mean the game is called The Phantom Pain, in allusion to the feeling that amputees still have even after their limb is gone). It's possible that Kojima knew of his inevitable firing from Konami, and wanted the player to feel that emptiness in the gameplay. I'm sure in 10 years we will all have some newfound appreciation for this game and its themes, but for those just wanting a surface level story, the game leaves me wanting.

I'd recommend you play this game for the gameplay alone, as it is possible the single best example of freedom in a stealth game ever. Ignore the story, or pay attention to it once and then leave it alone as you do missions and you will certainly have a great time with this game. 

I give it a Perfect for the Gameplay, and an Almost Good for the Story.

[h1]Mistakes only make it more fun[/h1]

[b]The Good[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Absolute Game Play[/b] - As I said, 'mistakes only make it more fun'. I enjoy the game best when I screw up and everything turns to crap. I start to improvise and am always impressed on what the game lets me get away with. This is when the MGSV shines.  
[*][b]Deep Armory[/b] - I was impressed with the selection of weapons and tools you're allowed to choose from and bring into a mission. This contributed to the fun I had in the game, as I got to experiment with the toys they let me have.  
[*][b]Mission Design[/b] - Strictly talking about the main missions and a few critical side missions, their design delivers maximum fun. Having me move to places to complete my objective, or an event/ twist that completely flips my situation are more than welcome. 
[/list]

[b]The Bad[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Chapter 2[/b] - I'm currently working on Chapter 2, and I noticed that its got me repeating missions at higher difficulty. So I did some research, and learned that Chapter 2 contains 19 missions, 12 of which are repeats. This feels like padding / fillers. Seems like they were trying to hit a certain amount of hours of game play for chapter 2 to make it out of the door. Luckily the game play is really good so maybe, I just might do these to get to the stories of some of the other characters in the game.
[*][b]Vertically Challenged[/b] - MINOR ISSUE here, I think the level design could do with a bit more of vertical design. The entirety of the game will have you infiltrating wide flat spaces. To be honest though, I would imagine facilities of these nature, to look like how they're designed in the game, flat and wide. So why ask for verticality?? - To vary the game play and challenges of course! We've got giant robots, psychics, and a living burning man, so might as well get liberal with some of the level design. 

[/list]

[b]The Recommendation[/b]

Given that Chapter 1 is a bigger part of the game, and Chapter 2 is just a handful of missions with most of which are re-do's, I'd give this game an 8/10. I can look past recycled missions because of good game play, varied mission designs and generous story telling. 
[b]8/10[/b]

TL;DR: Game is great, something everyone should sample. My personal issues with the game lie within somewhat abrupt ending and some problems with game design. A strong 7/10 even if I'm being rough on the game.

 Level design feels great. There are a lot of different ways to go about solving majority of the missions -- go in guns blazing, sneak, let your allies do the work or all at once. Weather and time of day will play a huge part in how you approach the mission, and I enjoyed how seamlessly it's integrated. The freeroam world often sadly feels like a filler. You can collect animal species and capture outposts, but personally I saw traversing the map as a nuisance rather than a feature. This opens up a lot of grind for post-endgame though. The control over character felt very fluid once I got used to the keybindings. The terrain interaction is another issue. Often you can't get up some slopes that should be passable. You'll see a lot of this in the wild, restricting your movement or limiting your options. Shooting felt a little off for me as well, which is why I resorted to CQC and buddies majority of the time. I absolutely loved how customizable everything feels by the way, feels like there's almost too much to choose from. 

Story. Not going to spoil anything too specific. The story finally got its claws in me somewhere after the tenth mission, and kept going pretty strong until the end of chapter 1 which was an entire story on its own. It felt really packed and tight. Chapter 2 had some really memorable moments that I will absolutely cherish, but the story just... ended? You get a bunch of recycled challenge missions during chapter 2 and the new story missions are pretty much drip-fed to you which I heavily disliked. It's just a shame The Phantom Pain didn't get more closure as a whole when it came to the storylines. That being said, I love the method of telling the player (extra) background story in ambiguous cassette tapes, filling in gaps where necessary. The cutscenes are also amazingly directed, camerawork especially stands out. 

Furthermore on the cassette tapes - I'm a sucker when it comes to 80's music and you can actually collect some of the hits in the vast open world and listen to them while playing. Thought that was a pretty cool addition to have. The soundtrack as a whole really suits the game and is totally worth listening on its own. Shortly on other aspects of the game - graphics look good, the game also ran really well on my rig that was bottlenecked by my CPU. The locations didn't look exactly stellar, but were quite memorable. There are microtransactions to buy some in-game currency. Overall they don't impact your experience too much (I had no use for them whatsoever) and you sometimes even get them for free so I didn't almost bother to mention it.

Overall I was really amazed by the possibilites and the worldbuilding and gripped by story, It's a shame a lot of what I liked fell off towards the end though and caused my last 10-15 hours to turn into a slog. In the future I'll probably look at the game in a very positive light though as those flaws don't really distract from the whole experience as a whole, so there's that.

MGS:V is a great example of a AAA game made with heart and love. I've played this game on and off for a while and very little of it disappoints. That isn't to say it doesn't have problems of its own despite this.

For one thing, combat is a little awkward, and stiff. This game was designed probably intended to be played on the controller, and the autoaim seems to cause problems for anyone playing by keyboard and mouse. Sure it delivers better movement and control over the game, but the stiff aiming makes it difficult to play out as that sort of action man. The controls are good, and even great sometimes, but they suffer from being intended for controller. Driving around in any vehicle that isn't the horse or the D-Walker is problematic, and I never can get around to making smooth turns or maneuver around common obstacles like rocks or tree's that are littered all over the maps in the game.

The gameplay besides that is great though. Carries a fun loop of going to the objective, checking everyone to decide which character gets to be in your personal army with their special skills, before going in and doing all that before completing the objective. It's organic, natural gameplay in a way surpasses MGS:3 in its own competing strength. The stealth itself is very fun as well, smooth and enjoyable. Though I wouldn't recommend trying to get an S rank on every mission you encounter the first run through. It requires a perfect stealth with no kills, and you'd have to have good knowledge of the mission to even attempt this safely. It is however very satisfying, even in the second or seventeenth run through. Though again, charging in with combat in mind is still awkward on its own due to the aforementioned PC controls.

And as someone who's never played an MGS game, this game is good as a primer to the proceeding events of the story... I think. I dont follow overly complicated story lines, and I wouldn't recommend thinking too hard about it unless you want to undergo the insanity that is Hideo Kojima's writing. It isn't terrible, it gets interesting up to a point in the early twenty missions, but from what I've heard in what I played, it's even weaker than every other MGS game released. As far as I understand, this game was sadly affected in a negative light due to Konami completely ruining Kojima and having some of the story cut. The story boards and voice acting can be found online for this sort of missing chapter of the game, but if you're here for story, I advise you be warned for it to cut halfway through.

All in all, the game itself is wonderful to play rather than invest in. It's core loop is fun and creative with how it plays. The stealth action and the base management all compliment each other, and even features base raiding down the line once you play enough of the game. Even with a cut story, it is something I'd recommend. It's sales usually go pretty low, which makes it worthy of a buy down the line. It's hard for me not to recommend this game, because when I end every session feeling like I did something significant and accomplishing with a smile on my face, then it is worth.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is my favorite MGS game. The open world helps this game stand out from other MGS games where there were often singular areas where one could travel. The replay ability is very high with side-ops in the open world that can be done any time. I've had fun completing them even after the main story as there are so many options for how to use complex weapons/tools in them.

[b] Positives [/b]
+ Outstanding gameplay - I think it's second to none in the stealth-action genre. The amount of true freedom to tackle missions is on par with or better than Zelda: Breath of the Wild, rivaling Hitman's legendary sandbox design laser-focused on player choice. Getting the elusive 'S' rank on missions is also a rewarding experience that makes you feel like a Boss!
+ The controls are on point. Snake handles like a dream, and the animation transitions are godlike!
+ Smart and challenging AI. How the AI adapts to your tactics, is a thing of beauty that makes sneaking past exhilarating, as well as satisfying!
+ The Fox Engine is a total gem. The day-night cycle, dynamic weather, lighting, draw distance, along with facial animations are among the best-of-the-best. The game still looks spectacular, and it has been over 4 years since release.
+ With the Mother base, building a private army is neat. It does take constant management to get the most mileage.
+ The soundtrack, along with selection of collectible in-game music are quite superb.
+ Impeccable PC optimization. Moreover, zero bugs in 600+ hours of playtime! Quality control from Kojima and team have never been less than extraordinary, so no surprises here.

[b] Didn't bother me much [/b]
= The open world/sandbox is a bit barren, chiefly the first region. There aren't various different adventures waiting around every corner. It does gets a tad better with time, and there are memorable locations along the way.
= If you came in to get many answers on the Metal Gear saga, you'll get very few.
= Boss fights could've been better. Although there are some good ones, I've witnessed so many solid boss fights in the series that I expected more quality and complexity.
= Side ops are numerous, but they are repetitive with recurring themes. The plus side is, you are not graded during these missions, so feel free to experiment. Option to go full-ninja, or full-Rambo (or anything in between) on those chumps!

[b] The not so positives [/b]
- Game is unfinished towards the end. Be prepared to read up on the internet for info on the unfinished episode that attempts to tie up a crucial story arc. If only Konami cared.
- The "time-gating" mechanic aka waiting for real world time to elapse, in order to develop items, is plain stupid and a poor excuse. Optional, but there is a lot of grinding involved, if you choose to do the online FOB missions. Oh, did I mention that microtransactions are available on this mode? (Thankfully the only place in the entire game.) Absolutely deserves plenty of F-Konami rants for their atrocious decisions here.
- The twist at the end was bittersweet. [spoiler] Kojima and team's effort to retcon makes sense for Big Boss' journey/Metal Gear lore. However, it still was disappointing when the truth was revealed.[/spoiler]

[h1] Overall [/h1]
Had a blast, and the S++ gameplay keeps me going back for more! There's so much this game does effortlessly right that the positives far outweigh the negatives. RIP Metal Gear franchise, you were one of a kind.

This may sound awesome to a certain type of person, but it ruined XCOM for me, and ruined this game for me. I don't want to be boggled down by micro managing and staring at menus in a base when I could be out on the field. The appeal of the Metal Gear games are the ridiculous storyline and stealth action. There's no action in deciding Corporal Roberts should be on Research and Development so I can learn how to make cardboard boxes. I've heard people compare this game to Peacewalker, one of the only Metal Gear games i've never played, so maybe this isn't new to the series, but it was new to me. 

This may sound petty or small to some people, but it was a dealbreaker for me. Again, this game is great, i'm sure of it, but i'm not recommending it to the demographic of players that are like me and wanted a game like the first 4 games. To start with, the game runs surprisingly well on my dinky HP laptop, a 5-year-old, off-the-shelf model with no real power to speak of (i5-5200U 2.2ghz, Intel HD Graphics 5500, and a piddly 6gb RAM) . Now I obviously don't run the game with the settings anywhere close to their maximum on this machine, but what I do use is good enough to play the game in a satisfying fashion. There is some rare slowdown, mostly during cutscenes--like Big Boss's flashback to the Mother Base attack early in the game--that don't use the game's own engine, but aside from that it runs quite smoothly.

While there is some truth to claims that the game's structure is repetitive and grindy, I actually don't see that as much of an issue, particularly as the early missions are completed and the game's full features--mostly in the form of a base with increasing capabilities, and more responsive enemies--unlock and come into play. And being able to repeat missions at any time for increased rank, funds and resources, or staff is more interesting than "one and done" that I'm used to in other games. Further, as you develop better weapons, you'll have steadily expanding options for HOW you go through a mission that makes repeats not quite as dull as they might first seem; full stealth like a ghost, long-range headshots for everyone, one punch man, all-out assaults, and more are possible.

Above, I made mention of responsive enemies. What that means is that, as you play missions in a certain way--always at night, always using tranqs or headshots, etc.--the enemy forces will begin to respond accordingly. You'll start to see guards with helmets and body armor, NV goggles and flashlights, and even gas masks, all as a result of how you choose to hit their bases. It's a neat feature, in my opinion, that keeps you from settling in to brainlessly hit every single mission with the same tired bag of tricks.

I haven't done more than casually poke a toe into the online side of the game, but doesn't seem terribly lively and I haven't gotten to the point where game's FOB missions are available, so I can't comment on those either.

For those who somehow don't know this detail, MGS V: TPP has a prequel in the form of Ground Zeroes, and I very much recommend that game as well. Not only does it offer a fuller exploration of how Big Boss and the others came to be in their current circumstances, but completing certain tasks in the game's small collection of available missions will unlock useful bonuses in this game.

MGSV: The Phantom Pain subsequently proved to be one of the funnest games I ever played.


[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

MGSV has some of the best gameplay I have ever got the pleasure to experience in a video game. The gameplay is extremely nuanced, vibrant and varied. The open world is extremely malleable and can be approached from too many angles/directions for me to describe right now. You start off light, only a few selection of clothes, weapons and equipment. Over the course of the game you'll go from mounting a horse and tranqing people with a low-end WU.Pistol to wearing parasite suits that allow you to become invisible or indestructible, riding a walker gear that can carry flamethrowers, fulton-extract people through metaphysical wormholes, utilise a rocket launcher that can fulton people and throw balloon decoys of yourself that speak short lines like "Kept you waiting, huh" to distract enemy guards. You can slide in cardboard boxes with posters of nude models (or anime girls) on them, you can order your d-dog to stun people with an electric bat, you can call down a thunderstorm that stuns everyone in a 50 meter radius with the highest level stun-arm, you can call weather-modification to induce rain, sandstorms or clear weather, you can also call fire support with chaff that cuts enemy comms, sleeping gas, conventional bombardment, etc. The game is just loaded to the brim with sandbox stuff that you can do and has an amazing and interesting backdrop that is your mother base (struts in the Seychelles that your private army inhabits, you can develop them over the course of the game, fill them with your soldiers that you either kidnap, rescue or recruit, fill them with vehicles and weapons and security cameras to defend them from intruders, and you can visit them and see all this growth in real-time). The controls are amazing (some of the UI and IDroid controls are awkward and stupid, but everything else is fine), the engine is one of the best I have ever got to enjoy, all of this converges into a massive game where you can do a great deal of actions and things and you keep getting even more new toys to play with as you progress the game through development or mother-base growth. The boss fights, as few as they are, are amazing, the Skulls are some of the coolest enemies ever presented in a video game. There are countless mechanics you will discover only after hundreds of hours of playing and cracking all the secret stuff (holding up people with guns, CQC chain take-downs and gun-steals, air-dropping boxes on top of enemies, etc). Your mother base is composed of staff you extract from the battlefield or those that volunteer to your ranks, so a lot of the gameplay involves extracting materials, equipment and soldiers (given they have good stats) to growing your mother base This element might seem tedious to some and fun to others (such as me), so ascertain this is the type of gameplay you are searching for (although you can largely ignore this element of the game, but you will be punished by having the ability to develop less weapons, items and equipment to utilise in the game.


[h1]STORY/LORE[/h1]

This game is widely criticised for having an unfinished story, which I can corroborate. But I still do not feel like it deserves all the flak it gets. The story is there, it's kind-of complete, it has a brutal plot twist in the end, I personally enjoyed it and found it really good (I really love plot twists, so it's subjective). The characters are also one of the biggest carrying weights of Metal Gear Solid V: The -Phantom Pain-. This subtitle almost tells the story on it's own - this game is about the phantom pain, experienced by Venom Snake for losing his arm and his former self, experienced by Kaz for all the limbs he lost (and all the comrades he lost), and finally, experienced by the player, for the big boss he lost. Phantom Pain is this game's story and theme. 
You start-off as Big boss, bed-riddened in a Cypriot hospital, hidden away for the duration of his 9-year long coma after the events of Ground Zeroes, you escape the hospital with the help of a certain Ishmael as Cipher, MSF's old enemy, learns of your where-abouts and attacks the hospital and kills everyone. From there, you go on to rebuild your old Mother base, as things progress, you will find some shocking surprises regarding the origins of your own protagonist, Venom Snake.
I would normally write alot more on the story, but I will not dilate any further on this as I will enter heavy spoiler-territory.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

The Fox engine needs no more praise than it receives, it's one of the most breathtakingly cinematic engines, as cinematic as it can get. The lighting alone is stupendous, the textures are (for the most part) amazing, the level of detail on alot of the world is commensurate. But it does feel like there is definitely some level of down-grade from Ground Zeroes (especially in the textures & lighting areas), but overall, it still looks amazing enough that it's easily going to hold up on the visuals department for the next few years. It is easily one of the most beautiful games I have ever enjoyed, and Kojima made no expense or hesitation to make it as beautiful and realistic as possible.

[h1]PERFORMANCE[/h1]

The performance of MGSV is one of it's highest and strongest points, despite being a Japanese console port (which are notoriously under-performing or gimped in some way or another, Nier;Automata and Dark Souls PTDE as examples of this), MGSV has exemplary performance with dips being a rare rarity. I can alt-tab and tumble around in my browser tabs while the game is running at borderless window @ 1440p and be able to tab-back and resume playing seamlessly, in my book, that is a standard for solid video game performance.

There are very rare framerate drops in the games with the usual suspects behind them (Severe dust kick-up, usually from fultoning a cargo container), otherwise, I have absolutely nothing to complain from this game's performance even while playing it supersampled at 4K, a resolution higher than my monitor, and it runs at smooth 60 FPS at all points of the game that matter.

I first picked up GZ in September 2019 and after beating it, I picked up TPP. The game is amazing! The intro had me sooooooo hooked! My heart was racing, my assh0l3 clenched, my eyes wide open and my brain thinking, "Kojima is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ genius! I'm gonna have a blast with this game. This is epic, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! My first Metal Gear game and it's such a blast!" 30 hours in- the charm was gone. I was sick of the desert and the sand. I was tired of the same copy-paste missions. I had no idea what I was even trying to achieve half the time by scrolling mindlessly through the entire complexity-ridden list of Motherbase chores and I haven't had the same adrenaline rush I got at the beginning of the game in days. I felt disappointed and lost.

Don't get me wrong, I love the game. The graphics are groundbreaking, the AI some of the smartest I've ever seen, the story had a lot of potential, the environment was breathtaking at first and the level of realism put into the game is mind-blowing. Yet, something feels missing. It's like they hooked me into the game with that nail-bitingly well-done prologue but seems like they spent 80% of the development time and resources into designing and polishing that prologue and the rest of the game is basically you jumping between the Motherbase, Helicopter and enemy posts. Same stuff all around- infiltrate the enemy outpost, retrieve something/kill or extract someone. It's gotten to a point where I've memorized each and every outpost's layout. In the beginning, I was getting A ranks on my first tries. But now even if I try not to, I end up getting S ranks. My last mission was to infiltrate the same outpost I've infiltrated for numerous side missions before. So I decided to ♥♥♥♥ around and explore. Alas... before I knew it, I had pacified the enemies in the immediate area (because they were so closely bunched together that if one of them sees you and you put him down, the others come looking and then you have to basically pacify everyone or they raise the alarm). With this done, I had no choice but to extract the VIPs I had pacified earlier before they woke up and sounded the alarm. 15 minutes was all it took. And bam! Just like that, another main repetitive mission was over. No cutscenes, no story, nothing special going on to drive the narrative further. And I've got three more missions like those on my to-do list right now. It's not even fun. The open world was meant to give you freedom of approach for your missions and for exploration. But every game mechanic so far just limits this in its own way.

- You can't kill enemies because otherwise that lowers your ratings and gives you demon points and changes your character's look.

- You can't explore or be patient about your stealth approach if you wish to pacify enemies because they wake up or are woken up and sound the alarm, making it difficult for you to complete the mission

- Suppressors get worn out fast and you can't even find replacements in the enemy outposts.

- You can't explore even in free mode because most of the map is unscaleable mountains and the roads which you can explore are filled with enemy outposts and patrols every few meters.

- What little you can explore is basically either bland and dead desert or just some vegetation after a few levels anyways.

- Not much do in Motherbase or in the Helicopter either (excluding Staff/Resources and R&D management which is unnecessarily cluttered and gives me migraines).

- AI sometimes reacts unpredictably (turning on generators from 4 walls away while doing the animation as if they're right next to it, running in the player's direction for no reason at all even when you're completely still and no one is suspicious or alarmed, reacting to deaths of fellow soldiers for which they're directly responsible (mowing them down with their truck, losing them in a mine placed by themselves) and blaming it on the player who is hitherto a complete ghost btw, sometimes reacting to loss of resources and other times not, some times spotting a player helicopter flying right above and other times not, etc.).

So despite a passionately carved and extremely detailed open world, millions of lines voiced by expensive voice actors, countless lines of code written to make the graphics so wonderful, there's not really much to the game in the way of content. Most stealth games I know of (Splinter Cell, Dishonored, Deus Ex, Hitman) reward patience and encourage exploration yet this game only seems to condone speedruns. If you avoid exploring (by avoiding enemies) and run straight for the mission objective and exfiltrate right out in record time, you get rewarded. If you ♥♥♥♥ around, take your time, carefully mark enemies, sabotage equipment and pacify guards to give yourself an edge, you get punished for it. I've never seen a game which is so confused about what it wants to be- an open world game (which are known to condone exploration) or a stealth game (which are known for amazing level design, and for rewarding patience and planning) or an RPG game (which are known to have a good story at least).

I love this game for it's (mostly) flawless mechanics, weapons/gadgets variety, multiple playable characters ability, buddies system and amazing graphics but... it appears Hideo Kojima was given an unlimited amount of time and money for this game and he just squandered it all on the first few minutes of intensely directed cutscenes and left the rest of the game to a braindead, uncreative team of interns which basically copy-pasted similar missions across the same three or four enemy outposts. 160+ hours in, 62% of the game finished, story completed and I still have a bad taste in my mouth. Yes, I am very well-impressed with MGSV. This is definitely up there with Mad Max, Wildlands and The Division in terms of immersive third person open world gameplay. It's slower-paced, for sure, but strategising and working out where to go and what you have to do in each mission brings that extra sense of realism and immersion to the table. It really does a sterling job in making the player believe they're in the thick of a full-blown major military operation. It is also pretty challenging stuff at times which is also a refreshing change.

Progress comes in the form of resource gathering while out-in-the-field and then spending said resources on buildings and upgrades to weapons and armour etc between missions. You have a "mother-ship" consisting of departments manned by personnel that you also collect (by attaching a fulton balloon to them) while out and about.

The environment is mainly the desert or barren landscapes which is rendered well-enough and you can carry only two weapon types at a time with two added devices/gadgets. As mentioned, gameplay is slow-paced. This is a thinking-person's third person shooter where thought is always necessary for completing tasks successfully. You can't go in all guns blazing. MGSV, however, is not open-world in the strictest sense. Missions are listed in a menu while your character is resting between missions in his helicopter or visiting the mother ship. You pick a mission and are then air-lifted into a specific area of the map for you to start. You get a handful of objectives which will usually take multiple "runs" to complete. 

The Cons:

1) I found the roster of soldiers who work for you - and how to employ them - very confusing. They are graded A-E but I found the UI to be cumbersome and just had the AI assign them their best roles. I am still quite unclear as to how that system really works.  

2) The map is badly rendered, hard to decipher and totally dull and boring. I know it's supposed to be a realistic satellite-style map but surely, for the sake of better gameplay or user-friendliness, realism has to sometimes be compromised to make way for something aesthetically pleasing.

3) It's capped at 60fps and I have a 144hz monitor. YES, 144hz monitors ARE made for a reason and IT DOES make a noticeable difference.

4) An over-complicated UI with some bizarre key-bindings.

This game is amazing. I cant put into words how much this game means to me. Because of that i'll try to put this review into catagories, like many others do too.

---GAMEPLAY---

This is the peak of open world freedom. Every Outpost, base, airfield, etc has dozens of ways to tackle them. How bout being sneaky and taking out everyone with nothing but a silenced pistol and a knife? Maybe make yourself a living tank with armor and an LMG to gun down everyone standing in front of you? Maybe put c4 on a sheep and make it run inside, and detonate it? There are limitless possibilities. Nomatter how you want to play, the game lets you, from sneaky snitch, to armed gorilla, to deadly sniper, to whatever else. 

From here on there are spoilers by the way.

The game also has "buddys". They are 4 Friendos you can take along on your missions (spoiler alert, D-Dog is the best by far). D-Horse, D-Dog, Quiet and D-Walker. Lets cover all of them.

-D-Horse:-

MGSV's world is giant, and getting a rideable friend to carry you to your target makes stuff easier!
D-Horse, the ♥♥♥♥-on-command, bullet proof mount, the first buddy you get in the game, actually.
You can ride him/her (is its gender ever mentioned?) and lean on a side to hide yourself from enemys. Its the best tool to get around the world. It some one thing to customize, its armor, either making it stylish or deadly, or rather undeadly.... it has more health, okay? With that it gives you the ability to run and gun on it, as you can pull out guns on it. Its not the worst strategy, however its still unmatched to quiet and D-Dog.

-D-Dog:-

D-Dog is the most OP woofer i have ever seen. His main ability is to mark any target close to him. And with close we mean like 100m or so. With that it makes him insanely useful. No need to sneak around and mark targets, only to get shot by some rando that you didnt see, D-Dog gotcha back!

Oh, but it doesnt end at that. He also can get customized. You remember that one Dark Souls dog that had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sword in its mouth? Yeah, want that to kill a bunch of russians? Well, the game gives you the option to give D-Dog a knife. You can look at any target, and tell the good boy to brutally murder him, which is stealthy, somehow. So you got a silent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemy radar, which is also your personal hitman. But wait, theres more! He can also get a fulton device, a electric bat, and another knife to injure his targets. However stock and knife are by far the best. BUT WAIT THERES MORE. He also has the ability to bark. Put him anywhere, and make people distracted. So he isnt just a radar, isnt just a personal hitman he is also a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ distraction device + you can pet him :)

-Quiet:-

Ironic. She uses a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loud ass sniper rifle and her name is quiet. 

Anyway, this is your personal sniper! She is in my personal buddy tierlist the second best option, right after Death Dog. She can either scan an outpost for enemys and/or get to any position to snipe at your desired target. She can also knock around grenades you threw and cover you (go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). In her arsenal are various sniper rifles. From silenced, to sleep dart ammo, to "i want to use bullets, the size of quiets chest".

She also has multiple outfits, however they dont change stats and only one of them actually give her clothes.

S P O I L E R    S T A R T

On the last mission quiet dies. You can play her fight (i think mission 14 or something) 7 or 8 times to get her back.

S P O I L E R    E N D


-D-Walker:-

D-Walker sucks. He costs a ton to even get into a mission, has tons of unsilenced weapons, those that are are better in venoms hands. He isnt useful for stealth, as he's way to big to hide, and for going in loud hes too annoying to carry around. Just grab a rocket launcher or something instead. Even in tank unit destroy missions its smarter to just use a launcher. I dont like Walker at all. You can customize him a lot, but i dont really use it a lot, because who cares? Venom himself is way more effective.


The game also gives you a lot to customize. From what weapons (you can even make your own weapons),  to what outfit/armor, to what gear, to what helicopter to pick you up/help you in fights, to what vehicle you want to spawn with (you can customize their looks, however not stats.), etc etc etc.

Then theres the mother base.

The big boy base is the central of everything. The people you fulton out, to the development, to the materials are all kept here. Its kinda underwhelming, you need to visit every once in a while for demon points (ill cover and explain later), your smell and the bases charisma. The only important thing is your defense from FOB missions. You can infiltrade others bases and steal their weapons, materials and nukes. To defend yourself from your stuff being snagged you can buy cameras, drones and equipment for your staff. Its really fun to steal, and kinda boring to defend. However the concept and its execution is done better than expected, and actually really fun at times.

So MGS: V was the first game in the series I played. I watched the other games to get the story and such, but gameplay-wise, this was my first delve into the world of Metal Gear Solid. And I can say that it was an overall positive experience.

The gameplay itself is smooth, responsive, and fun. I'm terrible at stealth games (I get too impatient, or just throw a wrench into a multistep grand plan that ruins everything) and even I had a lot of fun with sneaking around as Snake. There's so many options and tactics to use in MGS:V's Far Cry-esque gameplay loop of: Find outpost > plan approach via marking enemies > tackle it from any way you can.  It was quite fun... for awhile. I'll admit I burned myself out on it because of a few reasons:

1. Every time I got caught, I felt like I lost the mission. You don't lose, and in fact it's quite easily recoverable, but I still felt like I failed each time. And I'm pretty sure I died at least once on nearly every story mission, which sucks as you see it penalize you in the score at the end of each mission for it. I honestly think if there was an option to skip the post-mission grades and credits, I'd be a lot more satisfied with my own gameplay.

2. I tried to do a TON of side-ops in between story missions, and these become kind of tedious after a few hours, and ultimately made me end up liking some of the main story missions less because I had spent hours prior doing essentially the same thing. 

3. The game doesn't do an amazing job of explaining just how vast of an array of options you have, which led me to fall into the trap of doing the same, path-of-least-resistance stealth tactics for the first few hours of the game. Combined with the feeling of getting penalized for screwing up anything than perfect stealth, and I had to force myself to experiment with cool little stealth options/tactics/items beyond just interrogating and throat-slitting enemies.

Other than the few gripes above, the rest of my gameplay experience was pretty darn good!

Story-wise, however, it's... a bit of a mixed bag, for me. Snake doesn't talk much, leading to awkward cutscenes where he SHOULD say something in Kiefer Sutherland's gruff voice, but just... doesn't. Like, not reacting to major plot developments is just jarring. Especially when it's not this is a blank-slate character; he's established!

The story itself is pretty... predictable if you've seen any of the other MGS games. There's a few character reveals and developments that were so obvious I had tricked myself into thinking this was gonna be some crazy multi-layered plot twist but... nope. The game is not subtle about it's main plot points.
The plot elements are a bit long-winded and silly to take in through the hours of cassette tapes you have to listen to in order to flesh out the rather lacking mission stories (meaning the vast majority of story elements are not given while you play... they're given as background loredumps). 

And I'm sure you've heard the infamous news about this game: it isn't finished. And it sucks. Major plot threads just abandoned. Literally left flying off into the distance. "I have to go now, my planet needs me," style. At least you can look it up online to watch the unfinished cutscenes.

Another gripe I had is with Quiet. Sigh... Kojima... If you've seen any of his games, you know he's not subtle with how he ogles practically every single woman in his games, but like... It's never sat quite right with me, and it's frankly disturbing in this game. To the point where I would be so embarrassed if anybody walked in on a cutscene that featured Quiet. And I can't get over how he thought he roasted everyone who was like, "This is too much" by saying, "You'll regret you're words and deeds" when he reveals why she's a half-naked bikini sniper... but it's not even a good justification (especially when other characters in the series were revealed to have had similar ...circumstances as her, but shocker, they were a male and as such weren't delegated to be creeped heavily upon. It's a shame really because her story arc is pretty good.

The game's visuals were absolutely fantastic. I love all of the cinematic lighting effects to highlight things in cutscenes, the way the search-lights, headlights, and sun all produce lens flares that also have sound cues. The facial capture is great, and the vast majority of the motion capture is great. The voice acting is all good, though I will admit I thought that it was a bit jarring soldiers didn't have fully voiced interrogation lines (once you get a translator, I feel like they should say their lines to you instead of just grunting and groaning at you. Shoutouts to the one voice actor for random russian soldiers who sputters like Grandpa Simpson when you interrogate them). My game ran at perfectly, never even dipping from 60 fps during intense battles with a ton of effects going on.

Overall, the game was fun and I do recommend at least giving it a go. The main chunk of the gameplay is fun enough to overlook the gripes I had with it, and though the story is overall just alright, it is a fun romp to go through. If you enjoy Far Cry, Assassin's Creed-style open-world stealth-action games, you'll probably like this one too!

Would I reccomend this game?
Yes, absolutely, but there are a few things you should know going in.
First, this game is desperately unfinished, it’s very clear when Kojima left development and it got an “ending” stapled onto it.
If you’re at all familiar with the MGS franchise, everything that happens in this game probably won’t surprise you. I’m only moderately familiar with the timeline, so certain things didn’t make sense to me, and other things that were probably obvious were complete surprises.
Without spoiling anything, the game is sorta building this mystery around some key characters, then without warning, and not in a cutscene (well, not really anyway), a key character basically explains the story to you in a none-too-subtle “We desperately had to wrap this up and we didn’t know how” kinda way. Which then culminates in a mission that might feel like the end, but isn’t happens, and the game moves onto chapter two.
Chapter two is basically just a bunch of challenge missions locking off a few key story events to wrap up a few dangling plot threads. Which felt cheap to me, since they just recycle old story missions with some arbitrary difficulty ramps. It’s disconcerting because I definitely felt the game was building to something, but then the game just kinda pads itself out for a few hours. A few key characters stories get quickly taken care of, then boom, game over, please come again, maybe give us a few bucks and buy our asset flip “Metal Gear Survive”.
It’s a fun game for sure, I sunk about 50 hours into it and I mostly don’t regret that, but it’s a lot of buildup for no payoff. I can’t think of many other games that feel as distinct as this, and the pseudo open world benefits the series. I felt like I had a great deal of control over how I approached objectives, and the game didn’t really railroad me into pure stealth or pure action. It’s kinda like Batman or Deus Ex, where slipping up on the stealth doesn’t mean game over, and while Snake isn’t a bullet sponge like Gordon Freeman, it’s 100% possible to fight your way to your objective.
The gunplay is different than most 3rd person action games, but it feels very clean and to the point. The stealth is top notch, and the addition of an upgrade system allows you the freedom to approach things very differently as the game goes on.
The fulton mechanic is pretty neat too. If you upgrade it enough, you can basically extract anything from the battlefield, which can drastically change how you approach missions. Here’s an example.  A late game mission had me destroying a few convoys of armored vehicles and then a chopper. In a similar previous mission, I might have laid down mines or C4, but now I just waited on the side of the road, ran up to where the cannons couldn’t hit me, and extracted them without ever firing a shot. And that’s a totally viable strategy. The game recognized I had done that and I got a personnel bonus for all the tank commanders. The game is surprisingly fluid in how it allows you to get things done.
If you’re looking for the TLDR, yeah, buy it when it’s on sale or something, but basically know you’re definitely there for the journey, not the destination. It’s a unique game that you won’t really get anywhere else, it’s just sad that company politics robbed us of what might have been an outstanding overall experience.

METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is an open world third person stealth (optional) game. It is a combination of a movie and a video game, it got hours of cutscenes and the lore is more complex than any other video game or movie i know. I am not a big fan of lore in games and sometimes i just skip it and go straight after the gameplay, but it is not the same for this game. It made me read lots of long wiki pages on some characters, organizations and places (Do not do the same before completing the game for your own good. Spoilers are not fun).
The gameplay is great, as i mentioned earlier the stealth is optional and it can be played and enjoyed by loud and ruthless players too. It is a really long game so it is worth your money 3 or 4 times more than the average AAA title without counting replayability. There are a lot of options in weapons, vehicles and backup and you can choose one of the 4 available buddies to help you in your mission. Each buddy has different abilities that you unlock by increasing the bond level (which is also pretty easy, just don't let them get hurt and order them to do stuff a lot). The enemies also get small upgrades along the story, you have to change your techniques if they don't work anymore and i find this a great way of stopping the gameplay from being repetitive. I personally finished all the main missions and a few side ones in 100 hours and still have some other side missions and new difficulty ones to do. There are FOB raidings too, pretty much the only online part that is still alive. MGS online seems dead, couldn't find anyone to try it out with. FOB missions are about invading player bases for stealing resources and crew, its cost is that if you fail or get spotted the one invaded knows who you are and can invade back.
The graphics are pretty damn good and the optimization is great, i ran it on almost max settings with stable 60 fps (capped) on GTX 1050 4GB (laptop), i5-8250U and 8GB RAM DDR4. My laptop didn't even make a lot of noise and it didn't get very hot, so if you got a similar system i bet you can run it on max easily. The soundtrack is nice and there are featured licensed songs released in the early '80s, which is good for the game's atmosphere, since that is when the story takes place. There are a lot of menus in this game, they look good and have satisfying sound effects.
 
There are parts i didn't like too. The helicopter takes too much time artificially. After doing a mission you are all bloody and want to go to Mother Base and take a shower. You have to call the helicopter, wait for it, get in, wait for it to traver long enough so you would close its door, wait for the game to load and press a button, use your idroid and go to mother base, wait for the loading screen again to press a button, waiting for it to get down and FINALLY getting out of the helicopter. It takes too much time and you can't do something else meanwhile, because you still need to press a few buttons. If you want to get to other platforms of the Mother Base you have to drive there in a vehicle. The road is too long and again, you can't do other stuff while doing it, maybe listening to cassettes at best. There is no reason for them to be this long, i think the road to other platforms should be at least half as long.
The upgrades take too much time. I understand it would be ridiculous to upgrade weapons instantly, but it goes from instantly for low tier to 18m, 36m, 1 hour and a few minutes, a few hours and to my surprise, one weapon that i didn't really need, but that i upgraded only because i had money made me wait 4 days. If i really wanted that gold tier heavy machine gun i would be pissed off badly.
The DLCs are ridiculous, at how much content there is in this game they are almost nothing and shouldn't cost money, yet they do. I never used the suits, i have them only because the bundle that included Ground Zeroes had them too and was only a few dollars more. Honestly there is no reason to buy them, you're wasting money.
The main story wasn't finished, Snake gets robbed of his secret weapon by an annoying brat and you don't get to see him again. If that scene wasn't in the game i would consider it complete, it's like starting a new chapter and leaving it after the introduction.
You see credits everywhere. Even if you don't want you will remember Hideo Kojima's name. At the start of every mission you will see his name credited, then some other credits for the people that made the missions. I think they did a great job making this game but i'd rather have all the credits at the end of the game only. I guess it's just his ego.

I see this game as the spiritual successor to MGS2; Both games were heavily criticised when they were released, but their stories and their messages are the most impactful of all the MGS games. The two games also changed the gameplay quite a lot compared to their predecessors. These two games are my favorite games of all time. It's sad there is no MGS2 on steam, but here is why MGSV is the best MGS game of all time.

The story:
The story takes place after the events of MGS3 and MGS-Peace Walker. I recommend you play these games first. But here's a short take away [heavy spoilers for the aforementioned games]: [spoiler]Big Boss aka Naked Snake aka Jack kills his former mentor The Boss, in order to save the relationship between the US and the Soviet Union, sacrifices herself. Snake, left feeling mistreated by his government and leaders, leaves the US and forms his own private army. The army is meant to serve the good, but ends up being nothing more than the tool of those who can afford them. Kaz (one of Snake’s companions) works for an ideology close to marxisme, but it is the soldiers being oppressed by the higher ups.[/spoiler]
More importantly the phantom pain is a direct sequel to Ground Zero, playing this game is a must.

I highly recommend that you read the book Moby ♥♥♥♥ to get the full story. Without spoiling the story, the story of MGSV parallels the story of Moby ♥♥♥♥, which is a story of descent into madness, how Snake and his crew falls into madness mirrors how we in the quest for peace (a big theme in MGS) end up doing the opposite. [spoiler] The crew fights for the liberation of soldiers, but end up being used by those who can afford them [/spoiler].
MGSV also uses the song ‘The Man Who Sold The World’ by midge ure to great effect, a song about two identities with one body in common, like how the song is a cover a song by the same name by David Bowie.

A big theme in MGS is identity. This came continues where MGS2 left off on the topic of identity. It raises the questions: Who am [b]I[/b]? Am [b]I[/b] fighting for others when [b]I[/b]fight for [i]myself[/i]? You might end up asking yourself these questions when you are hit with the twist.
A big question is: where do we as humans come from? Is our identity our gene, that we inherit from our parents, or is it the meme that we affect how we live our lives and how society shapes us. 

The story has, however, taken a bit of a back seat when compared to other MGS games. And this game’s story is not super crucial for the overall story of the series. The story and themes are still far better executed than other games on the market (even though the game has been out for over five years now)

In between the story you are treated to the greatest gameplay the series has to offer. Throughout the series, I feel like you have always been on some sort of rail; not being able to do everything that an almost super human should be able to do. However MGSV  nails something as basic as walking. Everything you do has a certain weight, yet every action is performed rapidly. 
With all the ways you can move, a great many ways of engaging enemies is possible (sneaking, guns blazing and more). All of these ways to engage let down a path of almost exclusively sneaking, mostly defeating the sandbox because I could run around doing everything the way I felt was correct, however the game does shake things up, when you are forced into combat-only missions.

I am late to the party on this one, but I swear to God I have never played a game less deserving of all the accolades it received since Watch Dogs.

The story just does not work on any level. As a main entry, it's freaking confusing since a lot of characters are from the HANDHELD GAMES! As part of the MGS lore, it constantly contradicts previous entries. And as a standalone narrative, it is completely unengaging and pointless. It is woefully lacking in narrative flow, since it plays out with you doing unrelated missions until the game decides to drop a cutscene on you. You end up with a sense of aimlessness as you blow up this tank or rescue this prisoner, not knowing how any of it relates to your goals or your adversary's.

Characters either have no personality (Quiet and Code Talker are prime examples) or are ridiculously annoying. Huey and Eli are especially grating, between the former's complusive lying & hypocrisy and the latter's whiny angst. Heck, "Snake" in this game has no agency whatsoever, only existing in the story to do whatever Miller and Ocelot tell him to do. That's not to mention how Ocelot and Miller, MAINSTAYS OF THE FRANCHISE, are relegated to dumping exposition on you for the majority of the game.

The gameplay is mechanically sound, favouring stealth gameplay over run-and-gun tactics. There's not really much to say on that since I don't really have big complaints about it other than cover is too sticky, which is troublesome when things invariably go sideways and you need to sprint. It's especially an issue during Mission 45, which is an absolute dumpster fire of level design. Also the lack of vehicle stealth. Are you driving a tank? Too bad! They know it's you.

By far, the biggest offenders are the level design and mission structure. The decision to make MGSV sandbox was absolutely the wrong one, as it introduces so much dead space into gameplay by forcing you to traverse an empty map for minutes at a time. Just to reach a mission area. Most of the camps and outposts scattered throughout the map are also fairly repetitive, and are positioned such that it's pretty cumbersome just to avoid if you don't want to deal with them.

In terms of mission structure, its biggest weakness begin to rear its head in Chapter 2, which basically forces you to play hard mode by recycling Chapter 1 missions, but making them harder (which by this game's standard is stripping you of gameplay mechanics you have grown used to). There are few original missions in this chapter, and the ones it does have are incredibly uninspired. Except Mission 45, which is specifically designed to be the worst MGS mission of all time. It forces you to use these controls, so finely tuned for stealth gameplay, to participate in wave defense. With tanks that can withstand 3 rocket blasts. And can kill you in one hit. And come in waves of threes at a time. And you cannot abort the mission once you start. Because whoever made that level tortures Satan as his hobby.

I have genuinely never felt so much like I wasted my time. Avoid like the plague.
