Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is one of the greatest scams ever pulled off in the history of videogames.

First there were trailers, with promises of open-world gameplay and freedom unprecedented in Metal Gear franchise, or any other game for that matter, and an epic conclusion to the story of Big Boss, the missing link of the Metal Gear saga. And these trailers, man! I still have chills watching one with Mike Oldfield’s song to this day, even with the context of that game.

Then there was Ground Zeroes, the glorified demo and a piece of misleading marketing, but a damn good one. Actually, it was not just “misleading marketing”, I am willing to say, that was a demo for a game which was never made. 

I am not easily separated from my money, but I decided to bite the bullet, and that was actually a great time. I really tried very hard to squeeze as much value from that game as I possibly could, but I think I’ve got my money's worth. And my hype for the Phantom Pain was through the roof. 

But, as I’ve said - I am not easily separated from my money. So I’ve waited for the reviews, and wouldn’t you know - these were perfect 10s front to back. Everybody seemed to think that it was a perfect stealth game, everyone pointing out the intricate guard AI, the multitude of systems interacting with one another, the amazing technical performance of FoxEngine on PCs, and so on, and so forth, just barely mentioning some problems with the plot. There were, of course detractors, trying to put the spotlight on some massive  problems this game carries. But then, there were also amazing gameplay videos by guys like videogamedunkey, who just had a great time messing with the guards. 

So again, I’ve gave in. After 30GB download I’ve sunk into the game for 10 hours straight. And what those 10 hours are! The opening, with its downright psychedelic atmosphere, the first missions, where the stealth sandbox opens up, and the plot gets its gears going. The introduction of its various systems just blew my brain away. “This really is the best Metal Gear Solid game Kojima is a GOD!”.

But then, around the ten hour mark, a weird feeling started to set in. Suddenly, the story cutscenes became few and far between. Sure, there were a multitude of ways I could approach every mission… But all of them were inferior to tranq pistol + tranq sniper rifle + stun gun and just headshotting/CQC slamming every guard. Sure, the guards would “change their tactics” which meant “they wear helmets/night vision now”, but effects of that felt negligible at best.

Suddenly the realization hit me - I was scammed. The game is super unfinished, not just from a story perspective (by the way, you gonna love the “twist” of the “real” ending), but on the game design front. There are a multitude of systems, sure - but you can ignore most of them safely, and just do whatever you feel like. 

They say that given the opportunity players will optimize the fun out of the game, and after playing MGSV, I can confidently say I’ve experienced that myself. I understand that some players (like aforementioned videogamedunkey) find freedom this type of sandbox provides liberating, and can pull a ton of fun from such experiences. And the game is a masterpiece from a technical perspective, FoxEngine is really that good. 

Hoverwer, I won’t be finishing the game for its devs, and imposing challenges on myself just so I can have some fun. It’s not my work, I’ve paid for this game to play it, not the other way around to test it. 

It is a scam, a front loaded production, a ten hours game stretched to last for days. And we helped to make it what it is, hyping the game mindlessly. We are all guilty. 

Maybe that was the true Phantom Pain?

Metal Gear Solid V is a masterpiece on par with titles such as Halflife 2 and Elder Scrolls:Morrowind.    There is nothing more that needs to be said. 


(One small caveat.) MGSV is not for casual gaming. You need a fair amount of free time to commit to this title before it pays you back in triple.  The first few  missions make the game appear sparse, confusing, or even boring. Keep at it, and that will soon turn into a honeymoon.

It's like a metal gear game, except you have to walk for 5 minutes between anything interesting.  Even in the supposedly curated missions, you will go to one location, then have to walk somewhere else kilometers away.  That's in addition to the normal stealthing around, so the game's pacing is terrible.

Bullets don't go where you aim, which is really annoying in a shooter.  Additionally, eventually guards get body armor, and there's really no way to tell until you shoot them.  There are probably some fun guns in the game, but they're locked behind base-building.

Stealthing around is actually fun, but frequently missions require you to just wait around without getting caught, while some guy takes 20 minutes to go visit stuff around the map.  I frequently got caught just playing around because I got bored, because that's boring.

Finally, you put up with all of that for a piecemeal, mediocre story without a satisfying ending.

There's a reason Kojima got canned.

Alright, just in case you guys weren't aware, if you played this game at ANY point and built up an FOB, you'll find yourself with a ton of GMP over time. Stopped playing for 2 years and returned, only to find out that my FOB on the old savefile ended up making me like 11 million GMP and tons of resources. 
With that out of the way, I CANNOT see this as an MGS game so much as a "Mercenary Army Man" simulator with incomplete elements from MGS sprinkled in. That said, the gameplay makes it into a FUN Mercenary Army Man simulator. There is no end to the amount of shenanigans you can get up to clearing bases silently while taking their best dudes as your own. The gunplay is absolutely fantastic, as is the weapon customization system(retro tacticool is best tacticool, I challenge all dissenters to a boxing match). Kojima did a great job with making you FEEL like a proper mercenary as seen from a 1980's Soldier of Fortune magazine. Only trouble is though, if you end up shooting it out with rival mercs or pinko red bastages, the game basically says "you're not supposed to do that, but we can't stop you", You also miss out on nice bonuses when you're mowing down S+ everything guys by the truckload, as fun as that is. 
Personally, if this rendition of the MGS series were to continue as a standalone game focused on the mercenary stuff, I would be beyond happy. Only things I'd really do are 3 things: make it feel like less of a punishment to get into fights, expand on character customization to include different outfits and gear, and finally, expand the buddy system so you can effectively control a squad. Unfortunately, it's become obvious that you cannot trust Konami to do ANYTHING right, and as sad as I am to say it, I hope this sleeping dog gets left to lie.

A lot has been said about this game, about the final chapter of one of the most long-running and narratively complex videogame series in history. After playing through all the story missions and the vast majority of side ops, having spent a lot of time with side objectives, base developing and a good amount of FOB missions, I think it's time for me to give a verdict as well. But first, I'm gonna leave a brief list of what are in my opinion the best and worst aspects of this title.

PROs:

+ Varied, smooth and engaging gameplay, by far the best that the series has ever seen. It seems like the series has fallen for the "open-world" meme at first, but you soon realize it's more of a hub system with different operation zones that can be freely explored or faced mission-per-mission, at free will.
+ Lots of freedom in approaching mission objectives. There's never a single way to reach a mission goal and the player is encouraged to experiment new tactics.
+ Tons of different equipment, items and customization options available.
+ Micro-management of Mother Base is simple and efficient.
+ The plot contains interesting insights and food for thoughts, like the role of language in defining individuals and such.

CONs:

- Extremely grind-based resources management, with lots of options tied to online play. If you don't participate in events or online rankings you're gonna have a really hard time farming all the materials you need for base and items developing and you'll be on shortage of GMP for most of the time.
- Related to the grinding for resources, there's the massive waiting time needed to develop all the advanced items. That can be shortened by spending in-game value. A cheap trick to lure people into online play and spend real money to get MB points. Awful.
- Said online play only consists in trying to capture another player's base, which practically means repeating the exact same task again and again while remaining confined in the same base all the time, since FOBs can't be customized in any way. Then there's MGO, but I doubt anyone actually plays the stealth version of Counter-Strike.
- Ranking system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and can really ruin the whole need for stealth approach for some missions. Since it takes into account the time as well as the player performance, sometimes the best approach for getting an S rank is just taking your chopper and heavy equipment, get right in the middle of the enemy base, kill everyone with the gatling and finish any survivor with heavy firearms, then snatch your mission target and get away. Sometimes you don't even have to leave the chopper if the mission objective is about eliminating a specific target, so you just get there, make a mess with the gatling and go away. Boom, S rank. It's ridiculous for a Metal Gear game.
- Badly explained briefings. Sometimes the explanation of the mission objective is so vague that you don't really have an idea of what you're going to do until you actually start the mission, which can lead you to bring the wrong equipment or choose a wrong deployment zone. At that point, it's better to just restart the mission from the beginning.
- Lots of useless side objectives meant purely for wasting the player's time. What's unnerving about them is that they're not explicitely pointed out until you finish a mission once, and even then you're often forced to replay the mission multiple times since a certain objective cannot be obtained without missing another.
- Main missions are for a good 80% either completely disconnected from the story or lowly relevant, which makes a lot of the game's content feel like little more than a filler. Even worse, after a certain point the game forces you to replay the same old missions with higher difficulty in order to unlock the final episodes. It's clear that they needed to dilute things and make the game longer, but there are more subtle ways to do it.
- Stupid enemy AI that makes them unable to see a man crawling 10 meters in front of them or to notice a vehicle passing at full speed amid rocks and dirt a few meters outside the main road. Metal Gear guards have never been a particularly good example of brilliance, but that is no excuse. Funny enough, once you've been spotted everybody seem to miraculously get their sights back and it becomes extremely hard to hide since they'll start shooting immediately at the minimum movement while in evasion mode.
- Excessively long waiting time when using the chopper, especially to move inside the Mother Base. I don't know if this was intended to mask loading times, but it's very annoying in the long run.
- Lastly and worst of all, the story is rushed and chopped in half. Some aspects of the plot sound ridiculous even for a Metal Gear game ([spoiler]like Skull Face's motivations being nothing much than a personal revenge directed against the whole world, making him a rather pathetic character[/spoiler]) and the fact that lots of important revelations have just been left on cassette tapes instead of being properly presented with a cutscene etc leaves a giant void that makes the whole game feel empty and soulless. The last mission is a big ol' explanation of what actually happened - which is YET ANOTHER RECYCLED MISSION - that is thrown in the middle of a bunch of secondary stuff and leaves important events unresolved, as if they never happened. [spoiler]Eli going away with a psychich friend and stealing a giant bipedal weapon? Nah, let's just forget about that.[/spoiler] It got so bad that Konami eventually had to make an extra scene on the special edition blu-ray (PS4 only, haha) to try and explain all that stuff a minimum. You can find it on youtube as the infamous "Episode 51".

After playing this game myself I understand why people got mad about it and I can't put the blame entirely on Konami either. They might've been making pressure on the developing team, but if Hideo Kojima invested half the time he wasted writing useless missions and implementing tons of utterly redundant equipments into actually writing a decent ending, things would've been way different and long-time fans like me wouldn't have felt so disappointed. The whole development planning of this title was lacking in every possible way, which is easily proved by comparing the amount of resources invested in making the intro and the useless pieces of equipment with the downfall of writing and mission variety from the end of chapter 1 onwards. It's almost as if the game's ending was left out of the schedule while waiting for Kojima to finally get his ♥♥♥♥ together and think about something to write. It's embarassing.

MGSV might be a neat game gameplay-wise but it's a disaster as storytelling and fails miserably where it was expected to excel the most. I have no idea what the hell Kojima was thinking about to leave a game in this state, he must've been tremendously burned out for sure but that's no excuse. Metal Gear deserved a better swansong than this.

Pessimistic Review:

Metal Gear Solid V is the long awaited prequel to the first Metal Gear game and a story line sequel to MGS 3 and Peacewalker. Overall the game received universal praise from the mainstream gaming media but in general I feel like a lot of it was reactionary in nature and the praise doesn't look in depth at the mechanics and the most important part of the Metal Gear Series, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story.

To start off with, I feel like the mechanics in MGS V feels fantastic to use and control, you really do have a lot freedom with how the main character, Vemon Snake, can move. But the main issue is the game is entirely open world so the polished controls aren't always complemented by good level design or good enemy placement. (For me) It offers either no challenge in some areas or way too much in others, the issue isn't that there it's any middle ground areas and that they are few and far between. This gets even worse with the upgrading and Mother Base building mechanics that are thrown in as well. In certain areas of the game you are either way too good with all the weapons you have or you are way too weak with the lack of decent upgrade further enforcing this idea of either too easy or too hard. Now, others claim that the way you play the game in MGS V crafts the difficulty for you, but I somewhat disagree. In open world games such as these, players are dropped into the game with almost complete freedom and test out most of the mechanics and or weapons of the game, but when they find a system that works for them they usual stick to that system for the rest of the game as it is usually the easiest for them. Now, that might not be a problem if the developer of the game makes varied level design to complement the varied weapon choices so you have to use other weapons to tackle different threats but they don't in this game. So, the player sticks with the same weapons until they are sick of playing the game due to their own lack of change, the main issue is whose fault that is, the player or the developer. In this game I would state the developer but that is up for interpretation.

I usually really like the story of a Metal Gear game but MGS V is one my exceptions for this rule. It has some of the worst story telling in the whole series but to be fair the series has somewhat of a high standard. First of all, it doesn't seem to cover up the plot holes of some of the previous games and actually makes it worse by adding new plot holes all together. Now, you might think that isn't too bad at first but when you have 100 hours + of gameplay and one of key selling points of a MGS game is it's story the Missions might ware on you quickly, as most of them are pretty generic with some amazing exceptions. You also might think that they are leaving plot holes for the next MGS game but this was supposed to be the climatic finale to the MGS series that answered all of our questions we had. Instead, the game added a bunch of new character which range from "Good" and "Weird but enjoyable" to "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ James Bond Villain #543" and also ruined (ruin is a strong word) some old characters by changing their character motivations and personality (looking at you Ocelot) for little to no reason. Overall though, the biggest sin this game commits story wise is the final chapter that was never finish. Look, I understand Kojima was rushed through development by Konami and due to the fact he had a big vision for the game he never was able to complete it on time, but that does not give the game a pass at it's certain state. I am not blaming Kojima, the blame solely rests on Konami but the issues with the game's story still stands. 

Overall, would I, an obsessed fan boy of the series recommend the game? Depends, if you are an obsessed fan boy like me, please take this game lightly and you'll love it. For everyone else, the game is pretty good with some holes in the gameplay but it's still super fun.

As someone who'd never played a Metal Gear title before this, I cannot recommend this game enough, especially if you think of yourself as a creative person. This game rewards creativity in a way that no other title (in the world, as far as I'm aware) does. If you come up with some crazy solution to a problem and wonder, "Will this work?", the answer will almost always be yes. The more "out there" your ideas are, the better your experience playing this will be. 
So don't sneak through levels. Slap a sticker of an enemy soldier on your cardboard box and MARCH through as if you're one of them. Or lure guards away from their post with a picture of a scantily-clad woman. Power move.
Don't just run-and-gun through levels. Find a good toilet and rig it with enough traps to incapacitate everyone who walks into it. I promise it's a lot more satisfying.

Just as good as the creativity aspect of MGSV is its difficulty. The game never feels too easy, but at the same time never feels unfair. Enemies will, over long stretches of time, learn your techniques and adapt to them. This would suck in any other game, but MGSV gives you enough options that even these adaptations feel fair to play against. (If sleep darts stop working on a certain enemy, for example, you can still lure them onto mines, distract them with lewd posters, or make them so paranoid that they'll investigate anything, even if you're nowhere near it.) It's hard, but never punishing, which is probably what makes this game so easy to get into. 

I should probably mention that the story isn't great, but isn't bad either (7/10). Online play is weird, but can totally be ignored. Soundtrack is absolutely outstanding. Wholeheartedly recommend, even if you're not normally a fan of stealth games.

MGS5 is the end result of the design that Kojima was fooling around with starting with Portable Ops on PSP, continuing through Peace Walker and Ground Zeroes. It's a game built around assembling a team, taking on missions, and growing your influence - a prominent part of the storyline of the series. 

I really love this game. It's a lot of fun to explore, take on missions, experiment with the different weapons and tools, and make it your own. There are a ton of different ways to approach each mission and the game actively encourages you to do so - of course the scoring system emphasizes stealth but that is only one way. The base building is a lot of fun and very addictive. It's easy to lose hour upon hour into this game. Most stealth in videogames has moments that feel arbitrary and frustrating, but MGS5, like the older titles, has an AI that follows a defined logic that is easy to understand and makes the game very transparent and logical. 

Hardcore MGS fans didn't like this title and I understand why. The story is rather threadbare and for some reason Snake barely speaks. It's incredibly weird by the standards of this series. Most of the story is delivered on optional cassettes from your underlings. The bad guys in the game are weird and don't make a lot of sense, and the main story missions (which pop up every 6-7 main missions, and are the ones tied to achievements) are far less fun than the other ones in my opinion. However, in spite of this, it's most definitely a MGS game and full of the characters, moments, and level of detail that are part of the series. 

I think MGS5 is a far more approachable and accessible game for a broader audience - it's probably the only title in the series I can say that about, except for the first title arguably. I think it's easy for a newcomer to pop in and pick things up. The game also runs great - it isn't the most advanced title graphically, seeing as it was designed to run on an Xbox 360, and scales really well - I have a powerful PC and can play it at 4K and 60fps maxed without any problems. There's a ton of content, it's a lot of fun, and it plays great - an easy recommend. Give it a try!

So when the mouse moves to what is equal to one pixel (or whatever the game uses internally to handle mouse look) it may be multiplied. If your in game sensitivity is set to, say 5 it may move 5 units (pixels or whatever) per mouse move. This means that you skip 5 units that you cannot ever reach over. Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain had a very rough development, culminating in the departure of many key developers from Konami, the company that made it and keeps the rights on MGS franchise even though it's "soul", the team that stood behind other entries in the series is no longer there. This shows in almost every aspect of the game, but overall it's still very enjoyable package.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay shines. Even though sometimes you can clearly see how rushed the game was, it is still one of the most refined gameplay-wise games in the series, with controls being the best without any doubt. Open world aspect might be dull and uninteresting, but infiltrating each outpost and base feels magnificent, especially how much variety it has not only depending on your loadout, but also on the weather, time of the day, alert level and your previous actions, which soldiers fairly quickly adapt to.
For those who played previous MGS games i will describe it in a little more detail; 
Camo system is dumbed down to binary matching/non matching camo, which slightly affects visibility.
There are comparatively few gadgets at your disposal - NVG, sonar, box, a variety of stun gun, inflatible mockup of player character, pentazemin and pills that allow you to see through walls - but none of them feel useless.
There is a lot of weapons to choose from, and even a weapon customization option. The gunplay in general is very good too, though gun sounds are a little uninspired.
Mother Base mechanics are interesting, but i quickly forgot about it entirely when i got my levels and GMP high enough.
The level design though leaves much to be desired. MGS3 did open environments much better, and GZ was head above V in regards to that. It's nothing too bad, but it's very bland, and there are very few unique environments or opportuinites.
Stealth itself handles pretty well. Alert is almost instant, there is almost no report time like in MGS2 when only one soldier is alerted. There is a feature called "reflex" which turns on slow mo on alert, but it comes with a penalty to a score (which matters because you have to earn money to operate here) so i turned it off after a couple of missions since it's not that much of a helper. There is a search phase, and caution phase stays on for three ingame days (!) which i find very fitting and welcome change. Vision and hearing distances are comparable to "hard" or "extreme" difficulty of earlier installments, but due to how much better gameplay loop is, and open environment of levels this is not a problem at all.

So core gameplay is a solid 5/5 if i were to rate it, though i'm not a big fan of levels and mother base.

[h1]Activities[/h1]
Main missions are amazing. They are quite unique, have many ways to approach them, and generally very well designed. But. Then they start to repeat. Due to how rushed the game was the team had to repurpose game's hardmode into being the part of main campaign, so in the end of the game you'll be replaying same missions but with harder difficulty. Nothing against hardmode, but having it as part of main line is kinda lame. Also some of the mission onjectives are very bugged, which is a problem, but one that does not count to mission design itself.
Now it's gonna get worse.
Side ops are uninspired, and very poorly thought out. With a few exceptions it boils down to blowing an armored convoy in a middle of nowhere up or abducting a guy with an escort. That's it. And there are ~150 of them. This is plain stupid. Not only that, but some of them are so bad, that they manage to be objectively insulting to the person playing. Foxtrot Uniform Charlie Kilo mission 45. If you are going for 100% - god help you.
Animal hunting looks like a little fun minigame on paper, but in reality it's a game of dice with mr. Kojima. Only 22/47 animals can be found in game, tranquilized/stunned and captured by player. For the rest you will have to use Capture Cage set up in a specific area which is in no way communicated to a player. Capture cages are ONLY retreived when leaving an area through a helicopter, and beleive me, even with a guide it will take you up to 20 hours to catch 'em all. It's tedious, boring, nd it's required for an acheivement and 100% completion.
Dispatch missions are nothing like their predecessor in Peace Walker. You just send your team and wait up to 3 hours. No simulation, no  team assembly, nothing. Just a probablilty number, another dice game. Better start this early if you are going for 100%, if you don't want to have the game open for 3 hours just to see if stars lined up for you today.
Mother base itself is meh. You can travel there to boost morale, see a couple of cutscenes, complete one [b]heart wrenching, tearjerking,  soul crushing[/b] side story involving one very tragic character you have seen before, see a zoo and take a shower. But nothing more. It's very boring overall, to the point that it might as well not be there.
Forward operating bases are equally as boring, since you are infiltrating an [i]identical[/i] base with slight variation in security system. It's unbalanced, filled with cheaters, and overall unengaging. But it's a good way to boost your resources since nobody plays it and it's almost a guarantee that nobody will infiltrate your base.
There is also an online mode, which was very promising, but since rules there are massively different - stealth with AI and living players is [b]not[/b] the same - it quickly died. You can fire up a dedicated server, if you have friends, and have a fair bit of fun.

In conclusion the game is very lacking in activities. But ones that work - are great. If you have completed main story - there's not much to return for.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Now for the main disappointment of the game. Spoilers ahead.
[spoiler]The story is unfinished, but even if it were it's pretty bad. It is obvious that team has ran out of steam, and have wanted to depart from Metal Gear for a long time. You can see that writers are very skilled and know how to work with given material, but main story line of the game outside of hooks to the rest of the franchise don't make sense at all. Skull Face is the worst MGS villain period. He's unrelatable, stupidly cruel, stupidly evil, and his motivation is paper thin. All the buildup from Ground Zeroes goes nowhere, since he doesn't even get a satistfying sendoff. Huey turning to an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥ doesn't make sense also, but at least it works with the rest of the narrative. I never thought i'd say this but i was tired of seeing Psycho Mantis. His gimmick is stretched way too far here, to the point that when the new question was raised in the story i was telling myself "please let it not be Psycho Mantis rage/psyche magic [i]again[/i]". The Phantom plan of Big Boss is very ambitious, but leaves me with many questions, if not to label it pointless outright. Language parasite mumbo jumbo is well written, but makes for a poor story element, nanomachines were handled much better.[/spoiler]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
MGSV has a very interesting and fun core gameplay loop, providing you with many cool tools, but leaves you with very few things to do with them, and very little motivation to do so, given how poor the overall story was.
It's worth playing, but not worth 100%ing - there's nothing there.

I have nearly 2 hours in this game and just experienced my first bit of actual gameplay. I don't know how it's possible to fail so hard at an introduction. People play games to play games, not to watch a terrible movie. From what I can see: Atrociously bad menu design and popups that tell me to use a right stick to move the character, the worst gunplay I have ever experienced, and a requirement to go into my Logitech software to bind M4 and M5. In the first "outpost" you encounter you have a guy (who you have no reason to care about despite the game beginning with two hours of cut scenes, completely blowing any reason for this amount of "exposition" to exist) telling you to be sneaky, find a vantage point and scout, but there is zero consequence for running in and doming every person you see. Zero world building. Yikes. Refunded.

Edit: I caved and bought the game again hoping the gameplay would be passable, and I could overcome the cut scene wankfest. 

The "tactics" elements are suitably fleshed out, and the missions are adequately enjoyable. You recon a compound, sneak up on guards and kill them. The stealth works, but stealth is apparently easy to accomplish: Assassin's Creed, Far Cry, and Dishonored, of games I've played, all have the same systems. MGSV features a forced slow motion effect, whereas the aforementioned games all have it as an upgrade in the progression path which I tend to forgo because I find slow motion effects cheesy. It's fine, but not my cup of tea. 

This is not an open world game. The game is a set of linear missions and you are strongly encouraged to "extract" from the main map to a base totally unconnected from that map after handling a couple at a time. Perhaps I am still in the tutorial phase, but that would be another strike against the already slow pacing. Are you really going to make me play the game 10 hours before you reveal your awesome open world? If so, pass. 

Moving around and exploring feel terrible. You are given a horse, but it handles strangely. Traversing the rocky terrain on foot is a chore; anything beyond a mild incline requires the use of a vaulting animation which can only be triggered when the character is positioned directly facing whatever cliff face you want to get up. The kicker is that you can only trigger this animation if the surface is high enough. So a small rock is impassable, but a slightly larger rock is a climbing surface. The result is that you're basically just moving along a road. A map with mission selection would genuinely be more enjoyable. 

The decision to use M+KB or gamepad further complicates. While this is a shooter that rewards head shots with instant kills, it's also an objectively poorly ported console game that ties your movement speed and the sound produced by movement to an analog walking system. The nuances of delicately tilting your left stick to creep towards an enemy, knowing that if you go to fast you'll get discovered, are lost on keyboard. The cover system, similarly, becomes totally unusable on keyboard. The game is clearly built and tested for gamepad. In the end, I found myself just putting down the gamepad and using the mouse whenever I got in a situation where quick headshots were necessary. Not great. 

The illegible menu system hinders an otherwise passable loot-based progression system. I'm the sort of player that really enjoys finding every trinket in a compound, but here I have no idea if I'm even being rewarded for doing so. There is no readily viewable inventory of these items you pickup as far as I can tell, and if there is, the game certainly didn't draw attention to it. Everything about looting is just dull. When you upgrade a weapon, the menu gives you a yellow list of things of stats (I guess?) that are changed, with no real indication of how these stats affect anything in gameplay. There are a bunch of guns, but why would I want another gun when all of them one hit headshot and what I really want is more durability on my silencer? If you put loot in your game, please make it enjoyable. Give me that weird, psychotic adrenaline rush from finding an absurd amount of a rare resource. 

The big takeaway here is that this game is on sale for $12, all DLCs and the short prequel included. You think, 100+ hour modern game for $12? Great deal! Not when the biggest cost of this game is lost time. Time lost to interminable cut scenes, time lost to missions that mean nothing to progression. I imagine every MGS fan had already purchased this game at full price and got more than their money's worth, hence the positive review score here. But in 2019, the game just feels like a failed attempt to hitch an old franchise to the giant open world and progression bandwagon of the early 2010s.

Let me get this out the way. This game is 80% gameplay and 20% story. It lacks the traditional cinematic cutscenes that has been expected of the MGS series since 1998 and the story is instead told through various cassette tapes that you unlock as you complete more missions. For newcomers to the series, don't expect to understand what is going on. For people that have a decent amount of knowledge of the series, expect to only understand a quarter of what's going on. Though the cinematic cutscenes are preferred to the cassette tapes, there's still a lot of lore to sift through that goes between the events of Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater to the original Metal Gear on the MSX2, as well as helps bridge a few things past that point.

As for the gameplay, there is a large amount of freedom to play with. Stealth is not required unlike past MGS games. This is a double edged sword as it puts non-lethal tactics in the shadow of lethal methods, but allows for crazy experimentation. You're encouraged to replay missions and complete them in different ways. 

Speaking of missions, there are 2 different acts and they're both lacking. Unfortunately, the second act is even more empty than the first as it repeats missions from act one with some difficulty modifiers (total stealth, on-site procurement, extreme difficulty, etc.) with a couple of unique missions here and there. However, the lack of story and unique missions doesn't mean that the game lacks emotional depth to it. Be careful of getting attached to certain things in the game.

Overall, this is a good game. Whether it's a good Metal Gear Solid game is up for debate, but I think the gameplay makes up for the lack of story.

As someone who's played every game since Metal Gear Solid at release I still love this game although it's easily the weakest of the Kojima made games. The gameplay itself is great although the side quests are very repetitive (go extract/destroy tanks, clear this minefield) but the game lacks the depth of previous Kojima games. In previous games you could call experts who would tell you about guns/equipment but in this game they just state the obvious, telling me what it is and stopping at that. I do love the level design though and how Kojima used the open world to let the player take lots of different approaches to a mission. The story is told mostly through tapes and even then snake barely talks although I do like him when he does, his voice is much better than it was in ground zeroes but still no David Hayter. Enemies are deaf and blind however they can call in reinforcements and a helicopter and they search your last location if they lose you and you can always bump into those reinforcements while escaping. You can of course disable these and it can make for useful distractions, getting certain guards to move out of the way while you go in and rescue a prisoner. The Kojima humour is still present, the funniest thing is having DD on lethal, sending him into a camp and just watching him jump on enemies and slitting their throats. You can also have Quiet snipe an outpost and sit back and laugh as they're picked off or give her a loud sniper and laugh as she comes under fire from the whole outpost and you get to sneak in.
I love that you can drive vehicles in this game, giving you another way to complete objectives, drive straight in and use the armour to tank the shots then quickly fulton a prisoner or attack the base with it while playing 80s hits. If you don't fancy driving you could also have the helicopter transport you, ride on your horse or use a small mech. Speaking of mechs, there is a boss metal gear which is a fun and unique fight and quite tough. The skulls you fight are also very tough. It took me hours to beat both versions the first time through and the sniper battle when you first meet quiet is also fun, especially on extreme where one mistake spells your death. This is a very good open world stealth/action game but it is not a perfect one. I'll just list pros and cons of the single player game and then review FOB missions separately.


[b]Pros (Single Player):[/b]

- A pretty good story. I didn't like some aspects of it but overall it was well told and had interesting characters.
- Excellent open world with lots to do.
- Very good stealth aspects, it is very punishing at the start but more and more rewarding as you get better at the game.
- Decent loud action but I feel that this isn't the way this game is meant to be played.
- Lots and lots of guns, most of them are behind expensive upgrades but the point still stands.
- A vast upgrade system, there is plenty of endgame content here and plenty of options of approaching the same missions differently.
- Excellent graphics, even for 2019.
- A metric tonne of content, there is easily over a hundred hours of SP content here.


[b]Cons (Single Player)[/b]

- The helicopter ride at the start of every mission is just wasted time and could have been a skippable cut-scene.
- The second half of the game was mostly harder versions of the first half's missions which I thought was lazy.
- Some secondary mission objectives are absolutely terrible so if you are a completionist you are in for a bad time with a lot of the end game content.
- Collect-a-crap achievements which are absolutely ridiculous in their scope, again completionists are going to have a bad time with this.
- Getting around the Afghanistan map is needlessly tedious due to large sections of impassible terrain.
- Some of the endgame gun/item upgrades take a ridiculous amount of time to complete.

Overall, despite the downsides, this is an excellent game in its SP portion.

FOBs are the online portion of MGSV and this is the weakest part of the package. The amount of guards and security measures on the advanced FOBs is so heavy that even the most careful run and with plenty of experience you will likely end up in a shootout after inevitable discovery. The PvP combat in FOB's is hilariously bad and as a new player to FOB's or even one with weeks of experience you will stand absolutely zero chance against players who have grinded the endgame gear for this game. To be fair, you can just run away when someone invades your game and I highly recommend doing exactly that because PvP is a complete waste of your time. The endgame upgrades related to FOBs take an insane amount of time to complete, I've come across one that will take 10 days (no exaggeration) to complete. 

One aspect of FOBs that some will deny is the fact and it is a fact that microtransations related to FOBs (MB coins) are PtW. Well, they absolutely are pay to win. The reasons are as follows:

- Insane upgrade grind I mentioned earlier, you can skip that altogether with MB coins. 
- MB coins allow you to buy extra FOBs which will give you a massive resource and research boost.
- MB coins can buy you FOB insurance which sounds like a protection racket and that's because it is.
- MB coins also allow you to complete dispatch missions (missions where you send your minions on headhunting/resource gathering missions) which means you will be swimming in resources and high level soldiers if you can pony up real world cash.

This is my first MGS game, and I was hesitant to get into it considering I knew next to nothing about the story or the franchise in general. 54 hours in, and having completed only about 24% of the main story, I have one word to describe this gem. Phenomenal. The story weaves itself completely organically against the backdrop of some of the tightest gun-play and tactical operations. The base-building component is woven in beautifully with the core gameplay mechanics, and yet never impedes on the main focus of the game itself. Even though the pattern of the side-missions can get repetitive, as others may have pointed out, the absolute freedom with which to approach a situation is so liberating that it never really gets boring unlike in so many other titles. Stealth works wonderfully and the diverse pattern of enemy takedowns, interrogations, and hiding bodies (or extracting them) creates this consistent hypnotic rhythm which allows for this amazing and immersive experience. The main missions feel fresh so far and can quickly get very challenging, especially, if the focus is to get higher mission rankings. The game truly comes alive if one leans towards stealth-based and tactical strategies with the occasional gleeful killing spree on side missions. Make no mistake the gameplay is most rewarding when trying to be a ghost, or should I say, Phantom , in completion of the objectives. 
 
MGSV looks stunning, and at times while riding thru the deserts of Afghanistan, one can't but be reminded of memorable moments  from the The Witcher 3. Some have complained about the gameworld being rather barren, and the lack of NPCs but then again, this isn't an RPG. That said the sandbox style open world and the way it is populated works perfectly within the context and scope of the game.  Surprisingly for a console port, I didn't have to change a single keybinding and the controls and mapping feel transparent in their functionality (considering there are multiple possibilities of equipping support gear on the fly or accessing the iDroid for tac support). 

There are so many other details that are taken care of so well in the game (for instance the Buddy system), that go on make this such a unique and engaging experience. Highly recommend this game, particularly to those on the fence because they haven't the prior titles. Just go for it!

You can use the weaponry and tools you've acquired to accomplish anything that's thrown at you in just about any way you could imagine. 

There is a bit of a grind involved in MGSV and while I felt it was unnecessary, I was able to get rid of the issue with mods, and yes there are a fair amount of mods available for the game as well. Just be aware that if you're going to purchase MGSV you will be purchasing it for the game mechanics and not for the story. If you're buying it for the story you may very well feel disappointed. For the price of the game vs what it has to offer I do feel this is a title I can recommend.

My only question at this point is,  "Who ruined the game?"  Was it the Kojima development team, or was it Konami?  The game has everything needed to be outstanding... but there is always some corporate BS feature added in to ruin the experience. Here is my short list of such features:

- Insane crafting requirements for weapons and items:  After you get half way through the game, some of the guns and items require millions of GMP (the in-game currency) to "develop".  Who is going to re-play 18 missions just to get a dot sight upgrade on ONE gun? 
- Forced time-delays on crafting: Let's say you grind for days to gather all the necessary resources to develop a gun you want.  The game rewards you with a big "F^%$ YOU!".  You get a timer put up over the item that you wanted.  The timers range from a few minutes to WEEKS!  
- Forced gameplay styles:  Once you have grinded for days to get the required resources, then waited another week for the forced time delay to expire after leaving the game running 24/7, finally you can use your shiny new gun.  Except you can't.  If you shoot too many people in the game, your "Demon meter" fills up.  Once it gets to a certain point your character becomes PERMANENTLY covered in blood and has a huge pointy rock sticking out of his head.  
- Microtransations:  So the in-game money is called "GMP".  Except it's not the in-game money.  The real in-game money is called "MB Coins".  You earn MB coins by ... spending real life money to buy them? 
- Pay to win:  If you are willing to pay an extra $100 dollars, on top of the $60 for the game, on gun and item upgrades then you can be pretty much unstoppable in this game.    
- Near-impossible objectives:  Did you ever feel like riding around the entire country of Afghanistan looking for one prisoner hiding in a random cave?  Me neither.  That is what a lot of the game objectives are like.  
- Deceptive leveling system: If the soldiers you already have at your base are at a low level (E rank), you are only going to see low-level soldiers on the battlefield (E rank).  If you paid a bunch of extra money on microtransactions to level-up your base fast (why in the HELL would you?), and your soldiers are all high levels (S rank), then you are going to see high-level soldiers in the battlefield (S rank). Completing harder missions, or playing better have NOTHING to do with the ranking of soldiers you find. 
- Stupid Base-Building Mechanics:  The first thousand or so soldiers that join you are worthless in terms of unlocking important weapons and items.  
People who buy this game are treated like horses being led around with a carrot on a stick.  Early on in the game, a little extra grinding reaps some good rewards.  However by the middle of the game you are being led on an endless wild goose chase.  Grinding, paying more money, and accomplishing obscure, almost impossible to find objectives earns you nothing but more of the same.

Even though I'm giving this game a recommendation, it's difficult to recommend for everyone; speaking as a fan of the Metal Gear franchise, this one in particular can be a bit of a mixed bag depending on what you're looking for.

In order to better understand the story of The Phantom Pain, hereby referred to as simply MGSV, I'd strongly recommend playing Ground Zeroes first, as that serves as the prologue to MGSV; it's included with the Definitive Experience.  If you haven't already, I'd encourage playing the earlier Metal Gear games as well, such as Peace Walker and MGS3, but they aren't necessary to play in order to understand MGSV's story.

Once again, you're the legendary soldier Snake, and you're in charge of your own private military force.   It's revealed not far in the game that the army Snake raised in the previous game, Peace Walker, was effectively wiped out by agents of Cipher, an organization Snake opposed during that game, and after some time out of action, Snake must rebuild his army and strike back at the ones that took everything away from him.  

Regarding gameplay, it's essentially Peace Walker 2.0 as a lot of the same ideas and mechanics return with some refinement here.  One of your goals is to make your army stronger by recruiting people to join your staff, obtain resources and materials that you can use to develop weapons, equipment, and even expanding your base itself.  It has a bit of an open-world mentality in that you can pretty much do things your own way and are actively encouraged to try different strategies, as the enemy forces adapt to your tactics and counter them in various ways (for example, if you infiltrate facilities at night too often, they'll start carrying flashlights and night-vision googles; if you rely on headshots extensively, they'll start wearing helmets, and so on; although you'll eventually have the ability to counter these yourself by sending some of your units on deployment missions).  Given the franchise's origins, stealth is encouraged; but you can also go in guns ablazing if you really want to, especially once you've developed stronger weapons and armor for yourself to use.  The game also has a buddy system where you can deploy with one of the various buddies once you have them available; you start with just the horse, which is good for traveling to places quickly especially towards the beginning of the game, but you'll also unlock a few others that have their own specialties and uses.  I'd recommend trying them once you have them and seeing for yourself how they work and which ones best suit your particular playstyle.

The controls are fantastic, everything is easy enough to do and your character has considerably more freedom in terms of movement and control then the previous games.  MGSV also has a few features to help make it a little more accessible to players, such as reflex mode which briefly slows down your perception of time if an enemy finds you, allowing you some time to take them out before your cover is completely blown, or escape depending on your situation (if you don't want this feature on, you're free to turn it off if you wish).

One minor point of criticism I have is that some aspects of MGSV are locked online, meaning you must have an Internet connection in order to use all the features MGSV has to offer.  After you've reached a certain point, you're given the ability to build Forward Operating Bases, or FOBs for short, giving players the means of expanding their army even greater then before.  Think of FOBs as secondary bases you can build that allow you to house more staff and resources, allowing you the ability to develop more things and harvest resources faster then you would without.  This sounds great, but here's the catch; once you've made an FOB, you'll be open to attack by other players: other players in the game can infiltrate your FOBs to steal your staff and resources from you and vice versa.  Generally speaking, as long as you don't partake in such invasions yourself and have sufficient security levels prepped up, you should be left alone; although you may occasionally still get a random player that will try to invade your base to steal your stuff, and there's not much you can really do about that unfortunately.  It should be noted that, even if you do get invaded and your defense fails once in a while, you really don't lose all that much that you can't get back relatively quickly, so it's really more of a minor inconvenience at best.  Another thing that kinda sucks is that a large portion of your resources get locked online as well (to put it one way, imagine most of your resources are being stored on those FOBs), so if you lose your Internet connection for whatever reason, you won't be able to use any of those online resources at all until your connection comes back.  If you don't want [i]anything[/i] to do with this though, just don't agree to the Terms of Service before you start playing the game and you won't be taken online, although you'll also lose stuff like daily bonuses and other similar perks until you decide to agree to the ToS.

Another object of some controversy is the story itself; which I admit is a bit weaker compared to the other Metal Gear games.  Without spoiling anything, after you finish the first segment of MGSV, the story kind of drags on from there and once it starts picking back up again, the ending suddenly shows up and you'll probably be left wondering “wait, that's it?” and the ending itself may leave a bit to be desired.  Being the very last game that the creator of the franchise, Hideo Kojima, worked on before his departure from Konami and knowing that MGSV had a bit of a rocky development due to internal issues between Konami and Kojima's team, it understandably can be quite disappointing as a grand finale to the franchise as we know it, although after enough time, you may come to accept it for what it is and may even be able to appreciate the message it left after the fact.  To get the most of MGSV's story, I'd suggest listening to the optional cassette tapes you can find under the Missions tab on the iDroid.

There's another online component in the form of Metal Gear Online, some kind of PvP team-orientated multiplayer shooting game loosely based on MGSV.  Personally, I don't care for these kind of games to begin with and never bothered to try it.  As I understand it as of this writing, there's a small player base out there and it's still possible to play games, although a portion of the player base are known to use cheats and hacks which is always frustrating to potential players, but your mileage may vary.

One more matter to bring up is DLC.  If you're going with the Definitive Experience, you'll have everything that was ever released for MGSV on Steam, including the previously unavailable day-one DLC that the console versions got, which consists of a few unique weapons, items, and uniforms for your character to wear; Definitive Experience is the only way to get that content on Steam, so be aware of that.  I don't find any of these DLC to be overpowered, especially the weapons as they are just weaker versions of weapons that you could develop yourself later in the game anyway.

Overall, as I initially wrote, it's difficult to fully recommend this title; it's definitely not for everyone, although I'd recommend it to fans of the franchise in general.  MGSV easily offers the best gameplay in the whole franchise; it's so much fun sneaking around and using all sorts of different gadgets and weapons and trying different strategies for each missions (almost anything you can think of is a legit tactic to try).  For those seeking something more like the previous games with a strong story, you may be a bit disappointed, but you may be able to make something positive out of it as well.  If you're interested at all, I'd definitely suggest picking up the Definitive Experience as it's more bang for your buck then just buying the base game.

When I first got MGSV I was only interested in the creative and fun ways you can do things stealthily, but I quickly got into the story and eventually I found myself invested in it, and it is because of that, that MGSV has become one of my favorite videogames of all time. And since I've finished the story, I've decided to write a review going over the key features and explaining the goods and bads of them.


Open world:
-There are two large maps each with their own unique environments, weather patterns, and locations.
 Both maps have outposts, bases and other special locations scattered throughout them. The open world part is great 
 because it allows you to tackle missions and objectives in many, many ways. Although there are many things to in free 
 roam from completing side ops to gathering resources to just capturing outposts, I found that these activities can become 
 repetitive and not fun if you do them very often, and once you've completed the story, there isn't much else to do 
 in singleplayer.
-You can build and upgrade your very own Mother Base, with several teams and platforms with their own unique functions 
 that you can level up by building more platforms and acquiring more staff to unlock new abilities and opportunities.
-There is a HUGE amount of weapons, items, and tools you can use to help you on your many missions, though I found 
 that you don't really need all of them. I wanted to unlock everything just for the sake of completion but eventually the 
 costs become so high that replaying missions and side ops just isn't enough to maintain a stable GMP level and develop 
 new equipment.


Story:
-The story for me was probably the best part of this game and like I said before, I wasn't interested in at all when I started.
 This game has an amazing story with amazing characters (thanks primarily to Kojima) and it is because of it that this game 
 is my number 2 favorite. Some would probably say that this game doesn't have the best story in the series, and they may 
 be right, I really can't say that it does or doesn't because I haven't played any other MGS games.
-Unfortunately, the story itself is unfinished; this I'm sure many of you know already. Once you finish chapter one, you get 
 a sortof teaser for chapter two, and when I first saw that I was like: "Sh*t's about to get crazy now." But chapter two is 
 mostly just extreme replays of earlier missions with only a few new missions.
-Another con of the story is that it's not completely replay-able, sure you can do the missions again as many times as you 
 want but you wont get the full story like you did when you first played through. The only real way to replay the story is to 
 start a new game, but screw that because I don't want to go through all that open world crap just to relive the story, I just 
 don't think it's worth all that time and effort. It's truly a shame because I really like the story in this game.


Multiplayer:
-I haven't played enough of MGO to have a well informed opinion of it, but I'm going to share my opinion of it anyway.
 To me, MGO is just Konomi's attempt at GTA Online, which to Rockstar and Take 2 is just a money farm. I'm not sure 
 exactly what it is but I am determined to avoid MGO completely.


Though it has many problems, I still love this game for it's story and openworld.
In the final words of my review, I shall say: Thank you, thank you Hideo Kojima, and curse you Konomi.

No game has left me feeling more bittersweet than MGSV. While being one of the best games I've ever played it also includes an incomplete story that will, likely, never get the ending it deserves. Gameplay is perfect with everything feeling tight and clean for a stealth shooter game. Enemies learn your patterns and adapt to your play style. I for one kept going for headshots only for enemy soldier to start wearing helmets. However, you can still land a headshot if you aim perfectly to just hit enemies in the face and miss the helmet. Some things feel a little dumbed down, such as slowing down time right as you are discovered giving you the split second to avoid detection by killing the spotter, but much of these elements can be changed with the difficulty slider. The story is also not on the same page as previous MGS games. It falls more to the wayside and is somehow the most grounded narrative of the series. One can only guess this was a result of complaints from MGS4 and it's ridiculous amount of cutscenes. Still the game is a perfect send off for the franchise at it feels like a culmination of everything the gameplay ever wanted to be. You feel like a super stealth agent who can handle themselves in any way they see fit, including dropping a supply box on an enemies head to make them unconscious.

To sum it up: this game has its storng points, but as it is, MGSV is only a phantom of what it could have been. And sometimes, a pain.

THE GOOD:
[list]
[*] Many different ways to complete an objective in singleplayer missions.
[*] Many different tricks up your sleeves in general.
[*] The freedom of open-world gameplay is fun. Run around plundering gold and gems and stuff (and soldiers who are not worthless.)
[*] Story by the legendary Hideo Kojima (until the second half, when things start getting hazy.)
[*] NPCs have appropriate reactions to common situations, up to and including "dude, where's our truck?"
[*] Graphics on par with any AAA title.
[*] Press-X-to-not-die events are actually somewhat intuitive.
[*] You can make your helicopter play your favorite songs as you deploy on a mission.
[*] A slow trickle of MB Coins for those who refuse to buy virtual money with real money.[/list]

THE BAD:
[list]
[*][b]Context-sensitive controls[/b] are bad at guessing the context. This really hurts in a stealth game because one wrong move can ruin your stealth.
[*][b]Movement.[/b] Though somewhat justified by Snake's injuries, movement controls are clumsy and obtrusive. There is a noticeable delay between motion keys and your character's motion. Do you like to play as a swift stealthy ninja? Have fun playing as a brain-damaged pirate.
[*][b]The environment.[/b] Unclimbable 30-degree slopes. Insurmountable waist-high fences. Invisible mission area boundaries that cause you to fail the mission. Some solid objects cannot be used as cover just because.
[*][b]AI.[/b] Enemies treat armored vehicles same as infantry. Your dog learns to sniff out land mines, but never learns to avoid them. Also never learns that jumping in front of your gun while you are shooting is a bad idea. NPCs get around their shortcomings by cheating: your dog is invisible to mines, and guards can see you through walls during combat alerts. [edit] Guards in singleplayer are oblivious to their own mines. Guards in online missions are invisible to their own mines.
[*][b]Obnoxious efforts to sell you virtual currency.[/b] Past the mid-game, you can literally buy in-game multiplayer insurance by spending real money.
[*][b]The grind.[/b] Optional mission objectives may require equipment that cannot be obtained until later in the game. You will need upgraded equipment for late-game and online missions. You unlock equipment by spending resources. Said resources take a long time to amass, and can be stolen from you by other players (unless you keep buying insurance.) You will be tempted to let this game idle in the background to get through the grind faster, but...
[*][b]No volume controls[/b] aside from helicopter music. (You can still disable the game's sound from the Windows Volume Mixer panel.)
[*][b]Fake difficulty.[/b] You will unlock more powerful equipment over time. So will your opponents. Skill is still very much a factor, especially for long-time players who unlocked EVERYTHING and are competing against similar players. Equipment becomes a big factor for mid-level players. For example, during online missions, you will meet armored NPCs that shrug off shotgun blasts to the head. With skill, luck, and a lot of experience from countless failed attempts, you can sneak past all of them without getting spotted. With progress, you can unlock a special gun that bypasses all their armor.
[*][b]Fake content.[/b] During the second half of the game, only half the missions are new. The rest are old missions on hard mode. Ocean platform missions are all the same, differing only by the opponents' strength.
[*]Cannot dispose of bodies on ocean platforms. Unconscious guards can be thrown overboard to their deaths just fine, but Snake refuses to pick up dead ones.
[*][b]Most side-ops[/b] are repetitive and boring. "Kill these." "Steal those." Even if you do not bother with side-ops, you will end up doing that stuff dozens of times just to make progress to better equipment.[/list]
[edit: found these later]
[list][*][b]Late-game[/b] progression is exponentially more grindy and somewhat bit pay-to-win. The only way to unlock the equipment you need to deal with invading players, is by unlocking all four FOBs. To do so, you'll either have to buy virtual currency with real money or spend a lot of time reaping daily login bonuses. It took me a year and two months and unlock the FOBs I wanted. If you do everything perfectly, logging in every Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday, and buy only the cheapest FOBs, you can get there in 350 days.
[*][b]Konami's own servers[/b] will occasionally disconnect you for no clear reason. In singleplayer, this is only an annoyance. Online missions, however, are automatically considered failed if Konami's servers disconnect you. Resources you spent on the mission - which can be a lot for online missions - WILL NOT be refunded.[/list]

THE UGLY:
[list]
[*][b]Venom Snake[/b], when he is covered in blood after you decide that your time is too valuable to spend on saving NPC lives (whose lives Snake would ruin anyway.)[/list]

I became a big fan of the Metal Gear Solid games since MGS1 and to this date, I never cared for any stealth action game because the player could get away with more screwups than its counterpart. It was easier to complete the games and experience its deep, if maybe convoluted story thread.

I bought MGSV day 1 and played tons of it.... before finally putting it down and moving on to other games and clearing my backlog instead. Why?

Well, for one, an the average playthrough of previous games varied from 6-15 hours. Meanwhile, average playtimes for MGSV can vary anywhere between 35 -120+ hours and it took me at least 110 to get the true ending and I was still missing out out special "re-run" missions", side ops, loads of gear upgrades, Paz sidequest, Metal Gear Online (MGO), and Forward Operating Bases (FOBs). You definitely get your money's worth of content, but if you want to reach the end, get the true ending and have a decent base and set of gear, it will certainly take you a while to "Just beat the damn thing and find out what is going on in the Metal Gear arc".

The open world, realistic design of the game is done extremely well here, and is also one of the features I never wanted in a Metal Gear solid game personally. In previous games, you could try to get past an area or neutralize most or all the enemies and if you failed, you could go to another area and reduce the alert status after time, or deal with guards one by one. In MGSV, enemies group up, become alot more aware of their surroundings, call in supporting guards, tanks and helicopters and have better equipment to deal with you. Its done very well here, but it is not what I wanted from MGS game, which let me get away with alot more nonense so I could get to the end. S Ranks are for hardcore stealth fans, not me.

Being stealthy and non-lethal here is arguably more important here than in the other games because recruiting staff and stealing resources and equipment is key to upgrading your own gear and Mother Base, which is neccesary for story progression.

Fans had the hope that MGSV would answer most if not all of the questions still lingering about the series, since this was the last game to be produced by the series creator Hideo Kojima. Development of the game was challenged due to corporate restructuring from Konami and their removal of his name from cover art and promotional material. Its arguable that the game was formed into a live service with microtransactions thanks to Konami instead of Kojima Productions, but we may never know that answer. With all the lengthy play time that me and other players had, MGSV left many questions unanswered and even created more in which you can read articles and forum threads about for details.

Ultimately the design flow of this game and the publisher-developer relationship nightmare tarnished the production of MGSV. There were some things about MGSV that makes it my least favorite in the main line of the series. However, I almost assuredly spent more time in this game than in the entire series combined and I often question if I want to keep it installed and play it more later or consider it done (I hate how often I get detected or I mess up one small thing, I honestly wish the game was easier).

[h1]MGSV is excellent and worthy of a purchase (especially at its $20 retail price) but it has caused consternation and disappointment among fans. A 10/10 it is not, but a heavily flawed amazing game it is.[/h1]

I wish there was a neutral rating option, but there isn't, so I have to give it a thumbs down for the forced online base raiding component and mobile-game-like microtransactions.

The online base raiding component to the game was supposed to be optional, but when the time comes, the tutorial literally forces you to build a FOB, which can then be raided by other players whether you're online or not.  Once built, you cannot destroy or dismantle it.  What's more, in order to have your R&D levels high enough to research good end-game level gear for the SP campaign, you HAVE to participate in this mode.  Do you need the good end-game gear to finish the SP campaign?  Not technically, but certain weapon options only unlock with very high R&D levels that can only come from having FOBs, so you're more limited in the SP campaign if you try to ignore the online component.  All of this is just bad game design.

On the plus side, though, the game looks good, runs well, and gives you a big, open world to play in with a good deal of freedom.  You can tackle most missions in a variety of ways, and you get a large assortment of helpful gadgets in addition to your weapons in order to help you through the missions.  I was actually fairly happy with the game until I came to the part where you're forced to build an FOB.  That pretty much killed all will to play for me.

I'm incredibly amazed at every aspect of this game. The gameplay mechanics, the graphics, the soundtrack, the progression system, the story, the easter eggs; it is unrivalled in the sense that nothing truly compares to this. The game itself is vast, expansive, and realistic, from the flora to the fauna, to the weather and the physics. It challenges, but is lenient. It establishes its rules and then lets you interpret them as you wish.

There is nothing more satisfying than successfully infiltrating a huge base, slowly working your way through the place, killing, subduing, and kidnapping as you go, knowing that every silenced bullet and every Fulton extraction is working towards a goal of being the absolute best and only of your kind. At the same time, there is a magnificent feeling to running around trigger happy with a machine gun and a rocket launcher, demolishing anything and everything that stands in your way as a friendly airstrike illuminates your field of vision with fire. 

The story never fails to surprise, entertain, and exceed expectations, and the format of the game is beautifully crafted, telling an interactive story. For a game that is relatively linear in nature, it allows you an array of options as to how you choose to play.

I bought the game on sale, shortly after it first came out, for about 30 euros, and after playing for no more than an hour or two, I was adamant that I would have happily paid the full 60. It is an experience which I would full-heartedly recommend.

[h1] My Brief and Totally Uninformed Review of [i] Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain [/i] [/h1]

People seem to almost worship Hideo Kojima for his narratives, and [i] MGS V [/i] is no exception... but I just don't get it! The whole [b] extremely tedious and drawn out [/b] introduction to this game failed to grip me in the slightest. You start off as Big Boss emerging from a nine-year coma, and spend - I ♥♥♥♥ you not - about fifteen to twenty minutes groggily waking up, designing a character (FOR NO REASON - I didn't pick up an MGS game to play online!), and crawling around the floor of a hospital after some bint tries to off you. Then the hospital is raided by some [i] mercs or something [/i] that want Big Boss' head as well as [i] Buff Human Torch [/i] and [i] Mini Psychomantis, [/i] who are... helping? Trying to off you? Who cares?! If you can't tell, at this point, after limping and dragging myself across a hospital, barely having any real gameplay, I wasn't invested in the slightest. What doesn't help is that I know that the primary gameplay loop hardly resembles this intro.

Anyways, this goes on [b] FOR AN HOUR AND A HALF! [/b] Bloody hell! I cannot wrap my head around how far this game is up its own arse! It concludes with this chase sequence involving [i] Buff Johnny Storm on a Horse [/i] and then transitions over to the primary local: Afghanistan.

This is where my primary gripe kicks in: Afghanistan sparsely littered with Russian military outposts, against the backdrop of a sandy desert, does not make for an interesting open world! After fleeing a [i] Fiery Dullahan, [/i] it's very hard to get excited about marking Russian soldiers with your binocs and stealthing into their bloody boring and samey campsites/outposts to find intel. 

This is where I turn my attention to the praise for Kojima's writing: How could you possibly believe that this does not have SEVERE pacing issues? 

So yeah. Maybe my expectations were far too high. So many people I know have sung this game's praises, it's absurd looking back. Honestly, this environment and the core gameplay loop has done absolutely nothing to grab me in the first few hours - and if it's the narrative that's supposed to sell me, please refer to my prior comment about it being "up its own arse." 

Maybe I'll return at a later stage and change my tune completely. That said, it's a pretty hard sell right now. I've a lot of [i] Hollow Knight [/i] and [i] Dark Souls [/i] to play before I even consider giving this another bash.

[h1]Shortly[/h1]
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an excellent game impeded by it's own mind-numbingly padded story that resembles a reality TV show. However, it manages to overcome these flaws through lore, gameplay and graphics.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
Pros
-Very well optimized.
-Enemies have interesting designs.
-Looks great.
-Realistic, when it is.
-Cutscenes have a shaky camera, as if an actual cameraman were there recording it.
-Weird handling. To see this in action, or to have fun, get a ZHUK BR3, find a flat area and hold A or D.

Cons
-Padded story.
-Lore is difficult to understand for first-time players.
-Toxic online community.
-You are forced to build an FOB for the game's online section.
-Has many of the issues that shows like Kitchen Nightmares or reality TV shows in general tend to have. For example, clichés, unnecessary slowmos and zooming when there's a reveal, or new character.
-No anticheat.
-The game's best weapons take days to unlock and are expensive, but how convenient that you can purchase what are essentially Konami Coins to skip the wait?
-Microtransactions and pay to win. The last tiers of weapons are ridiculous.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain manages to do what most games fail at; it manages to look great while playing very smooth at the same time. It is very well optimized, and only falls below 60 FPS when the screen is bombarded with particles or in the jungled areas of Africa.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As with all Metal Gear Solid games, you must sneak and not become spotted, however you still have a viable arsenal to use in case you get spotted.

[h1]Updates[/h1]
The only thing resembling updates are weekly new FOB events.

[h1]Online[/h1]
There is no point to playing MGSV's online portion, as the only players that play it are the fanatics who play the FOB mode, as with all games that have low online populations. Notably, the remaining fanatics are just sweats, sadly.

[b]There is no way to delete your FOB in order to remove your online progress, as keeping one is merely an unfun hassle.[/b]

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
Very clean with excellent tracks scattered about. Shame that some of the best tracks like Nuclear aren't ingame.


[h1]Rating[/h1]

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, at the same time, wants to be a videogame and a TV show.  It found a balance between those two, and plays great. While the online part of MGSV:TPP is not worth your time, it's singleplayer mode is sure to soak up quite a few hours from even the newest players of the Metal Gear Solid franchise.

Despite a wall of negative pros, it still manages to be a solid game, as long as you don't touch the online portion.. at all.
