What was originally meant to be Hideo Kojima’s masterpiece did end up being the most polished unfinished game I’ve ever seen, which it is likely to stay for a long time. Also, I now consider Assassin’s Creed calling itself a stealth game heresy.

Graphics: Nothing to criticize here. Sure, you do find some textures that look kinda off now and then, but considering how damn detailed your character and your weapons look, that isn’t even a nuisance. Besides that, this game has some great optimization; it’s the only AAA game I can run in 4k without suffering noticeable drops in FPS.

Sound: I highly recommend playing this with surround, this way you’re able to locate enemies fairly easily, as you can hear them breathe. Other than that, the local wildlife has a sound atmosphere as well, to the point that you can hear some flies buzzing around you. Concerning the OST, you have epic soundtracks playing during important missions and sad music during tear-jerking scenes. The background music is exactly that; background music, it’s decent but adds to the atmosphere. It sure does get repetitive, but any music would do so over the course of several hours of sneaking.

Gameplay: You can finish every mission in roundabout a million different ways, with the help of several hundred gadgets at your disposal, ranging from bio-weapon-suits to anti-material rifles. All of these are developed throughout the game, on your very own paramilitary base in the Indian Ocean, eventually sporting thousands of soldiers and a size of several square miles. Stealth works logically and flawlessly most of the time. Base management only gets annoying once you have to get your new weapons by online development, which takes some days unless you pay to speed up the process.

Atmosphere: This game switches from military espionage to zombie apocalypse to fighting giant mechas within a few minutes and still manages to maintain most of its credibility. If that isn’t a sign of quality I don’t know what is. Interaction between the main characters felt a bit flat though.

Balance: The stealth gameplay itself is well balanced in most cases; in some of the main missions it’s utterly ridiculous though. While normally being tough as ♥♥♥♥ they become a joke once you found an exploit. Due to the high number of gadgets at your disposal, there’s at least one such exploit for nearly every mission in the game. Another thing is the varying difficulty of the main missions; you’d expect them to rise in difficulty with the story progressing. This isn’t the case for this game’s main missions; they regularly switch from the hardest difficulty and the longest duration to cheap as ♥♥♥♥ and not difficult at all. Given the fact that said cheap missions barely deliver anything vital to the story, I consider them filler. The missions after the main story’s ending are poorly balanced as well; it isn’t exactly hard to notice that they were never supposed to be recycled this way.

Story: While having a pretty good presentation, which is executed excitingly and dramatically, this still is the game’s weakest point. That is because you don’t get a full story; the original finale was scrapped, essentially leaving an unsatisfying ending and several plot holes. I’d normally think of something like this as unforgivable. If I would’ve known that before buying the game I wouldn’t even have bothered to buy it. If someone would’ve told me that the second half of this game’s main missions consist of replaying the former ones, I would’ve dropped it right away. So, why am I still recommending this? Because the story still managed to keep me interested and the background information made me curious enough to go through it, even though it only consisted of voices on tape, which is only slightly more entertaining than reading a Wikipedia entry and way less informative. If you want to understand everything concerning the story of this game, however, especially if you never played another Metal Gear before, you’ll have to take some hours to read through the Wikia and watch the content which was cut from the final game on Youtube.

The deciding factor whether you’ll like this game or not depends on your valuation of storytelling, if you’re all about gameplay, or just someone who cares equally for each factor of a good game, then this won’t disappoint you, given you don’t dislike stealth games in the first place. If you’re all about the story, or a fan of previous Metal Gear games, or both, this probably isn’t your case and your disappointment may vary.

I'll give this one an "Ehhh". It is a high quality game, no doubt about that and therefore deserves a thumbs up. And yet it has some serious flaws that make it a rather mediocre, maybe even bad depending on your expectations, Metal Gear Solid title.

The gameplay itself is rather fun, albeit a bit lopsided for my taste: Sneaking is pretty difficult and unrewarding and can turn the game into a frustrating experience rather quickly. That would be okay if it meant that MGSV was simply a difficult game. But it's not. Because choosing the other strategy of "just shooting everybody in the face" is very viable and with all the weaponry, equipment and companions at your disposal really easy.

The open world is great and the amount of options you have in terms of weapons, vehicles, customization, recruitment, basebuilding, research and secrets to find is huge. However, some of these things are locked until you meet requirements that are hard to see through or even find out about in the first place. In my entire playthrough of the game, I never unlocked the weapon customization feature. I only found out that such a feature exists by reading about it online. And this even applies to Story missions: I had to look up guides on how to unlock the last couple of missions because the game simply doesn't tell you how to do it. In that regard MGSV is unnecessarily obscure (and not clever or complex).

The presentation is, as you'd expect, phenomenal, but the story...is quite the opposite. Even for Metal Gear Solid standards the story is more than absurd, but one could simply accept that and call it 'creative' if it wasnt for the fact that it feels (and as far as I know actually IS) unfinished. The game ends abruptly and many of the questions that you will undoubtedly have after "finishing" it, are only explained in audiologs which unfortunately arent very engaging. 

Hence, Metal Gear Solid V only felt like one half of a very ambitious, high quality game to me and not the full game that I was hoping for.

MGSV:TPP is a combination Stealth/Management/Action game, with the Stealth being the main gameplay mechanic and the action and management portions exist to modify the stealth.

You have an open world, with a huge map (two maps), and scripted missions take place in specific smaller sections of each map. You manage a small military base, and order people to research new weapons or gadgets.

The main gameplay loop is very fun. Usually on a mission, you will navigate to an outpost, scout the outpost, take down the guards silently, and do the objective (usually destroy/capture something), and then exfiltrate.

There is great replayability for this game, because there are around 20+ big bases, and maybe 50+ small outposts, and infiltrating a base from the opposite direction will force you to change your approach.

The "multiplayer" FOB feature is OK, but not great. The MGO online is not very fun in my opinion, but it's free with the Single player.

The "buddy" system is a great mechanic, which will give you an ally with special powers.

There is also a mod called Infinite Heaven which will let you play each mission in Subsistence Mode, meaning you will start with no weapons, similar to a battle royale. Despite this, nearly every mission can be completed in this way!

Despite some of the development management issues, the gameplay here is excellent.

Gonna start this review off by talking about the bad parts of this game as a nod to how bad the game starts off, but also to warn newcomers (like i was) about how you shouldn't let the first bad couple of hrs (which is the start of this game) ruin your experience. Personally, I took a break for a while from the game after this first part because its really boring and uninspired, I thought the rest of the game would be like that, however I was wrong and I am very glad I returned to give this game another try because it really does get a lot better.

Cons:
- Terrible Story. (the human torch riding a unicorn following a flying straightjacket bound woman with a massive fire whale leaping out of nowhere was dumb as hell) I understand that these crazy events depicted in the prologue are meant to intrigue you about cipher and take a supernatural approach but its just so utterly ridiculous that you can't take it seriously, the fire man is basically depicted as unkillable from the start so whats the point? its really dumb and I honestly wished this game couldve been a coherent story about tactical espionage and revenge rather than all this unnecessary supernatural crap that had me groaning each time it came out of nowhere.
- Not only is the story bad but its unfinished and the ending leaves more questions than it answers, which is really unfortunate. 
- Prologue Mission (Ep 1) is far too long and has some extremely ridiculous moments (see above)
- The game has some pretty tediously bad boss fights that play really awkwardly and rarely utilize the excellent gameplay mechanics, for example one boss fight is that you have to fight teleporting zombie soldiers with a missile launcher, they teleport and run you around to the point where theres no value in taking cover or strategizing, you just strafe and fire the launcher until they die.
- The first 2-3 hrs of the game are almost 8(?) uninspired cookie cutter missions of open world stealth which become incredibly dull as they are all in the same area, with similar buildings and you have extremely limited gadgets + guns to play with
- No cover button. Oh boy this was a design choice that I found infuriating, when games like Gears of War, The Division and even Grand Theft Auto have mastered this feature over the years it is just mind-boggling that the developers of MGSV decided to remove it and opt for an auto cover system which proves to be very frustrating to learn as it seems to only work 50% of the time and will get your cover blown many times. It really is astounding that a game so fundamentally based on stealth which punishes you for being spotted would remove this fantastic feature that works so much better than any auto system.
-  Spoiler titles. Every single mission you start in this game uses the same "Directed by Hideo Kojima" title credits that appear onscreen when Boss is in the helicopter, flying to the drop zone. Why is this a problem? Well, because it lists off every single person that will be involved in the mission you are about to partake in, including a 'guest starring' section that always tells you whether you are about to encounter skull face, that you are about to fight the parasite legion, that you are about to a fighting a giant mecha etc etc. The credits even specify the mecha you about to fight, its honestly just ridiculous and completely the spoils the surprise when skullface randomly shows up in the mission or the parasite legion attack you out of nowhere. It is clear with the way the missions are scripted these encounters are meant to be random and shocking but it is spoiled at the start of the mission. Why is this in the game? If Kojima was so desperate to strike back at Konami for removing his name from box credits why couldnt he just leave the mission credits at: "Written/Directed by Hideo Kojima"?.

Pros: 
- Excellent stealth mechanics (apart from the lack of cover button) that are really fun to play with
- Realistic, Challenging Gunplay that keeps the game stressful and punishing if you decide to abandon stealth
- Decent enough AI Enemies that will investigate, flank, communicate etc etc
- Massive array of gadgets, guns, tools and vehicle to use, customize and develop for use in the open world
- 'Buddy' companion system. Really fun and actually useful (unlike FO4's companion system) companion system that actually changes the way you approach different situations in combat. It works excellently and the companion AI is decent enough that it doesnt just get you or itself killed (Like in FO4)
- Large open world with plenty of bases, outposts, checkpoints and strongholds to conduct either main missions or side ops in. Unlike other open world games with bases like JC3, or FC3/4, your capture of enemy bases is only temporary and are swiftly retaken with reinforcements by the enemy in order to keep the world hostile and full of danger, which feels much better than an empty world full of captured bases like in JC3 or FC3/4 and also keeps the map from feeling small or completed.
- Music. Almost all bases you infiltrate will have a radio/cassette player with an iconic track on cassette tape from the 1980s which you can collect and play at any time. I really loved this little feature and it allows the player to experience some really fun moments, like driving a tank through the desert at night listening to "The Final Countdown" on the way to destroying some enemies was just an awesome and quite unique experience. You can even upgrade your helicopter to have speakers which can allow for some really enjoyable experiences like flying into a heavily guarded landing zone blasting "Ride of Valkyries".
- Developing weapons. Collecting materials, upgrading staff units and developing gadgets/weapons feels satisfying and makes missions really worth completing, as you gain more toys to play with in the open world.
- Weather Effects/Day and Night cycle. Weather effects such as heavy rain, clouds and sandstorms are all fantastic and change up the gameplay effectively, forcing the player to adapt and use it to their strengths, its a very enjoyable mechanic that can change missions completely and totally wreck or bolster your strategy. Being able to choose whether to deploy in daytime or nighttime is a nice touch and both have benefits and disadvantages, the time slowly going by is also great as it feels realistic and like your time actually matters, for example if you deploy on a big base at night and spend too much time gathering intel or crawling around you can get to sunrise and become alot easier to spot.
- Basebuilding/Management. I haven't delved too deep into this yet but its easy to understand and interesting to manage different areas, staff members etc etc
- Excellent UI and Menus. The UI and Menus, (which you spend alot of time in) are well thought-out and executed, everything feels intuitive and it isnt clunky or annoying to use.
- Beautiful textures/overall graphics, game looks fantastic and motion capture is excellent.
- Optimization. Running it on ultra settings with no stuttering or fps drops, its not that taxing on my hardware although the game is 3 years old now, however its safe to say its been pretty well optimized for pc.

Overall, this game's fantastic gameplay makes up for the various problems that plague its beginning, and it massively spikes up in quality and enjoyment around level 8. Its an excellent open world stealth game that is worth playing if you can stick with it.

This is the worst port from a console I have ever had the displeasure of playing. As a fan of smooth gameplay, seamless transitions and a responsive, intuitive control schemes, the pace of this gameplay feels like a new driver who has no concept of acceleration or braking discpline while the player, a mere passenger, is experiencing this all from the total control of the trunk.

The two most torturous aspects of this game are the Delays and the Saves.
Delays: The animations and unskippable transitions are numerous and intrusive. Getting into any vehicle or on a horse has an accompanying fanfare and disorienting swooping camera so that you KNOW you JUST. got into. a VEHICLE.
Every time you want to set foot in a mission zone you have to spend 60 seconds in an unskippable helicopter scene in which you... just... sit. And watch the sky. (If you don't believe 60 seconds is a long time try slowly counting to 60 while staring at a blank wall).

Saves: this game world is elaborate and the compounds are immense. The objectives in this game are always lofty enough to be intimidating but possible enough to be encouraging. That is...until you spend 30 minutes systematically eliminating an entire base only for a single mistake to cost you your life or objective. Most devs know people mess up. Restarting a lot is part of that whole Hard Game allure. But it's not fun at all to lose that much time and effort from a single mistake. To compare: if you screw up 4 times and you have to load a few minutes back, that's ten minutes spent LEARNING how to be better. If you have to load 30 minutes back each time, not only have you wasted 2 hours of your life failing one objective, but you only learn 1 thing each time. Replaying 30 minutes of gameplay in which you made no mistakes is tedious and dull.

Fortunately for us, the story elements and conventions that give me such extensive second hand embarrassment are mostly limited to the cutscenes (of which there are still too many). The redeeming part of this game, is in the gameplay. The stealth gameplay is super great. If you pride yourself on perfect stealth type stuff, boy, do I have a game for you. Less actiony than games like splinter cell, think more belly crawling around in the dark. The maps are open world, enormous and interesting. The missions, both main and side, are by and large a lot of fun to play with few exceptions. Customizing your home base, helicopter, buddies and gear is a lot of fun as is developing new weapons and equipment. In terms of endgame content, there is a multiplayer mode where you can infiltrate other player's bases and they can infiltrate yours. Not only can you manage your security setup and guard equipment for your various base platforms, which you construct more of over time, but you can steal resources and personnel from other players. Clearing bases and outposts quietly and kidnapping the skilled soldiers is always a blast and if you aren't feeling sneaking around every single outpost, you can always hop in a tank or ifv and roll right through.

In truth, I wish there was a "Mixed" option when it comes to reviewing products on Steam. Because that is what this game is in my opinion, a mixed bag. this is very much a Metal Gear Solid game in the sense that you can still go around, infiltrating bases/camps. But it doesn't hit the narrative points that previous titles had achieved. It is absolutely the weakest when it comes to not only providing the narrative, but also towards providing meaningful perspective for said narrative to exist. In theory, you could completely skip this game and you honestly wouldn't miss a whole lot. 46 missions compose the story, and most of the time the details leading up to said missions revolve around listening to cassette tapes, or by listening to support over the radio. It certainly does trim down the length of the game (where before, the details were explained in cutscenes), the issue is that it really doesn't help to provide a sense of depth or gravity to the situation. That may be a personal preference, but you also have to remember that this is the fifth game in a series where NARRATIVE DEPTH seemed to be priority one. But this isn't the only element to the game, there is also uh...A game...To this game...Anyways, now you have seemingly unlimited methods of completing tasks in this game. You can kill or tranquilize enemies (which is standard of MGS games since MGS2) but you also have additons to that system such as the fulton recovery system returning from Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker. You can drive vehicles, call in support from man's best friend, Quiet the mute sniper, or even a sort of miniature Metal Gear called a Walker Gear. Expansive gameplay is always appreciated in my book, and I admire that Kojima Productions took the task of making as many possible gameplay scenarios as possible. The game's setting comprises of (technically) three open worlds: Afghanistan, Africa, and Mother Base. You can recruit soldiers, fulton materials, vehicles, or even free roam just for the sake of free roaming. This is on one hand a unique idea since the worlds are massive in scale. However the potential is lost when you realize that it is just empty space. Occassionaly you may find soldiers out on patrol, or even some animals to rescue/fight. But %75-%90 of my experience has been traversing empty wastelands, getting from point A to point B is tedious in this game since it never varies the events that can occur between those points. Most of my playtime honestly revolved around traveling these distances, it's just driving, and driving...Also, more driving. Overall, the game is very much a mixed bag with a weak narrative, but also some fantastic means of experiencing. 

So why do I recommend Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain?

Because when you get right down to it's core, it is a fun game. There's a reason why my playtime is high (aside from the driving), it's because the game provides a fantastic experience in terms of gameplay that you really can't find anywhere else. Experiences in this game, (or methods on how to complete a task) rarely become the same between players. A lot of experiences are unique to that player BECAUSE of the variety it has with the gameplay. To give a scenario, this is my second time completing this game, the first time was on my PS3, the second time was here. Not only was my experience improved here, but it also was so varied that in a lot of ways it felt like I was playing it for the first time. Because the scenarios that you take can change that much between players and gameplay sessions. So I would absolutely recommend this game if you are looking for a game that can provide unique scenarios every time you play. Also because it is a great deal, $20 is a small price to pay to the Konami overlords for this one of a kind experience. Even better if you could get it for a cheaper price.

Metal Gear Solid 5 is a 3rd person stealth-focused infiltration game set in the 70-80s military era with some sci-fi sprinkled on top. However, right from the start, this game has mental issues; it's bipolar. Ground Zeroes is this, Phantom Pain is that. So, basic gameplay has to be split in 2...

First, let's cover Ground Zeroes.

It starts as a "playable demo" that was sold at a high price, which can be completed in about 1-2 hours, excluding any extras side-missions. These extra mission just re-uses the same map with different objectives and day/night setting.

However, I actually enjoyed my time in those 2 hours because it [i]felt[/i] like an actual Metal Gear game. Great presentation, good conversations, great stealth action. I was able to play it from start to finish without putting the controller down.

See, this demo had everything that made Metal Gear great in the first place. The story cues in and gives you motivation to persue your task. Even if it's linear or open-world, a good story makes you want to see what's next. This was the main driving force of previous MGS's.

After finishing Ground Zeroes, I was a bit bummed by the lenght, but told myself "well, Phantom Pain will probably rock".............

But then I boot up Phantom Pain...

The hospital intro was alright, nice little build up. However, I can't help to notice the bizarre/surreal presentation after leaving the bed. I wasn't sure if these soldiers were human or robots,  quickly noticing their mechanical movements and behavior.

Things happen and you escape the hospital, then follows a long cutscene. Then it hit me in the face as I started riding my horse in Afghanistan leaving Ocelot behind... Snake doesn't talk... At all. On the Muteness scale, he's worse than Tom Hardy in Mad Max. Moans and groans a lot, might say a sentence each half hour or so...

So, instead of intricate conversation exchanges that lays ground to a good story which in turn motivates you to play, you have these long monologue by each character you meet which quickly turn into a snoozefest. There is no emotional motivation coming from Snake like it used to, no chemistry between characters. You're just playing as a mute, crippled, near-brain-dead shell of a character that used to be a hero for each game. Snake yells more at his horse than he talks to others...

Phantom Pain's gameplay, unlike Ground Zeroes, shifts from a linear story-focused game to a free-roam open-world game where you have to rebuild your military empire in the likes of Peace Walker. Instead of taking missions from a static menu, you can take missions live on the field. Using your chopper and your horse, you go back and forth from your base to your next mission objective. You gain GMP (money) by completing missions and use it to expand your base, research better weapons/gears.

I do admit the gameplay is great as I enjoyed Peace Walker back then. However, PW had a great story, with some very neat QTE ideas during cutscene which made the PSP feel great for some reason. PW is one of the highest rated games for PSP, so I guess they did a great job there.

As I start clearing a few missions, I notice yet another thing that's quite irritating. Each time you start and finish a mission, each names of the characters appear on screen (Snake, Ocelot, Miller, etc) just like a TV episode, followed by the dev's names. Wether it's artistic liberty or childish corporate defiance doesn't matter, it's just irritating after a few times.

The big idea with this episodic naming thing is to annoy people like me, who used to enjoy long stretchs of gameplay with loads of conversations. Instead, this presentation style ruins any immersion the story might have, which is already hard to watch like mentioned above.

I've rescued Kaz (3rd story mission), and again, I'm treated to a long monologue with a simple one-liner from Snake. I'm not sure the game changes later, but I fear the more I'll play, the more of the same I'll see.

I'm not exactly sure to who or how I should recommend this to, since this hodgepodge of a bipolar game is a damnable mess, an under-handed bait & switch.

I rate this a solid 6/10 for gameplay, loose #ERROR#/10 for the absurd dual-game flame-out/troll.

One of the best opening scenes to any video game quickly fizzles out into a sparse chaotic and unfinished story.   

Most of the game's missions feel like filler including most of the main missions, which should've been where the story content is.  There are some strong ones at the beginning, towards the end, and then obviously the end in terms of story, but the vast majority of main missions have nothing to do with driving the story forward, they just feel like glorified side ops.  To make matters worse the game employs a tactic of forcing you to replay missions in higher difficulties to unlock the true ending.  In terms of story telling, if you thought the whole "nanomachines did it" meme that MGS4 created was bad, this one introduces an even worse one.  The prequel games had done a pretty good job of not reaching into the full ridiculous like MGS 2 and 4 did, but that ended with 5.  It's obvious development of this game was a struggle to tie loose ends.  The story is made worse by the fact that it's told in big bursts sparsely throughout the game. A dozen or so main missions, which have no story go by, then you get a heavy story main mission, which just feels like a sucker punch of absurdity, then nothing happens for a while again. There's also the infamous Mission 51, because there's an entire chunk of very important origin story for a character completely missing and it's pretty obvious they ran out of time for it.

You can probably map out Kojima's relationship with Konami as the game progresses and devolves into madness. 

That being said the gameplay in this game is the best the series has ever had.  This takes the Peace Walker formula to the next level and really fleshes out the base building and open world concept.  The core gameplay is excellent too and feels properly modern.  MGS games always had a problem of having weirdly unique gameplay and control systems, which did not lend themselves to aging properly at all.  This game's controls and combat system are tight, intuitive, relatively simple given it's an MGS game, fun to mess with, and above all else they feel like standard controls for what you'd expect for this type of game.  I can come back to the game and not be completely lost.

The game also has tons of content.  The open world is fairly big and varied and there's tons of side ops to do in addition to the main ops, all of which can be replayed in various difficulties.  There's a ton of weapons, equipment, and items, perhaps a bit too much.  There's an online aspect, which involves sending your crew out to complete some missions and also base invasion and your general MGO online multiplayer.  It's great, but it's also too much in some aspects.  If you're a completionist, but don't like online multiplayer, then you'll be in for a hard grind, a very hard grind.  The game's later aspects require tons of resources.  It becomes a grind fest.  The fastest way to get more resources is through the online multiplayer, which itself is fairly boring because there's a barren amount of variety to it.  There's also the problem of so much of this being real time based.  Building a base? Have to wait several days.  You can bypass this by paying real money, which is just stupid.

Even with all that mess it's a great game. If you focus on the story and enjoying a good amount of side ops on the way you'll have a great time, a long time, and be witness to an MGS level mind altering story.   It's sad to see MGS finally come to an end.  MGS was one of the games that got me into gaming as a kid and for almost two decades of my gaming life there was always that thought of looking forward to a new MGS game.  Nothing compares to an MGS game.  End of an era.

This game is what got me into the Metal Gear Solid franchise, and a lot of people will say that's a bad thing. Some of the most common complaints I hear about the game is that it doesn't add much to the overall story of the series, and the self contained story of this game is pretty lame, however I don't think that's a big enough complaint to call it a bad game. Yes, if you play the Metal Gear series for the story then you will most likely be disappointed by this game, however if you're new to the franchise or playing it for the game itself and not the plot, then you will most likely love this game, as I did. It's relatively kind to new players, not expecting you to have played the previous games to know what's going on, and the gameplay is the best in the entire series. Combined with the open world, what you have with Phantom Pain is essentially Breath of the Wild with guns, and Breath of the Wild was great. If you're a long time fan of the series, maybe decide what you want from this game before you play it, however if you're a newcomer, then this game is absolutely great.

PLUS SIDE :D 
         Best part of this title was the gameplay, attention to detail, and general amazingness of the gameworld. Another major plus was the way the gameworld reacted to your playstyles and the freedom you had to change methods, counter gameworld reactions, and upgrade weapons and gear to get an edge on the enemy. 
   Negative side :( 
         Gotta say, the cinematics were definitely trying to mirror an anime, dramtized, over the top kinda deal. The overall plot was pretty good and had some twists, but there were some moments that were very cliche and some downright cringy/awkward (a lengthy car ride with some very surprising guests while some chick sings in the background for example?) . Lets just say, if you're not a fan of random grunting, overplayed drama, or (trigger alert) anime vibes in general, might want to prepare yourself for a good cringe during the cutscnes.

***2018 
The story is weaker than MGS4, but the gameplay and missions are varied enough to keep the game fun and easy to move forward. It would've been better to actually have more cutscenes (which do look incredible). PC version is all round an amazing looking game maxed out at 60fps without any noteworthy crashes/glitches. Definitely worth it.

This wouldn't be a big issue if I could simply disconnect from servers, however, in doing that you can lose resources and GMP that is specifcally tied to the online component of the game.

Konami has clearly gone off their rocker, I would even say their online intergration is worse than Ubisoft.

A 9.5/10 experience offline (provided none of your resources are locked by online parts).

A 7/10 experience online.

First impressions:
- Lots of cutscenes. The beginning felt unnecessarily long with little to no gameplay other than crawling around on the floor. Could've been much shorter, or even a cutscene.
- Once I got into the meat and potatoes of the game, I quickly learned it's not much different from the first few Metal Gear games (gameplay wise). Stealth is almost too necessary, and completing anything can take ungodly amounts of time. Not only do you have to spend a lot of time scouting out areas, you also have to spend tons of time knocking out enemies or headshotting them with sleep darts. If you mess up... Well, I hope you enjoy lots of doing the same thing over and over until you learn all of your lessons.

So far, it's not my cup of tea. I like the idea of stealth, but not this restrictive. The stealth is what I dub "too realistic" sometimes. There are some deviations to the realism, but, so far, not much. 

If you really enjoy some hardcore stealth missions that make you feel like you're in an extremely dangerous situation in which getting caught means death, and you really enjoy planning out every single move you make, then this game is for sure for you.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Returning impressions:
- I've found more oppurtunity for action, but I'm still constantly running miles away from dangerous zones after killing maybe 2 to 5 people. Better than I was seeing at the beginning, but with the increased amount of soldiers to fight off, it doesn't change the pace much.
- Despite the pace of the game mostly being slow, the short bursts of fast-paced shoot outs i've been experiencing are extremely fun and almost have me jumping out of my chair in excitement/adrenaline. I'm starting to like the game better.
- The game still requires a lot of patience and dedication, which I don't have. I complete a mission or two then I have to take a break.
- [i]Getting tired of all of the intro cutscenes and credits showing in-game. I get it, Hideo Kojima made a game.[/i]

There isn't enough to be said about The Phantom Pain, and that is meant as a good thing.
This is by far my favorite game I've ever played, and I've played a few.
Rumored to be the swan song of the Metal Gear franchise, TPP is as amazing an experience as was expected of Hideo Kojima.
I've played every Metal Gear game and never imagined I would play a title that was better than Snake Eater, but I was proven wrong.
This game has been my staple through two tours in Afghanistan, and it ran fairly on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ windows laptop.
My point is, this is the greatest optimization I have ever seen in a video game, and it really shouldn't be.
The graphics are among the best of its time, and mods can further them even more.
The gameplay is so fluid, that it will never bore you, as I have completed this game several times.
As is typical of Hideo Kojima, the story and character progression are top notch and leave you wanting more after every taste.
There is nods to older games, appearances of old characters, funny scenes, drama, romance, action, and serious themes that dwell into the political.
As alternate history as this game is, it is still relatively informative, and I find myself listening to the same audio tapes over and over while I complete side quests.
On that note, there are 80's classics strewn about the dual play areas, and listening to The Final Countdown during Infiltration will never get old.
The music is but one of the pieces that was done to perfection, as the visual art is just as stunning.
Going on a journey with Big Boss and his crew has been one of the best experiences in video games.
Everyone loves a game that is easy to learn and hard to master.
With so many fine details in the gameplay, this is a gift that keeps on giving, and you'll discover things about this game every time you play it.
There's nothing more satisfying than infiltrating a base undetected and leaving no stone unturned.
Stealthily winding your way through a platoon of enemies, expertly dispatching every one.
Anyway, I could go on and on about how great this game is, but you just have to see for yourself.

Like many have said, I have a love/hate relationship with this game.

Mechanically, this game is a masterpiece. Every Metal Gear game prior to this has some kind of limitation that your character cannot perform due to the controller, engine, gameplay, etc. Some of those are baked-in features, like in MGS, MGS2, or the original release of MGS3. In regards to the over-the-shoulder type MGS games: Snake in MGS4 cannot track targets very well while crawling and shooting, or in the PSP version of Peace Walker has camera control issues. I felt like this game had none of those limits. Every character motion, action, item, cover wall, and gun performed in the exact way I was hoping it would. Venom is a natural extension of the player's hand motions and that is truly satisfying. Frankly, this game's character mechanics remain unmatched to this day. Building up Mother Base with personnel, equipment, and research gives a great sense of progression. Everything you actually DO in this game is fun.

The disappointment came with the story and the structure of the game. The episodic format of the game is taken from Peace Walker/Portible Ops and it doesn't translate too well to a big-time Metal Gear release. They feel too much like "challenge scenarios" rather than the single-player aspects of the game. It feels too much like there's an "ideal" solution to each scenario instead of the intrinsic reward of story-based events. An unsatisfying ending and repeated "hard mode" scenarios are just two parts to the problem. The characteristic quirkiness is almost completely absent from this game; instead, it takes itself too seriously for most of its run time. For example, the most fun I had with the game's story was when I went to Mother Base on my birthday (a great and goofy Easter egg for those who haven't done this). Metal Gear used to be FULL of that kind of stuff which is why many of us enjoyed these games in the first place. Like Peace Walker, Codec/radio calls are replaced with (optional) audio tapes resulting in Venom being disconnected from the actual explanations of what's going on which only serves to alienate the player from the story even further.

I can see the thought process here: Portable Ops felt like an experiment, Peace Walker refined that experiment, and MGS5 was supposed to be the ultimate marriage of existing MGS mechanics with those PSP tryouts. Overall, I'd recommend the game for its mechanics alone, but don't go in expecting it to be the best Metal Gear game. It’s a well-made and enjoyable stealth action shooter but if I wanted to replay a Metal Gear game for funzies, it wouldn't be MGS5 (…maybe just Ground Zeroes).

Oh boy, so we come to the last game of the Humble Monthly Bundle of December 2018, and it’s Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. This is a big game, and I feel that it’s impossible to divorce this review from the company who made the game, the man who made it, and the situation surrounding it. In fact, any attempt to do so at this point would not be properly judging Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.

We go back to Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes, which we already have reviewed about a week ago. From there, Ground Zeroes was an expensive demo for consumers, but it still contained excellent gameplay, even if it didn’t have a ton of content. At that point, I remember thinking that there was no chance in my mind Phantom Pain could fail. A true Metal Gear Solid level story, tied with that gameplay would be incredible.

About a year later in March of 2015, there were rumblings of trouble. Konami and Kojima Productions seemed to be going separate ways after The Phantom Pain. No one was sure exactly what happened, but the rumors that were around was that Kojima would be leaving Konami after the completion of Metal Gear Solid V and the other rumors made people think it wasn’t very amicable.

Six months later, Konami released The Phantom Pain, and while there are far more parts of the story such as the removal of Kojima’s name from some promotional material, I’m not reviewing Konami’s business practices here. I’m focused on The Phantom Pain, however, there are parts of the game that I think directly relate to this. I do recommend anyone interest in the full story to research it further, as it was a rather interesting situation.

So looking at The Phantom Pain, I’m quite amazed at almost every part of it. The first thing that strikes me is the graphics are fantastic. Almost every scene and every visual is unbelievable. The level of detail is similar to Ground Zeroes and that’s amazing. Though, once the player reaches Afghanistan after the first level and starts playing the main game, I do have to admit that the graphics while great, never reach the height of the first mission in The Phantom Pain nor the Ground Zeroes opening mission.

At the same time, part of the reason is they are different types of games. The first mission is a typical level based game with limited scope and view, and Ground Zeroes only has a small area to render. The Phantom Pain instead takes the open world to the extreme and allows Snake to explore a very large map with a huge number of bases, guard posts and locations to check out. While the graphics aren’t as good, they’re still amazing and I found myself lost in the exploration and locations.

About halfway through Chapter One, Snake is allowed to go to a second location. Without saying where it is, I’ll say the graphics seem to improve there. No longer is the player stranded in the desert that has sand in almost every direction. Instead, they are surrounded by lush and beautiful foliage, water features and better vistas to see everything.

Still, the graphics of the game are beautiful and while there are trade-offs, such as a limited number of interiors there’s still a focus on the binoculars again and it really allows the game to shine. The Phantom Pain still impresses me with the visual quality it achieves, even three years after the release.

Graphically, I’m impressed, then we come to the story, and the good news is unlike Ground Zeroes we start to find a bigger and better story. The game starts with Snake heavily focused on the aftermath of Ground Zeroes. Without spoiling it, Snake has a lot to deal with early on and the first mission is very story heavy and develops Snake into an interesting character. I would even say the first mission gives players a false understanding of what the Phantom Pain is going to deliver. There’s a lot of story development and it almost feels like it comes from another of the series’ games.

After that mission though, the story flutters away, and for the rest of the game the player feels like he has to chase it incessantly. Chapter 1 has thirty-one missions in it. Of them, less than half feel like they have a strong tie to the main story, though the last five have heavy story elements, and even contain a continuation with “to be continued ”s at the end of each mission.

Those last five missions are unlike any other mission in the entire game. That shift in pacing, both the heavy focus to the main story as if it’s suddenly important and the continuation feels off. Suddenly after 25ish very open world missions, you have five heavy story-based missions in a row, and they just don’t fit. The game eschews the story until it brings it back with a vengeance and then later tosses it away again.

Every mission works from the gameplay side, however, The Phantom Pain exchanges cutscenes and story moments in the previous games in the series to an audio tape style delivery system for much of its dialogue. While the audio tapes are often good and flesh out large pieces of the story, it fails the fundamental first step of a story. “Show don’t tell”. The Phantom Pain is not a radio broadcast, yet it tries to use that in the tapes. However, it’s a visual medium as well as an interactive medium, so even if it was the best story, it’s not living up to the promise of the medium itself with it. Even if they were Picture in Picture videos, they would work better with the medium.

Similarly, since they’re audio tapes, they almost always just tell a story, and for Metal Gear Solid, that’s not good enough. After most missions Snake will receive a couple of tapes that attempt to fill more pieces of the story. You’ll hear discussions of the villain (Skullface), different characters, and a lot of dialogue, and it can work if you put the time in.

At the beginning of each mission, the game shows credits, and sadly the credits hurt the story a bit as if you pay attention to them you’ll see surprise guest stars in many missions, in fact, there are great reveals of enemies and even the newest metal gear, but watch the credits and you’ll see their name so the surprise of their appearance is gone.

While most missions are free form and exploratory, some missions have a story based “Metal Gear Solid” feel. This is when you are ushered into a location with only one real entrance, you’ll notice something has changed with the game. Oftentimes you’ll get that strong story cutscene system again. Sadly they don’t happen often, but when they do the story shines. In fact, your first face to face meeting with Skullface is brilliant and every time I see that scene I instantly realize why it’s a “Metal Gear Solid” game, or at least what my heart really wants from a Metal Gear Solid game. The cutscene, the delivery, and the presentation are all there. It’s just a shame that you then play ten more missions trying to find another mission that has that same delivery, and ten missions after that chasing that second story moment.

I recieved this from a friend who got a second copy of the game through a Humble Bundle. Usually stealth games feel fairly binary, either you're doing well and you succeed flawlessly, or someone sees you and you restart from scratch because you're instaneously dead. Being spotted in this one isn't as immediately lethal as in older Metal Gear games (my only experience other than this game is Snake Eater as kid) or as forgiving as something like say, a Bethesda game. Reflex Mode (a time slow down effect that occurs when an enemy spots you, giving you time to react) can make it a bit cheesy if you're a good shot, but it's an option you can turn off and with it off it isn't so punishing as to seem unfair. The actual gameplay feel is lightyears ahead of the older titles, and the AIs ability to react to what you're doing is solid. I've only had maybe two instances where I felt the game was being unfair.
If you like open world games, this is a solid choice. If you enjoy tactical shooters/stealth, this is also a good pick. If you're a Metal Gear Purist, this game diverges some from what the previous games were, gameplay wise, but for the most part you can play it the same way those games did.
The only parts about this game I don't really like is the online component (that being said, I generally don't enjoy multiplayer anyways, so I'm biased in this opinion) losing staff members and resources to other players raiding your base is frustrating, and to hit the real end-game equipment, you have to either invest a huge amount of time into the game (coming back to get the daily reward and hoping it's MB Coins, the premium currency used to buy expansions for your online bases) or shell out extra cash for more bases online. Also, the game needs an online connection to function correctly, and if you DC you can find yourself without a large portion of your materials and assets, which can cause staff members to leave. With that being said, at the time of writing I've played for just over one hundred hours and I don't feel like the game is pressuring me to buy, or like i'm being punished for not engaging in the online aspects.

A fantastic game, everyone will find something to enjoy. It is a Kojima game, so expect a truly ludicrous and confusing story, but don't be put off; that's not where the substance of this game lies.

It certainly has its flaws, some highlights for me being:
- The generally perfect hitboxes struggle to distinguish between a helmet and a face, so sometimes you'll shoot a pesky guard in the eyes, in slow motion no less, and be rewarded with a loud [b]*clang*[/b] for your trouble. When the graphics and smooth gameplay keep leading you to believe you're safe from such oversights, it's pretty jarring each time it happens.
- There are occasional mission-breaking bugs, for example someone you're spying on won't have the conversation they're supposed to have and you have to give up and reset.
- The visual treatment of the game's silent deuteragonist/eye candy, Quiet, is pretty problematic. While there is canonical reason for all the bare skin, I couldn't really see one for the constant camera lingering, or the inclusion of jiggle physics. You can eventually unlock actual clothes for her, but[spoiler]this may well come too late[/spoiler].
- The game makes you watch the cutscene of Snake wearing a classic pre-mission grim expression on his helicopter before every time you go into the field. [b]Every time[/b]. Mission or no, and also when you go to your base. And it's almost a minute, and unskippable.

One popularly touted flaw I'm not mentioning, however, is that most of the game's latter missions are repeats of earlier ones with various 'hard mode' constraints. Total stealth, on-site procurement of items, that sort of thing. And I didn't mention it, because I don't think it's a flaw. It serves its purpose perfectly, which is to prompt you to approach the tasks differently.

And that's the really iconic thing about this game, its invigorating focus on freedom of gameplay. In most games such a choice means [i]'loud or quiet'[/i], or [i]'nice or nasty'[/i] or even [i]'hard or easy'[/i]. But not here. Snake's tasks can be accomplished by near limitless means, the variety is astounding. There are fully fledged gameplay mechanics for things you'd never even considered.

Here's an example of just a tiny corner, the timeless cardboard box.
- Get in the cardboard box to hide from enemies.
- Hide in the box on the road to stop a jeep, then burst out and blast the drivers!
- Too crude? Try leaving the box on the road and sneaking past, or even quietly[spoiler]fulton[/spoiler]the truck when it stops, drivers and all.
- Not wacky enough? Try putting the box over your head, jumping into it like a toboggan, sliding down a hill and body checking the drivers!
- Prefer mind games? Try putting a sticker of a pretty lady on the box and put it over your head and watch the drivers swoon and fall to their knees. Or put a sticker of a Soviet officer on the box and watch them salute and drive swiftly away.

You can always go on YouTube and find incredibly creative ways to get the job done, but don't do it too much; it's so rewarding to devise or stumble across these ideas for yourself! 

And new things will keep revealing themselves to you. I pretty quickly found the audio tapes, and worked out that you can have a cool 80s soundtrack to your adventures. And soon after, I found that I could play the tapes on speaker instead, and enemies would respond to them. Hours later, I would figure out that didn't just mean pop songs, and that playing an Afghan lullaby would send enemies off to sleep. I also found that I could have my helicopter blast out these songs as it came to the rendezvous, striking fear into enemies. But it would be dozens of hours later that I discovered I could put mp3s into the directory and have my heavily armed helicopter arrive to any song I felt like (Iggy Azalea's [i]Fancy[/i]) instead.

This is the game's strength. Not its own creativity, but the way it allows and encourages the player's creativity to flourish.

I was lucky, as I started my adventure with Ground Zeroes "Prequel", because first mission of TPP is terrible (long crawling sequence), and there is living man on fire, and floating child. I probably would've given up back then - and i'm grateful I hadn't.
I don't really know where to start. This and GZ are by far only MGS games I played (well, there is Survive, but thats for another time). I'm still unfamiliar to tangled story of the series, but TPP story picks up where GZ left - Big Boss is a leader of Private Mercenary Army, known as Militaries Sans Frontieres (love the play on Doctors without borders), returns to the Mother Base after rescuing former commrades from USA Blacksite. Upon arrival, he discovers that base under attack by hostile force known as XOF (Kisses and Hugs followed by F...). Moreover, one of the prisoners rescued from blacksite was implanted with a bomb, causing escape helicopter to crash. Big Boss spends 9 years in coma, and wakes up just as XOF discovers his survival, and sends forces to finish the job. With help of another patient, he manages to escape both XOF, and previously mentioned Man on Fire and Floating Boy. With help of man called Revolver Ocelot, he reaches Afghanistan just in time to rescue one of the former commanders of MSF and creates another mercenary army, known as Diamond Dogs (this isn't a spoler, these are 2 first missions). 
Story is... long. There are around 50 missions, 35-40 of them being unique story missions, rest are reused missions with a twist, such as mandatory stealth, no statring equipment, and so on. There are also 150 Side Ops - quite repetitive missions, with few types - couple of prisoner rescues, elimination of heavily armored enemies, tank units, and similar ones. 
One of the main elements of the game, besided story, is working on Diamond Dogs. Sure, you can just live on volounteers, but... enemy soldiers can also be experienced. Therefore, player is encouraged to [strike]capture[/strike] kidnap (lets not lie to ourselves) enemy soldier with good stats (solders are described by their suitability to specific Mother Base unit - Combat Unit, R&D, Maintenance, Medical, Intelligence or Support), or even unique abilities, such as decreasing costs of researching specific weapon types. Researching - because as leader of the unit, you can order research on various types of weapons and equipment that can be later used by player on missions, or by Staff in asimetric PVP component (later). Researches require specific level of Mother Base units, which can be increased by assigning staff with higher ranks in given unit. There are also resources scattered around the Area of Operations, and they are needed for research purposes, or to resupply before deployment. So if you are bored of eliminating enemy forces, you can go and collect flowers. Or go hunting, as there are animals present (they can be put to sleep, and extracted from conflict zones, for small payment from Natural Protection NGO). There are also collectibles, such as cassete tapes with '80s music.
Okay, so we know more or less what to do in the game - but where do we do it? Apart from Maltan Hospital, seen in two missions, player conducts operations in Soviet-controlled part of Afghanistan, and Angola-Zaire border region, full of various PMCs. Moreover, players can travel to their own Motherbases to increase staff morale (just by going near patrolling soldiers, but for some weird reason, staff seems to be happy when beaten up by their Boss. I dont ask, and i dont want to know). Last but not least - you can "visit" other players Forward Operating Bases and "recruit" their staff, or "borrow" their supplies - this is earlier mentioned PVP component - usually player faces only Security Unit of attacked player, but should he or his supporter be in-game at the moment, invarder may have to deal with better equipped enemy player. FOB construction and upgrading allows to hire more soldires, and increases Mother Base Units' staff limits.  
Attention Kojima paid to details is astounding. These small things maybe aren't that important, but certainly make game more enjoyable. For example, broken power lines falling into puddles of water during rain will stun nearby enemies. Enemy vehicles will stop and scare off animals from the road. You can use water gun to destroy communication equipment, or delay alarm by splashing water into face of guard which spots you. Enemy soldier reporting missing resorces, or get laughed at when reporting moving cardboard box. Unless using special Sneaking Suit, enemies may hear your footsteps when you try to eliminate them from close up. Enemies respond to your activities - attacking at night and scoring headshoots with make enemies equip helmets and NV googles. Just a few examples. 
There are few flaws in TPP as well. Some items are overpowered - Big Boss has prostethic arm, which can be replaced with models that have special abilities. Third level Stun Arm can, after ~30 seconds of charging, stun all enemies in 30-40 meters radius, being extremly useful during FOB raids. Game automaticly equips best uniform, but at some level, they restrict mission completion rank (sometimes it's stupid, like when GZ Sneaking Suit earns first level of Health regen - upgrade regular Sneaking Suit has without restricting level completion rank). But these are minor "offences". What really sucks is cut content - player can find Pastho Interpreters, but no Pastho Soldiers anywhere. There is at least one mission  that is missing from the game - mission name was Kingdom of Flies and it offers closure on story of one of the major characters. It's concept art was added to one of PlayStation Editions, and cutscenes can be found on Youtube - it seemed to be nearly done, which makes it's cut weird. Some say that there was supposed to be 3rd chapter - which allegedly can still be unlocked by disarming all the nukes on FOBs. Nobody knows for sure though. 
I know this review is a mess, but there were so many things I wanted to mention at once. I just wish i could forget about this game just so I could experience it again.

After a while, however, I started to love it, despite how annoying certain parts of the game are (maintaining a good balance of GMP, having to walk everywhere, [b]everything[/b] costing money to use - which makes sense). Though this may not be Kojima's greatest game (and I cannot veritably say that it is or is not, having not played anything else he directed), it is certainly a good one, and would have been potentially the best Metal Gear game (in terms of gameplay, at least) had the third chapter been finished and released.
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is, at times, a slow and casual experience, for instance when out in the open world, dealing with random encounters or clearing outposts over and over again - but it can quickly become demanding and anxious, such as in sudden stealth scenarios (e.g. coming across a helicopter or a tank squad). I believe that it's this dynamic that makes the game fun to experience, and engaging enough to keep players wanting to come back again.
The multiplayer element to this is, to be honest, lacking. The level progression system and the creativity of defence placement means that FOB raids are either stupidly easy, or ridiculously hard. Metal Gear Online is... interesting, to say the least.

Worth every single penny, really loved this from top to bottom.

The game runs smoothly and the controls are pretty intuitive, though weirdly I got a better experience using a controller rather than mouse and keyboard (and even weirder was the fact the controller feels more accurate when aiming). Stealth works well and there’s a wide array of moves and situational advantages such as weather effects. The story is pure Kojima crazy; it’s set in the ‘80s yet we have giant mechs, humans with preternatural powers and advanced cybernetics.  

Sadly a forced multiplayer aspect mars the game. In summary other players can attack bases you set up and steal your men and resources unless you stop what you’re doing (IE: having fun with a story mission) or pay Konami for “insurance”. This wouldn’t even be a negative if you could just play offline. However playing offline denies you access to about 90% of your crafting resources, GMP (basically cash), and effectively limits the size of your R&D teams. Since this became part of the game it’s killed my motivation to continue.

I’m recommending it though as recently so few games demonstrate such craftsmanship, and I imagine that if you’re not a misanthrope like me you’ll probably enjoy the multiplayer aspect.

The gameplay is also vastly improved from Peace Walker, although it's more comparable to Metal Gear Solid 4's gameplay. You can still crouch walk which is pretty convenient. Overall, I'd say this game is a solid 8/10. The gameplay makes up for almost all of the shortcomings of the story.

MGS5 is a strange game. It got huge amounts of praise when it came out and still does today sometimes, but its not that good of a game. Its definetly the weakest in the series.

The prolouge is a slog to sit through. Its like an hour long and its one of those things were you "play" through it, bit the controls are very limiting and the game takes control away from you every 5 seconds. Its not fun.

The first and biggest problem is that this game is tedious. The game is open world, bu the world is very empty almost to the point of uselessness. All it does is make the player run from mission to mission and its slow and boring.  Mother Base is also insanely huge and not in a good way. Its not that interesting to explore and it takes so long to get from one place to another. 

The missions vary from good to medicore and most are medicore. In fact i wanna say half of the missions in chapter 2 are just the same missions from chapter one just harder.  The side ops missions are even worse. 90% of the side op missions are downrite bad and i didn't even bother doing them after a while. The only ones i did was the imprtant ones. Unfortanatly theres a few points in the game were it forces you to do side op missions to unlock new main missions. 

The story is also very weak. It feels like it doesnt have a point. All the big and imprtant stuff happen in the other games and everything that happens here feels weak. And the twist is kinda stupid honsetly. 

Now whith that all being said there are a few things in this game that i really loved. 

The first is the graphics. It looks and runs damn good. 

The second is the gameplay. Its still the stealth/action that was great in the previous games and its one the things thats kept me playing. Its just fun to play once your in the groove of things. 

Developing new items/weapons at mother base is also really fun to mess with with all the methods you can use in missions. Unfortanatly if you develope a weapon/item you want to use you have to wait in real time to use it Which ranges from 16 to and hour and 35 minutes. 

The buddy system is sweet as well. D-dog and Quiet being my favorite. Quiet is is actually my favorite new character in the game. Shes bad ass as ♥♥♥♥, very usefull and her story in the game along with her relationship with Big Boss was sweet. She does lack depth though. 

And the cutscenes are very well directed and are fun as hell to watch. 

So overall MGS5 is a mixed bag. Honestly i wouldn't even say its a good game, but the game has charm and it kept me invested with its good qualities. Its a guilty pleasure. The majority of the games problems can probably traced back to Konami screwing over devolopment to which i saw ♥♥♥♥ KONAMI. 

Do i recommend this game? I'd say yes if your already invested in the series. If you've never played a MGS game before than this is a hard sell.

MGSV is probably the most technically sound in the series, brought low by its poor pacing and repitition. While I count most of the MGS titles as some of my absolute favorites games, MGSV lacks a lot of what made those before it so appealing. It lacks the impressive environments, the engrossing and sometimes whacky story, and any real need to use your brain to find a way to progress through your surrondings, the kind of things the series is praised for. Instead you're going to spend a lot of your time either in a desert clearing the occasional guard post, or as the HR manager, worried about staffing and recruitment for Mother Base. The story is cut up in a sort of pseudo episodic fashion, showing Kojima still wants to be a film director more than a gameplay designer. This leads to the story being shown as little bite size chunks that ultimately don't flow in any meaningful direction. All of that aside, probably the greatest sin of this game is when you find out that most of the first half of the game is recycled in the second, making it hard to justify spending another thirty hours of tranqing and kidnapping the same soldiers, in the same outposts, just for another half an hour of its shaky story.

It's like I can get to the ending and find some positive interpretation of it, but to get there I had to go through some stupid nonsensical missions and interactions that went nowhere, so what was even the point? I have such a love hate relationship with this game. 

On a boring Sunday night, I stumbbled upon a MGS3 PS2 ROM I had downloaded months ago, played for 7 hours straight, and have been hooked on MGS ever since. I played my way up to this game, playing the MG series chronologically from MGS3, so I came to this game without the shiny eyed nostalgia from the other classic MGS games, but with extremely high expectations as the only main line MGS game I had played before this was MGS3 (argueably the best in the series). 

Ground Zeros made alot of canonical sense to me coming, jumping to it mere minutes after finishing MGS: Peace Walker. The massive leap in mechanical fluidity, and the direct story continuity was boarderline erotic to me. It was a perfect taste of the full game to me (I got GZ and MGSV in a cheap bundle, so the price didn't affect my view of the game). The exclusion of the legendary David Hayter stuck out like an orgy in the middle of a Pope inauguration, but aside from that, I loved it.

But then I jump on MGSV. Within the first hour or so, I see a shriviled up 'Snake' crawling around with a weird personification of a last minute Halloween costume, whos voice actor was so distracting that by the time Johnny Storm and the floating Trippe Redd showed up, I was completely detached. It was weird. And i was expecting weird. I knew Kojima was known for weird. But this section, along with the rest of the game felt so drab and serious, that even the weird quirky parts seemed either depressing, shoe-horned, or horribly obnxious. And I still do not believe that Ocelot is the real Ocelot. Especially now that I've gone through the rest of the series.

While the gameplay is hands down the best the series has ever been (and one of the most mechanically satisfying games my virgin hands have ever navigated through), the story, in an effort to be as dense as it usually is, ends up saying so much less than the run-time would suggest. The episodic nature makes the story seem more like disjointed flashbacks rather than a flowing, concise storyline. The basically mute Venom Snake, the seemingly lobotomized Ocelot, the walking (actually, limping) temper tamtrum Miller, and the comically evil Huey Emmerich as the main cast all felt out of place in the dark and depressing story. Snake felt more like he was reluctantly being dragged out of bed to fulfill his legacy as "Future Main Baddy", which even the true ending couldn't really explain.  The only potentially interesting characters, Eli and Quiet, were so criminally ignored, that having them in the game at all just felt like an after thought. "How can we put an easter egg, and a pair of juicy, edgy tits in the promotional material?" was what they felt like.

The idea behind the story, when looked as as pure concept, is such a sweet premise. It sets up the real Big Boss as a manipulative, sadistic war monger, that has no remorse for friends or comrades and is not above using them to better his own goals. The fact that Snake is not really Snake partly explains away the disconnect the player might feel with this Venom Snake character. But the padding around this concept, and the fact that this reveal was hidden behind arbitrary requirements means that most people won't see this. This really feels like it was tacked on last minute as well. 

Its a shame, because the game is still distinctly Kojima, but its Kojima at his most stressed, tired and uninspired. Its an amazing game, and while the story is not a good Metal Gear story, its still a decent story. And mechanically., this is one of the best games of our generation, although the game play loop can get repetitive after a while.
Why can't i kill children? I thought this game was a realistic take on war, not some bromance simulator with your men and some skelly guy who keeps yelling about erasing English.

While the story is incomplete (though you can check episode 51 on youtube and fill the gaps) it may be the best stealth action game ever made, nothing comes close in terms of player agency, systemic gameplay and responsive controls than The Phantom Pain.

Skull Face looks cool as ♥♥♥♥, and even though the execution of the [spoiler] vocal cord parasite virus [/spoiler] is not the best, the idea is really interesting and something to think about (read 1984 if you want  something similar, it's amazing). Quiet, Ocelot, Miller  and all the other supporting characters are back and are there to help you out while you learn how to manage your Base of Operations. Speaking of which, collecting herbs, soldiers, and adding extra wings to your motherbase could be a game of its own, and will easily take you 10-20 hours to complete. 

Now to the gameplay. The big new mechanic here is the Fulton Device that lets you extract people/cargo/animals back to your Motherbase. It's interesting and there's plenty you can do with it, but certainly the best part about the gameplay is the amount of ways you can approach each different scenario and mission. So, let's say for example, that you want to get rid of a guard without raising an alarm. How can you do that? Well, you could throw a magazine and get his attention that way, there's also the decoy device, if you've unlocked it. If that's not really your style, you could also use a sleeping gas grenade or a mine, or just tranq people and put them in the trash can. Whatever you want to achieve in this game, there are always multiple ways to do it, and that's what makes MGSV so great.

All in all, while not great as Peace Walker or 3, MGS V's gameplay and dynamic missions makes this a blast to play through atleast once, and earns the game a solid 8/10.

That last part's a bit of a joke but seriously, everyone I've convinced into playing this game had the exact same experience. You play it at first, think it's neat.... but then you miss it and give it another go and before you know you are legitimately addicted not just to this game but to the entire franchise. These games are a culmination of genius game design and writing and the Phantom Pain is the perfect place for anyone to start. Don't be discouraged by thinking you might not be caught up with the lore of the series, because this game still tells an excellent story, especially for newcomers to the series.
And building your own private military from the ground up is way more fun than it might lead on.
 
As I described above this game has lasted me years and I still play it to this day, constantly working to improve my base of operations, staff, weapons, etc... For how cheap this game can get (EDIT: I'm seeing it as low as $5-6) there is so much you can get out of it. I bought my copy back in 2016 for $16 and today I'm seeing it as low as $10 if you look hard enough. This is literally one of the greatest games I've ever played in my lifetime. It's so good it's painful and I wish I was exaggerating or overselling it. You'll be a huge fan of Metal Gear and Kojima's work after playing this.

Though I can recommend MGS5 without a doubt it is definitely not without it's flaws. 
For it's current price you will get your money's worth, you don't need to worry about that, even when you stop playing the game after about 10 to 15 hours when the game's repetitiveness kicks in, because in those first 10 hours when everything is still new and you're still figuring out all the game mechanics you'll be treated to a gorgeous looking stealth adventure chock full of exciting gameplay where you feel everything is possible. Not that that stops after those first so many hours, it's just that once you've got the hang of things (and get your hands on a tranquilizer rifle) the shine starts to wear off quickly and you're left with an open world sandbox like any other where being stealthy and sneaky has turned in to primarily tranqing and airlifting. 

And that's where I think MGS5's biggest flaw lies, it not being it's lineair story driven self anymore. Because for all the fun and interesting mechanics it has to offer in an open world setting I still prefer being led in a single directions and more or less being forced to experience a rollercoaster ride full of corkscrews and loop-de-loops. That is where the franchise's core strength is at and has always been at, and the game's 1 to 2 hour long prologue/tutorial seems to agree with that because ironically enough it is hands down the best part of the entire game. Albeit a bit over the top, but hey, we're talking Kojima here.

So to sum up this recommendation; if this is not your first Metal Gear and you've always loved the series this will most likely be one of your least favorite entries in the franchise (Metal Gear Survive? Never heard of it.) yet still being far from a bad game. While if you're just a nut for sandboxes and love being sneaky this will probably be a match made in heaven for you.

Oh boy. What can I say about Metal Gear Solid V? I suppose I can start off by saying that I do recommend this game solely because it is a very fun game to play. The gameplay and mechanics are very open-ended, there is a ton of customization, tons of exploration, and a lot of freedom (there is no right way of approaching situations). The controls are really top notch as well when playing on a gamepad. It just feels very intuitive, which I cannot say about many other Metal Gear games hahaha. As fun as the gameplay is and as much enjoyment I got out of it, I am still conflicted about Phantom Pain because it just doesn't feel like a Metal Gear game in many respects. The characters, whacky story, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy elements from Kojima's other games are all still there, but it just doesn't quite fit in with the rest of the series, especially when you know the full story of Phantom Pain. The gameplay, while awesome, also doesn't quite feel like Metal Gear. There is less emphasis on stealth, it's not very challenging and the RPG elements feel so out of place. In fact, the RPG elements nearly ruined this game for me. I never thought I would see the day where I needed to grind in a Metal Gear game. I know many other people liked the RPG-like gameplay, but it just doesn't work for me, especially in Metal Gear.  I also don't like that the true ending of the game is locked behind post-game missions that are simply just harder versions of previous missions, and one insanely hard to find and contextual mission. It's ridiculous. Not everyone has time to be a completionist.

TL;DR The game is fun to play, but by no means is it a MGS game that tells a story well.

It's...it was difficult to decide whether to recommend this game or not. The main cause for such ambivalence is that this is an unfinished game. However, before I whine about that, I must say that this is a very well made game that provides a plethora of reasons for a purchase.

1) Ports: One of the best PC ports I've seen

2) Graphics: Beautiful and runs on piece of ♥♥♥♥ computers as well

3) Gameplay

a) Stealth is not overly difficult nor punishing for small mistakes. It's very engaging and rewarding. It's slow paced unlike a lot of modern stealth games but it is slow paced done right like earlier splinter cell series.

b) Non-stealth combat is fun and epic. Vehicles are implemented beautifully and act like the war machines that infantry should be afraid of in (what i think to be) an actual battlefield. 

c) Vast amounts of customization. You can even design your own guns by reassembling parts of different guns you own! Customize your companions, helicopter, guns, base, your gear, which there is an insane amount of. You can even put loudspeakers on your heli! Getting detected in the middle of an enemy base, popping a flare for a rescue heli gunship, then hearing AC/DC getting louder and louder and seeing said gunship destroy the enemies with rocket barrages was one of the most memorable scenes ever.

d) The World: very vast, very immersive and beautiful. You actually get 2 sandbox areas, which are the wetlands/safari zones of africa and the desert Afghanistan. very nice.

Now, thats a lot of praises so far. The game definitely has its downsides, but I felt like they could all be contained in this verdict. Gameplay, missions, plot, the crucial things that keep you playing fall incredibly flat after 40+ hours. No doubt is this an incredible game, a worthy GOTY contender for 2015 had it not been for witcher 3. However, this doesn't hide the fact that this is an unfinished game. Just to give you an idea, there are 50 main story missions divided into 2 chapters. Over 1/3 of the 50 missions are basically the exact same missions but in hard mode, or in harder modes. Like what in the ****? and said 1/3 missions are mostly contained in chapter 2, which just leaves the game in a middle of nowhere in terms of plot. Digging existing files reveal that there are 3 chapters, with chapter 1's length being most likely to be the planned length for each chapters. On youtube there are actually finished elaborate cutscenes for mission 51. Ugh! This vexes me so much. The game reels you in with an incredible game and setting then konami just punches you in the guts for falling in love. 

Also, gameplay difficulty at end game is incredibly askewed. You will find it way too easy for both stealth and non combat options. Aside from being overpowered, you just...won't get any enemies.
