The game does get very hard when you can infiltrate other bases like multiplayer, and it is fun for a while but it's not the same. You cannot use vehicles and you do not get the same degree of freedom.

So there you have it. I cannot possibly give this a thumbs down just like many bitter fans who have used the review medium to get their hurt feelings out of the way after playing it for 60+ hours. This is a great game, but it might leave you feeling angry and sad once you get drawn into it.

This game is a great example of a great game on its own that can be better with fine-tuning and additions.   

Now, I haven't been "in the loop".  I don't know much about the Konami and Kojima thing, how a third chapter of the game was apparently planned but not delivered, or the behind the scenes issues like that.  On the surface, Metal Gear Solid V is a strong open-world stealth game that has charm and a more interesting world in the same vein as Metal Gear Solid does, but with a short story that feels more like a reason behind the context of the mission actions.  

Gameplay wise, this game is a knock-out for the most part.  The player's given an arsenal of weapons to research and develop, making this feel like a very custom stealth, open-world experience.  In terms of a Metal Gear Solid experience, the conventional gameplay is still very much used in the same way, but the way the maps are stretched out and laid flat makes the core experience feel less restrictive.  In a way, this is a double-edged sword.  You're given multiple options, even more than prior Metal Gears, to plan beforehand and really tackle challenges the way you want to.  The game is at its best when it gives you multiple decisions to make before, during, and after you go stealthing.  

There are, however, a few issues with this game that I feel can be remedied simply.  For one, playing this game on a computer with keyboard controls is pretty fun, but there are times during gameplay where you can get spotted because of one stupid mistake.  The key used to go from crouching, crawling, and walking, all important stances for stealth, is a tad problematic.  In tense, "do or die" situations, this key can easily screw you over if you don't press down enough.  In a heated moment, you'll have to remember to press C in a specific way otherwise you could get spotted, ruining your cover all because you wanted to crawl but your character stood up instead.  

A few missions have painful checkpoint issues.  Obviously, if you're good at the game, you don't NEED checkpoints, but everyone makes mistakes.  That being said, in missions such as Chapter 9, the mission never offers you any checkpoints throughout the entire foray.  If you plan to get everything possible out of that mission, (missions offer plenty of rewards) failing once sends you back to the beginning of the mission.  Another mission, one with a prominent boss battle, sends you back to the beginning too.  For a boss fight, that may not sound bad, but for the first people playing for the first time, losing means losing several minutes of progress seeing as the boss takes a while to take down.  The checkpoints on most missions work well, but the checkpoint system usually only works after your character crosses a large enough section of the map instead of it being saved manually like in other Metal Gear Solid games, which is annoying if you don't want to play SUPER STEALTH NINJA-LIKE.  

There's a lot of this game that doesn't require the same "stealthy action" as prior Metal Gear games and offers a more "action" to it.  That being said, there is a system within the game that penalizes you for taking more action-oriented routes, going in guns blazing.  It's a bit of an annoyance.  While understandable that this game is trying to be a stealth game, offering up all these options for weapons and strategies, making one strategy seem like a bad option and preferance for stealth can make the game less interesting if there are just times where you want to say, "Alright, sneak time over, gun time now".  Especially since this is a departure from normal Metal Gear Solid routines.  

Another negative or positive depending on taste that this game has is its emphasis on "waiting".  Again, stealth game, patience is the name of the game, but with its introduction of things like base construction and weapons development, you'll be doing a lot of waiting on weapons you want developed for you.  But before you can research weapons, you need to get your base to a certain level.  Before you can do that, you need to Fulton enemy soldiers to your base.  Assuming you do that, next you need to level up your base, but you have to earn GMP (money) and materials to do that.  The mission and stealth gameplay are usually long, which would complement these options, but for those who just want to stealth gameplay, it's such a chore to get the things you might need in order to pull off a good mission.  

It's invents a little bit of a new thing to go along with its Metal Gear Solid side while giving people something to do while in the open world side.  Playing the game can be a chore alongside a game or a minigame within a game depending on your tastes.  

That being said, the regular game is probably fast if you don't mind the cutscenes and base/weapons development.  I'd say, if you're willing to put time into stealth experiences like this, and I mean TIME, then go ahead.  If you just want to spend the normal, long waiting times in stealth games, something else might be a bit faster for you.

This game is very weird.

The first 15-20 minutes of this game are a trip. I didn’t know what the hell was going on and it just kept getting incrementally weirder. I assumed its because I had never played a metal gear game, but then I logged in and found out how many people were just as confused as I was.

If you buy this game, you may have to fight the impulse to turn it off and return it. Do yourself a favour and hang around  until you get to Afghanistan. It takes about 20 minutes where the game makes you feel like you are in a supernatural dream sequence. I promise, the game eventually does get around to explaining what the hell is going on, but it’s a very odd design choice to immediately dump the player into that. The story is complex, weird, and spans 5 games, and this game dumps you into the deep end with no apologies.

Once you are into the main part of the game, you are treated to one of the greatest open world strategic shooters ever made. This part of the game alone (the clear majority of the game) is totally worth the price of admission. You are basically dumped into a world and have the freedom to handle each objective any way you please. There are hundreds of weapons to choose from (lethel and non-lethal) and an assortment of high-tech toys. Sometimes the action is purely ridiculous, but you won’t mind, because its so damn enjoyable. You will be spending about 80-90% of this game in an open world, encouraged to try different approaches to each objective. It’s hugely fun. 

The gameplay is periodically broken up by cut-scenes from a story that is totally off-the-wall. Full off unrealistic actions sequences, weird science fiction moments, cheesy 80’s action characters, and corny melodramatic dialogue. The developers clearly had a thing for 1980’s B-movies. Don’t let that turn you off. This game works better if you embrace the cheese.

My major complaint about this game is that about 40% of the way through the main story, your single-player experience gets abruptly interrupted by introducing this stupid multi-player forward operating base mechanic which is shoved down your throat. It sort-of ruined the game for me, since I usually despise multiplayer. The developers would due well to release a patch to turn this stupid feature off, instead of forcing it on you. Its ham-fisted and immersion breaking.

Overall, I think the game is worth the asking price.

Thumbs up. Highly recommended. Another incredible game from Hideo Kojima that everyone should experience. For the most part. Unfortunately, it's obvious that they were not given time to finish properly (due to Konami), so it lacks the polish and perfection of previous Metal Gears. A considerable disappointment for longtime fans, especially evident during "Chapter 2", but there's still plenty to love.

First and foremost: Incredible cutscenes and acting, as usual from Kojima Productions! Absolutely stunning. Beautiful graphics and art design (Yoji Shinkawa, Fox Engine teams). Creative writing, characters and narrative, an increasingly difficult task for the complex MG universe. Brand new "open" world to explore, set in Afghanistan and Africa. Fantastic soundtrack, including score and music from various MG games, as well as some 80's hits.

Buddies! Buddies are amazing: From DD (dog), Quiet (mysterious semi-nude sniper), Walker Gear (mini ridable Metal Gears, they can pack a punch), and "Roach" (okay, not Geralt's, but an equally welcome horse); they all have extremely useful functions and bring a ton of enjoyment to the game. Huge variety of weapons, gear and tools (too expansive for this review) that will definitely satisfy. Home of "Motherbase" and other ocean platforms (as well as home-away-from-home heli) is unique, expansive and customizable.

Cons: As already stated, the game simply was not finished, so there is a lot of missing content, but at least the team did a great job "closing the wound" quickly and not allowing technical issues to creep in. Everything seems a bit too expensive, from weapon upgrades to simple deployment costs, which unnecessarily encourages a "grind" to gain credits and materials. It also turns the novel Fulton process into a boring routine. FOB and late-game online content gets stale quickly, and is even more overpriced if not unattainable (millions of GMP for many items). Also: I missed David Hayter.

Stable and exceptionally bug-free (very few bugs or crashes in my experience, but do stay clear of the Walker Gear Ballista). Main campaign feels the right length (about 100 hours), and full exploration, including side ops and achievements, extends that considerably (over 200 hours). Bravo to Kojima Productions. Shame on Konami for causing most of the problems with what should have been a masterpiece. My rating for METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN: 4 out of 5 wormhole Fultons.

[h1] SPOILER-FREE REVIEW [/h1]

(and by "spoiler-free" I mean that I won't reveal large elements of the plot or twists unless its details within the first hour or something inconsequential and minor.)

[b][u]For the first 50 hours[/u][/b] this game was, quite possibly, one of the greatest games I've ever played. It's the first of its kind: an open-world stealth game, with the primary objectives in the game world being infiltration, exfiltration, and elimination. It's not the first game to have a large, open-world and stealth elements mixed in, but its the first to [b]primarily be[/b] a stealth game and actively discourage going in loud. Most importantly, it [i]works[/i] in an open world just as well as it did in linear games.

[b][u]After 100 hours[/u][/b] I would only play this game and for long play sessions. The game has roughly 160 side operations, which are seperate from the story and allow facilitate exploration of the game world, as well as fueling the highly addictive base building element of the game. The pattern is as follows: go on side ops for monetary rewards, collecting soldiers for your units along the way. There are different units to level up with soldiers, and each soldier is unique in which one he excels at. More soldiers increases that units level which allows development of new materials (suits, weaponry, helicopter equipment). And there is a [b]lot[/b] to unlock, which becomes progressively expensive as you continue onwards leading to a need for more money and more missions. 

[b][u]160 hours in[/u][/b] I was left confused and disappointed. The plot is the main culprit here, which is more akin to a plot summary. It feels like you caught the gist of a plot off a wikipedia entry, but didn't actually [i]delve[/i] into it. What's here is a competent beginning that sets the stage, and then the actors actually come on stage and they [i]half-a*s the sh*t out of it[/i]. To add insult to injury: some of the actors come on, introduce themselves, partake in the plot, then just leave the stage abruptly. In other words, not only is the plot bare-bones, but some story elements are just dropped or introduced and never actually developed. I assumed the game began with filler content somewhere around a third of the way in because I was in it for the long haul, but it just ends abruptly thereafter. 

[b][u]After 170 hours[/u][/b] the game's open world elements and side content felt repetitive and somewhat restrictive. Sure, I was building up motherbase but the mission names started having increasingly large numbers at the end of them: "capture the wandering soldier 10" or "Defeat the armored tank unit 12". The plot's pathetic, neutered state didn't help impressions any further. I realized that the side missions are unlocked out of order because they're pretty repetitive, which leaves you wanting for more variety in such an open world. 

So lets neatly summarize this wall, with the good:

[list]
    [*] Open world stealth that works seamlessly
    [*] Addictive base building side game
    [*] A lot of side missions and items to unlock
    [*] Good setting for the gameworld and plot
    [*] optional mission objectives and grading system that keeps you coming back
[/list]

The bad:

[list]
    [*] Repetitive side missions
    [*] Horribly paced plot and large swaths of plot left undeveloped
    [*] A lot of 'filler missions' in the main campaign
[/list]

This is ironically the greatest MGS game in terms of game mechanics, but the worst entry in the series story-wise. In a series primarily known for its plot that's saying a lot. If Kojima was given another 100 million USD and 5 more years I'm sure he would have finished up the plot. You know, when he wasn't busy working on meaningless things like foliage textures or eating out with Hollywood directors. Despite Kojima's absolute trash ablity to properly manage time and budgets, It's still sad that this was Kojima's final entry into the series, as you can [i]see[/i] various areas in the plot where he [i]intended[/i] to take the game. 

But his vision was [b]FAR[/b] too grand; Ground Zeroes (the stand-alone prequel to this game) was a [i]part[/i] of this game, meant to be a prequel chapter rather than a seperate title. There is an entire part 2 post-game chapter that [i]continues[/i] the story past the end-boss. You start wondering just how long he meant for this game to be, and what exactly he spent all those 5 years of development doing. [i]And why there is a post-game chapter when the main game was lacking in the plot department[/i]

Having one of the largest budgets in video game development history and a lengthy development time, Konami grew both fearful of the ballooning budget and worried with all the constant delays. Coupled with Kojimas personality and drive for perfection and this game was doomed to never see the light of day in anything other than an unfinished state. It's a shame too because if he was somehow able to complete his vision this game would have been more than a dissapointing masterpiece. As it stands I still recommend it, but [i]♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥[/i] could this have been more than just 'good'.

There are more than enough reviews of the gameplay and open world elements of this game and I won't waste your time - those things alone are done better than in most if not all games I've played, starting with PSX.

Instead I'd like to point out that the story in this game is more complete than average reviewer could be bothered to mention. I'll explain.

A story can be told in a variety of ways. In the west we are used to games and movies that offer a linear storytelling experience. It relies on you taking a seat and trying your best to sit through a 3-4 hour narrative told mainly in explosions and gunshots. With RPG genre dying you could see even Fallout series have devolved into that one-choice narration because they can't think of a story in a non-linear way.

[list]
[*]With the new Metal Gear the narrative is shandified, and is told through a variety of levers you pull through the time you afford to this game. If you take your time and think over the things you do while putting yourself in the army boots of the protagonist you'll be rewarded with a story that unfolds at just the right pace for you.

[*]I found that trying to speedrun Metal Gear Solid V leaves you wanting for more. I did exactly that during my first playthrough and while I enjoyed the game a lot, and could safely rate it as one of the best games I ever played, something was definitely missing.

[*]On my second playthrough, after almost three years, having a bit of a Metal Gear nostalgia I replayed the previous installments with exception to MGS4, Acid and Portable Ops, and decided to take another swing at MGSV. Boy, was I surprised. Not only the story connects exactly the way it should to the first Metal Gear, it answers pretty much all the questions you ever had if you bothered to give the previous games a chance. 

[*]Acting and cinematography is on a whole other level here. You can call it Hideo Kojima's movie and you won't be wrong. Snake finally speaks like a human being well over the age of 14, who now has a man's voice and speech maners. Face capture and emotions portrayed through the facial expressions and especially eyes are so well done it's such an important aspect of cinematic experience and such a rare pleasure.
[/list]

Without spoiling anything at all I'd like to say - Pay Attention. Listen to the heroes and villains and most importantly watch over their actions. Try to speculate what you would do and respond via the persona of Venom Snake.

There are so many hidden gems in this game you never get this level of quality anywhere else. Do the side missions. Find secret plot revealing tapes, listen to them if you want to. But don't worry you'll get the most interesting ones anyway.

There are also some topics covered by the narrative that aren't easy to digest. And that's what I love about the game the most. It's not always clear who is your enemy and who isn't. Some good-willed people make for the worst of them.

Like the ending of a good movie it's really all up for your personal interpretation. And that's what good art does it makes you wander around after you experienced it thinking if you've seen it all or there's more and you end up setting off to explore the unknown.

I genuinely think this is the Metal Gear that Hideo always wanted to make but couldn't either due to restrains in budget, production management overreach or w/e. Regardless whether you like his direction or not, it's the metal gear game you told everyone you were a fan of the series of. We see many recurrent themes that are finally complete and are sent off into the legacy of gaming. I'm fairly certain people will still remember this game in twenty years.

(Spoilers ahead - only people who finished the game should read the following)

[spoiler] You won't be wrong to suggest that you aren't the game's Main Character. We've seen the Silent Protagonist method of storytelling before, though Snake takes his stand and raises voice for what is right, I could suggest that the main protagonist is Quiet. Hear me out.

We could summarize the post-Boss world of Metal Gear as basically boys (and some girls) running around killing each other trying to essentially push the non-believers in their ways into submission.

You know by know that Quiet was a three-vector attack on Snake, the Big Boss. 

First her mission was to kill Big Boss in the Hospital and with her immense ego making her feel like the assassin we players often play as, she took too long to get rid of helpless man V, so much that Big Boss eventually made her pay.

Second time you see her should have been your last, yet you defeat her in sniper combat and she lets you put a bullet in her head, until you decide otherwise and she tries to do it instead as you stop her seconds from blowing her own brains out. We know could easily destroy you on the spot. But chooses not to.

She then has complete freedom to run away or kill everyone on the mother base including Big Boss. Does she know which one?

She can also go out infect the rest of the world and kill everyone who speaks English, but chooses not to.

Quiet is the only character to break the cycle of Revenge that is so prevalent in Metal Gear Solid series. Not only she does forgive her captor, but ultimately sacrifices her life to save Snake before his insides melt into bloody soup.

Then she runs off to die all alone in the desert. You hear it all in the song titled Quiet's Theme. And it's near impossible to complete her arc and feel nothing while listening to the theme.

Part of the experience is losing her, the only person who genuinely did good for V. While Ocelot knows who he serves and Miller plays his toy soldiers, V serves more of a Samurai role to defend the Man Who Sold The World. Look at the stylistics of the main poster.

This game, the story is an unparalleled experience and it opens fully to those who genuinely want to understand.
[/spoiler]

Not only is this one of the worst "Metal Gear Solid" game ever made, it's simply not a very good video game at all.

Everything wrong with The Phantom Pain:

1. Story is ridiculously bad. It's the typical Kojima nonsense but this time it feels like a poorly translated Tom Clancy novel written by someone with schizophrenia. The dialogs and motion capture actings are all terrible.

2. Mother base and FOB building/managing is basically a freemium mobile game concept implemented into an AAA title. It is incredibly tedious and ruined the pacing on the game.

3. The game punishes you for simply playing it. If you perform well in game, enemies becomes harder and more well equipped. The better you managed your Mother base, the higher the chance for someone to invade and steal your resources. It's an endless loop of tedium, frustration and dissatisfaction. Every time you take a step forward, the game take two steps back.

4. Even if you decline the "Terms and agreement" and start the game in "Offline mode" the game still connects you online. It will eventually drop the connection in the middle of gameplay or cutscene. 

5. Core gameplay is extremely repetitive. Main mission or side ops boils down to only two types of gameplay. "Seek & destroy" and "Search & rescue". Every missions feels the same.

6. Both Afghanistan and Africa settings are bland and boring. You spent a lot of time traversing these boring landscape without seeing anything interesting.

7. Giving the large amount of times you will be dispatching for Missions and Side Ops, the helicopter "fly-in" scene is extremely repetitive and annoying. They should include the option to skip it but they didn't.

8. Hiring Kiefer Sutherland is a total waste of money and it added nothing to the series. It's just Kojima's personal obsession with the TV show "24" and the fictional character "Jack Bauer".

Overall, the game feels very unsatisfied to play. Story never pays off, gameplay becomes grindy and tedious, online is pointless and full of cheaters. This marked the end of the Metal Gear series.

Graphics:

The graphics are excellent in this game, although I would have liked to not have a 60fps cap (playing on a higher refresh rate monitor)

Gameplay:

The gunplay and stealth (which are both massive parts of the game) are both great. I wasn't a huge fan of either to begin with, but once I was accustomed to them, they felt amazing.
I enjoy the way you can expand upon your motherbase, adding new platforms and upgrading existing once. I also enjoy the developpement system that goes alongside it.  Both give you stuff to do when you're not out doing missions, and offer something to work towards.

Story:

My only real issue with this game is the story. It starts strong, especially having played the prologue "ground zeroes", but it falls apart near the end. Once you reach the final few hours of the game, it feels awfully rushed. But that's no coincidence. It's well known that this game was released before developpement of the final mission was completed, giving us a real ending to the story (the incomplete cutscenes are visible on youtube however.)

The ending you get under certain conditions decent and gives a pretty cool twist, but it feels like more of a twist than an ending.

The pacing issues in the endgame are only strengthened by the fact that most of the final missions are just higher-difficulty replays of older missions. The added difficulty might be a turn on for some players, but I felt it made the game drag on a bit because i was unable to progress further without completing some of them.

Overall I highly recomend this game for everything other than the story.

OK, first off, I gave this a recommended review because Steam doesn't allow an in-between.  Really, I rate it as a definite maybe.  I'll explain.

It's an enjoyable game.  Truly, it is.  I wouldn't have 300+ hours in it and still haven't finished it otherwise.  It's a very enjoyable sandbox to play in.  But if you're looking for a Metal Gear quality story, it's a bit lacking.  It starts out great.  Especially if you get Ground Zeroes (but get it on a steep sale, because it is very short.  Like 2-3 hours short.)  The prologue starts out like you'd expect from a Metal Gear game, but it falls downhill quickly.  Part of it is there is so much to do.  Not a bad thing, but a lot of it is busy work to build up your base.  And there are a LOT of repetitive side quests.  But you can skip those, you say.  Nope.  You must do at least a certain amount to move the missions forward.  And again, if you're a single player like myself, they're the best way (along with just straight out raiding in open world) to build up your base.

If you're into multiplayer?  Don't get this game for multiplayer.  MGO is dead.  And the FOB portion is overrun with hackers and cheaters that are not under any control.  Sometimes they might get banned, but mostly they don't.  

The controls.  Don't get me started on the controls.  I would say maybe it's KB&M problem since this is obviously meant for consoles.  But still, unless they don't repeat controls like they do for kb&m, it's still going to be very aggravating.  With kb&m, at least, there are many commands used for the same button.  The result?  Snake can't decide if you want him to climb on something (and don't get me started on the fact that there is NO jump command), extract it, use it, or hide behind it.  Usually he picks the absolute wrong one for the context and blows cover.  

And checkpoints.  I hate checkpoints.  Give me F5 save any day.  To make it worse, I've had instances where I reach a checkpoint after much work, die, and it puts me back... at the previous checkpoint.  

In spite of all that, it's a really fun game.  But expect your swearing vocabulary to expand greatly, and try not to break your controller.

This review is based on having just finished the game after about 555 hours of play!

MGS5TPP is my first MGS game, and is IMO a very good stealth game, with a vast open world and tons of resource collecting/leveling up to do.

[b]Upsides (90%)[/b] are the big open world, the graphics, the sound, the weapons, the freedom to do what you want, well working AI, the "realism", the 80s atmosphere.

[b]Downsides (10%)[/b] are a - to me - the supernatural and unrealistic parts of MGS. Flying kids with gasmasks, burning villains on unicorns (!) are really not my cup of tea! Long time fans of the series will probably view this differently, but for a first timer, it felt really odd.


[b][u]Details[/u][/b]

I focused on a very good stealth game set in the 1980s with tons of atmosphere, realism, player choice, exploration, base building, using companions, and acquiring weapons and equipment.

The Afghanistan and Africa maps are huge, beautiful and full of stuff to do.

I decided to try and play as realistic and as tactical as I could, and that worked out fantastic. The only thing I had to "live with" was the rediculous way of "extracting" personnel and resources, called a Fulton device. A giant balloon that you attach to enemies, sheep, tanks and containers to have them magically extracted and appearing back at your base.

Back at base (a giant rig in the ocean), the base building and development felt OK. However, it felt strange to have this massive massive structure you could walk around on for an hour, but nothing you could do on it. All rooms being locked and nowere to go, did not make me feel like the "BOSS" of the whole operation.

The personnel managing part of the game felt unfinished, and the interface to manage them felt clunky.

There are 50 main missions in MGS5TPP. Most of them are really cool and interesting. To me, that was the realistic, military themed ones. The supernatural missions, I skipped as fast as I could, but they are not that many - especially in the beginning. The game lacks a real ending, I think. For example, the last 3 missions I was given in the game, was just repetitions of earlier missions, as if the game had nothing more to give me. But no problem, I had just about all i could eat after 555 hours anyway :)

There are about 150 side missions, which are also great. However, there are basically only about 10 different types of side missions (extract prisoner, eliminate armored vehicle unit, extract the high skilled soldier etc), but they are set in different locations, which makes each one unique and a lot of fun. However, some people found them to be too repetetive. I loved them, as I tried to use different tactics in each one.

There are 3 companions that you can use in the game. A sniper girl in a skimpy dress with big bouncy boobs (dont ask me why), a horse and a dog. The horse is very useful for getting around on the map without drawing attention to your self, so that was the companion I preferred. The dog's use is limited, but it will alert you of nearby enemies. The sniper girl, was somewhat useful, but was also difficult to control precisely if you were trying to play in a tactical way, but was a lot of fun when you just wanted to have a blast and run-and-gun an enemy post.

The FOX game engine is very impressive, and it is well optimised for PC. I did not have any crashes or glitches in 555 hours of play! Not many games can make a similar claim. Only the keybinding on the PC left something to be desired. Also, the game is missing a FOV slider, which I had to fix with a mod. Read more in the section below.

The game feels somewhat unfinished, and I think it actually is. I have read about the problems that the game faced in the end of its development, and it was probably cut short in order to be released.

I dont care though, as I was not here for the MGS lore, but for a ton of realistic, tactical, stealthy gameplay. And that was exactly what I got. And lots of it.

As a die hard fan of Metal Gear, I simply cannot recommend this game.   

Lets start with the pros
+ The stealth mechanics are good. Taking out enemies feels like past MG games. 
+ Graphics are good
+ You can decline the TOS when the game starts up, which gives you an option to start it in offline mode = you can avoid having multiplayer forced upon you. 


Now the cons
- First and foremost, there is only one audio slider for overall volume, which means no way to turn down the music volume (and it gets extremely loud)  This is completely unacceptable in a modern game. 
- The open world is too big and empty. Much of your time will be spent just running across empty desert. 
- Very little variety between outposts. A lot of copy/pasting took place in making the map. 
- There's a base building aspect (motherbase) that heavily encourages you to extract (fulton) every enemy soldier you encounter.  This turns the game into "knock everyone out and extract them" and it gets quite boring. You are punished heavily if you do not extract enough soldiers (cannot research better gear/upgrades)


I could also list a few more negatives, but to do so would spoil part of the story so I'll leave them out.  Needless to say I consider it among the worst of the Metal Gear games. 

There is so much potential here (especially with how they polished certain mechanics, such as boxes for example) but sadly the open world aspect, deafening music, need to extract soldiers, and lack of variety really kill it. 


It's entertaining enough for one play through, but after that it's just boring and repetitive. If you're a big fan of Metal Gear and want to play it to see the story, I'd say wait for 70% off at least.

Metal Gear Solid V (MGSV) is an incredibly enjoyable experience to a fault.  

It doesn’t just provide the freedom to choose.  MGSV injects the player into a world where choices must be made.  Without player ingenuity, nothing happens in this game, everyone lives, no soldier ever sleeps.  It's incredibly unfortunate then that the game's moments of originality be almost entirely sabotaged by it's creator's total inability to organize his thoughts.  

After nearly 40 hours of gameplay, I have finished Chapter 1 of 2.  I played this game on my TV via the Steamlink, using a Steam Controller.  My brother played through the PS4 version of MGSV in tandem and we related our experiences with one another mission by mission.  It speaks volumes about the game to say that we both regularly sought necessary relief in relaying profanities via text to find an appropriate voice with which to express the intense frustration that we felt, at times simultaneously, with MGSV.  

When MGSV puts you in the field with an assortment of tools you collected, a village to investigate, and a reason to interrogate, it is the epitome of infiltration simulation.  When MGSV tries to tell you a story, reward you, or fill your time between missions, it is one of the worst gaming experiences you will ever have.  It's a milkshake with rocks at the bottom.  It's an expression of Hideo Kojima's insanity, an unmasking of his vanity, and a quagmire of mechanics.  Hideo Kojima is the George Lucas of Japan and the second they let the man loose he suffocated his own genius with a pillow of profane and manic design.

I've played all the other Metal Gear Solid titles.  I know how wacky this all gets, how indiscriminately absurd some of the set-pieces are.  The best thing about Kojima's universe was that he could get away with anything and keep his players human.  The worst thing about his universe is that he tried and along the way his players realized they were human and by consequence very stupid.  

When MGSV let me play MGSV, it was amazing.  When MGSV told me to watch a ten minute tutorial on how to walk around my grotesquely large base and quarantine my staff as to avoid the spread of an infectious disease that two story missions later would be eradicated, I felt like looking away.  When MGSV let me develop a sleep grenade and go drop some A++ soldiers silently and air mail them home to base, I felt like a creative badass.  When I realized that the game straight-up killed off seventy of some of my highest ranked soldiers for the sheer sake of the formerly mentioned, short-lived, and totally uninteresting infectious plot device, I wondered why I ever cared to put those soldiers to sleep in the first place.

After 10 to 15 hours of gameplay, Hideo's inability to create a coherent story and total disrespect for some of the games initially most enticing mechanics left both me and my brother wondering what the hell the point was.  By mission 25 I wasn't even allowed to play MGSV any more, I was fighting zombies of all things, every weapon I had developed served no real distinct purpose as playstyle and rating were made to be mere backseat riders to an award story and force-fed online micro-transaction time-sink online mode.

The best decision Hideo Kojima made here was the inclusion of credits after the first chapter.  I generally always force myself to see a credit roll, no matter the difficulty, no matter the pain.  Thank you Mr. Kojima for that epic credit roll.  While the game may have another credit roll after chapter 2, I have yet to stipulate the difference between a mid-game and an end-game credit roll in my personal contract to myself, and by god, thanks to MGSV, I don't think I ever will.



EDIT (7/24/2018):  In pursuit of the final credit roll (NO STORY SPOILERS)

My brother hasn't gone as far as to forge a personal contract with himself; he's more at peace when he sets the controller down, credit roll or not.  That said, he volunteered to see this one out, and I was able to sit by and bear witness to the story pillars of our final Metal Gear Solid as he played through them.

Simply put, Metal Gear Solid V had one of the most convoluted, nonsensical roundups I think I've entertained bar none.  

Suffice it to say that the most genuinely interesting, most coherent moment of this game, scrolled by too quickly for me to read.

I'm being literal.  In an attempt to reel Kojima back in, an intern inserted some rebellious clarity in the form of scrolling 16-font text.  And, while I understand it's difficult to sneak a steak past a bloodhound, thirty-seconds of scrolling block-text is not the best way to help us connect the dots.  

It was such an unexpected and intrusive story telling device that I thought maybe I was being communicated with, that somehow, I had stumbled upon a secret message of sorts, unplanned and alien to the original framework of the game; that I was being hacked?

By the time I realized I was reading a list of Metal Gear Solid's most important dates, inserted directly into the ending cutscenes of the game, I had skimmed so much that the insult of it all was distracting me from believing that this was anything but Konami's best "bag it and tag it" routine of Hideo's confoundingly praised story-telling.  The whole affair was as useful as rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic.

I love a good game.

All told, I admit that I tend to enshrine the memory of the games I grew up with; that comparing every RPG I play to Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy 7 has stilted my enthusiasm, and likely my enjoyment, of the genres newest releases.  I do not understand the psychological science of why, but am party to the act of criticizing games for attempting to tell stories in new and creative ways when there can be nothing better for the industry than experimentation.

Still, I will never understand how such an utterly flawed game was held so high: 

10! 10! 10! 9.8! 10!

Metal Gear was a world of dark characters with ambitions mutated by cruel pasts.  It was a world of political satire that strayed into the paranormal, but only so far as to stretch our perceptions of reality, never break with them.  It transported gamers.

Metal Gear Solid V has a super hero, a rambling super villain, a zany scientist, a babe with a rifle, some angry children, a futuristic super-mech that can't destroy a 1960's Huey and roars apparently, and the same catchy song on both ends.

I swear to god Hideo's smart refrigerator plays the applause from E3, 2018, every time he opens it; that every time his dog comes in through the backyard doggy door, the refrain from The Man Who Sold the World plays from a speaker in the corner of every room of his house.  

Left unchecked, Hideo Kojima's Death Stranding, due for release in 2019, will be an absolute abomination of creativity.

The Fox Engine delivers beautiful and smooth graphics and ensures one of the top sneaking experiences ever. The only sad thing was that you have to manually hack the 60 FPS framerate cap but there are tons of instructions on how to do it. The sound world is also very rich, the enemies speak local languages etc.

The gameplay is extremely smooth and responsive. You can do tons of different things with your character. However, learning all the tricks properly takes a considerable amount of time. Probably longer than average game. I really feel jealous because more realistic games I like more can not get into this combat experience. 

The new open-world perspective works mostly well. The main idea is to collect animals and loot guard posts between main missions using different vehicles. Towards the end the two countries are simply not enough though. Especially when grinding all the side ops it would require more variation in the environment. It also would refresh the missions aswell. 

The marriage between the plot and open-world could have been a bit better. There are not a lot of things going on actually. About half of the missions relate to the plot only indirectly (someone might know something and needs to be taken out, captured or etc). It feels like the missions are mainly planned to cover the land and somewhere between happens something. But hidden scenes and subplots help alot.

When I first saw the main base I thought "Okay, lets give it a try". At first, it seemed difficult with all the menus and sub-menus. To be honest some of the features opened to me after the game was already 100% completed. I think the base is a good idea - the game would be simply too boring or monotonous without it in the open-world.  

And then there were the forward operating bases better known as FOBs. Pretty much everyone whom I have asked have said that when the FOBs were introduced in the early middle game or so, the game got much more stupid. "I just want this main plot completed why I'm under constant threat by the others?". In addition you have another or several other bases to run, upgrade and protect. In this stage I ALMOST stopped playing. When I eventually finished the whole game I tried it - the FOB missions. They were ultimately boring to grind and you can't stop thinking why this huge feature (online credits, online dispatch missions, online weapons, online... aaarghh) was ever created to serve this purpose. 

Also how you enjoy your main plot affects your online performance! The tanks, flowers and other ♥♥♥♥ you collected should never be sold because they affect your virtual league performance. The online playing should be purely optional and separate mode!

After the disappointment the game was happily played through with every little thing possible. Every animal collected, every mission played as S rank and every mission task completed. 

I warmly recommend this game because of its overwhelming game engine, plot and open world.

The Metal Gear Solid series is known for its amazing stealth gameplay, and although this may be the most flawed in terms of story, it makes up for it by having some of the best gameplay in the series.

The game's sandbox element is one of the most fun parts of the game. With all the gadgets at hand, you can complete missions in any way you want.

MGSV has been out for a couple years now and though I am still yet to finish the story (Which I'm less invested in than most anyway as this was my first full MGS game) I can't possibly hesitate to recommend it. The cinematic nature and curious tone of the story aside, MGSV is bursting at the seams with character and functionality, there really is a lot to do in this game, or rather, a lot of ways to do things. 

While it's true that there are only two open worlds the game has to offer, they're hardly small and do not lack in diversity. For anyone not used to the Metal Gear franchise, you'll likely find the combat (of which there is a lot) refreshing and entertaining. Though if you are new to it, like I was, I wouldn't expect the story to feel too... Normal? It's odd, there are a lot of things I know I missed due to lack of knowledge but it's still enjoyable nonetheless. 

Ultimately, MGSV was something not quite like anything I had played previously and something I'm glad to have invested in. I know I will be getting back into it to finish the peculiar story and, in line with a good amount of other nice systems, to research more gear to add to my arsenal.

MGSV is 100% worth the buy if not at least a good try.

Wow where to get started.

The game was fun at first but after the first chapter it becomes a mess, the story is easy to follow but even for a fictional game it just ridiculous and uninteresting, my guess fans of the serious can actually see some sense in the story but I wasn’t able to.

There are only two maps Afghanistan and Africa, technically three if you count motherbase but since there nothing to there at all, you can’t really count it. After an hour in each you’ve seen all that they have to offer with both maps becoming bland as there isn’t much to do other than the missions and some side ops which become repetitive fast an example would rescue the prisoner 1 - 6 or destroy the heavy infantry 1 - 6, the terrain doesn't differ whether you look north or south with some buildings speckled throughout, what I find odd is that there is some buildings that are completely closed off as if they got lazy and decided not to make them but if you see any of they other buildings, there very basic in there design.

The game essentially boils down to half assing every mechanic. Base building doesn't provide any actually use, mother base is bland even if you customize the color scheme, there's nothing to there except some shooting games and looking at your recruits who will repeat the same line over and over. its was also designed to be a maze for some reason, if you want to get to the top of certain buildings you have to climb a different pipes, ladders and hidden ledges to get to it and for some reason they decided to separate the platforms using long roads instead of making them closer together, so that there more accessible if you want to go from one to the other. there is a fast travel system implemented using boxes.

The combat was odd as well, I could be sniping some soldiers from a fair distance away but all they need to do is spray in my general direction and they would be able to hit me multiple times. One mission which was egregious with its difficulty, decided to have snake and quiet survive an enemy onslaught from tanks, apc’s and a single gunship. What I don't understand is that the game is designed majorly around stealth, so why would I have to upgrade my rocket launcher or any other explosive to take out tanks? and the difficulty seemed to spike by making the tank’s, apc’s and gunship able to take multiple hits from a upgraded rocket (I had to abort the mission and make the rocket launcher). They game also seems to nerf your vehicles on the same mission I called in a supply drop for one the tanks I had previously stolen from the enemy in a different mission but to my surprise it was only able to take a single hit from the enemy tank and it was destroyed.

Developing weapons and upgrades for either yourself or your buddy also took an odd turn, most games allow you get an upgrade and have it instantly made (there are some low level stuff which can be made instantly in the game) others being tied to story and you have to proceed through story to complete them but what the phantom pain does, Ive never seen it in a game ever, when you set item to be developed it take can different completion times such as eighteen minutes or over two hours (base building) and you would think that you could exit the game and come back to it completed. Absolutely not you have to stay in game for those items to continue developing, I have no clue why this was implemented, especially when you need that item to continue the story because your stuck and you want to take a break.

The main reason I can't recommend this game to anyone as there are two chapters in the game but chapter two only has a few missions and then you have to repeat missions from the first chapter with harder difficulty or complete the repetitive side ops, why you can't just continue the games story is beyond me, it's as if they designed in a way to make the game seem longer when its not or that they didn't want you to finish the story as they had not faith in it.

If you have an interest in this game all I have to say is look up the cutscenes online and hope you can understand the story and I can guarantee you'll have more fun doing so. I payed for a game with repetitive objectives, lackluster environments and a convoluted story that I ended up not finishing as I simply couldn't get the ending without wasting time.

Metal Gear Solid V - The Phantom Pain was released in 2015 and received praise from critics and fans until people started reaching the end of the game, which I will discuss more later. For now, let me just say that the critics were completely right giving high scores for this game - it's indeed a masterpiece even with its problems. 

Anyway, let's start this review by looking into how the PC version performs. I played this game with a GTX 780Ti, i5 6600K and 6GB RAM and the game ran without any problems. It also scales very well from what I tested, and it's quite good looking considering the year of its release. Make no mistake, it's not visually incredible as The Witcher 3, but no Fallout 4 either. As performance goes, I was able to maintain 60FPS most of time, with a few exceptions. There's some areas where your FPS get nuked - OKB Zero and Motherbase are some which came to my mind right now but there's a couple others that are reminiscent of the problems that we will, again, talk later. 

As far as it goes for bugs and problems, I had two main bugs in my entire 60+ hours playthrough. It's worth to mention that sometimes I couldn't connect to Konami servers. This caused some problems as a big part of my budget was on their servers and I couldn't progress with my tools and guns development until I could reconnect.

Gameplay-wise, the game exceeds every previous title in the franchise. Kojima Productions nailed the gun play and movement. Wandering around the open-world scenario of Afghanistan and the Angola-Zaire border is smooth as one can hope. You have access to a big array of transport methods. Once in a while in big open areas guards will notice you behind a wall for some reason and this is more recurrent in FOB invasions with can be a deal breaker sometimes. Still, most of time the IA will act according to what it's expected of it and taking your way sneaking into missions is completely possible. Overall, MGSV is a great TPS control-wise.

You will never be out of ways to make your way into a base. Guns-blazing? Sure, if you developed the correct weaponry, of course. Sneaking, passing by every guard? Go on, make sure you have enough tools to distract then if you need. Want to take out everyone without killing? You also can, this is the way I took most of time and I felt rewarded for capturing a captain instead of killing him even if I had to go the extra mile to accomplish it. If you're interested, YouTube has a lot of videos showing different ways to sneak, invade and capture bases and as your team rank up, more tools are going to be available.

The customization in MGS V is also in another level. You can paint and modify your guns, your motherbase, your vehicles and your partners. The Motherbase that is like a hub in the game it's a very well developed element that makes all the difference. Going after top-ranked soldiers so you can level up your staff, which allows you to develop better guns and equipment, alongside searching for resources to improve MB so it allows more staff to work feels great, not grindy at all.

The online element is another aspect which needs mention. MGSV features FOBs, which are offshore extensions of your mother base that can hold nukes and be invaded. The development of your FOBs are just the same of the main MB which a few difference. There you can deploy security devices like cameras to make invasions harder, and you can also develop your team to fight against other in a weekly league that the game runs by itself and rewards the winners with points that you can exchange for resources, highly-skilled soldiers, tanks and etc. You can invade other people FOBs too, which it's fun as each FOB is different from the other. 

The game also has a system where you send your soldiers to accomplish missions online or offline. Online missions rewards you with top level soldiers and big amounts of money and resources, while offline missions allow you to get an advantage for yourself on the field. For example, you can send a squad to take out a shipment of helmets, which will reflect as less enemies wearing a helmet in your missions and so on. It's pretty interesting and developed, there's even a mini-storyline that goes as a main deployment task.

I don't have any problems with the sounds in the game, dialogues are well written and the voice actors did their jobs to pass emotion as their characters speak. The soundtrack for the game is what deserves the spotlight though. Collecting cassette tapes (they're like collectables) over will allow a selection of classic songs like "The Man Who Sold the World", "Take on Me" and "The Final Countdown". Musics that play in determined moments were also well-thought and fits perfectly with the theme. 

Now it comes the hard part to review this title - the story. In the Metal Gear storyline, MGSV - The Phantom Pain is placed between Ground Zeroes (2014, prequel to TPP) and Metal Gear (1988, the first title released of the franchise). If you're new to the franchise, or if you don't played MGS3 and Peace Walker you might get a bit lost but after you finish the prologue you will be given a set of Codec's - audio files - which will inform you about what is what - who's Ocelot, what happened that you were in the hospital and more. More of those files are discovered as you progress. 

It's here that I will be explaining the problems that the game have that were mentioned above. The story is incomplete. Basically, the game suffered with how Konami turned out to be and while the game ends on Chapter 2, there's rumors that the game was supposed to go over 5 chapters which would properly close MGSV and connect it directly with the start of Metal Gear. Why I chose to believe in these rumors is that they just align which leaked before the game release, take this one as an example - the first two chapters indeed have mostly of their missions listed there with the correct names, why someone would report the first two correctly and then proceed to falsely report the rest of the three missing chapters? Not only this but the final phase of the game simply don't make sense. Out of nothing, you start losing things and the story concludes completely out of place. Coincidence that this happened while Kojima v Konami fight was on its peak? Who knows. It's up to the individual player judge it though, I decided to believe, you might not. 

While it's unknown if the game indeed was supposed to have 5 chapters, it's clear that there was more to it. Skull Face, the villain of Ground Zeroes and Phantom Pain simply isn't developed enough as a MGS villain and its clear that some missions and places were changed in last minute, mission 30 and OKB Zero were clearly changed in the last months of productions (the area is one of these that tanks the FPS on PC, and according to rumors was supposed to be way bigger, a level by it self, which would make sense in Mission 30 instead of the awkward encounter that we got in the final game).

So, the story feels rushed. Every step of the way you have the ability to research new weapons and tech that both broadens your arsenal and provides fresh new abilities with previously inaccessible mechanics. While the iDroid and menu controls need some acclimation, the overall UI experience is glorious e.g. the weapon wheel is customizable and fast. Forward Operating Bases (FOB) are completely optional but provide a PvP challenge for skilled players to tackle after 100% the game. 

Over time, minor problems will start to repeat themselves that doesn't hinder gameplay, but causes a lot of annoyance. The major issues are only apparent once you're deep into the game, which the magic of stealth doesn't conceal and it shows that development petered out on Chapter 2. The finale is just dissatisfying and disappointing. While there is plenty to do in free roam and side quests, the forced usage of loud weapons and interminable combat alert in the final missions built up my frustration and ruined the end and post game experience for me. I would highly recommend you fully experiencing this game's nuances and intricacies through weapon and item mechanics and the enemies' reaction, buddy interactions, weapon playstyles and freedom of open world, and so on (don't be afraid to use those Rank A mission limiters, they have a lot of depth). But I cannot recommend how endgame locks you into a single playstyle (loud destructive weapons without stealth) and Konami's staunch commitment to not fix bugs and issues.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
I like many things about MGSV. It's a big ambitious game. Big title with big living world consists of 2 huge maps with loads of missions and side quests. It has multiple ways to complete a mission, wide range of arsenal, guns, equipment, weapon upgrades, vehicles, and buddies. Full loads of actions with a unique feature of human trafficking and base management. Fulton hostile soldiers and assets to make your own militia nation. Each individual soldier has their unique name, background, and skill levels. And once they are transferred to your base you can track their progress, see them get developed, sending them on missions, and more. Ultimately this creates a bond with these NPCs throughout the game.

[h1]Cons[/h1]
Downside? Super long UNSKIPPABLE mission-briefs/heli arrival scenes. It was cool at first then once it got old it became the most annoying part of the game. All you can do is waiting till you can upgrade the heli to make it move faster. And one more thing, re-cycled missions. The game is divided into chapters. Apparently, there are the main 2 of them in the game. The first chapter was a masterpiece, amazing, and considered as the "main story". The second one is basically "post-game missions". After mission 30, there are full of the re-used old missions with few new missions. This wasn't supposed to happen. It was supposed to be full of unique missions and complete the story. This was due to the conflict between what Kojima wanted, Konami's limited budget and the game's deadline. However, Considering the quality contents it's got, it's worth enough.

The game is awesome, but more in-depth melee fighting, smoother parkour and maybe even random events would add a lot. I know that Konami has fallen off but it would be cool if at least there was a mod to add these things.

As someone who has been a fan of MGS, I really anticipated the direction that the series was going towards. But, MGSV is such a let down in terms of furthering the series explanation to Big Boss' history. In terms of content for an MGS game, it doesn't come close to the care or attention that other games were garnished with. MGSV is this bloated shell that lacks any meaningful content. I believed the hype behind the marketing, to finally see the time before Metal Gear (MSX) started. I really don't know how much of this has to do with Kojima and the confliction that he had with Konami, but regardless the final product is a hollow game compared to other MGS games. Konami was fine pushing this game out in the state that it was in. It just doesn't sit right as a finished game in terms of plot and other problems that I have with the game. 

Gameplay wise, it's essentially Peace Walker but bigger. The game looks great on ultra and have personally never had technical issues in terms of running it on a consistant fps. Movement is probably the best in the series for its fluidity. Everything in terms of player choice like movement, combat, and sneaking feels actually good and not clunky. This game in terms of mechanics feels like an evolution of Peace Walker. However, I think that the environments that you are inserted to is really a letdown when you have such good player mechanics. Both maps feel empty with long stretches of barren gaps that you traverse until you get to your destination. The key geographical locations feel not diverse especially when you have to grind for side ops. The game feels great when you're into a fresh start, but later it feels repetitive to go to the same kind of locations. If you're the person that doesn't mind grinding by capturing better grade enemies for better items, etc. I think the game is ok when discussing how to progress. The missions though are not all treated with equal care. A majority of the missions for myself do feel repetitive and stupidly simple, especially the side ones. Only a few main missions that serve to further the story are ok, while other missions feel awkward in explaining anything. 

As judging this as a "complete MGS" game, MGSV is really not the game that fans of the series wanted. Cutscenes are not what they were from the previous games. We instead get these audio files in order to give us more context for the story. They almost if not completely explain everything that cutscenes don't. I get that Kojima took it to heart about the criticism from how long cutscenes were in MGS4, but that game was supposed to be the final MGS game that Kojima thought he would work on. It's just impossible for MGS fans to overlook the lack of care that use to be in the franchise (this is probably due to Konami's interference). There is more questions that are created from this game rather than answers. In looking at the timeline of the Metal Gear series, you can honestly skip right over this game because of how little it does to add to the series. 

The game, regardless if you look at it from the perspective of a MGS fan or not, feels really empty compared to how other MGS felt. From the perspective of a new player, I think the gameplay is appealing and that's it. It's a great looking and playing game, but the lack of content in terms of plot and care of a sandbox environment are evident. I've played this on PS4 and PC roughly 100 hours on both platforms in hoping to see what others are praising the game for, but I do not agree with this game being "masterfully done". You're given a set of great mechanics in an empty sandbox, which is a letdown because you go to the same kinds of locations doing the same thing. I can't really recommend MGSV for anyone unless you think that the other MGS games are not accessable when it comes to gameplay. I know I'm mainly speaking for the single player of the game, this is Peace Walker with great graphics that lacks any of the care of story telling and missions that the previous MGS titles had. MGSV is not a quality game when comparing it to other MGS games, let alone other sandbox games that have done the formula better.

I gave this game a second try, the first one I was kinda confused and can't get used to the stealth gameplay. I used to play the PS1 MGS and you can see the "light cone" of enemy's vision so you know exactly if you're in their line of sight.

With this one, my first attempt was a mess, I kept getting spotted and even the first few mission was hard. So I stopped playing for a while.

The second attempt after about a year buying the game, I finally learn the stealth mechanics and the "gun-blazing" mechanic, it's now much easier and now I can say I can really enjoy the game, there are so many ways you can tackle a missions. Even though (just like any game) missions are mostly rescuing somebody, or killing someone / destroying facilities, but the variety of items and options you have at hand make it not boring, and I truly feel the game has that magical feeling everytime you do something new or different.

With that said, this game is not perfect, there are many flaw I can find:

* Sometimes when I get hit, Snake will fall down and crouch, it is so unintuitive and often times I ended up dying because he won't run.
* I wish the keyboard movement is just a smooth as the controller, because aiming with mouse is so much better.
* Add to that, why can't we use the menu / iDroid navigation with mouse?
* A little delay in the iDroid navigation always annoyed me, for example, when I wanted to request a resupply quickly, because with keyboard you can type fast, the menu transition couldn't catch up to it and often times I ended up selecting a wrong menu item
* Man oh man the chopper animation gets old real fast, there's no way to skip it. Everytime I go into the mission, returning to mother base, getting into the chopper, etc, there's like 30 seconds to 1 minute spent in there just watching Snake sitting.
* What's with the mission repetition after chapter 1? Just filler without variety.
* I know intro gameplay is kinda necessary, but this one is just long, I had to play "crippled" Snake getting away from the hospital and I don't feel like there's any significance to the scene anytime during the actual gameplay after the intro.

There are many other points, but still this is a great game that sometimes go on sale, I really recommend picking this up if you're into stealth game. Quirks aside, this is by far the best stealth game I've ever play (and it's really fun too, even if you're not into stealth).

This is my second-most played game on Steam. I am in love with it. 
Consider this a decently unbiased review, because I have never played another Metal Gear Solid game, so I cannot comment on how it lives up to its predecessors. 

This is an adventure like no other. I'll start with the gameplay, because the story, while endearing, is ridiculous. The gameplay really is this game's best feature. 
This is first and foremost a stealth game, but to say it's *just* a stealth game would be to do the game a disservice, because it allows you to approach encounters in a truly gargantuan number of ways. Although nothing works quite as well as simply tossing an empty magazine away from you and then knocking out a guard, the amount of time I've spent experimenting with the different goofy gadgets is probably the amount of time it would take to do something productive like learn a foreign language or something. Admittedly, most of these gadgets I barely use, but they're fun to play around with. 

MGSV is one of those rare open-world games like Skyrim or Just Cause 3 that actually make something of the fact that they're open world and give you an enormous amount of freedom that's actually worth having. The maps are dotted with outposts for you to play around in, and the mechanics of the game are so much fun to screw around with that I completed the game at around the 70 hour mark (that's just a guess) and the rest of my play time has just been screwing around. 

Now, the story. I am aware that this is nothing new for Metal Gear or Kojima in general, but the story is ridiculous. I want you to understand that I don't intend that as an insult. If you want clear, concise writing and a plot that makes sense, you're in the wrong place, because that's not what you'll find here. You'll find very cheesy writing and a good amount of ludicrous technobabble. However, this is not a game you are intended to take seriously. It's not outwardly comedic, but it's fairly tongue-in-cheek. 

The musical score is great, there's a tremendous number of things to collect and weapons to use, the Mother Base recruiting system that allows you to knock out guards and extract them to use as essentially indentured servants actually encourages stealth gameplay because you want as many talented people on your team as possible, and the story is completely batsh*t but endearingly so. The cutscenes are dozens of minutes long in some cases, but it is a Japanese game, so you have to expect that to some extent. 

This is a very fun game, and given events surrounding Kojima and Konami, it's the last good Metal Gear game you are ever likely to see.

There is so much here it's hard to fit it all into a review.

The Stealth/Action of the game is done really well, there is a ton of different weapons to choose from, Pistols, SMGs, Rifles, Grenade Launchers, sniper rifles, rocket launchers, etc. (most of these weapons have a sleep or stun option as well).   On top of that there is support weapons like grenades, decoys, mines, etc... and lastly you get a robotic arm to control with various abilities as well.  If all that doesn't appeal you can go full stealth and take down enemies with knockouts or knifing them.  The only negative is the enemy AI, it gets very predicatable where and how an enemy moves and what their reactions are to certain tactics.  By end game I was just running around with a sleeper sniper rifle and would have entire groups of enemies down in seconds.

On top of all the cool weapons/gadgets you get a buddy that accompanies you on missions, a horse, a dog, a sniper and a bipedal mech.  The Horse is useful early game, but once I got the dog I never used anything else, the dog just does to much where I found the other buddies just didn't do enough, the horse was good for fast travel but once you got a stockpile of vehicles there was no need for the horse.  The sniper is cool, but I just felt didn't do enough and was kinda clunky to control.  While the mech was the hardest to control of the bunch and didn't work well with the stealth kinda of game play I liked, so I used it once and that was it.  The only negative here was that the buddy AI was clunky at the best of times, you would have to issue certain orders multiple times to get it to work properly.

On top of all the missions, stealth/action and buddy system, there is also a base building element to the game.  You upgraded various part of you bases to get you access to more things, such as deployment missions you can send recruits on, ability to upgrade weapons, med bay to heal your recruits and more.  You find raw materials in the game to be able to do your upgrades as well as a mining system.  The system is fun but you realize that certain materials are used more often than others so you end up with GIANT stock piles of certain things and never have any of the other.  Couple of negatives here as well, a lot of the upgrades take a LONG time to complete, almost an obscene amoount of time, as well if you are working on a mission and you fail it, you lose the time towards completetion, which is stupid.

The last thing I'll touch on is the story, the last metal gear game I played was for the Gamecube, so the backstory of everyone here was lost on me, however you don't really need the backstory to enjoy this story though.  THe story is a little out there and convuluted but was overall enjoyable and good reason to keep pushing through the game.

The only big negative I have for the whole game is that damn hospital level, it's needlessly long with a lot of parts that could just not be there.  It could be trimmed down a bunch and make for a much better opening to the game.

I like to give it a while before I review a game and I decided I'd give 100 hours to fully let it sink in. This is the first Metal Gear game I've played and I'm not dissapointed in the least bit.

The Phantom Pain plays like a cinematic masterpiece melded with a Splinter Cell type stealth game on steroids. It's a giant sandbox that once fully unlocked leaves you with almost unlimited potential for fun.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is really what makes the game. It took me the full 100 hours to finish the final chapter and it was well worth it. It's like a good book or tv series, you want to know what happens even if you don't know what's going on necessarily. So many of the elements like the tape recordings and character development add something that most modern games leave by the wayside for giant multiplayer traps. If you like spy/military themes and over the top action this is your game. 

[h1]Mechanics[/h1]
The game feels very fluid, I used an Xbox gamepad as my go to, and once you have everything down you'll be extracting everything in sight in no time. The real shining star is the basebuilding, it gives you something to do when you're not out in the field or just need a break. Granted the wait times to research things do get long, but by the time you can fully equip yourself with a custom loadout and you're producing a decent amount of resources it's mostly a management sink.

[h1]Only Gripe[/h1]
The only thing that sticks out as a negative are the Skull units. They're overpowered god enemies that thankfully only appear in a few of the missions, and are the worst part of the game. If you want to be productive in the game you take a stealth approach to most things when it comes to infiltrating bases which is what most of the game is, then you have to jump into a boss fight you weren't prepared for. You'll learn quick that running or hiding against them rarely works unless you have D-Horse or D-Walker.

[h1]Final Conclusion[/h1]
I think if you like AAA games that are actually worth their money this is one of the best games in the form of content I've played in a while. In the end you want the most bang for your buck, I have 100 hours in and I could easily see another 50 trying to complete everything or if you wanted to climb the infiltration boards. Hats off to Hideo Kojima and his team for this masterpiece.

Although I haven’t played this game in a while - Just wanted to revise my review and show it some love because of how brilliant it was for me. This is the only Metal Gear game I’ve played and it’s been good for me as you can tell by the hours I’ve clocked in. 

The game play mechanics in the game is stellar and one of the best I’ve experienced so far, at least from a 3rd person shooter perspective as I’m not an 'FPS gamer.' The game rewards being stealthy in tackling missions and side ops as opposed to going in loud and killing enemy soldiers.  [b]'Quiet'[/b] was my most used buddy - as she makes scouting and taking out enemy outposts less of a chore especially when the game gets kind of repetitive with the countless times you get to do similar side ops. You can also use her as a little hack, where you send her to scout a mission area, and if you're low on supplies just restart from a checkpoint, and she'll have a resupply of ammo and supplies ready at certain spots in the mission area, saving you from having to use your GMP to call for a supply drop. 

The enemy AI in this game is dynamic and fun to tackle as they adapt to your play style, and also get more skilful the higher you level up by investing in your off shore mother base. And if I’m not mistaken, doing the side ops also felt a bit more challenging after completing all the main campaign missions, especially those where you have to take out the enemy gunships. 

The game got a lot of flak for its story, as many found it to be incomplete or incoherent, but I still found it to be quite immersive and compelling with its ‘cold war’ lore and cinematic cut scenes, that can often escalate tension of impending doom especially with regards to the [b]Skulls[/b]; some sort of supernatural soldiers. There may be some loopholes in the story that doesn’t feel like a cohesive unit but often these stories can be patched together if you are patient enough to play through the tapes that you collect throughout missions and important side ops. 

The only little gripe I had with the game was having to sit through an entire animation of your chopper dropping you off to the mission area every time you start a mission from the Aerial Command Center, along with the rolling credits at the end of each mission (but I think that part might have been skippable). Other than that I’m all praise for the game as it is really optimized and even playable on Intel's integrated graphics. 

I didn’t really get into much of the multiplayer aspect of the game, as that is not my forte, and only did the  [b]FOB Events[/b] in order to farm S+ and S++ soldiers. There’s also a bonus for new and returning players – as you can now play as  Quiet and Ocelot for FOB infiltration (unfortunately this was after I’d kinda lost interest in the game). 

[b]P.S. ‘Subsistence’ [/b] missions are also quite gratifying, even though I didn’t like it initially, but the bare bones approach to tackling a mission is sort of akin to [b]The Division’s ‘Survival’ [/b]mode. But ‘Survival’ in the Division is a lot more addictive. Maybe I’ll save that for another review 😉

Anyway, I thoroughly recommend this game to any one inquisitive about it.
