By far the greatest stealth action game to be released for PC. 

[b]Pros[/b]:
•Unparalleled strategic and tactical freedom in how to approach and undertake a task.
•Vast array of weapons and items at your disposal ranging from a water pistol to a pill that slows down time.
•Creative and challenging boss fights. 
•Everything from your clothing to your movement has an impact on how well the enemy can see you.
•The AI continually adapts to your playstyle, expect more enemies wearing NVGs if you like the night time. 
•150 Side Ops that are unique and help in progressing the story and unlocking higher level staff for Mother Base, e.g. The Legendary Gunsmith.
•Innovative buddies with their own customization options, from the versatile D-Walker to the controversial Quiet. (My personal favourite is D-Dog)
•FOB Infiltration is a very well executed and fun PvP mode, even despite not being a PvP mode most of the time.
•Base management is actually fun and interesting, because depending on which teams you focus more on, your playstyle and availability of gear and resources can vary.
•Resource and blueprint gathering can help out a lot in building Mother Base and developing gear. E.g. I randomly came across the WU-S333 blueprint, which allowed me to develop the Tornado-6, Ocelot's revolver and the best one in the game.
•The fulton is a great tool that allows for some really ludicrous moments, but is also extremely useful. 
•Recruiting (or should I say kidnapping) staff is a lot of fun. Many a times I've infiltrated entire outposts just for one guy who's an S rank.   
•Features a variety of intense themes including poverty, betrayal, trauma, guilt, race, the horrors of war, and perhaps the most apparent of all, truth and deception. However, unlike games like Homefront, none of these ideas are forced down the players throat, and the player is free to interpret and experience the story as they wish to. The choices Snake makes throughout the course of the game are questioned by NPCs as well as the player, yet they never feel preposterous. E.g. sparing Quiet and bringing her to Mother Base provides you with a useful buddy, but her bond with Snake negatively affects staff morale. 
•Box sled. Hell yes.
•[spoiler]Volgin as the Man on Fire. Now that's some good nostalgia-inducing stuff[/spoiler]

[b]Cons[/b]:
•Not a whole lot of mindblowing sequences as compared to previous MGS titles. The only mission that didn't disappoint in this regard would be the Prologue. (ITS A WHALE) The prologue perhaps set the bar too high for the rest of the game to  follow.
•A very lacklustre story with a bland main villain. Centered primarily on revenge and fighting fire with fire, I believe the theme song sums it up very well with the line, "The thirst must be quenched to fuel hypocrisy".
•The ending makes the game fall flat on its face, and was greatly panned by fans and critics alike.
•The online component, Metal Gear Online, has no anti-hack, limited and fairly uncreative gamemodes, and I think only like 5 people play it these days.
•Fairly empty open-world. Though it doesn't matter much, the lack of content in the open world is measly when compared to games like The Witcher 3 or Skyrim.
•The Aerial Command Center. It's just stupid. Why would your actual base not be in your base? Really makes you think.
•The lack of a co-operative story mode is just a whole lot of missed opportunity.

[b]Final Verdict[/b]:
Despite the shortcomings of the story, Metal gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an amazing stealth/action game and there are none like it. Hideo Kojima had cemented himself as a legendary game-maker with Snake Eater, but the Phantom Pain just goes to show that he is yet to lose his skill.
I highly recommend you play this game, regardless of whether you know anything about MGS or have never played a stealth game before, and I give it a [h1] 9.5/10[/h1] I have put in 70 hours at the time of writing this review, and it has been less than a month since I bought it on Steam. I'm very excited for both Metal Gear Survive and Death Stranding, as I am very curious to see how Konami and Kojima do without each other's support.

This game is incredible. In the first few hours, it throws all of the peices to its puzzles on the table for you to look at, and to try and see how they all fit together. Not only does it form the picture of what happened previously in the Big Boss timeline of the Metal Gear franchise, but it also connects how the Big Boss timeline bleeds into the Solid Snake timeline. The fate of Master Miller is all but said to your face at the end of the game, and the fall of Big Boss from hero of MGS3 to the villain of Metal Gear and Metal Gear II is revealed to us all. Not only does it do all of that and more, but the story also adds entirely new sci-fi elements that are entirely its own, and includes it all without breaking the reality of the universe the game is set in, respecting the year that it takes place in, and isolates itself so as to preserve the integrity and logic for the previous games that are set after the events of this game.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain was a game built on almost impossible conditions, and pretty much any other game would have been cancelled, handed off to a new team, or released in an unfinished state. This game is a little bit of it all, but simultaneously held together by a team of geniuses. There is obviously some missing content that was hinted at and removed for time constraints, but this content was so specifically chosen so as to make sure that anything that was removed would not impact the main stories and themes of the game, and in fact, would actually leave the players feeling like the protagonist; feeling a phantom pain, like something you know is supposed to be there is missing. We've seen the Chapter 3 logo, we've seen the Mission 51 logo hidden in the files, and we've seen the cinematic that was 98% complete that shows how the arc of the character Eli ended, but was never finished and put into the game. It was all 'amputated', leaving the game completely functional, but still missing something. It is a phantom pain that we'll all feel, and we'll all know exactly what's missing, and it will never heal, nor will it ever go away.

That said... Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is not your daddy's Metal Gear. The camera is wholely unique, never before utilized like this even in Peace Walker. The same can be said about Reflex Mode, and everything else associated with the FOX Engine that runs this game, and its prologue, MGS5: Ground Zeroes. If you've never played a Metal Gear game, the story may just be too difficult to follow. Not only that, but the open-world and vehicles might feel stiff, jankey, and just plain wierd to you. And if you're a long-time fan who remembers when the franchise went 3D, then you'll still have a bit of a time adjusting to horseback and vehicle handling.

And then there's the biggest issue with this game; the intrusive, 'optional' always-online aspect where you're pretty much required to build Forward Operating Bases if you want to be able to develope all of the equipment in the game. If you want your units to be able to grow past level 85, you'll need an FOB to bypass the capacity limits of Mother Base. If you want to have more than 5,000,000 GMP, you'll need and FOB. If you want to be able to hold the resources required for some equipment to be developed, you'll need an FOB. And if you want to send out more than two Combat Deployments at a time, you'll need an FOB. I'd like to say that this isn't a problem, but the FOB is always online, always vulnerable to other players attacking and stealing your resources, armaments, and soldiers, and you cannot get rid of them when you decide you don't want them anymore. Your personnel, equipment, and resources will always be at risk of being taken from you. Some equipment in the game requires your teams be at level 120 or higher, but without an FOB, you will never get any higher than around level 85, even if your Mother Base is staffed entirely with S++ soldiers. You'll need an FOB.

TL;DR: This is by far the best game I have played in 2016. Everything about it is excellent, from the graphics to the story and the gameplay, this game is almost flawless. Hideo Kojima has really outdone himself on this one. Don't be afraid of buying this if you have no previous Metal Gear experience/knowledge. That is the same situation I was in and I became a fan in a matter of days. You'll have no problem enjoying the game nonetheless.

[h1][b]INTRODUCTION[/b][/h1]

I will begin by saying that this game won two awards back in 2015 when it was first released: best soundtrack and best action/adventure. Does it deserve them? Absolutely yes. This game is a masterpiece, not that it wouldn't be expected from Kojima.  Right off the bat if you like good stealth experiences, variety in gameplay, an in-depth upgrade system and a magnificent plot, this game is for you. 

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]

There are a total of 50 missions in the game, even though the "main" story ends at mission 31. After that, there are some more of the old missions to play but with different twists, like total stealth or "extreme", and 7 missions which expand on the story, the "real" ending of the game being mission 46, which is the first mission in the game but iwth some bonus cutscenes that make for one of the most radical plot twists in gaming history. A brief introduction to the story: you are Punished "Venom" Snake, a soldier of legend fueled by a lust for revenge against the organization that destroyed everything he has built. From the ashes of his former team rises his own private military task force, the Diamond Dogs. Will you be able to exact your revenge?

[h1][b]GAMEPLAY[/b][/h1]

The main thing you do in the game is infiltrate enemy bases and gather intel. That can be either done by stealth or by going in guns blazing, which isn't really recommended. There are always alternate paths you can take and more than one way to complete a mission. The game encourages you to try out different strategies with the vast toolset at your disposal. You can also go for a non-lethal approach (by tranquilizing enemies) or a lethal one, having plenty of upgrade choices for your weapons and gadgets as well as getting different ranks in a mission based on your performance while playing.Also, the game uses negative feedback loops meaning that the AI will react to your playstyle. Infiltrating at night? If you do that several times, the guards will be supplied with night vision goggles. Going for headshots most of the time? Guards will wear helmets. And so on. This forces the player to adopt a more varied playstyle and try out different strategies and techniques. Or you could just say "♥♥♥♥ it" and still go for headshots (with a helmet it takes 2 shots to kill a guard, one for the helmet and one for him). It's your choice, really. The Fox Engine gives you so many options that it almost feels like a sandbox at times, the only thing that limits your approach being your imagination.

[h1][b]OTHER ASPECTS[/b][/h1]

The aforementioned Fox Engine can also make for not only varied gameplay but some quite beautiful moments. The game's take on Afghanistan and the Angola-Zaire border region (the two maps the action takes place in) is unique and even magnificent at times. In addition, the soundtrack perfectly fits the game's theme featuring some classics from the 80's. You are sure not to get bored with all the tasks Metal Gear Solid V puts on the table. From rescuing former mother base soldiers to finding cassette tapes and upgrade blueprints, your average completionist will feel right at home. There is also an aspect of the game in which you have to rebuild Mother Base's platforms in the Seychelles. Different upgrades feature different resources being mined or new technologies for weapon upgrades being unlocked. There is a multiplayer component as well besides Metal Gear Online (in which you fight other players in deathmatch environments). FOBs (forward operations bases) let you build a second "Mother Base" for other players to test their skills in by infiltrating it, and it also allows you to infiltrate those players' bases so you can get to hone your tactical skills too.

[h1][b]CONCLUSION[/b][/h1]

In the end, it all boils down to how you want to play the game or how much time you are willing to invest into it. I assure you it will take you 50+ hours to complete the story of this amazing game and at least 100 more if you are a completionist like me and want to find all the blueprints and to get the S rank in every mission. I can safely say, that, with 230 hours of playtime at the time of writing this review, I don't see myself getting bored soon thanks to the online play. If you want a solid stealth experience, just buy this game. You won't regret it.

I have been a big fan of the Metal Gear series since I was in middle school, but I had never actually played a game in the series prior to this one, so I had a lot of anticipation to truly experience the franchise. For all this hype and grandiose marketing for this game, I personally also had a bit of worry going in as well. Knowing the strife that happened in development and the ultimate falling out between publisher Konami and series creator Hideo Kojima I tried to balance my feelings of being a fan of the series, what the game was marketed as and the grim future of the series in evaluating the game. I’m happy to report that the game on it’s own merits was quite enjoyable but suffers from flaws created by how much potential it could have had to be the grand send off to the franchise it wanted to be. Starting off with the gameplay, Metal Gear Solid 5 has the most refined the series has offered so far. The game presents itself in a series of missions the player can tackle at their own pace, with a series of side ops and free roaming to collect resources and money to increase Big Boss’s private army, Diamond Dogs, and his personal arsenal of gear. When selecting a mission a prep screen opens which is used to pick and choose Snake takes with him. This creates a range of possibilities with some weapons being lethal and non-lethal, choosing to go with less tools to save money, or spend more money to bring in gear if the mission requires combat. In the start of the game Snake will start with a basic gun and gear, but building up resources gives the opportunity to develop and use much stronger weapons. This progression feels quite natural and I felt so satisfied unlocking all types of heavy weapons using them to replay missions ultimately changing my strategy from my first attempts. In addition Snake can also bring in buddies with him D-Horse for faster travel, D-Dog a wolf with the ability to find enemies and prisoners to rescue, Quiet a sniper who can provide combat support, and D-Walker a robot that’s a combination of the three. Personally I found D-Dog the most useful, but each has their own advantage and aside from D-Walker I liked using the variety and skills each had to offer. All of this variety creates a range of possible strategies, which while the game suffers from one or two dominant plans created such a wide amount of options that I played over and over to see them play out. The gameplay just flows so well and naturally and is easily one of the highlights the game has to offer. In addition to field missions, Snake must also build up his private army Diamond Dogs by rescuing prisoners and capturing enemy soldiers. These soldiers provide the ability to create better weapons in the R&D team, locate enemy and resource positions on the map, and the combat team can do missions for you to obtain more resources. There is also a main hub base where some of the soldiers walk around you can travel to, which helped the immersion and made me feel like an infamous warlord with a global organization at my command. Not only was the gunplay fun, but the resource manager elements were not bad and gave me a sense of power especially knowing it would loopback to help me perform missions that much easier. For all the praise gameplay-wise the story is a bit more of a mixed bag for me. While having prior knowledge of the characters and stories is useful, the plot is more self-contained than most and I think could be an okay game to enter the series with. The plot centers on Big Boss (also named Snake) as he and his allies track down the villainous Skull Face, who destroyed their old operation. Snake will not stop in his quest to stop Skull Face’s plans and ultimately exact his revenge. Ultimately the game's theme of revenge drives the story the majority of the game and while it has some insightful things to say at times, it gets a little pretentious. The game does suffer from a massive pacing problem and sometimes it is easy to forget the plot developments that have happened because of it. The game also divides itself into two chapters and when the game enters chapter two it can really drag with not much feeling of progression. Finally there’s a final plot twist at the end which is a bit divisive, I did not have a problem with it but I felt it was a little flat. With that Metal Gear Solid 5 was a fantastic game. The gameplay is the best in the series and has provided me with hours of enjoyment and satisfaction. The story is all over the place, but is entertaining sometimes for better or worse when it does pickup. This game has a lot of incredible things it does well, however it is noticeable that it is missing features and has cut some of the story which holds it back. It had a whole lot more potential, but that doesn’t stop it from being a great game and makes me wish they can build off what this game presents if the franchise were to continue. 8/10

This might be a little long, but I wanted to address my biggest problem with this game first and then a simple list of issues I had with the game.

I'm a huge fan of this series. I've beaten every game in the canon multiple times. I love this game for its gameplay and I'm sad to say that's it. 

The game is an upgraded version of its predecessor Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, a handheld game. That game focused on resource and base building and nearly every mission could be completed within 5 to 10 minutes, depending on how powerful your weapons and tactics were. Everytime you completed a mission, upgrades to your weapons and items would be finished or would require you to do a few more before they were done.

The Phantom Pain uses the same systems, but to its own detriment, it also took in mobile phone game tactics. What this means is that if you want more powerful soldiers or a decent amount of resources, but dont want to leave the game running, you have to send out some of your forces and wait set number of real world hours or pay to have the time reduced with an in-game currency you only get a small amount of each day or pay with real money to get more of this currency.

To be clear, the game still has these missions you can send your forces out to complete, but they only complete them within the time you are in the game proper. So this means that you have to be in the game's central hub or in the field for these missions to be completed and some take over 2 hours. This also applies to your weapons and items.

My other issues:
- Too many weapons and the variation method they use just means that you probably will just have a cluttered mess of weapons you'll never bother to use anyway.
- I honestly couldn't tell if it really mattered what camo I was wearing or if the stealth suit was the only difference.
- Barely any boss fights. The ones they have aren't bad, but there could have been more.
- The main story is lacking in terms of content, especially given how gruesome the prologue, Ground Zeroes, and the opening section of this game are and it relies heavily on Tapes to give you more backstory. What could have been a cutscene, is instead an audio clip.
- Snake barely talks and though I had issues with David Hayter being pushed out, Kiefer Sutherland isn't given much in terms of lines and I think he does a fine job when he actually is given some.
- The open world is as vast as an ocean and as deep as a lake. There aren't any NPCs to interact with outside of the main base and the world just feels empty. Your methods and tactics are commented on by the enemy patrols, but its rare if you hear anything from them, unless you wait to see if two soldiers are about to talk.
- Certain cutscene events will never happen again unless you delete the save data and start over.

Everything else I can't talk about without spoiling the game.

I didn't really play online, though I did find the base sneaking to be lacking because at a certain point, everything is the same in terms of defenses and the only difference is where you land and the layout. The multiplayer was okay. I think I liked MGS4's variant more.

I can't recommend this game as a fan and I hate that Ground Zeroes, which had a good setup for this game, was letdown by the following product.

MGS V TPP is pretty much an open world stealth army-building simulator.

The first chapter of the game is very good but it's all downhill from there and the last chapter was actually cut out of the game leaving it with a very anticlimactic ending. Actually I think the more you know about the MGS universe the more mad you will get that the story is the way it is so it might be a good thing if you come in blind.

That being said it definitely has the best gameplay of the whole series. The FOX engine renders the game beautifully and it runs very well on mid-range hardware. Surprisingly it works very well with keyboard and mouse as well even though MGS is generally thought of as a console franchise. This game is also open world, a first in the MGS series. The open world itself is pretty good! It adapts to they way you play like if you headshot a lot of enemies they will start wearing helmets. Headshots are mandatory for the tranquilizer gun to work well so you can either send out a dispatch team from your private army to destroy their warehouses which will make them stop wearing helmets, or just adapt yourself like for instance use CQC, just sneak by or call in an airstrike, the choice is yours!  Aside from the main story this game also has side-ops. They can be pretty fun in the beginning and rewarding since you get blueprints for defenses in your base but they quickly become a chore if you want to 100% the game. The game lacks any efficient fast-travel system, a must have in an open world of this size!
Despite all of these negatives I love the game. Gameplay wise, it's easily one of the best open world action games of all time and the best stealth game of all time.

Now you just gotta decide if you want to support Konami or not. If you are unaware, Konami forced Hideo Kojima out of the company, the man behind the MGS series! If you haven’t played Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes then do that first before starting Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. If you have then strap yourself in for a fun, roller-coaster ride of betrayal, intrigue and murder as you slither and sneak your way across Afghanistan, Africa and your Diamond dogs base in order to enact revenge on those who destroyed your MSF base and killed all who were stationed on it.

This game is a masterpiece- the story twists and turns at every angle, and there are so many references to the Phantom Pain suffered by all major characters (not just the loss of your arm before being fitted with a replacement). Those who are new to the series might be confused as to who everyone is and about some of the previous events as they are mentioned regularly, but there is enough information provided (either through direct cut scenes or collectables) that by the middle to end of the game you can figure out majority of what is happening, only for the rug to be pulled out from underneath your feet right at the end.

The game is controlled as a open world 3rd person shooter, but vastly rewards players for not killing (killing will lower your overall mission rank). The 3rd person viewpoint is critical as it allows you to see a wider range, so you can spot anything that might detect you and give you away. It’s mostly open world, with missions limiting you to parts of the overall map, but giving you the freedom to tackle the mission how you want. I thought this was a great setup, and when the mission is done you can usually continue on your way with the open world exploration- there is lots to see, do and collect. You can use support characters that you gain throughout the game to support you in each mission, from Quiet, the mute female sniper to D.D. an orphaned wolf puppy that you find and raise. Each comes with their own equipment and abilities, and their usefulness will vary depending on mission. If you don’t look after them in mission then you have to wait for them to heal, so you can’t just send them in and expect them to do all the work. If you feel like a challenge you can do missions as someone other than Snake, each character has a full bio of abilities and stats. You can request supply drops and extra equipment as needed though it will cost you either money, materials or vehicles. The missions themselves are great, and many aren’t unlocked until others are complete, some just seeming to be there as filler, but others advancing side stories in conjunction of the main story as all the plot pieces slowly fall into place.

The graphics and attention to detail are amazing, you can see the rain roll down Snakes armor, when you do kill an enemy if you pick them up (to hide the body) Snake gets covered in blood. If you don’t shower when returning to base the soldiers stationed there will comment on your appearance and stench. Your actions in game also influence your appearance- if you continuously murder enemies or commit immoral actions (building a nuke) then you will gain a darker appearance, blood will always be on your armor and the shrapnel in your head will look like a large horn. If you perform good actions, such as rescuing hostages, stunning enemies (or destroying nukes) then this effect is reversed.

The music soundtrack is amazing as well, you pick up cassettes throughout the game and play them in your Walkman. You will likely need to stop listening to it quite regularly as you need to listen to mission briefs and updates that happen throughout the game, but that’s not an issue, and the voice work for all the characters is amazing.

The characterization and growth of characters displayed is amazing, from watching Snake try and fumble his way out of the hospital in the first mission, to replaying it at the end but with all the knowledge you have learned and seeing all the details that were initially missed is an eye opener. Watching Snake cope with the signs of PSTD when discovering mementoes of Paz, and dealing with Huey to finding out Quiets history all add character development and keeps on reinforcing the idea of Phantom Pain. The base building concept is great, making you want to go out of your way to collect base materials and collect soldiers with good stats. There is a point in the middle of the game where this concept is turned on its head (I thought it was an evil trick and I didn’t see it coming but well played) that again really drives home the concept of Phantom Pain.

The multiplayer component comes in the form of raiding other players bases for resources, staff and nukes. This adds an interesting dimension to the game, as you need all of the above items (except nukes) to upgrade your base and equipment, but if you stockpile it too long others can take it. If you don’t have the hero status, you can’t assault a base that has a nuke, but having a nuke makes you a very large target (and ruins your appearance).

If you are aiming for 100% achievements then it’s possible, but you will have to sink a lot of hours into the game, as there are a lot of side missions and collectables. I would recommend doing it, or at least finishing all the side missions as a fair chuck of the games plot isn’t explained until you do (Quiets disappearance)

There is a lot of DLC, but none of it is needed unless you like extra costumes for your characters to dress in, many which are references to previous games.

Speaking of breathtaking: the Fox Engine amazes me every single time I boot the game up. It's gorgeous, it's versatile, and it's incredibly stable. The team that made it needs a medal.

What of the problems? The story is the main offender. Kojima has always been scatterbrained and unrefined (but that hasn't stopped his rabid fans from trying to rationalize the most asinine of mistakes) but this is just unfinished. You play chapter 1 and you think "How could they mess it up from here?" Then you play chapter 2 and you can almost pinpoint the second when Konami pulled the plug on the funding. In retrospect, even the second environment seems smaller and underdeveloped compared to the first.

Next, although the action elements of the gameplay are perfect, the base building sections feel soulless. Mother Base was clearly intended to be less of a plot device and series of menus than it turned out to be. Even the UI feels primitive. Development project trees are somehow confusing in their simplicity. Soldiers are pretty much a spreadsheet management minigame, and the game does expect you to care about them both narratively and mechanically. However, even with these faults, MGS5 isn't a game to skip. You can wait for a sale if you want, but the game is worth it.

I'll say this right up front - this is the first Metal Gear game that I played. As such, I can't compare this to older games in the series, but I can tell you this; it is an amazing game. The soundtrack, the gameplay mechanics, the open world, they're all just perfect. The story starts out strong as well, but the ending lacks finality, and it seems rushed. This review will delve into some technical aspects of the game, then cover the game's story, soundtrack, etc. 

[h1] 21:9 Support [/h1]

Right out of the box the game does not fully support 21:9, but there is a fix to get it working. It involves editing some .ini files, and then the game will show more on the sides of the screen correctly. The only problem left to fix after this is the markers; the 21:9 fix breaks them. In order to fix them, watch this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ke6d8AOXmKg

After all the fixes, the game will work perfectly at 21:9 (Cutscenes, gameplay, and even aiming down sights). 

[h1] Frame Rate Lock [/h1]

The game has a set frame rate limit of 60 FPS, but there is a fix to remove this. Joker Productions made a video on it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XJ304NoyJTA

After the fix, the game will have an uncapped frame rate, and from what I can tell, it doesn't break the game. 

[h1] Performance [/h1]

I have a GTX 970M, an i7 - 4710HQ, and 16 GB of RAM. I'm running the game at 2560 x 1080, with all graphics at high or ultra. That being said, I'm above 60 FPS at almost all moments, sometimes dipping into the mid-to-high 40's, but quickly jumping back up. That being said, I understand that the 970M is still a pretty powerful card, so I did some searching. LowSpecGamer has a good video in which he's able to get the game running in a build with Intel HD Graphics 4000, an i5-3317U, and 4 GB of RAM. Check it out here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I9z0qQctnXE

All in all, the performance is impressive, and thanks to LowSpecGamer's fixes, anyone can enjoy the game. 

[h1] Story [/h1]

The story starts out strong right from the get-go, albeit confusing. After all, it is a Metal Gear Solid game, and the story is never simple. Near the last few missions, however, it's obvious that the game was rushed and the story feels lacking. The ending was not sufficient, and you can pinpoint the exact time when Kojima left Konami; the story really does become that bad. That being said, it's only the last few missions, and there are plenty of memorable experiences throughout the course of the game. Overall, it's a great tale. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

This is where the game really sets itself apart from others. There is a saying that's used often when revealing a new open world game; "You can approach the mission any way you want". This isn't always the case, however, and few games actually manage to give you the freedom to approach a mission in a variety of ways. This is one of those games. The game promotes player ingenuity, rewards them for being tactical, employing new strategies that just wouldn't work in other games. Or, you can go guns blazing into an enemy stronghold and complete the mission that way. Really, the possibilities are endless. The only problem is the side quests - they're short, unoriginal, and not even close to being as good as the story quests. I'm the type of person who enjoys doing every quest possible, but I just couldn't bring myself to do the side quests in this game.  

[h1] Graphics [/h1]

This game takes place in Afghanistan and Africa, and as such, you will traverse deserts and lush forests. The graphics aren't anything groundbreaking, but they aren't terrible either. Think of it this way - the graphics are just good enough to get you immersed in the world. 

[h1] Soundtrack [/h1]

This is one of the better aspects of the game. You can find cassette tapes lying around the world, and listen to 80's music as you explore the world. The music during cutscenes adds to the depth and immersion, making you feel as though you're in an action movie. 

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Overall, the game checks all the right boxes. If you're a 21:9 gamer with a 166 Hz monitor like I am, you'll need to do a bit of tinkering to get the best experience, but it's worth it. To end off, it's a really good game, and I'd highly recommend it.

[h1] METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN [/h1]
It's a new Metal Gear solid game, focused on missions and story, but with more options this time. The game is less focused on a solid storyline, but more so on a diverse, adaptive one. Each mission has countless opportunities for diverging from the standard playstyle, and each has a bunch of side quests in the same region. You upgrade and research your equipment/weapons and facilities. To do this you need to also research and kidnap soldiers in the region. You find suitable candidates, and fulton recover them to Mother Base. This develops a specific branch of your base in order to unlock new development options, defend your base, or attack your opponents. Not only do you fulton extract potential candidates, but also animals, vehicles, resources, and more. All of this is part of the game's developmental focus. Each mission can be completed in order, with little need to develop a lot of extra equipment. But by skipping the developmental cycle, you would be missing out on what the game does best. It is extremely satisfying to seek and recover super-soldiers, expand your base, and develop new and interesting methods to continue taking over the world.

[h1] Pros [/h1]
+ AI reacts to gameplay styles, encouraging various playstyles to develop
+ Missions are interesting and do not feel repetitive
+ Characters have interesting dialogue, and the cutscenes aren't boring/awful.
+ Research/development gameplay is intuitive. I spent a lot of time kidnapping Russians to make new guns.
+ Side missions don't suck like a lot of other games. A few of them have repeating versions, in different areas though.
+ The story isn't bad, I watched the cutscenes and paid attention to collectibles, which I don't normally.
+ Kidnapping Russian soldiers has never been so easy.
+ Visually impressive game. The hair and skin look very realistic.
+ Movement is fluid, never clunky.
+ Each mission encourages multiple approaches and replayability, especially when trying to get a high mission score.
+ The funny aspects are consistent, completing the whole off-the-wall vibe the game gives off.
+ Fantastic soundtrack.
+ Interesting recurring characters.
+ The 45 minute intro sequence with half of it being a man's butt was painstakingly created. It made me laugh a lot, and wonder what was going on. It drew me in immediately.

[h1] Cons [/h1]
- DLC list is a little long, but it is only filled with cosmetic stuff.
- Research/development sometimes has really long arbitrary wait times.
- The few side quests that repeat can be repetitive. (negigible)
- The first region of the game, Afghanistan is interesting and fun, but after you get to Africa (about halfway through the game), it begins to lose the charm it had.
- No audio level options.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is a great game. In comparison to the other Metal Gear games, it does not live up to the hype of being the best game in the series, but it is very good in its own right. The gameplay mix feels unique, and the story is not horrible, it's pretty good. The game is only $20 USD at the time of this review, and that is what I purchased it for. It's well worth this price, especially if you are interested in the online aspects the game offers. Ultimately, the mix of a fantastic soundtrack, memorable characters, intuitive gameplay design, and the opportunity to kidnap various Russian soldiers makes METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN a great option for anyone looking for a solid third-person action game.

Don't even worry about the overly complex and melodramatic story. The game is too fun to get caught up in the details. You play as cyborg Sam Fisher, with a team-building and customization mechanic that is somewhere between a JRPG and a Mechwarrior/Dawn of War game, with a classic RTS approach to research and development of your tech and capabilities, all set on a Battlefield 2 map with all the hilarious, game-breaking physics exploits that entails. Having trouble engaging a sniper? Call in a support drop to land right on his head. Need to abduct several enemy soldiers? Knock them unconscious, put them all in a car, and attach the car to a C-130 with a Fulton device. Trouble with armored units? Trick them into chasing you right off a cliff. Intense stealth action meets wacky exploding fun, when suddenly you're being attacked by a giant flaming monster right out of Final Fantasy.

Don't think too hard about it. Just pop your inflatable decoy, ready your C4 under your cardboard box, and enjoy your adjutant Miller's ridiculous commentary as you strafe dance around while jamming 80's hits on your Walkman. Imagine if The Boss from Saint's Row was the protagonist of HITMAN with some Resident Evil thrown in and you have just one small part of this massive game, tightly balanced and never repetitive.

It's a game and an experience that is only as serious as you take it, never impeding the sheer fun and challenge. Your vendetta against Skull Face is intense and engaging, in spite of the laborious Melville references, lengthy cutscenes, and Professor Kazuhira Miller's comically overserious ruminations. Yes Miller, things that are made of fire will tend to avoid water, and yes, you should have known the guys with lame disguises and evil mustaches were enemy infiltrators. The mid-game plot twist still reaches out of the screen and slaps you for not seeing it coming. Not to spoil it, but it makes you feel as stupid as Miller sounds, which is impressive. The plot is overwrought, sure, but it still adds a special dimension to the game.

You will not be disappointed.

MGSV: TPP would make a great stealth game but there is one HUGE problem with it. Score system encourages players to finish missions as fast as possible. In reality that means it doesn't really matter how well you execute the missions as long as you speedrun them. The score wouldn't bother me but game actually gives you rewards for getting S rank in missions so they aren't just meaningless numbers.

I'll give an example.

In one of the missions your objective is to eliminate 2 tanks and colonel. You can get bonus points for capturing him alive ofc. It took me about 3 hours of retries to execute the mission in the most perfect stealth way possible. Meaning I didn't kill anyone, didn't trigger reflex mode or any alerts whatsoever. I extracted the colonel alive, destroyed tanks with c4 instead of RPG so they never saw it coming. My final try took me around 30 minutes. Not bad huh? Well guess what.

After all this work the game rewarded me with A. If you want to get the highest possible rank (S) all u need to do is come to the convoy and slaughter everyone with RPG Saint's Row style in 5 minutes. As an extra time bonus you will get around 150 000 points. 

On the other side, capturing colonel alive is not a simple task at all since he is located in the middle of valley surrounded by guards. The game gives you 5000 points for it. 5000 points!!! 

That means I could probably commit a genocide if it happens within short time and still be rewarded with highest rank, it's just ridiculous. 

Punishing methodical stealth approach while rewarding dumb reckless tactics seems really unfair and kills most of the fun for me. It's a shame because gameplay is pretty smooth and addictive.

To begin my review I have to say that I didn't play with other titles in the franchise (except with Ground Zeroes) so I might be a little biased.

The intro sequence is a bit weird if this is your first MGS title but after it does a great job explaining the Big Boss mythology and the events of Ground Zeroes.  That brings me to one of the most critised part of the game, the storytelling. Unfortunately Kojima thought it would a good idea to switch to casette tapes when it comes to storytelling devices. That doesn't mean there aren't any cutscenes but they are far and few between. I believe the story suffers from this kind of storytelling because you feel so disconnected from the happenings during the game.

The gameplay is loads of fun because it feels like a real sandbox. You have a lot of opportunity to carry out your missions with variety of gadgets and devices that game provides (of course they are only available if you have good enough R&D department on your base). There are side ops which can be bit boring if you are doing the 20th mine clearing mission in a row. The basebuilding is fun early game but weeding out your troublesome soldiers will be a tedious task once you reach mid or late game. The only annoying thing is that most interfaces were designed with consoles in mind so they are a bit hard to navigate with a mouse and keyboard.

The soundtrack is mostly made up of licensed hit songs from '80s, they can be listened on your "iDroid" during missions, or you can set them to your helicopter's landing music. Of course you have get them from Soviet and milita camps.

The engine is a technical marvel. The optimisation is great, the game looks good even on older hardware. The controls are tight but unfortunately the game assumes you are using a controller so there are a few things that you have to find out yourself.

To conclude it, I must say that this is brilliant title with a few shortcomings. I recommend this title to everyone who loves stealth games and/or games that gives you a lot of freedom.

Ok... Where do we begin? This game has had SUCH an incredible journey, and I feel like it shouldn't end yet. We'll get back to that in a minute. So, this game has a LOT of awesome things, and I don't regret buying it for $20. (I don't think the price will go any lower than that, guys) It has a MASSIVE open world, from the wastes of Afghanistan to the lush greenery of the South African region and the customizability that the game posseses are absolutely ENDLESS. The detail given to the languages in the game is also admirable. Now, here's where it get's tricky;
____________
THE STORYLINE
____________

 The storyline... Is average. Not to say it didn't invoke any emotion, it REALLY did. No spoilers here, but although the game's main storyline was indeed short, it was very much filled with quality. However, it DOES leave the player slightly unsatisfied. MGS V IS NOT the game that ties the series together, and does not really compare to the other games in the Metal Gear Series. LOTS of holes, question marks and the like. There honestly needs to be one final one, in my opinion. One that's story driven. Although this game's story carries on well from the Peace Walker series, I feel like Kojima's abscence degraded a lot of things in a lot of places. It's good, but not THAT great. I still like it. Hits me in the feels, boi. 7/10
________________________________________
FORWARD OPERATING BASES (A DISPUTED ONLINE FEATURE)
_________________________________________
 
The other thing that's of note are the FOB's. They're bittersweet in my opinion. You'll have a bit of difficulty at first, but once you master patterns and such.... Well, they're still challenging, but managable. I've personally never owned a Nuke, and I feel like it isn't necessary for people to own one either. Even though it's 'just a game' there's still a moral obligation to be had with owning one. FOB's very much have the community split. There are those who don't even want to bother, there are those who play but use non-lethal weapons (thank you.), and those who prey on the weak, generally making life SO much more harder than it is, constantly having to worry about which one of the thousands of players out there is going to rob you blind. Though I still like it. 8/10

The game isn't bad per se. EDIT: oh god yes it is. All in all, it's a less well done Far Cry.
The problems start with the intro. The whole hour of intro mission is neither really connected to the rest of the game, at least not as far as I came yet, and it's "Cutscene: The game". for each 5 minutes of gameplay, there are 10 minutes of cutscenes. There are nonsensical things galore, like sprinklers not starting despite the fire all around but suddenly doing so when the main char (not you, as you can't play that part) shoots them, or people, not superhuman ones, being ablaze and still pretty determined to move towards the character, again in a cutscene.

Later in the game, many problems arise because it's an awful port. For example, in the menu, switching from one category to the next has you press the 1 and 3 number keys instead of, you know, using the mouse. Switching weapons in game can also only being done the same way, using the mouse wheel is way too novel a concept. In fact, the mouse wheel has no use at all, not for zooming (with weapons), not for switching, not for scrolling in menus, only for zooming with your binoculars.
The other things are mosty small problems that amass. Enemies being able to shoot you with an AK47 at a distance where you have problems hitting them with a sniper rifle, not being able to jump without any AC-style freerunning, having to slowly walk (or horsey ride) vast distances which are often long for no reason, like in your own base, because there's no usable fast travel system (there is a way with the copter, but it requires you to first go to the 'aerial command centre' and all in all takes ages), a checkpoint system that has it's checkpoints so weirdly set that I had to repeat 3 side missions at once because saving between them never occured to the devs (why can't console ports give us free save FFS?) and so on.
One last thing that bugged me were so many cutscenes that had cool stuff to play in them that would be playable in any game but this one.

Let me give you an example: There I was trying to go to a side mission. What looked like a way to squeeze in between two mountains wasn't so I had to use a huge detour. Suddenly at one place I was stopped dead in my tracks because a sniper shot at me, which started a main mission, 11, while I was at 6 or so. This in and on itself wouldn't be that bad, I would just have liked a warning because, well, I was trying to do the side mission. Anyway, a fight later and the dilemma of letting the sniper live or kill them comes up. Ocelot and a Miller (which I don't remember, maybe he appears in a mission between 6 and 11) both take the opposite position and tell me to kill or capture them respectively. I decided.. I decided for jack sh*t because the game didn't let me decide, it was all in a cutscene. After putting them in a copter, I ride off towards the side mission I was planning to do on my trusty steed. As soon as I leave the area, a cutscene played and the horse transformed in a copter, aparently, because I was flying it with the sniper. A jet attacks. All the while I was like "grab that friggin mounted machine gun already and let me shoot it!" Quite a while later, snake doesn't seem to be too fast on the uptake, he did grab the gun. And fell over. And grabbed it again. And fell again. And the same thing yet again. As so often in the game, I was screaming at the screen 'get ON with it!". Alas, instead of a sequence where I was shooting at the jet and letting loose flares when a rocket came, which would have been sweet.. none of that happened. it was all just a cutscene.

It's like that several times through the game.

The good parts of the game are pretty much points you could make about far cry. I enjoyed far cry so that's great, but it didn't feel any different. 

To wrap it up, MSG V is NOT a bad game. but it is way less than I expected from the hype.

Utterly ridiculous, vulgar, irreverent, laughable, and shameless: Metal Gear Solid V. In it, doctors perform hypnosis and plastic surgery on a medic loyal to the PF corporation commander Venom Snake so he can create Outer Heaven, a utopia of warriors with “No greater good. No just cause.” In the words of his enemy, Skull Face: 

The chain of retaliation is what will truly bind this world together as one … Sans lingua franca, the world will be torn asunder. And then, it shall be free. People will suffer, of course - a phantom pain. The world will need a new common tongue. A language of nukes. My Metal Gears shall be the thread by which all countries are bound together, in equality. No words will be needed. Every man will be forced to recognize his neighbor. People will swallow their pain. They will link lost hands. And the world will become one. This war is peace. 

This game is, undoubtedly, a masterpiece. The gameplay is incomparable. Every subtle shift in the route of an enemy, the redirecting of a turret, the coming of dawn is fluid and graceful--something lacking in many other stealth games. In MGSV, time seems to condense and expand at the sight of a chopper, a trigger, or the sudden recognition of red light blinking discretely in the foliage--blink, blink; be careful. But more importantly, the game is weird. No, absurd. It has the je ne sais quoi one sometimes witnesses in a certain an image, a 10-second sound, a story--anything, but very few things. This has it. It gives the deep impression of a long past and a bad future. Something bigger always seems hidden from view, poised, but ready to crash down at any moment. It seems important, that something deeply unsettling are at the center of Snake's actions. People complain about the story. The story is not about events, but a certain feeling or fear that lingers. Moreover, this game is deeply melancholy. Motherbase is silent except for the mechanical whirr of helicopters and the bark of a soldier. It has long, dead avenues. This game regrets life, but lives it to the fullest. MGSV is, in the best sense, a somber paradox. It is adolescent and immature on the surface, but has unintended valleys and trenches. People complain about the story because it seems giddy and cheap. Life is cheap.

This review is a comparative opinion on the series, with highlight of this game.

The series spans decades and multiple shifts in style, both in gameplay and story-telling. There are ups and downs. This game, MGS5, is definitely an Up.

The Up is firstly the gameplay, this game plays like a modern action game: with enough degrees of freedom, a sense of streamlined action to consequence feedback loop and impactful tactical elements. Previously in gameplay, either it was too tactical or non-actionable. 

Next Up, is story, the essence of MGS. Story is a sum of plots and character. We have plots deepening since the MGS1 but the characters start to shine when the serie take a look at Big Boss in Snake Eater. In TPP we get to witness a few fantasitic, lively characters that previous MGS games don't even have the materials for. In my opinion, the MGS series ended with Sons of Liberty in New York Manhatton. That game was more about philosophy than story, and was certainly entirely about post-modernism. The lack of character was on purpose. However Konami drags on to Guns of the patriots, so Kojima fill up all the plot holes to justify the drag. The TPP, however, has all the freedom it needs because it's not about Solid Snake the uninteresting, but the confounded yet determined 'freedom' warrior Big Boss (alert, there is a catch). So the character is a real person, flesh and blood real: we get to experience the bloody path he walks, understand his mission and give out sympathy as a human being. Drama, is an upgrade to this genre.

Finally, style. The setting sets the style. Blizzard (not the company) sets the tone for MGS1,  Ocean and sense of Isolation sets for MGS2, Jungle for 3 and Sand and Savanna for 5. There are limited factors in previous works that those settings are not well presented and resonated in the game but for TPP, with open world (somewhat) mechanism, they form a good synergy and it plays great.

At the end, MGS5 TPP is a fun game to play and thus time flies. 

p.p.p.s. I need to bash MGS4 before I hit the submit button. That game tarnished the MGS legacy, although I enjoyed the clichés and the plugged plot holes... But come on, MGS2 was an art. MGS4 was a forced interpretation of the said art.

Being that this was my first MGS game, I originally gave this game a negative review, because despite the game-play (largely) being fun, I also thought the story was a mess. 

A couple years later, and after beating the other games, I decided to play MGS 5 again, and my mind has been changed.
I won't say that the game is an utter masterpiece, it still feels a bit under-cooked, but as a final product I do see where the game was headed.  Especially since the game exists as both a sequel and a prequel... which is quite perplexing.  

The problem with talking about a game like this is that on the surface it seems lacking in substance, presented as a militaristic semi-sci-fi-fantasy game that pays homage to 80s action flicks and American culture.  In reality, the game contains layers and layers of coherent themes and subtext that are otherwise harder to understand if you have never been exposed to the other games, and if you otherwise ignored listen the to cassette tapes that you unlock.  Such themes include:

- The cold war 
- Nuclear deterrence (Remember, the game was created by a man whose country was hit by nukes... twice)
- Militarism and nationalism
- Colonialism
- language
- identity

I also really liked the twist.  I've always known about it, pretty much since the game came out, but the way that they revealed it by just recontextualizing the prologue was really satisfying.  

Least to say, I'd recommend playing the game.  If not for the story, than at least for the gameplay.  The way the game plays is really deep, like immersive sims level deep, and how you control Snake is really nice and snappy.  Just running around feels good.

Although MGS V may not have as much of a well developed story as many of its predecessors, its still a fantastic experience i would highly encourage everybody to play. For anybody unaware, Metal gear solid V: The Phantom Pain is a sequel to MGS: Peacewalker and a prequel to MGS 1, featuring hugely different gameplay to other metal gear solid games and an heavy emphasis on freedom while maintaining signature mechanics of previous games, and further developing Metal Gear Solids  lore while attempting to make sense of many plot elements and character arks.

The gameplay in MGS V feels far smoother and more modern than any other game in the franchise, while implementing a massive list of interesting and useful game mechanics that can be used to carry out the games massive amount of missions all accessible from the I droid, which is the players way of controlling the many variables of there very own mother base and developing a vast number of weapons and items to bring into the field. This includes a very interesting staff management mechanic that allows the player to extract targets in the field to be recruited as soldiers, much like the system from MGS: Peacewalker. Snake has a vast array of options when completing missions in mgs v, as the game is now fully open world, allowing the player to enter outposts and fulfill objectives in which ever manner they see fit. This make the game feel far less linear than previous entries in the series and allows the player to experiment to their hearts contents. Another new feature in MGS V is the buddy system, which allows players to recruit and fight along side a Sniper, a Dog, a horse, and a robot, which ads a new dimension to gameplay and allows for even more play styles while allowing the player to form a bond with your buddies.

MGS V's story is where the game starts to fall apart. Although the first chapter of the game is fantastic and the second chapter holds a lot of potential, chapter 2 feels very unfinished and rushed likely due to Konami losing their minds and kicking Kojima out of the team and pushing an early release date due to the projects high costs. This is a massive shame, as it is very clear that there was supposed to be a different ending to the game due to the sudden introduction of copy pasted missions just with a higher difficulty, the sudden ending, and open character threads or character threads with sudden, nonsense conclusions (Paz, Quiet). To make things worse, the physical definitive edition of the game featured massive amounts of unused dialoge and concept art, and even a cutscene from a cut mission that ties up Eli's insulting 
loose threads. Overall I think the story could have been incredible if Kojima productions were given a chance to u know, finish there game by the people over at konami and its a real shame that it ended the way it did.

MGS V's Graphics are still incredibly impressive even today, featuring high detail texture work, realistic shading and great modeling. Overall, there isnt much to say about this games graphics, other than that they add to the games immersion and differentiate the game from other entries in the MGS franchise.

Overall, MGS V is one of my favorite games of all time and I would highly recommend it to anybody. If you are reading this, unsure if you should buy this game, do yourself a favour and do it.

Pretty good game don't get me wrong, but barred by some highly questionable (downright infuriating) design decisions that soured my experience. Since i'm going to give this a bad review, i'll skip over the pro's and give my reasons as to why. As those are the things people will want to read if they agree and thus avoid it. I don't hate the game, but this can't be allowed to continue. And if I give this one a positive review, it will be swamped. I also like to state that it's probably the publisher, Konami, that is at fault for most of these gripes. They seem like tacked-on afterthoughts.

1; the fact that every main mission needs a creditroll. This whole game reeks of Kojima self-congratulating himself at every corner. Be it cameo's in the demo, or having to have his name plastered on the screen every mission. It was fairly obnoxious to be honest.

2: Overly long chopper transitions. Yes you can teleport to ACC, but you still need to wait for the cutscene of the chopper flying and touching down. If you could skip that whole thing, it would speed up the already lengthy playtime.

3: The base management/idroid screen is way, way too cluttered and the whole mechanic of base management I could do without. It's not fun and it's tedious busywork that you have to do in order to get any decent upgrades. It feels like a unncessary barrier between you and the gameplay. 

4: and this basically singlehandedly forced this negative review, the absolutely hamfisted approach to online play. First off, they don't explain what the online mode does, and default it on.
What it does is save about 90% of your GMP (the ingame currency) into a online depository which you can't access in offline mode. It does this every time you launch, sync or play the game in online mode. And it leaves you open to being attacked by online players. What essentially happens is that people just enter your base and steal all your stuff. Meaning you get interrupted in your game and have to either stop the player or get your stuff taken. You can also just use real-world money as insurance (wish I was joking). Chances are, by the time you get invaded by players, and decide you'd much rather play offline, that GMP amount which you lose is going to be substantial. Basicly meaning that they intentionally designed it as ransom mechanic to punish you if you decide to take it offline. 
Now comes the kicker. In order to play offline you need to disconnect in-game via the menu, do something that requires a checkpoint which needs to be synchronised next time the game goes online. Restart the game and decline the UELA license agreement, every single time you launch the game. Otherwise it will always first sync up before you enter the game and reset your online balance. 
Oh, and you can't drain that online GMP without getting a severe hit to base morale. Since you need to go into the red on your main account so it drains the online portion. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this is some next level villainry if I ever saw one. What were they thinking. To sell those shekelcoins?

5. Another reason to dislike the game are the arbitrary timedelays for upgrades to your base or equipment that can take literal hours before they complete. So if a particular mission would go better with a specific upgrade to your silenced sniper rifle, prepare to do vapid sidequests or exploration for a good hour for that upgrade to finish. And no you can't speed the ingame time to get it to finish. And no it doesn't continue to run the timer if you close the game.  #♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

6. Resources, especially Fuel, are scarce by design and required in every major base upgrade, again forcing the player to play online and steal it from others. The alternative is grinding ad nauseam for boxes and containers. My current gametime is 125 hours (though probably 50% of that is just idle time) and I still hadn't gotten enough materials to even max out my base. The latest upgrades to your base can take literally hours to grind/farm, and they've even patched in diminishing returns if you try to repeat missions to farm them. How nice of them. #♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

[b]TL;DR[/b] - In my opinion, the story is the worst of the entire series and really insults all that Kojima has done so far, but the gameplay is the absolute best in the series and likely the best of any third person stealth game ever made (as of 2017). However, a lack of any PC support outside of just being able to run on the PC (no mouse support in menus, no FOV changing, button prompts are half controller / half keyboard) further drives the negative vibe I get from this game down to a strong "Do not recommend". Only get this if you plan to play it like a console game but don't own a PS4/Xbox One.

[b]*EDIT[/b] - I should add that I played this on PS4, that is where my knowledge of the game comes from. I got rid of it a while back and thought maybe I would enjoy replaying it on PC, that maybe I could finally give the story another shot and like it more this time around. Unfortunately, the bad PC support and ridiculous opening of the game almost immediately turned me off and I am left not recommending it unless you know what you're getting into.

Gonna keep this one short, because most people probably know what they're getting into at this point.

I'm am/was a HUGE fan of MGS because of the characters and the story, but the story in MGS5 feels like (I'll be humble here; I could be completely wrong) some of the worst story I've seen in a game. It feels like Kojima, in his frustration with Konami, just kind of gave a huge middle finger to players and put zero effort into the story, meanwhile ensuring the expected Metal Gear twist at the end. However, the twist is so insulting that it's actually retroactively made Metal Gear a series that is difficult for me to enjoy anymore. Knowing that Metal Gear Solid 5 exists and is a terrible (imho) cap on an otherwise amazing series is just such a let down that I've lost all interest in playing MGS again, and I routinely play through the entire series most years, sometimes more than once.

That said, the gameplay is probably the best open world / third-person stealth gameplay I've ever played. It's so responsive, it's so varied, the animations are amazing, the amount of things you can actually DO is pretty incredible. The gameplay, for once (come on, until MGS4, the series had ♥♥♥♥ gameplay), is absolutely amazing. But man, that can hardly redeem such inane plot and characters this time around.

On top of all of this, I could PROBABLY get past all the negatives if the PC version was actually a decent port. The ONLY reason you should play this on PC is because you don't own an Xbox One or a PS4, or you intend to run it at 4k. The framerate is 60fps on all platforms, there's no FOV changing, and there's no mouse support during menus. Some of the button prompts in the game also show for the controller, while some will be for the keyboard. It's just a half-assed port that, while able to run well and be played with a controller, doesn't take advantage of ANY of the reasons someone would want to play on a PC over a console. It's basically the console game on PC, and you better expect to play it with a controller and sit 5ft back from your screen unless you can stomach the ridiculously close FOV while crouching and in tight spaces.

It's a shame, because MGS5 has plenty of reasons to be amazing, but story and characters are absolutely not one of them. Also, originally, I was pretty damn stoked for Keifer to voice Snake, and while I think he does a passable job, it highlights the HUGE disconnect MGS5 has with the series; they try to make it hyper realistic while also maintaining the hyper style and goofiness that the series is known for. It's just not good, in my opinion.

Six years and a hundred more hours later, this game holds up not just as the most mechanically satisfying game I've ever played, but as a narrative marvel. The original misgivings about the story that I had were proven wrong with the added context of Peace Walker (which I had not played at the time of initial review).

This game is truly a masterpiece, and given how many misunderstood games are given a critical re-evaluation several years after release, I'm sure we'll be seeing more and more people coming out to defend this game's narrative and the risky delivery method it chose to dole that narrative out.

The way this game deals with the warping of ideals, the concept of identity, the inherent oppression of shared language, the place of a soldier in a technologically evolving landscape, the banal rise of fascism... it juggles so many topics without ever dropping the ball. It's equally as dense in this single entry as the entire Metal Gear saga up to this point. It has more subtext than most novels.

I could go on all day about this, but there's better ways to experience what I'm talking about. Like playing this game. Even if you don't feel like pouring a hundred hours into the series so that this story makes sense, play it for the mechanics. Whatever your favorite third person shooter is, this game probably does it better.

The world probably doesn't need anymore Metal Gear Solid games, but we definitely need more games like Metal Gear Solid V.

Metal Gear Solid V is a great but very flawed game. I'll divide my review into two sections, gameplay and story.

Gameplay

While it does have the best gameplay in the series, it suffers from the usual problems of open world games. These problems are the open world being fairly empty, and gameplay repetition. MGSV has two big hub worlds, and inside both of them are outposts and more large scale bases, which you can infiltrate. These are all over the map, and in between them are vast expenses of nothing except scenery. This makes the open world kind of pointless, seeing as you only really want to get to the places you can infiltrate. Any time spent in the world besides infiltration is just a time consuming trek from one base to another, and all it really acts as is filler. Now getting to my other point, the repetition. MGSV has 50 main missons, and 37 of them are related to the games story. These missions are unique missions with different objectives, though they do usually share a similar theme of either retrieving a target, or eliminating a target, but this isnt always the case. The other 13 are challenge varations of the missions. I have yet to do them all, but they up the difficulty of past missions, and add a new twist to keep thing interesting. An example being a mission where you have to destroy a target located in an enemy base, but can now only use weapons and items you find while doing the mission. The ones I've played have been extremely fun, and a fresh challenge which still feels new, because of the added difficulty and new mission rules. These 50 main missions are the highlight of the game. Now lets talk about side-ops. Side-ops are very hit and miss. They have similar objectives to the main missions, but with no story. The problem with these side-ops is that they reuse many of the main mission areas, but just reuse them. No new rules or anything, just the same area with a different objective. Also, some side-ops sometimes have you go to random places in the wildermess on the map, only to usually do a quick 3 minute objective. So most of your time doing these ops is just spent traveling. And then the next side-op you want to do could be half-way across the map. So you either travel all the way over there, or call down a helicopter, which acts as the games fast travel and is used to leave the hub world. The problem is this still takes around 3 minutes. You need to travel to a helicopter pick up point, wait for the helicopter to arrive, and then your taken through another loading screen, and after that your finally allowed to pick another destination. Yet even after that you need to wait for the helicopter to make its way to the ground to drop you off. Travel time in this game is simply too long and tedious. So basically, main missions are good and side-ops are pretty boring and very repetitive. Now that I've talked about the basic aspects of the game design that effects the gameplay, I'll discuss solely how the game plays, and it plays beautifully. MGSV gives you so many options in how you can take on these missions, with multiple points of entry in a base and multiple ways to manipulate things inside and around the base. You also have a plethora of weapons which get better and better over time, giving you a great sense if progression. This progression also links with the motherbase building part of the game. This part being building your own mercenary group, Diamond Dogs, along with its base of opeartion. Throughout the game your able use GMP (the games currency) to expand your motherbase, allowing you to obtain more soilders. You obtain new soilders for your base by doing missions and recovering enemy soilders out in the field. You can scan any enemy soilder while in the hub world, check his stats, and knock him out and extract him back to mother base, he'll then be convinced into working for you, and become part of your team. The better people you have, the better your weapon and item arsenal. This is once again great progression, as it incentives not just running and gunning, but carefully considering your options when taking on a mission, as you'll want to maximize your rewards. There's also a multiplayer motherbase invasion mode, where people can invade your base, and you can invade theres, but I've had fairly little experience with this, as I've stuck mostly to the singleplayer, so I have no real opinion on it. So that covers the gameplay, MGSV does have some poor game design choices, along with some bad side-ops, but the gameplay and core 50 missions are more than worth the money, and has some of the best stealth gameplay to ever grace the industry.

Story (No Spoilers)

I've played every canonical Metal Gear game, and story wise, MGSV is the second worst, only beating out MGS: Peace Walker. MGSV's story is made up of two chapters, with chapter one consisting of 30 story missions, and chapter 2 consisting of 7 story missions, along with 13 missions that are past missions with different rules. Chapter 1 is pretty good, it has an interesting story and a solid antagonist. Though its not nearly as good as the other MGS games, its entertaining. The problems begin in chapter 2. Chapter 2 has pacing issues, where story missions just kind of appear after doing other various missions, and it all feels very loosely connected. Like, the ending mission of the game literally comes out if nowhere, and has absolutely no build up. Though I do like the ending itself and I think it sort of makes up for a lackluster chapter 2, it still feels out of left field. Also, one of chapter 2's arcs is unfinished. There was supposed to be a mission 51, which would explain a few stroy details in the game, but it was cut because of time constraints. Cutscenes and story details were released by konami though, so after finishing the game, be sure to look up these details for a better conclusion. Chapter 2 really isnt that good. But overall, I'd say the story isnt terrible, just really lacking, especially by MGS standards.

Conclusion

MGSV is an ingenious stealth game, muddled by some poor design choices and a lackluster story. So I'll sum up the game like this. If you solely play a game for gameplay and are a fan of the stealth genre, then this game is for you. If you play a game for story more than gameplay, and havent played prior MGS games, I wouldn't recommend it. Though I'd recommend MGS 1-4 as they are far more story rich. If you have played prior MGS games, I'd recommend this game either way, as it does give some story details MGS fans will want to hear, and I assume you like stealth games if you've played the other games, and the gameplay is great. So in conclusion, V delivers on gameplay but falls short on story, but I'd still recommend, as it truly is one of the best stealth games from a gameplay standpoint.
