[h1]What Made Me Fall In Love[/h1]
[hr][/hr] 
This game has unexaggerably THE best third person player locomotion system in the industry, not topped since 2015, and you simply will not find any other game that gives you more movement freedom and such a rock solid, slick yet precise and robust feel to it. All options are always to your disposal, and once you learn the controls, your character will always do exactly as you say, and you can even learn to command every singular step.

That's not all for freedom, of course, since this game also gives you one of the widest and deepest arrays of possibilities to interact with enemy characters. As a war game, you can expect to be clicking on their heads with many weapon types, sure; but then there's also CQC, you can 5 string combo them unconscious, pointing your gun to interrogate them, or stealing their weapon to interrogate them with it, also grabbing them with a choke-hold, and drag them around with your pistol pulled out for scouting, or use them as a meat shield when in combat, make them trip with a leg swipe, or pushing them to the ground with a dive to their stomach, and so much more. Let's not even get started with the amount of stealth gadgets, you can't even imagine.

But primarily, what really kept me playing this game for all these years were 2 things: the FOB endgame, and the modding community.


[h1]What Kept Me Coming Back[/h1]
[hr][/hr] 
To briefly explain this game's endgame; as you can imagine, sh*t's not over after the credits roll; not even after 100% completion, because of this game's multiplayer PvP mode, FOB invasions. Many people think of it as merely an opportunity for random players to pillage one's own base and opt out of it, but this is a common misconception. Maintaining an FOB risks it being invaded, sure, but FOB soldiers and materials can't affect your single-player experience in any other way than positively, since it will give you more material storage AND personnel capacity, and anything you could lose due to invasions is strictly limited to FOB bases and capacity. Multiplayer brings over the winnings to single-player, and keeps all the losses to itself.

Even if you don't ever interact, it will provide a net positive to your base economy overall, and if you do interact, you'll quickly be convinced that the winnings always far outweigh the losses. Sure, when invading you risk being detected and so opening up a revenge invasion, but until you get to the higher ranks, most bases you'll invade will be abandoned, owned by one-time players that left them there vulnerable forever. Even if you do get the weird invasion, recouping would at most take 2 invasions. FOB invasions are really fun and also really short, and the fact that you only have 1 shot gives it real stakes, and then the even weirder defence PvP encounters are really fun, and it's very rewarding to master the possible strategies and get into the meta.

Lastly, there is an entire aspect of the game that locks a huge part of it behind FOB base capacity, and that is the R&D higher grades of weapon and item upgrading; a great way to give endgame players one last long term checklist to complete. It's genius, since you can't really see the tree much further away from where you've so far made it, so you never really feel like you're missing out on the possibility of that much higher grade levels. But even if you did know, those levels would realistically only serve to be more effective at FOB PvP, since using such high gadgets on the single-player only makes the game way easier, which is the last thing you'd want at a point when you've dominated the game enough to unlock power levels that high, paradoxically. In fact, at that point you'll naturally try to challenge yourself, by limiting the equipment you bring to missions, or outright playing OSP, and perhaps even going the extra mile: modding.


[h1]What Made Me Settle Forever[/h1]
[hr][/hr] 
MGSV has one of the best modding communities on the internet, and I mean that on many levels. The game has been cracked open in so many incredible ways, to the point there's an entire community of people pumping out content that pretty much feels like official free DLC. New missions, new Side-ops, and even new entire maps, with someone currently working on a full re-implementation of Ground Zero's Camp Omega, which is already out and available for download, with frequent upgrades and a really high quality catalogue of Side-ops.

Many dreams left over by this game's troubled development are becoming true thanks to its modding scene, which found ways to add content to the game that doesn't need to replace any existing assets; for now these are maps, missions, side-ops, textured models for NPCs and soldier characters, and we're soon to be able to add new player costumes, vehicles, weapons and items. It's wild, and it's gonna get wilder.

You can mod your game to make it the experience you want. Tune up the difficulty by increasing enemy cone distance, reducing player health, removing NPC overhead markers and heat auras, and you can even download a mod that disables health regen, and another that adds a First-Aid Spray for healing (I made that one rawr). You can also enable random item drops when incapacitating enemies, random skull invasions on free roam, and even random landing events that force you out of your routine and mixes up the experience. And if you have your own mod idea, you can probably make it yourself rather easily.


[h1]What Made Me Feel Like Home[/h1]
[hr][/hr] 
And here's the other side of the coin; not the mods, the makers. Modders' Heaven is one of the most welcoming places I've ever found on the internet, and I'm not saying that just because I'm a part of it, I promise. Modders are really open to dumb newbie questions about what's currently possible and what stands on our way, and that's precisely how I interacted with them at first, and it was because of their hospitality that I got into making my first ever mod. 

Whenever you come up with a new mod idea, you can share it with the community and enough people will give you the assistance you need all the way until you have everything you need to carry it out. And even if you're shy, there's great effort in maintaining good documentation about the community's findings and useful tools. Though there are figureheads, there's no elitism; it's just good vibes all around. Hopefully, I've convinced you to come around!

[hr][/hr] 
Metal Gear Solid V quickly became one of my favourite games the first time I played it; player freedom, base building, army recruitment and its thought provoking story about race & language, dissociative identity disorder and the fruitlessness of revenge really grabbed me and kept me engaged all the way to the credits, then its great endgame experience, PvP meta and the drive for a "true" 100% completion turned it into my comfort game and kept me playing way afterwards, and it's now been the community of those like me, who enjoyed the game so much to make new content for it and urged me to do the same, what's made me stick around for so long and feel like I'm part of something greater.

Let me preface by saying that I've not played any other Metal Gear Solid title; I have no real basis of comparison.

This is a decent stealth/cover 3rd person action/shooter.  

Pros:

The gunplay feels fairly satisfying, and while the game would certainly prefer for you to take your enemies alive and Fulton them away to safety/employment, you're not really obligated to do so.  

The weapon customization is welcome.  Many of the choices are largely cosmetic, but the ability to choose a short barrel vs a long barrel, or swap your medium-power combat rifle ammo for a smaller supply of high power sniper rifle ammo, is helpful.  The most important aspects of customization, for me, are suppressor, optics, and underbarrel attachments.

Mission rewards feel tangible.  You do something, you get paid for it.

Lots of side missions that let you experiment with different play styles.  Open world lets you wander around and kill/extract whoever you want at your own pace.  Not a great way to make money, but a good way to get personnel and resources. 

Cons:

The cover and stealth mechanics don't feel as tight as those in, say, Splinter Cell: Blacklist.  They're functional enough for the game, but I frequently find myself trying to stick to a wall and getting spotted by an enemy 150 ft away, despite the fact that every other time I've immediately covered next to that wall.

The tech tree unlocks are clearly resource/time sinks, and unlocking the various trees frequently doesn't give any new customization parts, just a new base model.  As the game has no resource or time cap, it makes everything feel a little... unimportant.

I have no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on in the story.  None at all.  I'll admit I haven't prioritized it heavily, but I went from apparently nuclear powered robots the size of skyscrapers with unpronouncible names in Afghanistan, to rescuing war orphans and avoiding gratuitously nude zombie snipers in Africa, and there was something about a disease whose infection vector is the language you speak?  Like, this is all over the place.  What the hell?

The online connectivity is a little unstable.  Not usually a huge problem, but when a large portion of your cash and resources are stored online (why, exactly?), it's frustrating to suddenly lose access to them due to server instability.  Oh, also, if you are doing a FOB mission (Adversarial PvE with decent rewards) and you get disconnected?  Instant fail with maximum penalty.

Overall verdict: It's not a compelling narrative, but it's good casual fun.  I'd personally recommend picking up on sale, and playing with a gamepad.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is definitely one of my favourite games I have played this year. At the time of writing, I have been playing this since Halloween, all through November. I had a bit of a horror binge throughout October, and I should have totally been playing this instead.

MGSV has shown me some of my most enjoyed storylines, settings and characters this year. Having played other entries in the Metal Gear Solid series (never touched the first two Metal Gear games), I will admit that when I first heard Kiefer's voice I found it a little jarring. However, despite my love of David Hayter's quips and voice (which has more gravel than my garden path), I have come to enjoy Kiefer's performance. Once you play for a while, you warm up to it.

Furthermore, the endless attention to detail in this series, from character and story events taking places in an entirely plausible timeline across the whole series, as well as music and thematic choices, and the whole, gigantic, artistic vision that Hideo Kojima has created., come together to form a true marvel.

Additionally, some of the characters and themes explored within MGSV have made me feel so much more empathy, horror, dread, joy and countless other emotions. One of the biggest features in this game is the wide variety of possibilities. There are tons of weapons and gadgets in the game and what you take into battle and how you use them allows for so many different play styles. This is what impresses me the most about this game. The tools you have at your disposal and the design of the environments, there's just so much potential, so many ways to play.

A negative is the way you sometimes can walk over certain terrain and other times you just slide back. Sometimes you get the option to climb over stuff but sometimes it's inconsistent and doesn't show. It can be annoying. But you start to get used to it and be able to work around it.

To reiterate, this game is all about options, player freedom. And my impression is the developers have done a great job in designing a game that is extremely flexible, giving players the tools to play however they want.

There is a suprising amount of diversity in the gameplay and what you can do, the maps are big and well fleshed out, there is a fair amount of content (LOTS of micromanaging, FYI) for online/offline upgrades, online FOB mode is interesting but optional.

The story... it's a bizzare journey, though there are parts that are lacking. I suggest playing through MGS5 Ground Zero first to understand the setup for the first mission in this. The cutscenes are over the top MGS goodness for the most part. I will say the ending is... well you'll either like it or hate it. Overall though the same is worth it if you have a lot of time to spare to play through the game.

MGS V was a game, that both pissed off and in retrospect impressed both it's core and new audience. The characters were mostly less engaging, the story less intense, so, even if there may have been a subtle reason for it, whether on purpose or not, the overall narrative was less engaging than the previous installments. That being said, it is still interesting enough in my opinion probably above average on the industry's scale. 

On the other hand, this may well be the best transition of a traditionally somewhat (less so in MGS 3) directed level based gameplay to a vibrant, memorable open world ecosystem. From screwing around with your horse's crap to jumping into a walker and shooting up an enemy base, there is much to do and most of it is damn fun. So if that is what you are looking for, this is an amazing game made for you.

On the other hand, Konami can be a cruel mistress and the tacked on annoying online base is just as intrusive and pace killing as it needs to be to piss you off. If the first complaint would mostly be made just by veterans of the series, this is a global annoyance. It did not ruin the game for me, but it tried hard to do so.

TL;DR Overall, if you want an open world stealth game filled with many interesting interactions and tons of options for overcoming your adversaries, this game is for you, if you want an OK narative attached, it is still probably fine. If you want a fullfledged MGS narrative, I hope you still have your PS2 around.

The story is ludicrous fantasy, even by MGS standards, but it's the only blemish on what is undoubtedly one of the best games ever made. MGSV brings the series' unique blend of "tactical espionage action" to Africa and the Middle East, in a vast open world reminiscent of the Far Cry series.

With hundreds of pieces of equipment to chose from, you can complete each mission however you would like, be it perfect stealth or all guns blazing. There are countless ways to approach a situation, giving this game stellar replay value. Unlike other stealth/action games, MGSV doesn't pigeonhole you into a stealth mechanic: given proper preparation, all approaches are equally viables. Sometimes I'll go the "perfect stealth, no kills" route, carefully choosing camouflage, silenced tranquilizer weapons and non-lethal riot guns; wearing night-vision goggles, interrogating enemies, and scrounging for intel. Some other times, I want to get it over quick, so I drop in with a helicopter in the middle of the enemy compound, triggering a combat alert, and pumping round after round into waves of enemies with a LMG whilst wearing full body armor. Most often, I vie for stealth, but end up being detected one way or another, which spices things up.

Other highlights of the game include a kickass 80's New Wave soundtrack, [b]INCREDIBLY GORGEOUS GRAPHICS[/b] (don't forget to enable [u]Ambient Occlusion[/u] in the NVIDIA Control Panel), a fun staff management system (improving upon the system they developed for MGS: Portable Ops), decent online features (inluding free DLC you get for participating in events), tight controls, and an unbelievable attention to detail (as is cutomary with the series).

Don't forget to play [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/311340/METAL_GEAR_SOLID_V_GROUND_ZEROES/]MGSV: GROUND ZEROES[/url] first!

I'll start by my favourite aspect of this game: gameplay. It's by far its best feature, full of different approaches and options of advancing through the game. There's a huge amount of weapons, items and tools that grant such variety. As a stealth lover myself, I've been very pleased by the gameplay. The AI is also good, especially when they go on alert, and really act as a group, making it more believable.

Now, its story and ambientation are, IMO, good for the first half of the game (Chapter 1), but then they fall amazingly short. The story begins with lots of mysteries, which are solved little by little, but towards the end things get simply ridiculous, making it overall not a good story.

Another negative aspect of this game are its Side Ops, or secondary missions. At first they are presented with variety and they're cool, but after you've rescued your 10th prisioner, extracted your 10th soldier... it gets really repetitive. There are simply too many Side Ops with too few different types of them for them to be enjoyable.

Main missions are good, they range between infiltrations, extractions, boss fights... just that sometimes you'll need to restart the mission to go with different equipment, if you don't want to spend money on its delivery.

Also, the FOB mechanics, being forced, is just wrong. Basically, you can invade another player's base, and steal their resources and soldiers, and the same can happen to you. If you don't want to take part in it, you must play offline, which limits your max money earnings and locks challenges. I haven't been invaded ever, but just the possibility of it happening makes me hate that decision.

Overall, I give this game a recommended rating because of how fun it is to play, despite its shortcomings in some aspects. If you're a stealth fan, you'll enjoy the game for sure.

[b]Short Version[/b]: Play the game. Its probably one of the best open-world games out there. Great Characters and Story and an Engine that's easy to understand within a few minutes.

[b]Long Version[/b]:

Despite being partially incomplete, this is probably the only thing that connects makes the entire Metal Gear Timeline complete and is considered as the Final Game in Big Boss' Storyline.


[b]Gameplay[/b]: Like the game before it, The Phantom Pain uses the new FOX Engine. If you know how to actually play Metal Gear then you can easily understand the controls within a few minutes. Compared to Ground Zeroes, The FOX Engine is more developed and updated as this time the engine is tuned to for the open-world environment of Afghanistan and Africa. Mission-Wise, Its pretty well made with the right kind of difficulty and there are only a few times with some cheap deaths. Also Kojima's in the game (again).


[b]Story[/b]: [spoiler] Nine Years ago, Militaires Sans Frontières (MSF), A Private Military Group led by the Legendary Soldier Big Boss was attacked by an unknown force known as XOF. The attack led to the destruction of MSF and Big Boss fell to a coma. The Year now is 1984, Big Boss awakens and was attacked by XOF again, He escapes with the help of an old friend, Revolver "Shalashaska" Ocelot, who then brings him to Northern Kabul, Afghanistan to rescue MSF's Second-in Command, Kazuhira Miller. After his rescue, They return to Mother Base, the off-shore base of their new Private Military Group, Diamond Dogs. Back on his feet, Big Boss will take revenge on those who destroyed MSF and take vengeance for his loss. [/spoiler]


[b]Connection with the next game[/b]: If you have Ground Zeroes, You can upload your save data to The Phantom Pain. Items acquired from the game such as the Uragan-5 Pistol can be in its default form. Characters extracted from Ground Zeroes can also be transferred to TPP such as Intel Agent Kojima, Glaz, Palitz, and The undercover CIA agent.

First of all, this is the first Metal Gear game that I have played, so don't expect me to compare it to other Metal Gear games. Second, for me gameplay is more important than story, so this is why I think this game is great: cause it has simply the best stealth/action 3rd person gameplay ever made

[h1]Story[/h1]

In this game, you are the mercenary legend Snake. You wake in hospital after a long come just to find out that your precious motherbase was destroyed. Then, you team up with your buddies Oceletot and Miller and try to rebuild Motherbase and puersue your dream of creating an army without borders. Along the missions you will also find out clues on who tried to kill you and destroy your base. You will meet up with interesting NPCs, like the sniper Quiet and the treacherous Skull Unit.
Now, I saw some people complaining that there is very little story on this game and so on... Well, I have to disagree. The long cutscenes are there, but they are split among the 50 missions, so to see the big picture you have to finish the entire game, instead of doing just the first missions, like most people do. The story is good and makes sense even though it has some exaggerated anime-esque stuff. Just the ending is kinda of dissappointing, like really bad... 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Now, the gameplay is what makes this game amazing: you press the button to shoot and Snake shots, you press the button to run and Snake runs immediately. It might sound dumb, but it's really impressive how responsive and precise the controls are in this game. The actions are fast and quick, with no winding up moves, unlike other games. Also, every time you are performing an action, like reloading, you can immediatelly interrupt that action with a defensive one, like running or taking cover. It's a really impressive work on what the devs have done with this game's controls.

Also, bear in mind that even if the game rellies heavely on stealth, you can also try other approaches to completing missions. You can even go Rambo with heavy weapons and heavy armor. I mostly played the sniper approach, taking down enemies from a distance, it kinda of worked for me

[h1]Motherbase management[/h1]

Now this is a game inside a game. To build the new motherbase is kinda of a strategy game by itself, and it's highly addictive! You need to find resourses like oil and metal to build base platforms, then you have to recruit men to work for you, then you can build stuff like new weapons or security items... The possibilities are nearly endless in how to improve and what to build for your motherbase.

[b]I give it 5.0/5.0[/b]

Colonel...Can you hear me?  As a gamer who grew up with the NES, SNES, and the introduction of the first major 3D systems (N64 and PS1), I definitely played the original MGS back in good old '98-'99.  As is widely known, the original was amazing and introduced unique gameplay elements (I'm thinking of Meryl's frequency on the jewel case, Psycho Mantis 'moving' your controller, etc.).  The core gameplay itself was fairly groundbreaking but its presentation was where the game broke true boundaries.  In any case, I've obviously been a fan of the series, and have kept up with most releases.  With this almost certainly being Kojima's last MGS foray, is it worthy of a true finale?  Does it still retain the MGS flavor? 

Yes and no.  Gone is the strong narrative and linear gameplay.  This sounds like heresy but the storyline is actually mission based.  You can also explore the game world at your whim; think of something akin to a Metal Gear GTA with bases to avoid or destroy, vehicles to shoot up or capture, etc.  Surprisingly, this doesn't feel like a Battlefield clone because the game stays close enough to its roots to give it that MGS feel; albeit in an open warzone.  There are too many details to describe how MGSV walks the line between your big budget military shooter and staying true to the Stealth-Action genre (Mother Base, FOB missions, weapons development) and they are almost all new to the franchise.  Having played the game fairly extensively, I can say with confidence that Kojima was able to create a MGS-esque type game with the aforementioned additions of generic action game type elements.  I have to admit my skepticism, but Kojima and friends pulled it off.  

With all this being said, I would recommend the game to MGS fans and action fans alike.  For better or worse, it will appease MGS fans (while feeling slightly watered-down), and invite those who prefer a more action-oriented playstyle (while feeling somewhat obscure).  Some missions do require absolute stealth (the vast majority do to get the best mission rank)  but it won't be the stunning stealth narrative you've experienced in the past.  However, I dare say it has enough of the latter peppered in to still feel like MGS.  The gameplay can be described similarly.  In fact, I was surprised by how much it did feel like MGS given it's GTA-like foundation.  It will give you plenty of Michael Bay-esque 'Wow! Explosions!' moments (Kojima does them well), while also giving you a healthly dose of the sneaking, hiding, and fear of capture that the series has evolved around (that can be optional given the aforementioned equipment development).  Frankly, that's exactly it.  MGS has evolved to accommodate modern gaming, and perhaps Konami's business model(?).  While still an enjoyable MGS game on a gameplay, presentation, and technical level, it has accomodated nonetheless.  Take it or leave it.

One last note: buy with the understanding that while the storyline reaches for excellence, it fails and is clearly unfinished (but not horrendous).  However, most other details (including the technical ones) are what you would expect from Kojima and crew; top notch.  Sad to see David Hayter not voice Snake as well.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (from now on referred to as MGSV:TPP) is a stealth third person shooter game that has many game mechanics.

MGSV:TPP offers a great deal of weapons to use with a lot of customasation options
you can paint the weapons and change configurations. there are a lot of fun gadgets in the game - if you want to destroy a tank you can either shoot a rocket at it or you can sneak behind it and parachute it away, taking it as your own. The only problem I have with MGSV:TPP is that some missions are just a harder variation of other mission.

Stealth is very important in this game - almost every mission lets you finish the mission without anyone noticing you, you can become invisible with a gadget, call your helicopter to make a sandstorm to blind the enemy, you can sneak behind enemies - take them hostage and force them to give you information, also there are tranquilizer and stun weapons that let you put someone unconscious.

Companions are another fun part of the game, you can have "friends" that help you - you start with your loyal horse, you can rescue a dog and get him as another optionto use, in one mission you will have to face off a sniper - after making the sniper unconscious (there are a lot of fun ways to do that. like requesting ammo to be dropped on her location - then the ammo box will drop on the sniper making the sniper unconscious) if you don't kill the sniper but choose to rescue her you will get her as a companion untill one mission in the story (after that mission to get her back you need to do the sniper face off and rescue her 20 times)
you will also unlock a robot that can use miniguns, blades, flame throwers and pistols after a mission

Story:
This game has story, but I didn't realy understand it, I also don't want to spoil the ending which was a bit wierd at first

In conclusion MGSV:TPP is  a great game worth buying as it offers many things to do!

Absolutely outstanding. Long time MGS fan, and this one has had me captivated as much, if not more so, as any prior entry. This game shows you a lot of things that you will wonder very deeply about and uses the rest of the series, in my opinion, as an explanation without always needing to shove the answer right in your face.

MGSV is the antithesis of the linear stories of MGS past. Cut scenes are shorter and can be sparsed out due to you having a choice of when you progress to the next main story mission. This can make the plot appear jilted at times but for those who care about the creative process, you have to appreciate Kojima for trying something new. The game plays out almost in episodic fashion, which actually compliments the open world gameplay.  To me this seemed natural, and quite frankly preferred. You aren't Solid Snake sneaking your way around Shadow Moses, you are Venom Snake building an army, interacting with local private forces, maintaining commucation with Mother Base, and on a whole different level of operation than any previous game save Peace Walker. The cut scenes we get are framed brilliantly and are great to watch. The visuals are SHARP and there is a real sense of gravity in the tone of the story and the way in which the characters carry themselves. The acting is superb and pushes video games forward as a medium of storytelling. The greatest artists always are in an effort to push their own envelope, and Kojima certainly does that with his one. His biggest project yet none the less.

The same soldier that just smartly called in another soldier to check the location where I just messed up my approach is completely unfazed when I use a box to hide. I sort of finished MGSV with mixed feelings. So, if I recommend it, than not wholeheartedly, but for some fun aspects of the game design and the idiosyncracities injected by the japanese producer Hideo Kojima. 

I am saying "sort of" because once the story finishes, the title screen tells me i have completed only about 58% of the game even after clearing a significant portion of side missions and all main missions relevant to the story. 

clearly, it is meant to be played on and on after story finish, perfecting your mission scores and clearing all side objectives and hunting the last animal that roams the semi-open world. 
this is strange to me and unexpected, since the other MGS game i played (MGS 4) was so story driven, to a point that it felt like watching a movie sometimes with gameplay sprinkled between rather than the other way around. 

to me this also illustrates the bipolar character of the game itself which in this open world setting seems to not fit quiet right from the story telling point of view. 
we have the stangely anachronistic world of MGS, with its typical humor (the first "end" for instance made me laugh out loud), the over the top heroes and characters, faithfull simulation of its time etc. yet, all this only exists in cut scenes wich are surprisingly disconnected from the world simulated. 
look at the motherbase for instance, many cut-scenes, many characters, but they are not actually to be found in the vast expands of the base. where are all your collegues and friends all day? where are conversations and interacions with them?

this is the main reasons i cannot wholeheartedly recommend.

let's look at the "end" of the game as another example. rarely in recent times, i have seen a more depressing conclusion to a game. i am not refering to the overall MGS ending of "truth" which was all nice and well. presumably, it satisfies die hard fans who played from MGS1 even more. 
no, I refer to [spoiler] the ending that strips off the only regular glimpse - or lets say - prospect of human interaction between missions from you. [/spoiler] 
how one could continue to play the remaining 42% is almost a mystery to me. 

yes, MGS5 presents an empty world devote of normal human interaction. the open world is not really a world. there are no stories to be discovered nothing there except plants, animals and soldiers. all there because they need to be collected as ressources.
in reality, the world only connects the tactical military simulation areas, but there is nothing in it like a simulation of a living environment. it often feels like an empty stage that would be filled in main story missions with at least a little life. 

compare it to the open world of the witcher 3 for instance which came out about the same time. there we also have a war torn country - yes, but there is life in it, too. there are actual people, third parties to be found with different stories from the main narrative. In MGS5, i have not seen a single civilian in it except burned corpse. everybody you "meet" is a soldier and will shoot at you immediately.
what difference would it have made if one of the groups of sheep that roam the world was accompanied by a shepard with dog, perhaps, or what about an actually inhabited village, i imagine... 
wasn't this even part of MGS4 where you would be punished for accidently shooting civilians?

what is working fairly well is the simulation of infiltration missions and military action in general. surely it is not an entirely realistic portrayal but it is immensly satisfying to clear out an enemy outpost with tranquilizers without being noticed once. 
granted, this will not work the first time around, since the game tends to throw a surprise boss fight in occasionally where you are than somewhat underpowered with your standard tranq gun...

well, expectations are a difficult thing. yet, i can't get over the open world failure. it seems such a waste to create a vast environment just for harvesting items. perhaps, the game Kojima imagined wasn't finished in time for release. some not fleshed out aspects of the story seem to indicate so, too. 
it is kind of sad because we can assume this is the last we saw from snake.

I know these games have a lot of fans, but as far as I'm conserned, Hideo Kojima is a hack who wants to make movies and doesn't understand the basics about games. Playing this game as a shooter is a miserable experience, you keep getting interrupted all the time by these stupid cutscenes, that try to tell this inane story about something I struggled to care about. Sure you can skip the cutscenes, but when you have to do it every 30 seconds for half of the duration of the first mission, it gets old really fast.

Now, don't get me wrong, this is a well-made game from a technical standpoint. But the way its parts are designed... The way you're punished for using your equipment (NVGs overheat, suppressors break after the first 10 shots, vehicles attract attention in an of themselves, even though they belong to the faction itself, so there would be no way for them to know who's actually behind the wheel, etc.), the way some objectives are placed, the way resource gathering is set up, even the base upgrading stuff is unintuitive, and to me felt simply tacked on for the sake of it, not having any inherent value.

And then you get to the juicy stuff, which is missions in the open world. And oh boy do they suck. This game revolves around stealth, but stealth is made unbelievably hard. You character moves very slowly, enemies are superhumanly perceptive and can hear you walk past them from dozens of meters away. If you dare and peek around a corner, they'll instantly see you from 20-30 meters. You're punished for the smallest mistakes. But if you just go "loud" and kill all of them, you're punished again (reinforcements come in in huge waves, also, you lose the ability to recruit anyone, because that requires subduing your targets and not killing them.

But what really sealed the deal, was the fact, that, as far as I can tell, the game is designed around completeling the same missions multiple times (you get tasks that you can complete in an area, but you don't have the means to do it on first try. You have to keep coming back for them. The thing is, if it was a seamless world, I'd have no problem traveling to the same location, but you actually have to go back to your base, pick your mission again, and start from the one of pre-placed insertion points (meaning you have to endure all those loading screens and cutscenes again). Couple that with the stupidest checkpoint system in the history of video games (checkpoint fire off when you exit the objective area, I assume, that's done to stop players from save scumming). After I lost several hours worth of progress again, I just uninstalled the game and wrote this review.

I have extremely mixed feelings about this game, being a huge Metal Gear fan.

1. Amazing gameplay, genuinely fun missions, enormous replay value. One of the best games I've played in years.

2. The story and game completely crashes and burns after Chapter 1. One of the most disappointing games I've played in years.

I'll keep it short and simple: this game is incredible, and had the potential to go down in history as one of the greatest games of the century. But, it didn't.

Let me compare this game to a book series, without spoiling any plotlines.

Lets say there are 3 books in a series that you have been reading since you were a kid. The first two are incredible, and you have to wait a long time for the third and final book to come out. It comes out, and it's HUGE. Encyclopedia huge. You're so excited, and start ripping through the pages. Chapter 1 is insanely long, about 1/3 of the entire book, but it's AMAZING. You can't believe how great it is. You get to the end of Chapter 1, and you're amazed that you still have 2/3 of the book left after such a breathtaking adventure. You've easily read 300 pages by the time you finish Chapter 1, and it feels like it's just getting started.

You take a breath, and start reading Chapter 2.

Something isn't right, and you immediately notice it. The story is not the same, it's not as rich. It starts to get confusing, and the author starts skipping much too quickly through important stuff, leaving out details. You notice scenes that feel like something you read back in Chapter 1, but slightly different. You're only ten pages into Chapter 2, and without warning, the entire plot starts to wrap itself up very quickly. You sit in shock and realize you are reading the end of the story, but there are so many pages left. 

15 pages into Chapter 2, you are horrified to read "The End". You flip the page, and it's blank. They're ALL blank. Frustrated and confused, you put the book away. Chapter 1 was so amazing that you can't stop thinking about it, but every time you think about it you just want more. Chapter 2 hurts to think about, and you feel slightly betrayed that it was even placed in the book. You would have waited for a second book to come out if it were as good as Chapter 2, but now it's all over and there wont' be any more books.

You find out afterwards that the publishing company secretly fired the author before he was able to finish Chapter 2, so they cobbled together what little had been written and ended the story quickly so they could publish the book and try to make some money back. You also find out that there was supposed to be so, so much more, but it was scrapped apart and never completed. You'll never really get to see the story end the right way.

This is MGSV in nutshell. 

However, it does have a lot of replay value. I'm still playing this game regularly, trying to beat the missions without being detected and turning off all helping icons and markers. It's really difficult, and a lot of fun. At it's core, the gameplay and stealth mechanics are revolutionary. 

I love this game, but I hate it at the same time.

I have a love/hate relationship with the Metal Gear series; I loved Metal Gear Solid, and I hated every other game in the series. That's not true. I haven't played all of them, and I also love Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance, a game whose gameplay is so out of place with the rest of the series as to not include it in the same breath. The point is that I feel Metal Gear Solid struck a perfect balance between excellent gameplay and over-indulgent creator nonsense that the other games in the series did not. I didn't get excited for Metal Gear Solid V when it was announced as two games, didn't get excited when it reviewed well, and really paid it no notice until it was selected as Giant Bomb's #2 game of the year. I always buy their game of the year, but I don't have a WiiU, so I deferred to the number two choice. I set my prejudices aside for a moment, and jumped into Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.

You are codename Punished "Venom" Snake, the legendary Big Boss, and it's 1984. Your Mother Base has been destroyed, your forces killed, and you've been hospitalized from critical injuries you received in the escape. After an explosive wake up, you're reunited with your lieutenants, Ocelot and Miller, and start about the task of rebuilding your private army (the Diamond Dogs), and tearing apart Afghanistan and the Angola-Zaire border in your search for the man who nearly killed you, Skull Face, to exact your revenge.

MGSV has a lot of interconnected systems in it, but for the sake of the "micro" in microreview, let's focus on the core gameplay loop. Storyline missions are broken into episodes. Each one starts you at one point in the open world map, and gives you an objective or two. How you achieve those objectives, such as eliminating an enemy commander or rescuing a POW, is up to you. At your disposal are a huge number of weapons (lethal and non-lethal) and utility items, ranging from the standard Metal Gear cardboard box, to inflatable decoys and smoke grenades that can summon your attack helicopter and fire support team. What works so well in these missions is that they encourage stealth and doing things quietly, but if you screw it up and have to shoot your way out, it doesn't really punish you in the way other Metal Gear games will. There are a ton of tools at your disposal. You can, should, and will need to use them all.

The sheer variety of missions and objectives and ways to accomplish them means MGSV rarely feels repetitive, arbitrary, or boring. Sometimes I was carefully scoping out enemy positions, creeping through their defenses, and quickly slipping out, POW in a fireman's carry, without a trace. Sometimes I would try to be sneaky, fail, and finish my objectives only after killing every single person in the area. In one mission, I was having trouble sneaking in, so I shot a rocket at an enemy position. It created a diversion, so while they were all facing in the direction of where I shot the rocket from, I was able to sneak around behind them, and finish the mission. With the exception of the very noisy rocket, I was neither seen nor heard.

There is a lot more going on, including side ops (side quests in other games), buddies and their relationships to you, base building, online mission dispatches, item and weapon research, and regular open world exploration and collectible finding. It's all great and none of it is jammed down your throat too fast. In fact, I'd estimate a solid 1/3 of the game is a steady tutorial ramping up to having all of your systems online and moving.

What doesn't work so hot is the story. It's less nonsense than some Metal Gears, but the conclusion is extremely underwhelming. It feels cut off, like the development team suddenly ran out of time or money or both. It leaves a lot of loose ends that aren't remotely addressed by the next game in the series timeline, which would be the original Metal Gear. It does one thing right at the end, but a dozen different things wrong.

I went into MGSV extremely skeptical, and was absolutely engrossed by it. It's hard for me not to be effusive about it. I just enjoyed this game so, so much. If I had played it earlier, it would've easily been one of my favorite games of 2015. Not quite good enough to unseat The Witcher 3, but it's excellent and they do have a lot of similarities. It's good enough to make me want to revisit those previous Metal Gear games that I didn't put a lot of time into. It's a real shame that Hideo Kojima has parted ways with Konami, and thus the Metal Gear series. The series may be at a functional end, but it went out on an extremely high note.

Side note: If you're likewise not a huge Metal Gear fan and not willing to jump headfirst into the full The Phantom Pain, check out Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes. It is more-or-less a demo for that excellent core gameplay loop, and it's a quarter of the price of the full game. Yes, it's a paid demo, but it contains an area not seen within The Phantom Pain, gives some backstory to the full product, and offers some items to carry over.

I love all canon MGS games, each games is unique and different in its own way, and MGSV is no exception. I've found MGS series to be the only video game series that realistically portrayed the military world in its both good and dark side, this is coming from an ex-soldier and I think MGSV is the one portrayed it best. MGSV captured the 80s global politics, its military industrial complex and the world through a soldier's eyes perfectly, I can say that I really appreciate what Hideo Kojima have achieved with the new narrative direction. 

The main story this time is minimal compared to the rest of the series, but world building and its surround events are being written with great attention to details, it makes the game world feels alive and if you pay attention to these events, it can serves as a great immersive tool for the nonlinear gameplay aspect. Listening to cassettes are not as interesting as having cutscenes, but they do offer great insight on the world and characters's motivation.

MGSV isn't just being open-world in terms of gameplay, but also the narrative itself. This is the world of your own actions which is you as a player rather than the main character. The narrative playfully try to tell the message that the narrative doesn't define your experience, but it's your experience that define the narrative.

In the end, MGSV isn't perfect, it's understandable that some people don't like how it is not the MGS they loved. But MGSV is still an achievement, a great story that given time, I think more people will come to appreciate its narrative.

PROS
[b]-Tactical gameplay.[/b] I loved the logistics os getting myself in position, doing recon, then executing a plan that I formulated on the go. It was rewarding and tense to wait for a group of enemies to enter the perfect position to produce the best results of my plan. To me, every mission was different, and it never got repetitive. Occasional upgraded enemies related to the story really threw a new curve in the game and put my upgrades to the test. Becuase with these upgrades, they did stand a chance.
[b]-Customization. [/b]You can literally build your weapon from scratch. Barrels. Receivers. Stocks. Scopes. Flash hiders. You name it, it's got it. It really adds a deeper connection to your weapons of choice than other games. Customizing your base is also cool, you can recruit soldiers by stealing them from the field, and each one has unique stats that eventually upgrade your equipment. Equipment upgrades are in depth too, with plenty of options to deck out your Venom Snake. Did I mention that any new gun attachments that you research are backwards compatible? Yeah. You can do that.
[b]-World.[/b] The game world is dividied in two parts, and each are distinct and fun to inhabit. It is very much like a Far Cry type of world.

CONS
[b]-Story.[/b] The overarching story is quite weak, and offers little resolution, so it's certainly not a selling point of this game. Simply put, it is unfinished. You may already be aware of the conspiracy that lasted many months after this game's release that new story content was coming; well, it hasn't.

OVERALL
I give this game a [b]9/10[/b]. The strengths of TPP's gameplay is so great, that it overpowers its  negative of an unfinished story. I believe that this is already a great game, but could have been one of the [i]greatest games of all time[/i] if the story matched the intensity of its gameplay.

MGSV does so many things right, yet so many wrong. My biggest complaint to the gameplay, which is pretty great when you think about it, is that it provides far too many advantages to you as a player. You have to actively choose to do things the more interesting, yet more difficult way. D-Dog makes stealth silly, and Quiet puts you in a position to rain death on everyone without ever pulling a trigger. Armored vehicles and indoor locations are about the only challenge, and the latter is still a breeze if you take D-Dog and actually try to sneak.

As I said, it's a pretty silly complaint, as you can disable reflex mode (which I did do), marking, and always play with a S rank, total stealth approach. I plan to take more of this approach in any subsequent playthroughs, but my first run through a MGS game is always whatever proves enjoyable and not incredibly difficult. It's a Kojima game with a ridiculous and highly convoluted story after all. Enjoying that craziness is always top priority on the initial run for me.

On to the story though. This is where the game does shine... eventually. The first dozen episodes of the story, perhaps longer as I can't remember how far it was before things happened, were incredibly slow and repetitive. I put the game down and forgot it for months. It just didn't hook me. Part of this, as it would turn out, is the result of this being a really long story. Still, it takes a long time to really get going, but once it does, it shines as another entry in the MGS franchise.

The characters all pull some sort of response, whether that be annoyance at Kaz's constant complaints, confusion as to how Ocelot has a different personality in every single game, a desire to punch Huey in the face every time he opens his damn mouth, and even Snake, who never quite grows on you, since David Hayter is Snake, and Kiefer Sutherland can't pronounce nuclear... Point being character development is great, and no new characters proved to be disappointing for me. At one point, even insignificant characters, ones you've never really interacted with, may put you on the verge of tears.

It's painfully obvious that the latter portions of the game were not presented in quite the fashion they should have been, but the story isn't seriously lacking or disappointing. It covers the transition between MGS3 and PW into MG/MG2, it explains the origins of things that occur in MGS1/2/4, and it does all of these things pretty well. Yes, a fair amount of it is presented purely as audio, but it's there, and it isn't horribly phoned in nonsense just to cover the gaps.

Overall, the game is great. It's not necessarily superior to any of the previous games, but it's also not inherently inferior. There's an argument to be had for any of them. Personally, V is at the bottom of the list (PW excluded as I never finished it) of MGS games, but it is solidly a MGS game, and as such, a great experience to be had.

They offer a storyline that I am hooked into more than just about any other game out there. The stealth/action gameplay is excellent, and the graphics are impressive even to this day. They have so much replay value, between my Xbox and PC playthroughs, I've spent more than 600 hours in MGS:V. That's far higher than any other game I've ever played. During a steam sale, $5 is a steal for the bundle of these games and I would recommend it to anybody.

Metal Gear Solid 5 feels like such a departure from Metal Gear Solid 4. The fourth entry in the long running stealth series felt more like an interactive movie: for 8 hours of actual gameplay, you had to watch 12 hours of cutscenes. 

MGS 5 is the exact opposite: I've spend more than 35 hours with the game and I haven't watched many cutscenes and the ones I've seen, weren't that lengthy. The fifth game - and unfortunately the last one under the helm of Hideo Kojima - is all about the fabulous gameplay. 

It's just so much fun, to figure out, how to infiltrate a base. Thanks to the Fulton-Device as a means to get rid of knocked out enemies, you can play MGS without killing anyone. 

It is ironic, that you can play the game, by not harming a soul and yet the story is all about the atrocities of war and you the player becoming a villainous murderer, driven by an obsession to avenge the destruction of your military operation. 

Kojima itself compared MGS5's story to Breaking Bad. But it doesn't feel that way. Maybe it has something to do, with Kojimas leaving Konami. Maybe Kojima never got the chance to produce the elaborate cutscenes, Metal Gear Solid is famous for, which would tell the story of Big Boss's downfall in the same fashion as all the other MGS games did.

I think, that MGS3 remains the best in the series. It may have aged badly, but MGS5 just doesn't have all the crazy characters, emotional showdowns and bizarre encounters MGS is known and loved for. 

From a pure gameplay perspective however, MGS5 feels like the most refined game in the series. 

Pros
+ Two huge game worlds to explore
+ Fulton-Device-Mechanic gives nice context to playing the game nonlethal
+ A wide variety of guns and gadgets at your disposal
+ You can upgrade your Mother Base, which is a physical place in the game
+ By uprading Mother Base you unlock weapons and items
+ Gorgeous looking game

Cons
- Lack of cinematic, jaw-dropping cutscenes
- Lack of crazy and unique characters
- Story feels like a missed opportunity
- Only two locations (Afghanistan and Central Africa) 

9/10

This is possibly the [b]best[/b] Metal Gear Solid game mechanically speaking. It is satisfying to go on stealth sprees taking over outposts, upgrading your base, going on missions with your trusty pet  and so on. The controls are tight, and feel very satisfying when you're able to manipulate the AI after carefully planning out your every move. This game deserves a purchase for its gameplay alone. [b]A great entry point for any newcomer[/b].

Unfortunatley this comes under the cost of the story. You see, the MGS series is basically about two characters: the Solid Snake and Bigboss. The Solid Snake games (1,2 & 4) take place in the near future (or now present day) whereas the Big Boss games (3, Peace Walker and V) take place from the onset of the Cold War too the soviet invasion of afghanistan. This game was meant to be the bridge between the Solid games and the Big Boss games, but what it ends up becoming is a useless filler. Newcomer characters all feel shoe horned in, some returning characters feel out of place, with seemingly undefined character motives. [b]The fact that the story abruptly ends[/b] doesnt help either. Whether this was supposed to be some form of "high level" prank on the fans by giving them sort of a phantom pain [strike] by our lord and saviour Kojima[/strike], or a result of Konami pulling th funding too early, we'll never know. As such, it is a much weaker game to its predecessers.

TL;DR: A great game. Just not a great Metal Gear Game

Pros: 
1. Gameplay. I don't think I've ever played a game with as fluid a gameplay as MGSV. 
2. Story, obviously! Hideo Kojima works his magic with Konami for a final time. The way the cutscenes have been meshed into the gameplay and just the story on its own, with all its allegories and metaphorical character references are really good. However, I wouldn't say that the story is complete in any way. 
3. Best stealth game ever! 
4. Graphics! 

Cons:
1. Structure. With the earlier MGS games, I'm more used to a linear story based structure. With this, and incroporating the open world scenario, you can do other missions and come back to doing the main mission and so on. And you actually need to do those at times to get necessary weapon upgrades. The intensity of the story can be dulled slightly. 
2. They've put too much into the game. There's base management and side ops which at times take away the feeling of playing an MGS game.

I would argue that this is the weakest or 2nd weakest game between MGS1,2,3,4,V, but it has by far the best gameplay. That may seem paradoxical, but the old games had stronger writing and themes in them. Overall I gotta say it was the first game of the PS4+Xbone era to feel actually next-gen, and it's a blast regardless of how little it actually does story wise for me and the other fans.

While the game does have some bugged and badly designed missions that will make it difficult to play at some points, I believe once you get an understanding of the mechanics it can be a very deep and exciting stealth game to play.

It was really difficult deciding how to recommend this game, a game which I played for quite a while and yet ultimately left me unsatisfied. People can often look at negative reviews in which the play time is 100+ hours and wonder what kept them around despite apparently not liking it. The answer to that is fairly enjoyable play mechanics and a decent gameplay loop padded to hell and back with what I can only describe as skinner box tricks and typical open world padding. Contained within this game is about maybe 6-8 hours of pure distilled original or noteworthy content, padded with tens if not possibly hundreds of hours of generic and bland but not outright painful or offensive content. If you are like me and somehow managed to avoid being spoiled as to what is actually in MGSV despite so much time passing since its release, you might get wrapped up in the potential which MGSV hits you with so strongly at the beginning. This potential was so potent to me that I wanted to fully engage in all of MGSV's mechanics, which besides the open world is primarily a base building minigame that the majority of the tools and mechanics are locked behind.

Well let me tell you that there is nothing at the end of the tunnel. THIS GAME HAS NO ENDING. This is not a spoiler,  but a great favor which will save you from expecting more. This game has no evolution either. What you see by the end of the FIRST MISSION in Afghanistan is a substantial representation of what the entire game looks like. You can get new gadgets and interaction methods but there is no new gameplay content waiting behind those hours of investment. Some people may spend hundreds of hours on this game before finding out that there's NOTHING AT THE OTHER END. 

The base building component is hardly a game either, its more like one of those phone based ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ner box games in which the "game" holds your time hostage over resource investments, but mixed inbetween the real time stealth action gameplay that MGS is so well known for it felt less offensive and the game certainly does a better job of contextualizing it. The meat of the game is playing with the intuitive stealth movement mechanics and various tools and applying them to AI soldiers in a sandbox environment. Since there are now hardly "levels" most of the content comes from finding new ways to interact with the mostly unchanging guards, who do gain new tools and counter-defenses to your tools but ultimately remain predictable. Other than a few levels which show more focused design than the average open world mission, there is not much else to say. The game promises something more and grants original content in short bursts but the game keeps you in the loop of hoping for something "more", while the novel play mechanics sort of monotonously tides you over.

This review is as much a justification for the time I spent on this game as it is the review of the game itself, and so here is what I have to say for myself: The game has a very fun mechanical core with a promise of interesting ways of applying that core seemingly always around the corner. Well, it was never around the corner and it never came.

Well, this game is hard to review because you have to review two separate things. The gameplay, and the story.

The gameplay is good. It's fun. You run around in an open world and if you want to, you can take twenty minutes to infiltrate an outpost without arousing the suspicion of anyone, or if you don't, you can call in airstrikes and ride in a mobile mech unit, guns blazing. It's pretty much anything you'd want from a game in this genre. Between that you can go back to your base, take a shower, and develop new gear. Customize your loadout to just how you like it. Unfortunately, it's painfully obvious the game was designed to be played with a controller, which means the menu system is _terrible_.

The downsides are that it takes a very, very long time to do everything. In order to expand and develop, you have to grind resources. A lot of them. Not only that, but the majority of resources you find are "unprocessed" and you have to wait until your base turns a teeny tiny amount of them into resources you can use every ten minutes. And that only happens while you actually have the game open and play it. So does the development of new gear, which at the later stages can take upwards of two hours. 

If you want to do everything in this game, expect to play it for many weeks. And that doesn't even cover the "online" aspect of the game, which I had to turn off because the servers were often unresponsive, making me wait anywhere between 3 and 30 seconds just to open the next iDroid page.


Now for part two: The Plot.
Yikes. It is awful. Just absolutely, mind blowingly terrible. Created by Hideo Kojima. The characters are all unbelievable and worse, unrelatable. There is little consistency to them, apart from the nerd-baiting Quiet. Created by Hideo Kojima. The entire game your "allies" are revolting mercenaries whose goal seems to be only to make money regardless of how many people you butcher so that you can fulfill some sort of dream to make the world a better place. Created by Hideo Kojima. And you're supposed to be one of them. Every single one of your compatriots is a massive, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, war mongering, ego centric ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (apart from the nerd bait). In fact they all behave so similarly you'll have a hard time keeping them apart. 

It feels like all the characters in the game were written by a single person who has no empathy, which reflects really poorly on the game's creator, Hideo Kojima.

If you can manage to get past that, you'll find out that the game is set in the Metal Gear universe. A universe with about a dozen of games in the series total. Except they weren't designed from the ground up, they just keep trying to make it work, and THE PHANTOM PAIN, created by Hideo Kojima, is smack dab in the middle of the timeline.

That means it has to somehow deal with all the garbage from the previous game, incorporate the retconned lore from the earlier timeline, and keep it consistent with the terrible tragedy of the later timeline. It's a mess. Created by Hideo Kojima.  The plot is banal, repetitive, and unfulfilling. The only thing these people do over and over and over is create mercenary groups to make money so they and develop more and better nukes to somehow save the world. 

Just thinking about how awful the Metal Gear universe is makes me angry.

I could probably rant about it for a lot longer, but I'm gonna end the review here.

Let me start off by saying that I enjoy this game a lot, however there are several flaws that if you're a fan of the Metal Gear franchise you may be dissapointed in. 

When I buy a Metal Gear game, a big part of the reason I'm buying is for the storyline and the writing. This franchise has one of the most interesting and engaging writing that caries through from game to game. Without getting into spoilers I felt that Phantom Pain was some pretty dang cheesy writing ... "Hamboogers" that's basically all I'll say for now. There are HUNDREDS of tapes that you're supposed to listen to to get bits of the story and side stories that usually I wouldn't mind taking the time to listen because usually i enjoy the story, but these tapes are absolute CRINGE. Phantom Pain's story is pretty lame, and overall a let down compared to the intense nail biting cut scenes you'll get in other Metal Gear games. 

OK, now let's get to the gameplay. 

It's great! Probably one of the best 3rd person stealth games on the market. The mechanics are fluid and you'll find yourself challenged in missions but not to the extent where you're smashing your keyboard in frustration like some other MG games. FOB missions where you attack other online users' bases end up being the main interactive part of the game, but these are fun as well. I find myself looking at different ways to defend and developing certain technologies to improve mother base, so theres a lot more to this game than the main storyline which I enjoyed. 

Anyway, enjoyed the game and still a fan of the franchise.

Ground Zeroes was an excellent, but a tad short and expensive prologue to The Phantom Pain. (much like the tanker was in MGS2, only sold as a seperate game) It sets up the events that lead to The Phantom Pain. I very much like the themes Kojima uses in TPP, which are primarly Revenge and Loss. I don't want to go too deep into the specifics of the story but i really like what Kojima Productions did here. However, it's delivery is not without its flaws. The amount of cutscenes are pretty lacking compared to previous MGS games, and a big chunk of the story is told through tapes. Much like Peacewalker, the codec conversations from previous entries are replaced with these tapes, and this has its up and down sides: the tapes can be listened to anytime you like, whether you're on a mission, hiding in a toilet, or chilling at the base or chopper, these tapes will not interrupt your gameplay like the codec did, very convenient! The downside is that it doesnt feel very urgent listening to a previous recording instead of a "live" conversation. The radio still plays a role, as your team can comment on the various things you see at the moment, but you wont get to choose use who you call, and snake wont really respond either. While Kiefer Sutherland does a great job as an older Big Boss, he doesnt get as many dialogue as David Hayter did before. Another thing is that later into the game, some missions get recycled, with different parameters more or less. So, to continue the story you need to replay some of these versions. While i personally didnt mind that much, it does slow down the pace of the story.

My biggest gripe with the story however is the fact that some story elements are just not finished. There was supposed to be an additional chapter dealing with these loose ends, but it never made it into the final release. While i still think its a solid story (and with a nice twist ending too) it has some loose ties in the end. Seeing how Kojima working at Konami is not a thing anymore, this means that there wont be any proper conclusion to this.
 
Gameplay:
But how's the gameplay? Well, as you can guess, i really love it!!! It was actually what i was waiting for in a MGS game. Scoping out a base, trying different approaches, screwing around with the guards, sabotaging their systems... MGS3 had some of these elements, and I remember thinking how cool it would be if the whole game was bigger in scale, like freeroam, which is what TPP does! TPP will give you loads of options to play however you feel like. You can go non-lethal and tranquilize guards and send them back home to reinforce your motherbase, receive suplies from motherbase, or you can just murderise everybody in hails of gunfire, artillery or gunship support. While the game encourages stealth, it surprising me in how much steam you can blow off in this. On top of that, the controls play like a dream. You can freeroam and scout bases for yourself, run into some side missions, or play any mission you like. Every mission has a few objectives (and some of them are hidden) and you're free to tackle them anyway you like. You will be ranked on your performances afterwards, and this adds replay value as you are free to replay the mission anytime, to improve your score for example. 

Base:
Like Portable Ops and Peace Walker, TPP once again lets you manage your own army. You can capture enemy units, and send them back home to Motherbase. Each soldier has its own set of stats, so its wise to place them were their stats are best suited for. Place the guys who are techsavy into the R&D division, and they will come up with new gear for you to use. Units with sharp senses belong in the Intel division, which will feed you more accurate info when your in the field. But nothing comes entirely free. To develop items, you need GMP. GMP is earned by doing missions, sending your units to side operations, or finding precious items on the field. You will also need to gain materials, which you generate depending on your Base Development staff, but you can also find them on the field, or as rewards. To actually deploy yourself, you will need these resources aswell. Higher end gear is of course better, but it will also cost you more to use it. Building your base is not only managing your units, but also building the base itself! Like Peace Walker, you will start with a single platform at sea, and the more you expand, the more platforms you get. You even get to build other bases in other places, called FOBS. This however introduces an element that im not so fond with. These FOBS can be attacked and raided for its resources by other players, and you can raid them for supplies as well. The FOB platforms resemble the Big Shell from MGS2, so i think its a nice throwback. It is a nice idea on paper, but its so annoying to get attacked when you're minding your own business during a mission. Even worse, you can get raided even if your not playing the game at all!! Losing resources to this is not that big an impact, but i find it very annoying.

So, to sum things up

Pro's
+ VERY interesting story themes and great story and characters overall (at least for me personally) 
+ Excellent gameplay and freedom
+ Smooth controls
+ Good visuals
+ Loads of replay value
+ Tapes are nice to listen to while still being able to play...

Con's
- ...but there are less cutscenes and urgent codecs because of the tapes
- Some story elements are literally unfinished
- Snake has less dialogue then before
- FOB mode can be VERY annoying
- Reuse of missions later on can feel very cheap (i dont mind that much though)

Id recommend playing the previous metal gears first as this will make you appreciate the references and throwbacks, but this is an amazing game, no doubt.

Their relevance to the single player mission come via the opportunity to build a FOB ...... which requires well over a thousand coins. Sure you can buy a 1.5 XP boost in online play but for the single player they are just a carrot. A very distant one. The AI is good though there is a caveat to this. It's clear the game is cheating a lot of the time. You fire that single sniper shot, scuttle into cover and move to flank your opponent/s ..... only to find them right in front of you again. That happens enough times for it not to be coincidence.

There is a lot of repetition here. The map becomes very familiar as do the side op missions. The only function they serve is to act as revenue streams. Everything in the game requires money so you end up looting as much as possible for resale so you can afford the upgrades to enable you to complete the "proper" missions.

Throughout the game shows an incredible level of detail. From conversations the guards have to the cut scene where you get a bucket of water chucked over you because you didn't shower enough. Throughout the map there are music tapes to collect. Each one is an 80's track that won't be unfamiliar to someone who grew up in that era. Though I'll probably have to google to get them all it is a touch of genius on the part of the designers.

I think I'll leave it there. I'm putting this up a a skin and bone review because there are plenty of other top to bottom jobs out there but very few touch on the MB coins BS. It's a good game but a slightly crippled one. And it will need an awful lot of your time.

MGS V the "stealth" game where you get immortal-self regenerating-bulletproof-shielded-teleporting-zombies as enemies who can see you through everything, while your hardly earned teammates and resources (back at mother base) got stolen  by an online idiot.

It's Metal Gear, but it also isn't. If you're used to the type of linear story of the previous Metal Gears, you're probably gonna feel a little bit weird about this one. 

First of all: you play as Big Boss, the man from whom Solid, Liquid, Solidus Snake were cloned. As such, the character itself will be familiar to you, as well as the way he controls and the majority of things you can do with him.

The major contention point with this game is its structure. Instead of following a story from beginning to end, you have a sort of "hub" in an helicopter, and then you have a list of missions to choose from (either main story or side missions). This, in my opinion, interrupts the flow of the game, and makes you feel like you're playing "levels" instead of a story. Combined with an open world you can explore and lose yourself in, it's very fun but you lose the sense of intimacy that the previous MGS games had.

It also wasn't finished very well, you will need to repeat a lot of missions in higher difficulties just so you can "finish" the game, you sort of have an "ending" at the middle of the game, but it's.... weird. You'll have to see for yourself.

In terms of content, if you count all the side missions and main missions, you have a lot of it. It's just a pity that most of it is rinse & repeat, with just some changes due to the specifics of each mission. Don't get me wrong, it's a lot of fun, and you can explore several different ways of finishing each mission, but it can get kind of boring or repetitive.

Just be ready for a little bit of weirdness if you expect a straight-up storyline, because the structure is a bit confusing. But it's still very much worth playing.
